qs.x: There is no contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, and maternal shock threatens the fetus. Left lateral positioning prevents the uterus from compressing the vena cava.
w: Withhold epinephrine because it may harm the fetus
Give only oxygen because pregnancy limits drug use
Position her supine and wait for ALS to evaluate her

qs.q: After assisting with an auto-injector for anaphylaxis, which reassessment finding best shows the drug is working?
qs.a: Stridor resolves and BP rises to 112/70
qs.x: Improving airway sounds and blood pressure show that anaphylaxis is being reversed. A rising heart rate, tremor, and local pallor are side effects, not measures of response.
w: Heart rate rises from 110 to 126
Hands become shaky and tremulous
The injection site is pale and sore

qs.q: A 68-year-old with coronary disease received an auto-injector for anaphylaxis. His wheezing has improved, but he now reports new chest pressure; HR 128, BP 176/98. What is the best action?
qs.a: Report the chest pain to ALS or medical direction
qs.x: Chest pain and severe hypertension are serious epinephrine adverse effects that need ALS or medical direction input. A second dose is not indicated because the anaphylaxis is improving.
w: Give a second auto-injector for the chest pressure
Assist with nitroglycerin without any order
Ignore it because epinephrine has no cardiac effects

qs.q: A 35-year-old in anaphylaxis becomes unresponsive and pulseless before you can use her auto-injector. What is your immediate priority?
qs.a: Begin CPR and apply the AED
qs.x: Once she is pulseless, high-quality CPR and early defibrillation come first; ALS gives arrest-dose epinephrine IV or IO. Compressions should not be delayed for an IM injection, which is poorly absorbed without circulation.
w: Give the auto-injector before CPR
Give an injector into each thigh
Place her in the recovery position

qs.q: A 40-year-old with no known allergies has hives, stridor, and BP 80/48 after a wasp sting. Your ambulance carries epinephrine auto-injectors under local protocol. He has no prescription. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give the ambulance auto-injector per protocol
qs.x: First-time anaphylaxis is still anaphylaxis; when the service stocks auto-injectors, protocol allows the EMT to give one without a prior prescription. Antihistamines do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
w: Withhold it because he has no prescription
Have a bystander find another person's device
Give oral diphenhydramine and wait for ALS

qs.q: After epinephrine, an anaphylaxis patient's stridor is improving, but SpO2 is 89% and she is working hard to breathe. Which oxygen decision is best?
qs.a: Give high-concentration oxygen; be ready to ventilate
qs.x: Hypoxia with increased work of breathing calls for high-concentration oxygen and readiness to assist ventilations. Epinephrine treats the cause but does not replace oxygen or ventilatory support.
w: Withhold oxygen since the epinephrine will correct the low SpO2 by itself
Use a nasal cannula at low flow to avoid toxicity
Delay oxygen until a second epinephrine dose is due

qs.q: A 50-year-old with a shellfish allergy has hives only on her forearms and mild itching after dinner. Breathing is normal, BP 134/82, and she has no GI symptoms. She has her auto-injector. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Monitor closely and be ready to give epinephrine
qs.x: Localized skin findings alone, with normal breathing and BP, do not meet anaphylaxis criteria. Reassess often and give epinephrine promptly if other systems become involved.
w: Give the auto-injector now due to her allergy
Give oral glucose and release her at the scene
Inject the deltoid now as a precaution

qs.q: A 9-year-old (32 kg) in anaphylaxis received his 0.3 mg auto-injector 10 minutes ago. Stridor is worse and he is pale and lethargic. No second injector is on scene, and ALS is 8 minutes out. What is the best action?
qs.a: Support the airway, give oxygen, and update ALS
qs.x: A used auto-injector cannot deliver another dose. Airway support, oxygen, and an urgent ALS update for further epinephrine are the priorities; albuterol does not treat upper airway swelling.
w: Inject the used device again into the other thigh
Give his albuterol inhaler instead of epinephrine
Lay him flat and give him water to drink

qs.q: After an auto-injector for anaphylaxis, a 40-year-old with BP 84/50 wants to stand up and walk to the ambulance. What is the best response?
qs.a: Keep him lying down and move him by stretcher
qs.x: Hypotensive anaphylaxis patients can collapse suddenly when upright because venous return falls. Keep him supine (or as breathing allows) and move him by stretcher.
w: Let him walk since the epinephrine is working
Have him sit upright on the curb to recover
Let him walk if he leans on a crew member

qs.q: A 26-year-old found next to a syringe responds only to pain, with pinpoint pupils, RR 8 and shallow, and SpO2 84%. You have opened the airway. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen, then give naloxone
qs.x: Slow, shallow breathing needs assisted ventilation first; a nonrebreather cannot fix hypoventilation. Naloxone is then given to restore adequate spontaneous breathing.
w: Give naloxone and wait for breathing to improve
Apply a nonrebreather at high flow and give naloxone
Place her in recovery position and recheck in 5 minutes

qs.q: Thirty minutes after intranasal naloxone, a patient who had been breathing well becomes harder to arouse during transport, and his RR falls to 8. What is the best action?
qs.a: Support ventilation and repeat naloxone per protocol
qs.x: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, causing recurrent respiratory depression. Support breathing and repeat naloxone per protocol.
w: Assume he is sleeping and let him rest quietly
Give oral glucose since sleepiness means hypoglycemia
Withhold naloxone because he already had a dose

qs.q: A 2-year-old found with an open bottle of her grandmother's oxycodone is sleepy, with pinpoint pupils and RR 8. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Support ventilation and give naloxone per pediatric protocol
qs.x: Pediatric opioid toxicity is treated with ventilation and weight-based naloxone. Charcoal and induced vomiting are dangerous in a child with a decreased level of consciousness.
w: Withhold naloxone because it is unsafe for toddlers under any circumstances
Induce vomiting to remove any remaining tablets
Give activated charcoal by mouth right away

qs.q: A 30-year-old who took a handful of alprazolam is sleepy but arousable, with RR 14, normal pupils, and SpO2 97%. No opioids were found or reported. Regarding naloxone, the best decision is:
qs.a: Not indicated; monitor the airway and transport
qs.x: Naloxone reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression; it does not reverse benzodiazepines, and this patient is ventilating adequately. Monitor the airway and transport.
w: Give it because every overdose responds to naloxone
Give it to keep the patient from falling asleep
Give two doses at once since benzodiazepines are strong

qs.q: After naloxone, a patient wakes, vomits, and begins to aspirate while still lying on his back. What is the priority?
qs.a: Roll him onto his side and suction the airway
qs.x: Vomiting is a common withdrawal effect after naloxone; protecting the airway by positioning and suctioning comes first. More naloxone would worsen withdrawal.
w: Give a second naloxone dose to stop the vomiting
Sit him upright and have him drink water
Give oral glucose to settle his stomach

qs.q: Three minutes after a 4 mg intranasal naloxone dose, a suspected fentanyl overdose patient still has RR 6 and SpO2 82% despite your BVM ventilations. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Keep ventilating and repeat naloxone per protocol
qs.x: Naloxone can be repeated every 2-3 minutes, and potent synthetic opioids may need more than one dose. Ventilation must continue until breathing is adequate.
w: Stop ventilating to see if he breathes on his own
Wait 15 minutes before considering another dose
Switch to a nonrebreather and stop the naloxone

qs.q: A 79-year-old hospice patient with a morphine pump for cancer pain is drowsy with RR 7 and SpO2 86%. Her POLST requests full treatment. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Assist ventilation; give naloxone aiming for adequate breathing
qs.x: In opioid-dependent patients, the lowest effective naloxone dose per protocol restores breathing while limiting severe withdrawal and a pain crisis. The goal is adequate ventilation, not full reversal.
w: Give a large dose to fully reverse the morphine
Withhold naloxone because the morphine is prescribed for her cancer pain
Turn off the pump and let her sleep it off

qs.q: A patient's RR improves from 4 to 14 after naloxone, but he remains unresponsive to voice and pain. His glucose has not been checked. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Check glucose and look for other causes
qs.x: Once breathing is adequate, continued unresponsiveness suggests another cause such as hypoglycemia, head injury, or co-ingestants. Charcoal is contraindicated with an unprotected airway.
w: Give more naloxone until he is fully awake
Assume he is asleep and transport without testing
Give activated charcoal for a co-ingestion

qs.q: A woman who is 30 weeks pregnant is found after injecting heroin with RR 6, cyanosis, and pinpoint pupils. What is the best action?
qs.a: Ventilate with a BVM and give naloxone per protocol
qs.x: Maternal hypoxia directly endangers the fetus, so ventilation and naloxone are indicated; titrating to adequate breathing limits withdrawal. A nasal cannula does not correct hypoventilation.
w: Withhold naloxone to avoid harming the fetus
Give oxygen by nasal cannula and observe only
Wait until she reaches the hospital before giving her any medication

qs.q: Seconds after naloxone, a patient wakes up combative, swinging at the crew, and trying to leave. RR is 18. What should you do first?
qs.a: Ensure crew safety and request additional help
qs.x: Agitation is a known naloxone withdrawal effect; crew safety comes first, and breathing is now adequate. More naloxone would worsen the withdrawal.
w: Give a second dose to calm the withdrawal
Hold him down alone to keep him on the cot
Give oral glucose to treat the agitation

qs.q: After naloxone, a patient breathes 16 times per minute with good chest rise, but SpO2 is 91% on room air. Which oxygen decision is best?
qs.a: Apply supplemental oxygen and titrate per protocol
qs.x: Ventilation is now adequate, so BVM support and more naloxone are not needed, but mild hypoxia (often from aspiration or lung injury) warrants titrated supplemental oxygen.
w: Continue BVM ventilations at a rapid rate
Withhold oxygen since breathing is now adequate
Give a second naloxone dose to raise the SpO2

qs.q: A 45-year-old is found with RR 8 and pinpoint pupils. His medical alert bracelet lists a severe allergic reaction to naloxone. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Ventilate with a BVM and contact medical direction
qs.x: Hypersensitivity is naloxone's contraindication. Effective BVM ventilation treats the life threat, and medical direction can guide further care.
w: Give a double dose to overcome the allergy
Give naloxone and then his EpiPen right after
Withhold ventilation until ALS gives an antidote

qs.q: After naloxone, a 33-year-old who used fentanyl 20 minutes ago is awake, alert, and breathing normally. He wants to refuse transport. What is the most important point to explain?
qs.a: The opioid may outlast naloxone and his breathing can slow again
qs.x: Naloxone's effect may end before the opioid's, so respiratory depression can recur after the crew leaves. It does not remove the opioid or give lasting protection.
w: Naloxone will keep protecting him from an overdose for the next several days
He can safely use again once the naloxone wears off
Naloxone fully removes the fentanyl from his body

qs.q: A 15-year-old having an asthma attack wants to use her friend's albuterol inhaler because she left hers at home. What is the best action?
qs.a: Contact medical direction; do not assist with the friend's inhaler
qs.x: EMTs assist only with a patient's own prescribed inhaler unless protocol or medical direction allows otherwise. Letting a bystander give it does not change that rule.
w: Assist with the friend's inhaler since it is the same drug
Let the friend administer it so you are not responsible
Have her take twice the usual puffs from the friend's inhaler

qs.q: After two treatments with her own inhaler, a 12-year-old asthmatic becomes drowsy, her wheezing is now barely audible, and SpO2 falls to 86%. What is the best action?
qs.a: Assist ventilations with a BVM and request ALS
qs.x: Drowsiness, a quiet chest, and falling SpO2 signal respiratory failure, not improvement. Assisted ventilation and ALS are needed; an inhaler cannot reach the lungs without adequate air movement.
w: Recognize improvement since the wheezing stopped
Assist with more puffs and recheck in 20 minutes
Have her sit upright and sleep until arrival

qs.q: After assisting with a prescribed albuterol MDI, which reassessment finding best shows the treatment worked?
qs.a: Speaking in full sentences with less wheezing
qs.x: Better speech and decreased wheezing show improved air movement. Tachycardia and tremor are side effects, and drowsiness with less effort may signal fatigue and failure.
w: Heart rate increasing from 98 to 112
Mild hand tremor and nervousness
Less respiratory effort with new drowsiness

qs.q: A 66-year-old with COPD and coronary disease used his albuterol inhaler with your assistance. He now reports new chest pain, and his pulse is 136 and irregular. What is the best action?
qs.a: Stop the albuterol and contact ALS or medical direction
qs.x: Chest pain, severe tachycardia, and dysrhythmias are reasons to stop albuterol and escalate care. Further doses could worsen cardiac ischemia.
w: Repeat the inhaler right away since he is still a little short of breath
Assist with his nitroglycerin without checking BP
Assume anxiety and coach him to breathe slower

qs.q: A 73-year-old with COPD has increased shortness of breath and wheezing. Which finding is most concerning?
qs.a: Confusion and one-word answers
qs.x: Altered mental status and the inability to speak more than a word signal impending respiratory failure. The other findings are common in COPD exacerbations.
w: Productive cough with yellow sputum
Wheezing on expiration in both lungs
Pursed-lip breathing at rest

qs.q: A 70-year-old with COPD and wheezing has SpO2 84% on room air and is working hard to breathe. He worries that oxygen is bad for him. Which oxygen decision is best?
qs.a: Give oxygen and titrate to the protocol's target range
qs.x: Hypoxia should never be left untreated in COPD; oxygen is titrated to the protocol's target range while you watch mental status and breathing. Withholding it or leaving it at maximum without reassessment are both wrong.
w: Withhold oxygen because COPD patients cannot receive it
Give high-flow oxygen and never reduce it in transport
Use his inhaler only and avoid oxygen until the hospital

qs.q: A 5-year-old with asthma has wheezing and retractions. His parent has his prescribed MDI with a spacer and mask. What is the best way to assist?
qs.a: Use the spacer and mask per protocol, then reassess
qs.x: A spacer with a mask helps young children inhale the medication effectively. Spraying directly into the mouth deposits most of the dose in the throat.
w: Remove the spacer so the medicine goes in faster
Spray the inhaler directly into his open mouth
Have him hold his breath for one full minute

qs.q: A 26-year-old who is 30 weeks pregnant has an asthma attack with wheezing and SpO2 92%. She has a prescribed albuterol inhaler. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give oxygen and assist with her inhaler per protocol
qs.x: Pregnancy is not a contraindication to albuterol, and maternal hypoxia endangers the fetus. Lying supine late in pregnancy can cause hypotension and worsen breathing.
w: Withhold albuterol because pregnancy is a contraindication
Wait until after delivery to treat her asthma
Have her lie flat on her back to rest

qs.q: A wheezing asthmatic says she broke out in hives and her lips swelled the last time she used albuterol. Her inhaler is on the table. What is the best action?
qs.a: Do not assist with it; contact medical direction
qs.x: Hypersensitivity to albuterol is its contraindication. Give oxygen, monitor for anaphylaxis, and get medical direction rather than repeating an exposure that caused a reaction.
w: Assist with half of the usual number of puffs
Assist with it since the wheezing is dangerous
Have her use it while you watch her lips closely

qs.q: A 35-year-old asthmatic used her inhaler twice in the last 5 minutes and is still wheezing with SpO2 93% and HR 112. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Contact medical direction about further doses and reassess
qs.x: Repeat dosing timing is set by protocol or medical direction, and unlimited puffs increase side effects. Aspirin can trigger bronchospasm in sensitive asthmatics.
w: Give as many puffs as she needs until the wheezing stops completely
Stop all treatment since the inhaler has failed
Give her aspirin to reduce airway inflammation

qs.q: A wheezing COPD patient hands you two inhalers: tiotropium (Spiriva) and albuterol. For acute bronchospasm, which should you assist with per protocol?
qs.a: Albuterol, a fast-acting rescue bronchodilator
qs.x: Albuterol is the short-acting rescue drug for acute bronchospasm; tiotropium is a long-acting maintenance inhaler not meant for acute relief.
w: Tiotropium, because it is the daily controller
Both at once to double the bronchodilation
Neither, since COPD wheezing cannot be treated

qs.q: A 2-year-old has a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and a low-grade fever. His older brother's albuterol inhaler is available. What is the best action?
qs.a: Do not use the inhaler; keep him calm and transport
qs.x: The findings suggest croup, an upper airway problem that albuterol does not treat, and the inhaler is not prescribed to this child. Keeping him calm avoids worsening the airway obstruction.
w: Assist with the brother's inhaler for the stridor
Give the inhaler with a spacer and repeat it often
Give it because stridor and wheezing are the same

qs.q: A 67-year-old with COPD says his albuterol inhaler is not helping. He now has a fever, a productive cough, SpO2 88%, and RR 30. What is the most important next step?
qs.a: Give oxygen titrated per protocol and transport
qs.x: A failing rescue inhaler with hypoxia and tachypnea signals a serious exacerbation that needs oxygen and hospital care. More puffs add side effects without fixing the underlying problem.
w: Assist with unlimited puffs until he feels better
Withhold oxygen because he has COPD
Advise a routine visit with his doctor

qs.q: A 9-year-old asthmatic used his own MDI with your help and now speaks in full sentences with SpO2 97% on room air. He still has faint end-expiratory wheezes. Which oxygen decision is best?
qs.a: No supplemental oxygen; keep reassessing
qs.x: With a normal SpO2 and good air movement, supplemental oxygen is not needed; ongoing reassessment catches any relapse. BVM ventilation is for inadequate breathing.
w: Apply a nonrebreather at high flow for the ride
Start BVM ventilations to clear the wheezes
Give oxygen only if the parent requests it

qs.q: A 62-year-old with chest pain has his own prescribed nitroglycerin. BP 146/88, HR 84. He denies erectile dysfunction drug use and has already chewed aspirin. With protocol approval, what is the best next action?
qs.a: Assist with one dose sublingually, then recheck BP
qs.x: Nitroglycerin is given one sublingual dose at a time, with BP rechecked before each repeat. Swallowing it or giving several doses together risks failure or hypotension.
w: Assist with three tablets at once for faster relief
Have him swallow the tablet with a glass of water
Give the tablet only after his chest pain resolves

qs.q: A 58-year-old with chest pain and BP 152/90 says he took tadalafil (Cialis) about 36 hours ago. What should you do about his nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Withhold it and notify medical direction
qs.x: Tadalafil is long-acting, so nitroglycerin is contraindicated within 48 hours of use. The 24-hour window applies to sildenafil and vardenafil, not tadalafil.
w: Assist with it since 24 hours have passed
Assist with half a tablet to reduce the risk
Assist with it if he lies flat during the dose

qs.q: A 70-year-old with chest pain usually has a BP around 170/100, according to his records. Today his BP is 128/78 and he feels lightheaded. What is the best decision about his nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Withhold it and contact medical direction
qs.x: A systolic BP more than 30 mmHg below baseline is a contraindication even when it is above 90. His lightheadedness suggests he is already relatively hypotensive.
w: Assist with it because his SBP is above 90
Assist with two tablets to relieve pain faster
Assist with it and have him walk to the cot

qs.q: A 66-year-old with chest pain and her own nitroglycerin has BP 104/70 and a pulse of 42, and she feels weak. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold nitroglycerin and request ALS
qs.x: Severe bradycardia is a contraindication to nitroglycerin, and the drug can cause further bradycardia and hypotension. A symptomatic slow pulse needs ALS evaluation.
w: Assist with it since the BP is above 90
Assist with it and recheck the pulse later
Give it with aspirin to protect her heart

qs.q: After a second nitroglycerin dose, a 60-year-old's chest pain resolves completely. BP 124/80, HR 80. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop nitroglycerin, keep monitoring, and transport
qs.x: Nitroglycerin is stopped when pain is relieved; the full series is not required. Relief does not rule out an MI, so transport and monitoring continue.
w: Give the third dose to complete the series
Cancel transport since the pain has resolved
Have him walk to the ambulance to see whether exertion brings the pain back

qs.q: A 65-year-old's chest pain persists after three nitroglycerin doses over 15 minutes. BP 132/84. ALS is still 10 minutes away. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give no more; continue care and update ALS
qs.x: The usual maximum is three doses in 15 minutes; pain persisting beyond that suggests an evolving MI that needs ALS and rapid transport. Extra doses or patches raise the risk of hypotension.
w: Assist with a fourth and fifth dose now
Apply his nitroglycerin patch in addition
Give an epinephrine auto-injector for the pain

qs.q: Before assisting an 80-year-old with her nitroglycerin, which positioning is safest?
qs.a: Seated or semi-reclined with legs supported
qs.x: Nitroglycerin can cause dizziness, hypotension, and syncope, especially in older adults. A seated or semi-reclined position reduces fall risk while allowing comfortable breathing.
w: Standing so the tablet dissolves faster
Prone on the cot to rest her chest
Walking to the ambulance to save time

qs.q: A 55-year-old with pulmonary hypertension takes riociguat daily and now has chest pain with BP 130/84. She also has prescribed nitroglycerin. What should you do?
qs.a: Withhold nitroglycerin and contact medical direction
qs.x: Riociguat, like PDE-5 inhibitors, can interact with nitrates and cause severe hypotension, so it is a contraindication. A normal BP now does not remove that risk.
w: Assist with it because her BP is above 90
Assist with it only if the pain gets worse
Assist with two doses since she is stable

qs.q: A 69-year-old with chest pain and crackles in both lung bases has SpO2 88% on room air and BP 160/96. He has his own nitroglycerin. Which action should come first?
qs.a: Apply oxygen and titrate to the protocol target
qs.x: Hypoxia is an immediate threat and is corrected first; oxygen is titrated to the protocol target. Lying flat worsens breathing with pulmonary congestion, and nitroglycerin is given one dose at a time.
w: Assist with three nitroglycerin doses at once
Lay him flat to rest during the assessment
Withhold oxygen because it narrows coronary arteries

qs.q: A 14-year-old has sharp chest pain after a soccer collision. His grandfather offers his own nitroglycerin. What is the best action?
qs.a: Decline it; it is not for this patient
qs.x: Nitroglycerin is rarely used in children, the tablets belong to someone else, and traumatic chest wall pain is not angina. Assess for injury and transport instead.
w: Give one tablet since chest pain is present
Give half a tablet because he is a teen
Give it only if his SBP is above 120

qs.q: Which chest pain patient is the best candidate for EMT-assisted nitroglycerin?
qs.a: BP 142/88, own prescription, no PDE-5 drug use
qs.x: EMTs assist with the patient's own nitroglycerin when SBP is adequate and no PDE-5 inhibitor has been used recently. An SBP under 90, someone else's prescription, or recent vardenafil rule it out.
w: BP 86/58, own prescription, no recent drug use
BP 150/92, wife's prescription, no allergies
BP 138/80, took vardenafil 12 hours ago, own Rx

qs.q: A 57-year-old has chest pain with BP 150/90. He has his own nitroglycerin and no aspirin allergy. Protocol allows both. Which plan is best?
qs.a: Give chewed aspirin, then nitroglycerin if BP allows
qs.x: Aspirin should be given early for suspected ACS and does not depend on pain relief, while nitroglycerin depends on BP checks. Delaying aspirin removes its early benefit.
w: Withhold aspirin until all nitroglycerin doses are used
Give nitroglycerin, then aspirin only if pain persists
Give both only after arriving at the emergency department

qs.q: After one nitroglycerin dose, a 61-year-old still has chest pain. Five minutes later his BP is 92/60, down from 136/82. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold further doses and notify medical direction
qs.x: A drop of more than 30 mmHg from baseline is a reason to stop nitroglycerin even though SBP is still above 90. Another dose could cause serious hypotension.
w: Give a second dose since the SBP is still above 90
Give a second dose with him lying flat
Give two tablets at once to finish faster

qs.q: A patient with chest pain took one of his own nitroglycerin tablets 3 minutes before you arrived. Pain persists. BP 140/84, HR 88. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Note the time, reassess, and follow protocol for the next dose
qs.x: The patient's own dose counts toward the series and timing; the next dose follows the protocol interval after a BP recheck. Doubling up or giving early increases the risk of hypotension.
w: Give another dose immediately, because he still has pain after his own tablet
Withhold all nitroglycerin because he self-treated
Give three tablets now to catch up on the missed doses

qs.q: A 59-year-old with chest pain is about to take her own nitroglycerin. She says she fainted the last time she took it. BP 138/84. What is the best action?
qs.a: Contact medical direction before assisting
qs.x: A prior syncopal reaction suggests she is prone to severe hypotension or a Bezold-Jarisch response. Medical direction should weigh in, and she must not stand during any dose.
w: Assist with three doses to prevent a repeat
Refuse to treat until the pain stops
Have her stand while taking the tablet

qs.q: A 22-year-old swallowed an unknown number of pills 45 minutes ago. She is now drowsy and responds only to a loud voice. Poison control is on the phone. What is the best decision about charcoal?
qs.a: Withhold it because her mental status is declining
qs.x: Altered mental status without a protected airway is a contraindication to activated charcoal because of aspiration risk. Her airway and transport are the priorities.
w: Give it quickly now, before she becomes completely unresponsive
Give it through a straw while she is lying flat
Mix it with soda so she drinks it faster

qs.q: A 3-year-old swallowed drain cleaner 20 minutes ago and is drooling, with burns around the mouth. What is the best action?
qs.a: Withhold charcoal, protect the airway, and transport
qs.x: Caustic ingestion is a contraindication to charcoal; it does not bind the agent and can hide injuries. Drooling suggests airway swelling, so airway protection comes first.
w: Give charcoal per protocol to bind the cleaner
Induce vomiting to remove the drain cleaner
Give charcoal mixed with cold milk to bind the cleaner and soothe the burns

qs.q: A 4-year-old drank lamp oil 15 minutes ago and is now coughing and breathing fast. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Do not give charcoal; monitor breathing and transport
qs.x: Hydrocarbon ingestion is a contraindication to charcoal because of aspiration risk, and coughing with tachypnea suggests aspiration has already occurred. Vomiting would worsen it.
w: Give charcoal right away to bind the lamp oil
Make him vomit to empty his stomach
Give water and observe at home for an hour

qs.q: An alert 30-year-old swallowed an overdose of her prescription pills 5 hours ago and feels fine. Poison control asks about charcoal. Which factor most limits its benefit?
qs.a: The ingestion was hours ago
qs.x: Charcoal works best when given within about 1 hour of ingestion, before much of the drug is absorbed. Being alert is required for safe use, not a limitation.
w: She is alert and cooperative
She swallowed tablets, not liquid
She weighs more than 50 kg

qs.q: While drinking charcoal ordered by medical direction, a 17-year-old with an intentional ingestion becomes sleepy and starts gagging. What is the best action?
qs.a: Stop the charcoal, turn her on her side, and suction
qs.x: Decreasing mental status with gagging means aspiration risk, which is a reason to stop charcoal. Lateral positioning and suction protect the airway.
w: Encourage her to finish the remaining dose quickly
Hold her nose so she swallows the rest of it
Lay her flat on her back and continue the dose

qs.q: Medical direction orders charcoal for an alert 25-year-old who swallowed a large amount of a medication 30 minutes ago. Which action best supports safe administration?
qs.a: Have her sit upright and drink it from a covered cup
qs.x: Sitting upright reduces aspiration risk, and a covered cup with a straw improves acceptance. Ice cream reduces charcoal's binding, and a drowsy patient should not receive it.
w: Have her lie flat on her back so it reaches the stomach and bowel faster
Mix it with ice cream to improve the taste
Wait until she becomes drowsy so she will not gag

qs.q: A 7-year-old has a fever of 102.4 F and is acting normally. His parent gave acetaminophen 1 hour ago and asks whether to give another dose now. What is the best response?
qs.a: Do not repeat it yet; doses are spaced 4-6 hours apart
qs.x: Pediatric acetaminophen is dosed every 4-6 hours by weight, and repeating early risks liver toxicity. Aspirin is avoided in children with viral illness because of Reye syndrome.
w: Give another dose right now, since the fever is still present after an hour
Switch to aspirin, which works faster in children
Give an adult tablet so the fever breaks sooner

qs.q: A 50-year-old with chronic alcohol use, known cirrhosis, yellow skin, and a swollen abdomen asks whether acetaminophen is safe for his headache. What is the best response?
qs.a: Avoid it; ask his physician about other options
qs.x: Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease is a contraindication because acetaminophen can cause hepatotoxicity. Higher doses or alcohol increase that risk.
w: It is safe in any amount despite liver disease
Take double the usual dose to cover the pain
Take it with alcohol to speed its absorption

qs.q: A 4-year-old with fever is lethargic, hard to arouse, and has a purple rash that does not blanch. The parent asks whether acetaminophen will be enough. What is the priority?
qs.a: Recognize possible serious infection and transport
qs.x: Lethargy with a non-blanching rash suggests a life-threatening infection such as meningococcemia. Fever medication treats a symptom and must not delay transport.
w: Give acetaminophen and observe at home
Add ibuprofen to the acetaminophen and recheck the temperature in an hour
Give a cool bath and recheck the rash tomorrow

qs.q: A 68-year-old with knee arthritis has taken high-dose ibuprofen daily for weeks. He now has dizziness, a pulse of 112, and black, tarry stools. What is the most likely concern?
qs.a: GI bleeding from NSAID use
qs.x: GI bleeding is a serious ibuprofen adverse effect, and tarry stools with tachycardia and dizziness suggest significant blood loss needing prompt transport.
w: An expected arthritis flare
Low blood sugar from skipped meals
An allergic reaction to ibuprofen

qs.q: A 29-year-old asthmatic with a sprained ankle asks for ibuprofen. She says aspirin once made her wheeze severely. What is the best response?
qs.a: Advise against ibuprofen due to NSAID-asthma risk
qs.x: Aspirin- or NSAID-induced asthma is a contraindication to ibuprofen because cross-reactivity can cause severe bronchospasm. Pretreating with an inhaler does not make it safe.
w: Ibuprofen is safe since it is not the same as aspirin
Take ibuprofen with her inhaler to block any wheezing
Take a double dose to avoid the need for repeat doses

qs.q: A 16-year-old with a sprained wrist took ibuprofen and now has hives, facial swelling, and wheezing. BP 88/54. What is the best action?
qs.a: Treat as anaphylaxis per protocol and request ALS
qs.x: Hives, facial swelling, wheezing, and hypotension after a drug indicate anaphylaxis, which needs epinephrine per protocol and ALS. Switching pain relievers does nothing for the reaction.
w: Give acetaminophen to replace the ibuprofen
Apply ice to the wrist and reassess later
Give more ibuprofen to treat the swelling

qs.q: A 58-year-old diabetic man is confused and combative, will not follow commands and has a blood glucose of 42 mg/dL. Your partner has a patent forearm IV. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Give IV dextrose per protocol, then recheck the glucose
qs.x: A patient who cannot follow commands cannot safely swallow oral glucose, and with IV access in place IV dextrose works fastest. Glucagon is the choice only when IV dextrose cannot be given.
w: Squeeze oral glucose gel into his cheek because he is still awake
Give IM glucagon first and save the IV line for fluids only
Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before giving any treatment

qs.q: You have given 100 mL of D10 to a hypoglycemic 66-year-old woman. Her glucose rose from 31 to 64 mg/dL, but she is still confused. What should you do next?
qs.a: Give another D10 aliquot and reassess glucose and mental status
qs.x: D10 is titrated in 5-10 g (50-100 mL) aliquots until glucose is normal and mental status improves. A glucose still in the low 60s with persistent confusion means treatment is not finished.
w: Stop dextrose because the glucose is now above 60 mg/dL
Give naloxone because the confusion did not fully clear
Give IM glucagon on top of the D10 already infused to boost it

qs.q: A 71-year-old man has sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech. BP is 178/96 and his blood glucose is 312 mg/dL. A bystander says "he is diabetic, give him sugar." What is the best action?
qs.a: Withhold dextrose and treat as a possible stroke with rapid transport
qs.x: Hyperglycemia is a contraindication to dextrose, and the glucose reading rules out hypoglycemia as the cause of his deficits. Giving sugar to a hyperglycemic stroke patient may worsen outcome and delays stroke care.
w: Give D10 because diabetics with altered speech are usually hypoglycemic
Give oral glucose because it is safer than IV dextrose
Give a half dose of D50 to be safe and recheck

qs.q: A 4-year-old weighing 16 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea for two days. She is lethargic, her glucose is 38 mg/dL, and you have a patent IV. What is the best treatment?
qs.a: D10 IV at 5-10 mL/kg, then recheck glucose
qs.x: For infants and children, D10 at 5-10 mL/kg IV is the listed dose. A lethargic child cannot safely take oral glucose, and an adult D50 dose is far too concentrated and too large for a 16 kg child.
w: Oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
Undiluted D50, the full 50 mL by slow IV push
IM glucagon 1 mg instead of IV dextrose

qs.q: A 49-year-old woman woke up after IV D10 and now has a glucose of 118 mg/dL. Which finding is most concerning?
qs.a: Swelling, coolness and blanching around the IV site
qs.x: Swelling, coolness and blanching at the site suggest extravasation, which can cause tissue necrosis with dextrose. Stop the infusion at that site; hunger and resolving sweating are expected after correction.
w: A mild headache she rates 2 out of 10
Hunger and asking for something to eat right away
Mild sweating that is now resolving

qs.q: You are titrating D10 for a 62-year-old hypoglycemic man. After 150 mL, he is alert, oriented and his glucose is 142 mg/dL. What should you do now?
qs.a: Stop further dextrose and keep reassessing glucose and mental status
qs.x: Dextrose is stopped when glucose is normal and mental status has improved. Pushing the full bag regardless of response risks hyperglycemia, which is the most common side effect.
w: Infuse the rest of the 250 mL bag to complete the full dose
Give IM glucagon to prevent the glucose from dropping again
Switch to D50 so the remaining full dose can be given faster

qs.q: A 40-year-old man of unknown history is found unresponsive in his apartment. RR is 14 and deep, SpO2 97%, pupils midsize and there is no trauma. Before giving any medication, what is the most important step?
qs.a: Check a blood glucose level
qs.x: Hypoglycemia is a common, quickly reversible cause of unresponsiveness, and a glucose check guides whether dextrose is needed. His breathing is adequate and his pupils are not pinpoint, so naloxone is not indicated.
w: Give naloxone intranasally
Give oral glucose gel in the cheek
Give an IV fluid bolus immediately

qs.q: A 6-year-old with type 1 diabetes received D10 at the pediatric dose. Ten minutes later she is still lethargic with a glucose of 50 mg/dL. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Repeat dextrose per protocol and recheck glucose and mental status
qs.x: Persistent hypoglycemia with altered mental status means the dose was not enough, so a repeat per protocol is indicated. A lethargic child still cannot protect her airway for oral glucose.
w: Consider her treated and transport without further medication
Give oral glucose now because she has already had IV dextrose
Change to undiluted adult D50 because the D10 did not work at all

qs.q: An 84-year-old malnourished woman with a glucose of 36 mg/dL received glucagon 1 mg IM 15 minutes ago because no IV could be placed. Her glucose is now 37 mg/dL and she is still unresponsive. What does this most likely mean, and what is next?
qs.a: Her glycogen stores are likely depleted; obtain IV or IO access for dextrose
qs.x: Glucagon works by releasing stored glycogen, so malnourished patients may not respond. When glucose does not rise within 15 minutes, dextrose by IV or IO is needed.
w: The glucagon needs another hour to work; keep monitoring only
She is having an allergic reaction to glucagon and needs IM epinephrine now
The meter is wrong because glucagon always works; transport only

qs.q: A 52-year-old man with a known pheochromocytoma is unresponsive with a glucose of 30 mg/dL. Two IV attempts have failed. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Avoid glucagon and obtain IO access to give dextrose per protocol
qs.x: Pheochromocytoma is a contraindication to glucagon because it can trigger a dangerous catecholamine surge. Dextrose can be given IO, and oral glucose is unsafe in an unresponsive patient.
w: Give glucagon 1 mg IM because it is the standard choice when an IV fails
Give oral glucose gel because he cannot get glucagon
Give glucagon at half the usual dose to limit side effects

qs.q: A 27-year-old diabetic received glucagon 1 mg IM. He is now awake, oriented, swallowing normally and his glucose is 92 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Give oral carbohydrates and continue to monitor during transport
qs.x: The effect of glucagon is short and uses up glycogen, so glucose can fall again. Once he can swallow, oral carbohydrates help maintain the glucose; another glucagon dose is not indicated.
w: Give a second dose of glucagon to keep the glucose up
Release him without further care since his glucose is normal now
Start a D50 push to build up his glucose reserves

qs.q: You are called for several diabetic patients at the same event. Which one is the best candidate for IM glucagon?
qs.a: Unresponsive, glucose 29 mg/dL, no IV obtainable
qs.x: Glucagon is indicated for severe hypoglycemia when IV dextrose cannot be given. The alert patient can take oral glucose, the patient with an IV should get IV dextrose, and the hyperglycemic patient needs no glucose-raising drug.
w: Alert, glucose 58 mg/dL, asking for juice
Confused, glucose 45 mg/dL, with a patent IV already in place
Alert, glucose 240 mg/dL, nauseated

qs.q: A parent gave a 9-year-old 3 mg of nasal glucagon 5 minutes before you arrived. The boy is starting to stir and moan but cannot answer questions. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Recheck glucose, protect the airway and reassess as the drug takes effect
qs.x: The child is responding, so the priority is airway protection (vomiting is common), a glucose recheck and reassessment. A drowsy child cannot safely take oral glucose, and repeating glucagon this early is not indicated.
w: Give IM glucagon now because the nasal form is unreliable in children
Give oral glucose gel immediately while he is stirring
Give naloxone because he is not fully awake yet

qs.q: A confused 45-year-old has a glucose of 33 mg/dL and a patent, flushing IV. Your partner hands you glucagon. What is the best response?
qs.a: Give IV dextrose instead, since IV access is available
qs.x: Glucagon is meant for severe hypoglycemia when IV dextrose cannot be given. With a working IV, dextrose acts faster and does not depend on liver glycogen.
w: Give the glucagon IM since it avoids any IV-related complications
Give glucagon IV push followed by oral glucose
Give both glucagon and dextrose to speed recovery

qs.q: A 67-year-old diabetic has new left arm weakness and facial droop that started an hour ago. Glucose is 41 mg/dL. He cannot swallow safely and no IV can be started. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give glucagon IM and recheck glucose and neurologic signs
qs.x: Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke, and focal deficits may resolve once glucose is corrected. With no IV and an unsafe swallow, glucagon is the appropriate route, followed by a neurologic reassessment.
w: Withhold all glucose because this looks like a stroke
Give oral glucose gel because he is still conscious
Skip glucose treatment and transport rapidly to a stroke center

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has crushing chest pain. BP is 150/90 and HR 84. He says he took tadalafil (Cialis) about 30 hours ago. What is the best decision about nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Withhold it; tadalafil within 48 hours is a contraindication
qs.x: Tadalafil lasts longer than other PDE-5 inhibitors, so nitrates are withheld for 48 hours. The 24-hour window applies to sildenafil and vardenafil, not tadalafil.
w: Give it, since more than 24 hours have passed since his last dose
Give a half dose and lay him flat to prevent hypotension
Give it only if his systolic pressure stays above 120

qs.q: A 63-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has chest pressure. BP is 132/78 and HR 92. Her medication list includes riociguat. What should you do about nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Withhold nitroglycerin and continue ACS care and transport
qs.x: Riociguat is listed with the PDE-5 inhibitors as a nitroglycerin contraindication because the combination can cause severe hypotension. A normal BP does not remove that risk.
w: Give nitroglycerin since her BP is above 90 systolic
Give nitroglycerin but only one dose
Give nitroglycerin and start a fluid bolus at the same time

qs.q: A 74-year-old man with chest pain says his BP is "always around 160." Today it is 118/70 with HR 96. He is pale and diaphoretic. What is the best decision about nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Withhold it; his BP is more than 30 below his baseline
qs.x: Nitroglycerin is contraindicated with SBP under 90 or more than 30 below baseline. A drop of over 40 from his usual pressure suggests poor perfusion, so a vasodilator could cause collapse.
w: Give it, since his systolic is well above 90
Give it, since a lower BP shows his heart workload is now reduced
Give two doses quickly before his BP drops further

qs.q: Two minutes after SL nitroglycerin, a 66-year-old woman becomes pale and lightheaded. HR falls from 78 to 44 and BP from 128/80 to 76/40. What is happening, and what should you do?
qs.a: Bezold-Jarisch reaction; lay her supine, no more nitro, fluids per protocol
qs.x: Sudden bradycardia with hypotension after nitroglycerin is a known Bezold-Jarisch reaction. Further nitrates are withheld, and supine positioning with a fluid bolus per protocol supports her pressure.
w: An expected headache response; give the next dose in 5 minutes as planned
A worsening heart attack that needs another nitroglycerin dose
An allergic reaction that requires IM epinephrine

qs.q: A 61-year-old man has received three SL nitroglycerin doses over 15 minutes. Pain is 5 out of 10, BP is 140/86 and HR 82. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Hold more SL doses unless protocol or medical control directs; transport
qs.x: The FDA label allows up to three doses in 15 minutes, so further doses need protocol or medical control direction. Persistent pain points to ongoing ischemia that needs rapid transport, not a larger dose.
w: Give a fourth dose right away, since his BP is still above 90 systolic
Double the next dose, since the first three were not enough
Stop treatment entirely because the medication has failed

qs.q: After one SL nitroglycerin, a 57-year-old woman's chest pain goes from 7 to 0 out of 10. BP is 130/80 and HR 76. What should the AEMT do now?
qs.a: Hold further doses and keep monitoring during transport
qs.x: Nitroglycerin is stopped once pain is relieved, so more doses add risk without benefit. Relief with nitroglycerin does not rule out ACS, so she still needs transport and monitoring.
w: Give the second dose in 5 minutes to complete the series
Give two more doses to prevent the pain from returning
Cancel transport since the pain is fully relieved

qs.q: A 69-year-old man with chest pain is ready for nitroglycerin. Which finding is most important to address before you give it?
qs.a: HR of 42 with dizziness
qs.x: Severe bradycardia is a listed contraindication, and adding a vasodilator can drop his BP further. The other findings do not change the decision to give nitroglycerin.
w: SpO2 of 95% on room air
A pain score of 8 out of 10
A history of high cholesterol

qs.q: You give a 64-year-old man an SL nitroglycerin tablet. A moment later you notice he is chewing and swallowing it. What is the best response?
qs.a: Teach him to let the next tablet dissolve under his tongue
qs.x: The SL route depends on absorption through the mucosa under the tongue; a swallowed tablet is poorly absorbed. Correct the technique and keep the usual dosing interval rather than doubling up.
w: Have him swallow the next tablet with a glass of water
Give the next tablet right away to make up for the lost dose
Stop nitroglycerin, since he is unable to use it correctly

qs.q: Five minutes after nitroglycerin, a 59-year-old woman says her chest pain went from 8 to 4, but she now has a pounding headache and flushing. BP is 138/84. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: An expected side effect; reassess and repeat per protocol
qs.x: Headache and flushing are common, expected effects of vasodilation. Her BP is stable and pain is improving, so a repeat dose per protocol is reasonable.
w: An allergic reaction; stop nitroglycerin and give IM epinephrine now
A stroke caused by the nitroglycerin; stop all medications
A sign of overdose; give a fluid bolus right away

qs.q: A 55-year-old man has chest pain that suggests ACS. BP is 142/88. He has asthma and says that aspirin once caused a severe asthma attack. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold aspirin and continue other ACS care
qs.x: Aspirin-induced asthma is a listed contraindication because aspirin can cause severe bronchospasm in these patients. A smaller dose does not prevent the reaction.
w: Give aspirin, since the benefit in ACS outweighs the risk
Give one 81 mg tablet instead of the full dose
Give aspirin with albuterol ready in case he wheezes

qs.q: A 68-year-old man has chest pressure and says he has had black, tarry stools for two days. He is pale with HR 108 and BP 104/66. What is the best decision about aspirin?
qs.a: Withhold aspirin due to signs of active GI bleeding
qs.x: Black, tarry stools with tachycardia point to an active GI bleed, which is a contraindication to aspirin. His chest pain may even be from anemia caused by blood loss.
w: Give aspirin, since ACS is more dangerous than bleeding
Give aspirin along with oral fluids to protect the stomach
Give aspirin and avoid nitroglycerin instead

qs.q: A 62-year-old woman with chest pain took her daily 81 mg enteric-coated aspirin this morning. She has no allergies or bleeding. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give 162-324 mg non-enteric-coated aspirin, chewed, per protocol
qs.x: A daily low-dose enteric-coated tablet does not provide the rapid antiplatelet effect needed in ACS. Chewed non-enteric-coated aspirin at 162-324 mg is recommended unless contraindicated.
w: Withhold aspirin, since she already took her daily dose
Give one 81 mg tablet to top up her morning dose
Have her swallow a 325 mg enteric-coated tablet whole with water

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with suspected ACS is pale and diaphoretic. BP is 84/50 and HR 104. Which medication can still be given?
qs.a: Aspirin, chewed per protocol
qs.x: Hypotension is a contraindication to nitroglycerin by any route, but it is not a contraindication to aspirin. Aspirin should not be delayed in suspected ACS when there is no allergy or bleeding.
w: Nitroglycerin, one SL dose
Nitroglycerin, half the usual dose
Nitroglycerin, as a skin patch only

qs.q: A 16-year-old with fever, cough and body aches for three days has chest pain when coughing. His mother asks if you can give him aspirin. What is the best response?
qs.a: Do not give aspirin due to the risk of Reye syndrome
qs.x: Aspirin is avoided in children and teens with viral illness because of Reye syndrome. His pain with coughing does not suggest ACS, and aspirin is not given for ACS in this age group.
w: Give 324 mg chewed in case this is a heart attack
Give 81 mg chewed, since he is a teen and not a small child
Give aspirin only if his fever is above 39 C (102.2 F)

qs.q: A 59-year-old man has chest pain and is about to chew aspirin. He then mentions his throat swelled and he got hives the last time he took ibuprofen. What should you do?
qs.a: Withhold aspirin due to his NSAID hypersensitivity
qs.x: Allergy or hypersensitivity to NSAIDs is a contraindication to aspirin because cross-reactions are common. A swelling reaction raises the concern for anaphylaxis.
w: Give aspirin, since his reaction was to a different drug
Give aspirin and watch closely for hives
Give a reduced dose of aspirin with oral fluids

qs.q: A 24-year-old was stung by a bee. She has diffuse hives, wheezing, throat tightness and BP 82/50. What is the first medication to give?
qs.a: Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL) in the lateral thigh
qs.x: This is anaphylaxis with airway and circulatory involvement, and IM epinephrine is the first-line treatment. Albuterol and fluids are add-ons, and IV epinephrine for a patient with a pulse is not an AEMT anaphylaxis dose.
w: Albuterol nebulized to treat the wheezing first
An IV fluid bolus before any medication
Epinephrine 1 mg IV push of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration right away

qs.q: Six minutes after 0.3 mg of IM epinephrine, a 35-year-old man with peanut anaphylaxis still has stridor and BP 84/52. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Repeat IM epinephrine and support the airway and BP
qs.x: IM epinephrine can be repeated every 5-10 minutes as needed when anaphylaxis persists. Antihistamines and albuterol do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
w: Wait 20 more minutes since epinephrine is slow by IM
Give albuterol instead, since epinephrine has failed
Give oral diphenhydramine and recheck in 15 minutes

qs.q: After IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis, a 30-year-old woman's wheezing has cleared and BP is 128/80. She now has HR 124, a fine tremor and feels anxious. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: Expected epinephrine side effects; reassess and monitor
qs.x: Tachycardia, tremor and anxiety are common, expected effects of epinephrine. Her improved breathing and BP show the drug worked, so monitoring is the right plan.
w: A new allergic reaction requiring a second epinephrine dose
An overdose requiring immediate medical reversal
Worsening anaphylaxis requiring a fluid bolus

qs.q: A 76-year-old man with coronary artery disease develops facial swelling, hives, wheezing and BP 80/46 after a new antibiotic. Your partner hesitates to give epinephrine because of his heart history. What is the correct decision?
qs.a: Give IM epinephrine; anaphylaxis has no contraindication
qs.x: There is no contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, and untreated shock is more dangerous to his heart than the drug. Monitor him closely for chest pain or dysrhythmias afterward.
w: Withhold epinephrine and give only IV fluids
Give half the adult dose to protect his heart
Give albuterol only, since it is much safer for an older heart

qs.q: A 6-year-old weighing 22 kg has lip swelling, hives and wheezing after eating cashews. Which epinephrine dose is appropriate?
qs.a: The 0.15 mg auto-injector IM in the lateral thigh
qs.x: The 0.15 mg auto-injector is listed for children 15-30 kg. The 0.3 mg auto-injector is for 30 kg or more, and IV epinephrine is not the AEMT route for anaphylaxis.
w: The 0.3 mg auto-injector IM in the lateral thigh
0.5 mg IM, the full adult anaphylaxis dose in the thigh
1 mg IV of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration

qs.q: A 13-month-old weighing 12 kg develops hives, vomiting and noisy breathing after eating egg. Using epinephrine 1 mg/mL at 0.01 mg/kg IM, what is the dose?
qs.x: 12 kg x 0.01 mg/kg = 0.12 mg, which is 0.12 mL of 1 mg/mL. This is under the 0.3 mg maximum for children under 30 kg.
w: 0.3 mg (0.3 mL) IM
1.2 mg (1.2 mL) IM

qs.q: A 41-year-old was stung by a wasp. Which finding most strongly indicates she needs IM epinephrine now?
qs.a: Hives all over the body with vomiting and lip swelling
qs.x: Reactions that involve more than one body system, such as skin plus GI plus swelling, indicate anaphylaxis and the need for epinephrine. Local swelling and pain at the site are not anaphylaxis.
w: A painful, red, swollen welt limited to the sting site only
Itching and swelling of the stung hand only
Anxiety and a HR of 104 with clear lungs

qs.q: A 28-year-old with shellfish anaphylaxis improved after IM epinephrine. Twenty minutes into transport, the hives return, she is wheezing again and BP is 88/56. What should you do now?
qs.a: Give another dose of IM epinephrine and reassess
qs.x: Symptoms can return as epinephrine wears off. Repeat IM dosing is allowed every 5-10 minutes as needed, and returning hypotension means she needs it now.
w: Watch only, since she already received epinephrine
Give albuterol and avoid a second epinephrine dose
Give oral antihistamines and recheck the BP later

qs.q: Five minutes after IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis, a 68-year-old woman's hives and wheezing are improving, but she now has chest pain and BP 196/108. What is the best action?
qs.a: Hold more epinephrine unless anaphylaxis worsens; call medical control
qs.x: Chest pain and severe hypertension are serious epinephrine adverse effects, and anaphylaxis is improving. The drug is held and medical control notified; nitroglycerin is not appropriate here and could worsen hypotension if anaphylaxis returns.
w: Give a second dose of epinephrine since the first one is working
Give nitroglycerin for the chest pain and hypertension
Ignore the chest pain because epinephrine has no effects on the heart

qs.q: A 29-year-old is found next to a syringe. He is unresponsive with RR 4, pinpoint pupils, cyanotic lips and SpO2 78%. What is the first action?
qs.a: Open the airway and ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
qs.x: Ventilation corrects the hypoxia immediately, while naloxone takes minutes to work. Naloxone is given after effective ventilation has started.
w: Give naloxone IN before touching the airway
Start an IV so naloxone can be given IV
Check a blood glucose level before any other care is given

qs.q: After 0.4 mg of IV naloxone, a 45-year-old woman's RR rises from 6 to 14 with good chest rise and SpO2 96%. She is drowsy but arousable. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Stop naloxone, monitor closely and keep her on oxygen
qs.x: The goal of naloxone is adequate ventilation, not full alertness. Further doses can trigger acute withdrawal without added benefit.
w: Give more naloxone until she is fully awake
Give a full 4 mg nasal dose to prevent any relapse later
Stop monitoring, since the overdose is reversed

qs.q: Two minutes after 4 mg IN naloxone, a 33-year-old man wakes up, is vomiting, sweating heavily and is agitated with HR 118. What is the best interpretation and action?
qs.a: Acute opioid withdrawal; protect the airway and monitor
qs.x: Vomiting, sweating, agitation and tachycardia after naloxone are signs of acute opioid withdrawal. The main risk is aspiration, so airway protection and monitoring come first; more naloxone would worsen it.
w: A naloxone allergy; give IM epinephrine
Not enough naloxone; give a second dose
Hypoglycemia from the overdose; give oral glucose right away

qs.q: A 50-year-old with a heroin overdose woke up after naloxone. Thirty minutes into a long transport he becomes drowsy and his RR drops to 6. What is the best action?
qs.a: Ventilate as needed and give another dose of naloxone
qs.x: Naloxone's effect can wear off before the opioid's, causing recurrent respiratory depression. Support ventilations and redose naloxone.
w: Wait until hospital arrival, since the naloxone already worked once
Give glucagon to reverse the sedation
Give oral glucose to help keep him awake

qs.q: A 38-year-old is unresponsive after using pain pills. Her pupils are pinpoint, but RR is 16 with good tidal volume and SpO2 is 97%. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Withhold naloxone, support the airway and monitor breathing
qs.x: Naloxone is given for respiratory depression, and her ventilation is adequate. Waking her without need can cause withdrawal, vomiting and aspiration; close monitoring is the right call.
w: Give naloxone now, since her pupils are pinpoint
Give naloxone IN at a full 4 mg dose to wake her
Give naloxone IV now to prevent any future respiratory depression

qs.q: A 26-year-old found after injecting fentanyl is pulseless and apneic. Your partner is getting naloxone ready. What is the priority?
qs.a: Begin CPR with ventilations and use the AED
qs.x: In cardiac arrest, high-quality CPR, ventilation and defibrillation take priority. Naloxone can be considered but must not delay CPR.
w: Give naloxone IN before starting compressions
Start an IV for naloxone before beginning CPR
Give naloxone IM and wait for a response

qs.q: A 3-year-old weighing 14 kg got into a grandparent's oxycodone. She is unresponsive with RR 6 and pinpoint pupils. After starting BVM ventilations, what is the best medication plan?
qs.a: Naloxone 0.1 mg/kg (max 2 mg) per protocol
qs.x: PALS-based dosing of 0.1 mg/kg (max 2 mg) gives full reversal in a pediatric opioid ingestion. Ventilation comes first, naloxone should not be delayed for IV access when IN or IM routes are available, and there is no reason to withhold it in a child.
w: Withhold naloxone until IV access is obtained
Oral glucose gel, since children get hypoglycemic
Hold naloxone because children should not receive it

qs.q: A 72-year-old hospice patient with cancer wears a fentanyl patch. He is very drowsy with RR 8 and SpO2 89%. What is the best naloxone approach?
qs.a: Titrate small IV doses until breathing is adequate
qs.x: For opioid-dependent patients, small starting doses titrated to RR restore breathing without causing sudden withdrawal and severe pain. Remove the patch, and note that hospice status alone does not mean withholding care; follow any advance directive.
w: Give a full 2 mg IV push for complete reversal
Give 4 mg IN and repeat it until he is fully awake and talking
Withhold naloxone because he is a hospice patient

qs.q: A 19-year-old woman with asthma is wheezing and speaking in short phrases. SpO2 is 91%, HR 118 and RR 28. What is the best next medication?
qs.a: Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized with oxygen
qs.x: Nebulized albuterol is first-line for acute bronchospasm. Her tachycardia comes from distress and hypoxia, not low volume, and albuterol is expected to help.
w: IM epinephrine before trying any albuterol
Ipratropium alone without albuterol
An IV fluid bolus for her tachycardia

qs.q: A 14-year-old with asthma is tripoding and drowsy. Breath sounds are faint with no wheezing, and SpO2 is 84%. What does the lack of wheezing suggest, and what is next?
qs.a: Poor air movement; assist ventilations, epinephrine per protocol
qs.x: A silent chest with drowsiness signals very little air movement and impending respiratory failure. Assisted ventilation (with in-line nebulizer) and epinephrine for severe asthma per protocol are needed.
w: Improving asthma; the albuterol is no longer needed
A non-respiratory cause of distress; withhold all bronchodilators
Mild asthma; coach slow breathing and reassess

qs.q: After an albuterol neb, a 25-year-old asthmatic's wheezing is louder, but she can now speak full sentences and SpO2 rose from 89% to 95%. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Improvement, since air is moving through opening airways
qs.x: Louder wheezing can mean more air is moving through narrowed airways. Full sentences and better SpO2 confirm that the treatment is working.
w: Worsening, since the wheezing is now louder
A side effect of albuterol requiring the treatment to stop
Paradoxical bronchospasm requiring epinephrine

qs.q: A 66-year-old with COPD is getting a second albuterol neb. He now reports chest pain and has a new irregular pulse of 136. What should you do?
qs.a: Stop the albuterol and contact medical control
qs.x: Chest pain and new dysrhythmias are reasons to stop albuterol. These are serious effects, not the common tremor or palpitations.
w: Finish the neb, since chest pain is a common side effect
Give a third neb right away to fix the breathing
Give nitroglycerin and continue the albuterol

qs.q: A 4-year-old with wheezing refuses to keep the nebulizer mouthpiece in and keeps pulling away. What is the best way to deliver albuterol?
qs.a: Use a pediatric mask attached to the nebulizer
qs.x: A snug pediatric mask delivers nebulized albuterol well in young children. Holding the mouthpiece away from the face (blow-by) wastes most of the drug, and refusing a mouthpiece is not an indication for epinephrine.
w: Hold the mouthpiece a few inches from his face
Switch to IM epinephrine since he will not cooperate
Wait until he stops crying before giving anything

qs.q: A 31-year-old asthmatic improved after one neb, but during transport she worsens: SpO2 86%, speaking one or two words and tiring. What is the best action now?
qs.a: Repeat albuterol per protocol and prepare to assist ventilations
qs.x: Albuterol can be repeated every 20 minutes, and back-to-back doses are used for worsening bronchospasm. Fatigue with low SpO2 means you should be ready to assist ventilations.
w: Stop the neb since it is causing the problem
Hold all medication until arrival at the hospital to avoid overdose
Switch to oral fluids to thin her secretions

qs.q: After her first albuterol neb, a 40-year-old woman's breathing improved, but she has a fine tremor, says she is jittery and HR is 112. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: Common albuterol side effects; continue to reassess
qs.x: Tremor, nervousness and tachycardia are common albuterol effects. Her breathing improved, so the plan is to reassess and monitor.
w: An allergic reaction; give IM epinephrine
An albuterol overdose requiring an IV fluid bolus right away
Paradoxical bronchospasm; stop all treatment

qs.q: A 71-year-old with COPD has a wheezing exacerbation. SpO2 is 87% and RR 26. Your protocol allows a combined neb. Why add ipratropium to albuterol?
qs.a: It adds anticholinergic bronchodilation in COPD
qs.x: Ipratropium is an anticholinergic bronchodilator used for COPD bronchospasm and acts by a different path than albuterol, so the effects add together. It does not prevent albuterol side effects.
w: It speeds up albuterol so less of it is needed
It reverses the tremor and racing heart that albuterol may cause
It thins mucus so the patient can cough it up

qs.q: A 78-year-old man with an enlarged prostate received several DuoNebs. He now reports lower abdominal fullness and cannot urinate. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Urinary retention from ipratropium's anticholinergic action
qs.x: Urinary retention is a listed serious effect of ipratropium, and an enlarged prostate raises the risk. It should be reported and further doses held per protocol.
w: Dehydration from the albuterol component
A kidney stone unrelated to any of the medications he received today
An allergic reaction to ipratropium

qs.q: Shortly after an ipratropium neb begins, a 64-year-old's wheezing gets much worse and SpO2 drops from 91% to 84%. What is the best action?
qs.a: Stop the ipratropium and treat as paradoxical bronchospasm
qs.x: Paradoxical bronchospasm is a listed reason to stop ipratropium. Worsening wheezing with falling SpO2 is not expected and needs urgent treatment.
w: Continue the neb since early wheezing worsening is expected
Double the ipratropium dose to overcome the spasm
Remove oxygen because it is worsening the wheezing

qs.q: After a DuoNeb, a 69-year-old woman with COPD breathes easier but complains of a dry mouth and a bitter taste. What is the best response?
qs.a: Reassure; these are common, expected side effects
qs.x: Dry mouth and bitter taste are common ipratropium effects and are not dangerous. Her breathing improved, so continue to reassess; serious anticholinergic effects would be urinary retention or blurred vision.
w: Stop all treatments due to an allergic reaction
Give IM epinephrine for a developing reaction
Hold further doses; these signal anticholinergic toxicity

qs.q: A 34-year-old asthmatic got hives and lip swelling the last time she used albuterol. Your partner suggests levalbuterol instead. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Avoid levalbuterol; albuterol allergy contraindicates it
qs.x: Levalbuterol is the active isomer of albuterol, so hypersensitivity to albuterol contraindicates it. Consider other treatments per protocol.
w: Give levalbuterol, since it is a different drug
Give levalbuterol at a lower dose to limit the allergic reaction
Give levalbuterol, then albuterol if she does not react

qs.q: Your service uses levalbuterol for asthma. A 42-year-old woman received one acute-dose neb 20 minutes ago. She is still wheezing and speaking in phrases, SpO2 91% and HR 108. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Repeat levalbuterol per protocol and reassess
qs.x: Acute bronchospasm is treated with levalbuterol repeated every 20 minutes x3 per NAEPP and EMS protocol, and she still has significant obstruction. Mild tachycardia is an expected effect; severe tachycardia or chest pain would be the reasons to stop.
w: Hold it, since a HR above 100 means she must stop
Switch to the lower dose used for children 6-11
Wait 4-6 hours before giving another dose

qs.q: During a levalbuterol neb, a 52-year-old asthmatic reports palpitations and chest pain. HR is 154. What is the best action?
qs.a: Stop the levalbuterol and notify medical control
qs.x: Severe tachycardia and chest pain are reasons to stop levalbuterol. Unlike mild tremor, these are not effects to ignore.
w: Finish the neb since this is a common side effect
Give a second neb to fix the bronchospasm faster
Give aspirin and continue the levalbuterol

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman is vomiting after a night of drinking. She mentions she was born with long QT syndrome. Your partner prepares ondansetron. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold ondansetron due to congenital long QT syndrome
qs.x: Congenital long QT syndrome is a contraindication because ondansetron can prolong the QT interval and cause dysrhythmias. The ODT form carries the same risk.
w: Give ondansetron, since nausea from alcohol is common
Give half the usual ondansetron dose
Give ondansetron ODT, since oral forms do not affect the heart

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with Parkinson disease is vomiting. His medications include apomorphine injections. What is the best decision about ondansetron?
qs.a: Withhold it due to the risk of profound hypotension
qs.x: Using ondansetron with apomorphine is contraindicated because the combination can cause profound hypotension and loss of consciousness. The route does not change that risk.
w: Give it, since Parkinson patients often have nausea
Give it IM rather than IV to reduce side effects
Give it only after an IV fluid bolus has been infused to raise BP

qs.q: A 9-year-old weighing 25 kg has been vomiting with gastroenteritis. Your protocol allows ondansetron ODT. What is the appropriate dose?
qs.a: 4 mg ODT
qs.x: For children 15-30 kg the ODT dose is 4 mg. 2 mg is for 8-15 kg, and 8 mg exceeds the dose for this weight band.
w: 2 mg ODT
8 mg ODT
0.5 mg ODT

qs.q: Fifteen minutes after 4 mg of IV ondansetron, a 45-year-old woman is still nauseated and has vomited once. Vitals are stable. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Repeat 4 mg once per protocol and reassess
qs.x: The 4 mg dose may be repeated once in 10-15 minutes. Large or repeated doses beyond that raise the risk of QT prolongation.
w: Give 16 mg IV because the first dose failed
Stop treatment since ondansetron did not work
Give ondansetron every 5 minutes until she stops

qs.q: After IV ondansetron, a 63-year-old who takes several heart medications reports palpitations and becomes lightheaded. Her pulse is now irregular. What is the best response?
qs.a: Suspect a QT-related dysrhythmia; monitor and call medical control
qs.x: QT prolongation and dysrhythmias are serious effects of ondansetron, and a new irregular pulse with symptoms needs close monitoring and medical direction. Mild dizziness alone would be common, but a new irregular rhythm is not.
w: Reassure her that headache and dizziness are common
Give a second ondansetron dose to settle her stomach
Give oral glucose because this is most likely hypoglycemia from fasting

qs.q: A 15-year-old drank drain cleaner 20 minutes ago. He has drooling and mouth pain but is alert. A parent asks about activated charcoal. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold charcoal, since caustic ingestion is a contraindication
qs.x: Activated charcoal does not bind caustics and can make injury and endoscopy worse. Being alert and within an hour does not change that contraindication.
w: Give charcoal, since he is alert and within the first hour
Give charcoal mixed with milk to neutralize the drain cleaner first
Give charcoal through a straw to protect the mouth

qs.q: A 36-year-old took a large amount of her prescription pills 40 minutes ago. While you prepare activated charcoal per protocol, she becomes drowsy and slurs her words. What is the best action?
qs.a: Withhold the charcoal and focus on airway and monitoring
qs.x: Decreasing mental status is a reason to stop charcoal because of aspiration risk. Airway protection and monitoring come first.
w: Give the charcoal quickly before she becomes less alert
Give half the dose so she can still swallow it
Have her lie flat on her back while she drinks the whole dose

qs.q: A mother has given her 3-year-old adult-strength acetaminophen every 3 hours for two days for fever. The child is now vomiting and has right upper abdominal pain. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold acetaminophen and transport for a suspected overdose
qs.x: Adult-strength doses given too often suggest a supratherapeutic ingestion, and abdominal pain with vomiting raise concern for hepatotoxicity. Suspected overdose is a reason to hold acetaminophen by any route.
w: Give another acetaminophen dose for the fever
Give acetaminophen rectally instead, since the child is vomiting
Give ibuprofen and acetaminophen together for the fever

qs.q: A 31-year-old woman who is 35 weeks pregnant has a headache and asks for ibuprofen. BP is 162/104. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold ibuprofen and treat the high BP as a warning sign
qs.x: Ibuprofen is contraindicated in the third trimester, and a headache with high BP late in pregnancy suggests preeclampsia. She needs evaluation and transport, not an NSAID.
w: Give ibuprofen, since it is a common and safe headache medication
Give a smaller ibuprofen dose because she is pregnant
Give ibuprofen with food to protect her stomach

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has had crushing chest pressure for 30 minutes. He is diaphoretic, BP 148/90, HR 96, and he took his usual daily enteric-coated low-dose aspirin this morning. What is the best next action regarding aspirin?
qs.a: Give chewed non-enteric-coated aspirin per protocol
qs.x: A routine daily low dose does not replace the ACS dose; chewed non-enteric-coated aspirin gives the fastest antiplatelet effect. Waiting for a STEMI is wrong because aspirin is indicated for any suspected ACS.
w: Withhold aspirin since he already took a daily dose
Have him swallow enteric-coated tablets whole with water
Wait to give aspirin until a STEMI is seen on the 12-lead

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman has substernal chest pain with ST depression in the lateral leads. HR 112, BP 104/66. She reports black, tarry stools for two days and feels lightheaded when standing. What should the paramedic do about aspirin?
qs.a: Withhold aspirin and report suspected GI bleeding
qs.x: Melena with tachycardia and orthostasis suggests active GI bleeding, a contraindication to aspirin. Changing the route to PR does not remove the systemic antiplatelet effect that worsens bleeding.
w: Give full-dose aspirin because ACS benefit outweighs risk
Give half the usual aspirin dose because of the stools
Give the aspirin rectally to avoid irritating the stomach

qs.q: A 52-year-old man with chest pain and anterior ST elevation is alert with BP 138/86. While you prepare aspirin, he mentions several facts. Which one most changes your aspirin decision?
qs.a: Ibuprofen once caused wheezing that required a hospital stay
qs.x: Severe bronchospasm from an NSAID suggests aspirin-sensitive asthma, which is a contraindication to aspirin. Smoking and statin use are risk factors or routine meds and do not change the aspirin decision.
w: He takes atorvastatin every night for his high cholesterol level
He has smoked one pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years
He ate a large meal about one hour before the pain began

qs.q: A 70-year-old man has an inferior STEMI. He is alert, BP 136/82, HR 74, SpO2 96% on room air, pain 7/10, no allergies, and has taken nothing today. Which medication should be given first?
qs.a: Chewed aspirin
qs.x: Early aspirin reduces mortality in STEMI and he has no contraindication. Morphine is not first-line and may hide ongoing ischemia; metoprolol and furosemide are not routine early prehospital STEMI treatment.
w: IV morphine for pain
IV metoprolol
IV furosemide

qs.q: A 59-year-old man has chest pressure with BP 142/88 and HR 84. While preparing nitroglycerin, you learn he took tadalafil about 36 hours ago. What is the best action?
qs.a: Withhold nitroglycerin and manage pain another way
qs.x: Tadalafil within 48 hours contraindicates nitrates because the combination can cause profound hypotension. The 24-hour window applies to sildenafil and vardenafil, not tadalafil.
w: Give nitroglycerin since more than 24 hours have passed
Give one nitroglycerin and recheck BP in 5 minutes
Give a nitroglycerin spray instead of a tablet

qs.q: A 64-year-old woman with chest pain had BP 138/82 and HR 80. Two minutes after her second nitroglycerin, she is pale and nauseated with BP 82/50 and HR 48. What is the next best action?
qs.a: Stop nitroglycerin, lay her supine, and give a fluid bolus
qs.x: Hypotension with bradycardia after nitroglycerin fits a Bezold-Jarisch type reaction; stop nitrates and restore preload, adding atropine if bradycardia persists with poor perfusion. A further dose would deepen the hypotension.
w: Give a third nitroglycerin dose because her chest pain persists
Give IV metoprolol to control the heart rate change
Sit her fully upright so she can breathe more easily

qs.q: A 74-year-old man in acute pulmonary edema had BP 218/124. After CPAP and repeated nitroglycerin per protocol, his breathing is much easier, but his BP is now 104/66. What should the paramedic do next?
qs.a: Hold further nitroglycerin and keep CPAP on with close BP checks
qs.x: His symptoms have improved and the SBP is now near the 90-100 stop range for nitroglycerin, so further doses are held while CPAP continues. Continuing the doses risks hypotension now that afterload has been reduced.
w: Continue the nitroglycerin doses every 3-5 minutes as before to keep the BP down
Remove CPAP since the patient is clearly improving now
Give IV furosemide to finish clearing the remaining fluid

qs.q: A 77-year-old woman has chest pressure, dizziness, and HR 42 in sinus bradycardia. BP is 104/62. She asks for her nitroglycerin. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold nitroglycerin and treat the bradycardia first
qs.x: Severe bradycardia is a contraindication to nitroglycerin, which can worsen hypotension and bradycardia. A BP above 90 alone does not make nitrates safe in a patient this slow and symptomatic.
w: Give nitroglycerin because the SBP is above 90
Give nitroglycerin and lay her flat if she gets more dizzy
Give nitroglycerin and atropine at the same time

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with a STEMI received IV morphine for refractory pain. Ten minutes later he is difficult to arouse, RR 8, SpO2 89%, BP 112/70. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Assist ventilations with a BVM and give naloxone per protocol
qs.x: An RR under 10-12 with oversedation is a stop point for morphine; support ventilation first and reverse with naloxone if needed. Low-flow oxygen alone does not fix hypoventilation.
w: Give a second morphine dose now since his chest pain has not returned
Place a nasal cannula and recheck him in 10 minutes
Give IV ondansetron to prevent vomiting and aspiration

qs.q: A 61-year-old woman has an inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R. She still has pain 8/10, BP 92/60, HR 66, lungs clear. Which is the most appropriate decision about morphine?
qs.a: Withhold morphine because of borderline hypotension
qs.x: Right ventricular involvement makes her preload-dependent, and morphine can cause hypotension. The IM route does not prevent hypotension and makes titration harder.
w: Give morphine because ongoing pain increases cardiac demand
Give morphine with nitroglycerin for better relief
Give morphine IM so it absorbs more gently

qs.q: A 71-year-old man with symptomatic third-degree block is being paced with good electrical and mechanical capture. BP is now 112/68 but he is grimacing and asking you to stop. What is the best next action?
