qs.a: Give titrated fentanyl analgesia per protocol
qs.x: Pacing is painful, and with capture and an adequate BP, titrated analgesia is appropriate. Dropping the current below threshold loses capture and returns him to the unstable rhythm.
w: Turn the pacer off until he is calmer
Withhold all analgesia because he is being actively paced
Lower the current below the capture threshold

qs.q: A 74-year-old woman with symptomatic third-degree block is being paced at 70 with confirmed electrical and mechanical capture. After a fluid bolus her BP is still 72/40, she remains confused, and her lungs are clear. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Start an epinephrine infusion per protocol and titrate
qs.x: With confirmed mechanical capture, persistent hypotension and poor perfusion call for a vasopressor or chronotropic infusion such as epinephrine. Atropine adds nothing while the pacer controls the rate, and stopping pacing returns her to the unstable rhythm.
w: Give atropine to raise the paced heart rate
Turn off the pacer and give amiodarone
Hold further treatment until hospital arrival

qs.q: A 63-year-old woman with a STEMI was given fentanyl after nitroglycerin failed to relieve her pain. Five minutes later: pain 3/10, RR 16, SpO2 96%, BP 124/78, alert. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Effective analgesia without adverse effects; keep monitoring
qs.x: Pain fell with normal breathing, SpO2, BP, and mental status, so the drug worked without side effects. There is no sign of respiratory depression, so naloxone is not indicated.
w: Early respiratory depression that requires naloxone now
Inadequate response that calls for a larger repeat dose of fentanyl
Hypotension from fentanyl that needs a fluid bolus now

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman has palpitations. The monitor shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia at 168 with no clear P waves. BP 124/80, alert. What is the most appropriate decision?
qs.a: Do not give adenosine; consider rate control per protocol
qs.x: This is atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, not reentrant SVT; adenosine is for regular reentrant rhythms. She is stable, so immediate cardioversion is not required.
w: Give adenosine to convert this reentrant rhythm
Give adenosine to slow the rate and then cardiovert her afterward
Perform immediate synchronized cardioversion

qs.q: A 55-year-old man with a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 receives adenosine. During the brief slowing, the monitor shows sawtooth waves at about 300 per minute before the rate returns to 150. What does this finding mean?
qs.a: The rhythm is atrial flutter, so repeat adenosine will not convert it
qs.x: Adenosine slowed AV conduction and unmasked flutter waves; flutter is not reentrant through the AV node, so adenosine will not convert it. The QRS stayed narrow, so this is not VT.
w: The adenosine was pushed too slowly and should be repeated at a faster rate
This is ventricular tachycardia and requires a shock right now
The rhythm is sinus tachycardia that needs a fluid bolus

qs.q: A 34-year-old woman with SVT at 210 was alert with BP 116/74 while you prepared adenosine. She now becomes confused, diaphoretic, and her BP is 76/40. What changes now?
qs.a: Proceed to synchronized cardioversion
qs.x: She is now unstable, so synchronized cardioversion is indicated rather than drug therapy. Adenosine may be tried while preparing only if it causes no delay; a fluid bolus does not treat the rhythm.
w: Give adenosine more slowly and wait
Repeat vagal maneuvers for one more minute
Give a fluid bolus and recheck later

qs.q: A 26-year-old with a history of asthma receives adenosine for SVT. The rhythm converts, but she now has diffuse wheezing and SpO2 88% that is not resolving after a minute. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Treat the bronchospasm and give no further adenosine
qs.x: Adenosine can cause bronchospasm, especially in patients with asthma; this needs treatment, not reassurance. Flushing and chest pressure are brief expected effects, but persistent wheezing with low SpO2 is a serious reaction.
w: Ignore it, as this is the normal flushing after adenosine
Give another adenosine dose to prevent the SVT returning
Give IV metoprolol to keep her from going back into SVT

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with stable monomorphic VT at 170 and a QRS of 140 ms is receiving procainamide. He remains alert with BP 124/78, but the rhythm has not converted and the QRS now measures 220 ms. What should the paramedic do?
qs.a: Stop the procainamide and reassess
qs.x: QRS widening of more than 50% from baseline is a procainamide endpoint and signals toxicity. Continuing or adding another antiarrhythmic raises the risk of hypotension, heart block, and worse dysrhythmias.
w: Continue, since a wider QRS shows drug effect
Increase the rate to convert him faster
Add amiodarone to complete the conversion

qs.q: A patient with stable monomorphic VT is receiving procainamide. Midway through the load the rhythm is unchanged, the QRS is a bit narrower, and the BP falls from 128/80 to 84/52. What should the paramedic do?
qs.a: Stop the infusion and reassess the patient
qs.x: Hypotension is one of the endpoints for stopping procainamide. Increasing the rate or adding another QT-prolonging antiarrhythmic raises the risk of hypotension and dysrhythmias.
w: Speed up the infusion to convert faster
Add amiodarone to the same IV line now
Continue at the same rate and recheck the BP in 10 minutes

qs.q: A 48-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has stable monomorphic VT at 160 with BP 130/84. She is alert and has no chest pain. Which antiarrhythmic decision is best?
qs.a: Avoid procainamide and choose another agent
qs.x: Myasthenia gravis is a contraindication to procainamide because it can worsen muscle weakness. Waiting for weakness to appear risks respiratory compromise.
w: Give procainamide since she is stable
Give procainamide but stop if she feels weak
Give procainamide and lidocaine together

qs.q: A 64-year-old man has a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 170 that looks like monomorphic VT. He is alert, BP 128/80, and has no chest pain or dyspnea. Which treatment is most appropriate?
qs.a: Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes
qs.x: Stable VT with a pulse is treated with amiodarone 150 mg infused over 10 minutes. The 300 mg push is the cardiac arrest dose, and diltiazem is contraindicated in wide-complex tachycardia of unknown origin.
w: Amiodarone 300 mg as a rapid IV push
Diltiazem IV over two minutes
Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation

qs.q: A patient with stable VT is receiving amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes. Halfway through, he is still in VT but his BP has fallen from 126/78 to 80/48 and he is now drowsy. What should the paramedic do?
qs.a: Stop the infusion and prepare for synchronized cardioversion
qs.x: Hypotension is a stop point for amiodarone, and a drop in BP with altered mental status makes him unstable, so cardioversion is indicated. Pushing it faster would worsen the hypotension.
w: Finish the amiodarone, since stopping it early makes it fail to convert
Push the rest of the amiodarone to convert him sooner
Add a dopamine infusion and keep the amiodarone going

qs.q: After his VT converted, a 69-year-old man has frequent PVCs. The new 12-lead shows second-degree type II AV block at a rate of 48. BP 98/62. Should amiodarone be given for the PVCs?
qs.a: No; AV block without a pacemaker contraindicates it
qs.x: Second- or third-degree AV block without a pacemaker is a contraindication to amiodarone, which can worsen the block. Suppressing ectopy is less important than avoiding a slower, more dangerous rhythm.
w: Yes; frequent PVCs after VT always need an antiarrhythmic
Yes; give the arrest dose so VT does not return
Yes, but give half of the usual dose this time

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman has monomorphic VT at 190. She is confused and pale with BP 70/40 and a weak radial pulse. Which action is the priority?
qs.a: Synchronized cardioversion
qs.x: VT with a pulse plus hypotension and altered mental status is unstable and needs synchronized cardioversion. Antiarrhythmic infusions are for stable patients and would delay definitive care.
w: Amiodarone infused over 10 minutes
Lidocaine IV bolus first
Adenosine rapid IV push

qs.q: During transport to a PCI center, a 60-year-old STEMI patient develops a regular wide-complex rhythm at 58 with no P waves. BP 112/70, he is alert and his pain is improving. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Monitor; do not suppress it with lidocaine
qs.x: A slow ventricular rhythm like this is often an accelerated idioventricular (reperfusion) rhythm; ventricular escape rhythms are a contraindication to lidocaine, which can remove the only pacemaker and cause asystole. The patient is stable, so cardioversion is not indicated.
w: Give lidocaine to suppress the ventricular rhythm
Give lidocaine and start an infusion after it
Perform synchronized cardioversion right away

qs.q: A 46-year-old woman on methadone has runs of polymorphic VT that twists around the baseline and stops on its own. Between runs she is alert, BP 104/68, and the QT is markedly prolonged. Which medication is the best choice?
qs.a: Magnesium sulfate
qs.x: This is torsades de pointes with a pulse, and magnesium is the drug of choice. Procainamide is contraindicated with torsades and long QT, and amiodarone also prolongs the QT.
w: Procainamide
Amiodarone
Adenosine

qs.q: A patient with torsades de pointes is about to receive magnesium when the rhythm continues without stopping and she becomes pulseless. What is the next best action?
qs.a: Defibrillate at once, then give magnesium
qs.x: Pulseless polymorphic VT is treated as VF with immediate unsynchronized defibrillation and CPR; magnesium can follow. Synchronization often fails in polymorphic VT because the device cannot track the QRS.
w: Give magnesium IV push before any shock
Perform synchronized cardioversion first
Give amiodarone before a shock is delivered

qs.q: A 79-year-old woman is dizzy and confused. The monitor shows sinus bradycardia at 38. BP 78/40, skin cool and pale, lungs clear. What is the best initial treatment?
qs.a: Atropine IV while preparing to pace
qs.x: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia with hypotension and altered mental status is treated with atropine first, with pacing ready if it fails. Nitroglycerin would lower her BP further.
w: Nitroglycerin SL for poor perfusion
Adenosine rapid push to reset the node
Wait for a 12-lead before any treatment

qs.q: A 75-year-old man has third-degree AV block with a wide-complex escape rhythm at 32. He is pale, confused, and has BP 70/38. Which action should not be delayed?
qs.a: Transcutaneous pacing
qs.x: A wide-complex escape rhythm in complete heart block is unlikely to respond to atropine, which works at the AV node. Pacing should start without delay; repeated atropine wastes time.
w: Repeat atropine doses every minute
Amiodarone infusion
Oral fluids and rest

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with an inferior STEMI and symptomatic bradycardia received atropine. His HR is now 136 and his chest pain is worse, with deeper ST changes. What should the paramedic do?
qs.a: Give no more atropine and reassess
qs.x: Tachycardia with worsening ischemia is a stop point for atropine because the higher rate increases myocardial oxygen demand. This is sinus tachycardia from the drug, so cardioversion or adenosine is not appropriate.
w: Give more atropine to reach a target
Give adenosine to slow the new rate
Prepare synchronized cardioversion

qs.q: A 7-month-old with bronchiolitis is limp and gray. HR 58, SpO2 76%, RR 8 and shallow. What is the first priority?
qs.a: Ventilate with a BVM and high-flow oxygen
qs.x: Bradycardia in infants is most often caused by hypoxia, so oxygenation and ventilation come first; start CPR if HR stays under 60 with poor perfusion. Atropine does not fix the underlying hypoxia.
w: Give atropine IV before anything else
Give epinephrine IV before ventilating the infant
Set up for transcutaneous pacing first

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman with symptomatic sinus bradycardia at 36 has received the maximum atropine dose with no change. Pacing will not capture despite pad repositioning. BP 70/40. What is the next best action?
qs.a: Start a dopamine infusion and titrate to effect
qs.x: Dopamine is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia after atropine when pacing fails or is unavailable. Atropine past the maximum adds no benefit, and amiodarone or adenosine would slow her further.
w: Give more atropine beyond the maximum dose until HR rises
Give amiodarone to stabilize the rhythm
Give adenosine to reset the sinus node

qs.q: A patient on a dopamine infusion for bradycardia and hypotension now has a HR of 118 with runs of nonsustained VT and new chest pain. BP 148/90. What is the best action?
qs.a: Reduce or stop the infusion and reassess
qs.x: Tachydysrhythmias and chest pain are signs of too much dopamine and are stop criteria. Adding an antiarrhythmic while keeping the cause running does not fix the problem.
w: Increase the infusion to reach a higher BP
Give amiodarone while keeping the same rate
Change to a larger IV site and keep it going

qs.q: A 67-year-old man with an anterior STEMI is cool and clammy with crackles halfway up both lungs. BP 74/48, HR 112, SpO2 88%. What is the most appropriate treatment for his BP?
qs.a: Start a norepinephrine infusion titrated per protocol
qs.x: This is cardiogenic shock with pulmonary edema, and a vasopressor such as norepinephrine supports perfusion. Large fluid boluses worsen pulmonary edema, and nitroglycerin and furosemide lower BP further.
w: Give a large fluid bolus to raise his preload and BP quickly
Give nitroglycerin to reduce cardiac workload
Give IV furosemide to remove the lung fluid

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman has ROSC after VF arrest. After a fluid bolus, her MAP is 55 and HR 104. She is intubated with good ventilation. What is the next best action?
qs.a: Start norepinephrine and titrate to a MAP of 65 or higher
qs.x: Post-ROSC hypotension that persists after fluids is treated with a vasopressor titrated to MAP goals. Arrest-dose epinephrine stops at ROSC and would cause severe hypertension and dysrhythmias.
w: Repeat cardiac arrest epinephrine doses every 3-5 minutes
Give amiodarone to prevent VF from returning
Withhold vasopressors since she now has a pulse

qs.q: A 62-year-old man has an inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R. BP 82/50, HR 68, lungs clear, no JVD. What is the best initial treatment for his hypotension?
qs.a: A fluid bolus first; vasopressor only if it persists
qs.x: Right ventricular infarction is preload-dependent, and clear lungs support careful volume first; vasopressors are for hypotension that persists after volume. Nitroglycerin and furosemide reduce preload and would worsen the hypotension.
w: Norepinephrine infusion first, then fluids if needed
Nitroglycerin to improve flow through the coronary arteries
Furosemide to reduce strain on the right ventricle

qs.q: A post-ROSC patient on a norepinephrine infusion now has BP 168/102 (MAP about 124), HR 54, and cool, mottled fingers. What is the best action?
qs.a: Titrate the norepinephrine down toward the MAP goal
qs.x: MAP well above goal is a stop or titrate-down point; reflex bradycardia and cool, mottled fingers are signs of too much vasoconstriction. Giving atropine treats a side effect instead of the cause.
w: Increase the infusion rate to improve the perfusion of his fingers
Give atropine for the HR and keep the same rate
Make no change; a high MAP protects the brain

qs.q: A 70-year-old man is in cardiac arrest. Asystole is confirmed in two leads, CPR is ongoing, and IV access is established. Which medication decision is best?
qs.a: Give epinephrine and continue CPR; atropine is not routine
qs.x: Epinephrine is the vasopressor for all arrest rhythms and should be given as soon as possible in asystole. Atropine is no longer routinely recommended in asystole, and amiodarone is for shock-refractory VF/VT.
w: Give atropine first because the underlying rhythm is very slow or absent
Give amiodarone to prevent VF from starting again
Withhold drugs until a shockable rhythm appears

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman regained a pulse after a VF arrest. Four minutes later her BP is 68/40 while a vasopressor infusion is still being prepared. What is the best bridging action?
qs.a: Give push-dose epinephrine per protocol and recheck
qs.x: Push-dose epinephrine in small doses is used as a short bridge for hypotension until an infusion runs. The 1 mg arrest dose is for pulseless patients and would cause severe hypertension and dysrhythmias.
w: Resume arrest-dose epinephrine every 3-5 minutes until BP improves
Wait for the infusion before treating her BP
Give a rapid amiodarone push to support her BP

qs.q: A 29-year-old man is found pulseless and apneic with a syringe nearby. CPR is in progress with a BVM, and the monitor shows asystole. Which action is the priority?
qs.a: High-quality CPR, ventilation, and epinephrine
qs.x: In opioid-associated cardiac arrest, high-quality CPR with ventilation and standard ACLS come first; naloxone may be given but should not delay or interrupt them. Naloxone cannot restore a pulse in a heart that is not perfusing.
w: Intranasal naloxone before continuing compressions
Stopping CPR to give IV naloxone and wait for effect
Repeating naloxone until he starts breathing on his own

qs.q: An 81-year-old man has atrial fibrillation at 156. He is lightheaded, BP 84/52, and his skin is cool. What is the best decision about diltiazem?
qs.a: Withhold it; consider cardioversion per protocol
qs.x: SBP under 90 is a contraindication to diltiazem, which causes hypotension. A smaller or slower dose does not remove that risk in a patient already showing poor perfusion.
w: Give the full weight-based dose to slow his heart rate quickly
Give a reduced elderly dose to protect his BP
Give it slowly over 10 minutes instead of 2

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman with AF at 148 and BP 128/80 was given IV metoprolol at an urgent care clinic 30 minutes ago with little effect. What should the paramedic do about diltiazem?
qs.a: Withhold diltiazem because of the recent IV beta blocker
qs.x: An IV beta blocker within hours is a contraindication to diltiazem because the combination can cause severe bradycardia, AV block, or hypotension. Lack of effect from metoprolol does not make adding diltiazem safe.
w: Give diltiazem now since the metoprolol did not work
Give diltiazem together with more IV metoprolol now to control the rate
Give diltiazem now but cut the dose in half to be safe

qs.q: A 65-year-old man with AF at 152 and BP 132/84 received diltiazem. Fifteen minutes later his HR is 92, BP 118/76, and his palpitations have eased. What is the best interpretation and action?
qs.a: Rate control achieved; monitor without another dose
qs.x: The HR is now controlled with a stable BP and better symptoms, so the drug worked and a second dose is not needed. A BP of 118/76 is not hypotension.
w: Rate is still too fast; give the second, higher weight-based dose
Early hypotension; stop and give a fluid bolus
Treatment failure; prepare for cardioversion

qs.q: A 32-year-old man has chest pain after using cocaine. He is agitated and diaphoretic, HR 128, BP 170/100. Which decision is most appropriate?
qs.a: Avoid metoprolol and treat agitation with a benzodiazepine
qs.x: Beta blockers are avoided in cocaine-associated ACS because they can leave alpha stimulation unopposed. Benzodiazepines reduce the sympathetic drive that causes the tachycardia and hypertension.
w: Give metoprolol to slow the HR and lower the BP
Give metoprolol only if the 12-lead shows no ST elevation at all
Give metoprolol, then give nitroglycerin afterward

qs.q: A 63-year-old man has an anterior STEMI with crackles at both bases, HR 104, BP 96/64, and SpO2 90%. A partner suggests IV metoprolol for the tachycardia. What is the best response?
qs.a: Withhold it due to heart failure and low BP
qs.x: Decompensated heart failure and SBP under 100 in acute MI are contraindications to metoprolol. The tachycardia is likely compensating for poor pump function, and blocking it can cause cardiogenic shock.
w: Give it because the tachycardia worsens ischemia
Give a single IV dose and then recheck the BP
Give it after furosemide clears the crackles

qs.q: A 78-year-old woman has crackles to the mid-lung fields, SpO2 86%, cool clammy skin, and BP 82/54. Her family asks why she is not getting her water pill. What finding makes furosemide inappropriate now?
qs.a: The hypotension
qs.x: Hypotension is a stop point for furosemide, and diuresis would worsen this picture of cardiogenic shock. The crackles and hypoxia are why a diuretic seems tempting, not reasons to withhold it.
w: The crackles
The low SpO2
Her advanced age

qs.q: A 59-year-old man on hemodialysis who makes no urine missed his last session. He has crackles, JVD, BP 196/108, and SpO2 85%. Which plan is most appropriate?
qs.a: CPAP and nitroglycerin; furosemide will not help an anuric patient
qs.x: Anuria is a contraindication to furosemide because the drug acts through urine production. CPAP and nitroglycerin reduce preload and afterload and help while he gets to dialysis.
w: IV furosemide at double his usual home dose to remove the excess fluid quickly
IV furosemide first, then CPAP if he does not improve
Withhold all drugs and transport without CPAP or treatment

qs.q: An 84-year-old man has had fever, cough, and poor oral intake for four days. He has crackles in the right lower lobe, dry mucous membranes, HR 118, and BP 98/60. Should furosemide be given?
qs.a: No; pneumonia with dehydration makes it harmful
qs.x: Focal crackles with fever suggest pneumonia, not heart failure, and dehydration is a contraindication to furosemide. Diuresis would worsen his volume depletion and hypotension.
w: Yes; crackles always point to fluid in the lungs
Yes; it will clear the crackles and raise SpO2
Yes; but only give half of the usual dose

qs.q: A 68-year-old man has a severe headache, blurred vision, and BP 226/124. The monitor shows third-degree AV block with a narrow escape rhythm at 46. Medical direction asks about labetalol. What is the best response?
qs.a: Avoid labetalol because of the complete heart block
qs.x: Second- and third-degree heart block and severe bradycardia are contraindications to labetalol, which can slow the escape rhythm further. Having atropine ready or lowering the dose does not make the drug safe.
w: Give labetalol, since the BP poses the greater danger
Give labetalol and keep atropine at the bedside
Give labetalol at a reduced first dose

qs.q: A 71-year-old woman has BP 224/118, crackles to the mid-lung fields, pink frothy sputum, and SpO2 85%. Your partner suggests labetalol to bring the BP down. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Use CPAP and nitroglycerin; avoid labetalol
qs.x: Overt heart failure is a contraindication to labetalol because beta blockade can further depress pump function. CPAP and nitroglycerin reduce preload and afterload and are first-line for hypertensive pulmonary edema.
w: Give labetalol first, then start CPAP
Give labetalol together with furosemide
Withhold all BP treatment until arrival

qs.q: A 57-year-old man has BP 244/136, a severe headache, blurred vision, and confusion. Labetalol is ordered. What is the most appropriate BP goal in the first minutes?
qs.a: Lower the BP gradually per protocol
qs.x: In hypertensive emergency the BP is lowered in a controlled way, not normalized in minutes, because a sudden drop can cause brain or heart ischemia. Leaving it untreated is also wrong when there are signs of end-organ damage.
w: Lower it to 120/80 as fast as possible
Lower it below 100 systolic for safety
Do not lower BP until he is at the ED

qs.q: A 61-year-old man with no kidney disease collapses at a gym. He is in VF; CPR is in progress, and he has received two shocks and one dose of epinephrine. A partner suggests calcium chloride. What is the best response?
qs.a: Calcium is not indicated; continue CPR and ACLS
qs.x: Calcium is contraindicated in VF that is not related to hyperkalemia and is not part of routine arrest care. It is reserved for causes such as suspected hyperkalemia or calcium channel blocker toxicity.
w: Give calcium chloride now to strengthen contractions
Give calcium chloride before the next shock
Give calcium chloride in place of an antiarrhythmic

qs.q: A 70-year-old man who takes metoprolol and insulin is found diaphoretic, responding only to loud voice and not following commands. HR 54, BP 112/70, RR 16, SpO2 97%, and a fingerstick glucose is 36 mg/dL. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Give IV dextrose and recheck the glucose
qs.x: Hypoglycemia explains his mental status, and his HR and BP are adequate, so IV dextrose is the priority; beta blockers can blunt the usual tachycardia. Oral glucose is unsafe because he cannot reliably swallow or protect his airway.
w: Give atropine for the slow heart rate
Begin transcutaneous pacing at once
Give oral glucose gel in his cheek

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman with AF at 150 and BP 132/80 received IV metoprolol per protocol. Five minutes later her HR is 54, BP 84/50, and she feels lightheaded. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Hold further metoprolol and treat the hypotension
qs.x: HR under 60 and SBP under 90 are stop points for metoprolol; more doses would worsen the bradycardia and hypotension. Adding diltiazem after an IV beta blocker is contraindicated.
w: Give the next scheduled metoprolol dose
Add diltiazem to keep the rate controlled
Give adenosine to reset the rhythm

qs.q: A 67-year-old woman with an NSTEMI is vomiting. She takes several QT-prolonging medicines, and her 12-lead shows a clearly prolonged QTc. What is the best decision about ondansetron?
qs.a: Withhold it and notify medical direction
qs.x: A prolonged QTc is a hold point for ondansetron, which can prolong the QT further and cause dysrhythmias. Changing the route does not remove the QT effect.
w: Give it at once to prevent vomiting and aspiration
Give it IM rather than IV to be safe
Give it with magnesium as a precaution

qs.q: A 61-year-old man has monomorphic VT at 180 with a weak pulse. He is unresponsive to voice and pain, BP 64/30. Your partner draws up midazolam for cardioversion. What is the best action?
qs.a: Cardiovert now; sedation is not needed
qs.x: An unresponsive, unstable patient needs immediate cardioversion, and sedation would delay it and worsen his hypotension. Sedation is for conscious patients when time allows.
w: Give midazolam first, then cardiovert
Give midazolam and fentanyl, then shock
Wait until the midazolam takes effect

qs.q: An 86-year-old woman is being paced for complete heart block. After IV midazolam for pacing discomfort, she becomes very drowsy with RR 8 and SpO2 87%. Pacing still captures. What is the next best action?
qs.a: Stop sedation and assist ventilations
qs.x: Respiratory depression and oversedation are stop points for midazolam, and older patients are more sensitive to it. She needs ventilatory support now; turning off the pacer would return her to the unstable rhythm.
w: Give more midazolam to keep her calm
Turn off the pacer to reduce stimulation
Place a nasal cannula and keep watching

qs.q: A 48-year-old man is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, shallow respirations at 5 per minute, and cyanosis. The monitor shows sinus bradycardia at 46 and BP is 98/60. Your partner reaches for atropine. What is the best action?
qs.a: Ventilate with a BVM, then give naloxone
qs.x: The bradycardia is most likely from hypoxia caused by opioid hypoventilation, so ventilation and naloxone treat the cause. Atropine, pacing, or dopamine do not correct the hypoxia driving the slow rate.
w: Give atropine first for the bradycardia
Begin transcutaneous pacing right away
Start a dopamine infusion for the HR

qs.q: A 64-year-old man with ongoing ischemic chest pain and BP 176/104 needs analgesia and sedation for transcutaneous pacing. Which concern makes ketamine a less suitable choice?
qs.a: It can raise BP and HR, adding cardiac demand
qs.x: Ketamine commonly causes hypertension and tachycardia, which increase myocardial oxygen demand in a patient with active ischemia. It does not usually cause hypotension, which is why it is chosen in other settings.
w: It almost always causes severe hypotension in older adults
It reliably causes complete heart block
It has no effect when given by IV route

qs.q: A 57-year-old woman with diabetes has ROSC after a PEA arrest. She is intubated with MAP 70, but a fingerstick glucose is 42 mg/dL. What is the best next action?
qs.a: Give IV dextrose and recheck the glucose
qs.x: Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of poor neurologic outcome after ROSC and should be corrected with IV dextrose and rechecked. Oral glucose is contraindicated in a patient who cannot swallow or protect the airway.
w: Give oral glucose gel through the tube
Recheck the glucose at the hospital
Give glucagon IV in place of the dextrose

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman with asthma has received two albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers. Her wheezing is now louder, she speaks in full sentences, SpO2 rose from 88% to 94% and HR went from 118 to 124. How should you interpret these findings?
qs.a: She is improving; louder wheezing reflects better air movement, so continue and reassess
qs.x: Better speech and SpO2 show improved airflow; wheezing often gets louder as air moves through narrowed airways. A small expected rise in heart rate is a common albuterol effect, not a reason to stop.
w: She is worsening; louder wheezing means bronchospasm is progressing and she needs intubation
She has albuterol toxicity; the rise in heart rate means all bronchodilators should stop
She has likely developed a pneumothorax and needs needle decompression before more treatment

qs.q: A 19-year-old with asthma has had three albuterol nebulizers en route. HR is 132, SpO2 86%, he is now drowsy, and breath sounds are barely audible bilaterally. Which finding is most concerning?
qs.a: Drowsiness with diminished breath sounds
qs.x: A quiet chest with falling mental status signals near-respiratory arrest from severe air trapping and fatigue; he needs assisted ventilation now. Tachycardia and tremor are expected albuterol effects and are less urgent.
w: Heart rate of 132 shortly after the third albuterol dose
A fine tremor of both hands
Expiratory wheezing on arrival

qs.q: A 30-year-old asthmatic was intubated 10 minutes ago. Waveform capnography shows a shark-fin pattern, the tube position is confirmed, breath sounds are equal with diffuse wheezing, and peak airway pressures are rising. What is the most appropriate medication step?
qs.a: Give albuterol in-line through the ventilator circuit
qs.x: With tube placement confirmed and a shark-fin capnogram, ongoing bronchospasm is the problem; albuterol can be delivered in-line through the ventilator. More paralytic does not treat bronchospasm.
w: Give a second dose of the paralytic and recheck
Extubate and return to BVM ventilation with a nasal airway
Give IV naloxone in case opioids are suppressing the drive

qs.q: A 66-year-old with COPD is wheezing after one albuterol nebulizer, and you are considering CPAP with in-line albuterol. Which finding makes CPAP inappropriate?
qs.a: GCS of 9 with active vomiting
qs.x: CPAP requires an alert patient who can protect the airway; a decreased GCS with vomiting creates aspiration risk, so ventilate with BVM and prepare for an advanced airway instead. Hypoxia and tachypnea are reasons to use CPAP, not to avoid it.
w: SpO2 of 89% on a nonrebreather
Respiratory rate of 28 with accessory muscle use
Heart rate of 112 after the albuterol

qs.q: A 71-year-old man with a COPD exacerbation is wheezing. While you prepare a combined albuterol and ipratropium nebulizer, he tells you he had a severe allergic reaction to atropine during surgery. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Give albuterol alone and withhold ipratropium
qs.x: Hypersensitivity to atropine or its derivatives is a contraindication to ipratropium, so give albuterol alone. Pretreating with diphenhydramine or reducing the dose does not make a contraindicated drug safe.
w: Give the combined nebulizer at half the usual dose
Give ipratropium alone because albuterol is riskier
Give diphenhydramine first, then the combined nebulizer

qs.q: An 80-year-old woman with COPD has received several albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers through a loose-fitting mask. She now reports a painful left eye with blurred vision and halos around lights. What is the best action?
qs.a: Stop the ipratropium and report possible acute angle-closure glaucoma
qs.x: Ipratropium mist reaching the eye can trigger acute angle-closure glaucoma, a serious effect that calls for stopping the drug and notifying the receiving facility. It is not an expected albuterol side effect.
w: Continue nebulizers since blurred vision is an expected albuterol effect
Increase the oxygen flow so the mist is cleared away from her eyes
Give another ipratropium dose because her wheezing has not resolved

qs.q: A 27-year-old with acute asthma needs a bronchodilator. Her allergy list shows hives and lip swelling after albuterol. The unit carries levalbuterol. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold levalbuterol because albuterol allergy is a contraindication
qs.x: Hypersensitivity to albuterol is a listed contraindication to levalbuterol, its closely related isomer. Choose another option per protocol rather than assume levalbuterol is safe.
w: Give levalbuterol because it is a different drug from albuterol
Give levalbuterol after pretreating her with IV diphenhydramine and steroids
Give levalbuterol by MDI instead of nebulizer to limit exposure

qs.q: A 58-year-old with asthma and known coronary disease received levalbuterol 1.25 mg. Ten minutes later he has new substernal chest pressure, HR 148 and frequent PVCs, though his wheezing has improved. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop levalbuterol, obtain a 12-lead ECG and reassess
qs.x: Chest pain, severe tachycardia and dysrhythmia are stop criteria for levalbuterol; evaluate for cardiac ischemia. Partial improvement in wheezing does not justify continuing a drug that is causing chest pain.
w: Give the second 1.25 mg dose since the wheezing improved
Switch to continuous albuterol for a smoother effect
Give IV metoprolol to slow the rate and continue nebulizers

qs.q: A 34-year-old man was stung by a bee. He has hives, a hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor and BP 84/50. Which medication should be given first?
qs.a: Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM in the lateral thigh
qs.x: Airway swelling and hypotension mean anaphylaxis; IM epinephrine is the first drug and is not delayed for IV access. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts that do not reverse airway edema or shock quickly.
w: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV followed by reassessment
Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV to reduce airway swelling
Nebulized albuterol to open the upper airway

qs.q: A 41-year-old woman with anaphylaxis has received two IM epinephrine doses and a fluid bolus. She still has diffuse hives and wheezing, with BP 78/44 and HR 132. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Start an epinephrine infusion per protocol
qs.x: Anaphylactic shock that persists after repeated IM doses and fluids needs a titrated epinephrine infusion. A 1 mg IV push is the cardiac arrest dose and can cause severe hypertension and dysrhythmias in a patient with a pulse.
w: Give 1 mg of epinephrine by IV push
Give diphenhydramine and wait for a response
Give methylprednisolone and recheck in 15 minutes

qs.q: A 74-year-old man with prior MI and stents develops wheezing, facial swelling and BP 82/48 after a new antibiotic. His wife worries that epinephrine will harm his heart. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Give IM epinephrine; there is no contraindication in anaphylaxis
qs.x: Epinephrine has no contraindication in anaphylaxis, and untreated shock is a far greater threat to the heart than the drug. Watch for chest pain or dysrhythmia afterward, but do not withhold or underdose it.
w: Withhold epinephrine and give diphenhydramine and steroids
Give half the usual IM dose to protect his damaged coronary arteries
Give nitroglycerin first, then epinephrine if needed

qs.q: An 82-year-old man with hives received diphenhydramine 50 mg IV. Twenty minutes later the hives are fading, but he is newly confused and picking at the air, with HR 112 and warm, dry skin. Airway and BP are normal. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: Anticholinergic side effect; hold further doses and monitor
qs.x: Confusion and tachycardia with warm, dry skin are anticholinergic effects of diphenhydramine, to which older adults are more sensitive; hold further doses. With a normal airway and BP and fading hives, this is not returning anaphylaxis.
w: Returning anaphylaxis; give IM epinephrine right away
Expected improvement; give a second dose for the hives
Opioid-like sedation; give naloxone and reassess

qs.q: A 20-month-old with croup received nebulized racemic epinephrine for stridor at rest. Ten minutes later the stridor is quieter, but she is drowsy, retractions persist, air movement is poor, and SpO2 is 86%. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Worsening obstruction with fatigue; assist ventilation
qs.x: Quieter stridor with drowsiness, poor air movement and falling SpO2 signals impending respiratory failure, not improvement. Racemic epinephrine causes tachycardia and anxiety, not sedation, so the drowsiness reflects hypoxia and fatigue.
w: Good drug response; reassess her in 20 minutes
Expected drowsiness from the racemic epinephrine
Mild croup now; switch to oral dexamethasone

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman who is not pregnant has a severe asthma attack and is moving so little air that nebulized albuterol is having little effect. She is alert, HR 128, with no chest pain. Which medication is most appropriate next?
qs.a: Terbutaline SQ per protocol
qs.x: When poor air movement limits nebulized delivery, SQ terbutaline gives a beta-agonist systemically. A steroid or ipratropium alone will not act fast enough, and diphenhydramine has no role in asthma.
w: Ipratropium nebulizer as the only next drug
Diphenhydramine IV to dry the airways
Methylprednisolone as the only next drug

qs.q: Thirty minutes after racemic epinephrine for croup, a 3-year-old has no stridor at rest and is playing. Her father asks to cancel transport. What is the best response?
qs.a: Advise transport, since stridor can return as the drug wears off
qs.x: Racemic epinephrine works for a limited time and stridor can come back, so these children need observation. Resolution of stridor is the expected response, not a sign the child is safe to leave.
w: Agree to cancel, since the stridor has fully resolved
Give a second racemic epinephrine dose now to prevent any recurrence
Advise an albuterol inhaler at home if stridor returns

qs.q: A 4-month-old weighing 6 kg has a temperature of 39.2 C (102.6 F) and a runny nose. She is alert, feeding well, and breathing normally. The parent asks you to give ibuprofen before transport. What is the best response?
qs.a: Do not give ibuprofen to an infant under 6 months
qs.x: Ibuprofen dosing in children starts at 6 months of age, so it is not given to this infant; consider acetaminophen per protocol and transport for evaluation. Aspirin is avoided in children with viral illness because of Reye syndrome.
w: Give ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO now
Give half of the 10 mg/kg dose to be safe
Give aspirin instead because she is so young

qs.q: A 45-year-old with asthma is receiving dexamethasone by IV push. Partway through, she suddenly reports intense burning and itching in her perineal area. Her vitals and airway are unchanged. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: A common effect of rapid IV push; slow the rate and reassure her
qs.x: Perineal burning is a known common effect of rapid IV dexamethasone and is not dangerous; slowing the push helps. With no airway, skin or BP changes, this is not anaphylaxis.
w: An allergic reaction; stop the drug and give IM epinephrine right away
A sign of GI bleeding; stop and start a fluid bolus
An extravasation injury; remove the IV catheter now

qs.q: Ten minutes after receiving methylprednisolone 125 mg IV with nebulized bronchodilators, an asthmatic patient asks why the steroid has not helped her breathing yet. What is the correct explanation and plan?
qs.a: Steroids work over hours; keep giving bronchodilators
qs.x: Corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation over hours, not minutes, so bronchodilators remain the immediate treatment. A lack of effect at 10 minutes is expected and is not a reason to redose.
w: The steroid has failed; give a second 125 mg IV dose right now
The steroid failed; this means she needs intubation
Steroids act within minutes; recheck the IV line

qs.q: A 50-year-old with an asthma exacerbation improves after nebulizers. You plan to give methylprednisolone, but he reports he is being treated in the hospital for a disseminated fungal infection. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold the steroid and report the fungal infection
qs.x: Systemic fungal infection is a contraindication to methylprednisolone because steroids suppress immunity. He is improving with bronchodilators, so withhold the steroid and let the receiving physician decide.
w: Give methylprednisolone anyway since the asthma takes priority
Give the steroid IM instead of IV to reduce risk
Give double the dose to overcome the infection

qs.q: A 28-year-old asthmatic has had three albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers. She still speaks in two-word phrases, with SpO2 89% and HR 128. She is alert. What is the most appropriate next medication?
qs.a: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 15-20 minutes
qs.x: For severe asthma not responding to nebulizers, magnesium is given as 2 g IV over 15-20 minutes. A rapid push increases the risk of hypotension and is reserved for cardiac arrest.
w: Magnesium sulfate 2 g by rapid IV push
Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV followed by reassessment
Morphine for air hunger and anxiety

qs.q: During a magnesium infusion for severe asthma, a 35-year-old reports flushing and warmth. BP has fallen from 128/80 to 84/50 and RR is 16. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the infusion, reassess, and treat the hypotension
qs.x: Flushing is common, but hypotension is a stop criterion for magnesium. Stop the infusion and support BP; continuing because flushing is expected ignores the significant BP drop.
w: Speed up the infusion so that the full dose finishes more quickly
Continue the infusion since flushing is expected
Give a second 2 g dose to improve bronchodilation

qs.q: A 32-year-old asthmatic received terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ 20 minutes ago. She is still wheezing, with HR 116 and no chest pain. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Repeat terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ once and reassess
qs.x: Terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ may be repeated once in 15-30 minutes, with a maximum of 0.5 mg in 4 hours. Higher or more frequent doses exceed that limit.
w: Give 0.5 mg SQ now because the first dose failed
Give terbutaline every 5 minutes until wheezing stops
Do not repeat; terbutaline is a single-dose drug

qs.q: A 78-year-old man with COPD and an enlarged prostate has received several albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers. His breathing is better, but he now has lower abdominal pain, a firm distended bladder, and cannot urinate. What is the best action?
qs.a: Hold further ipratropium and report urinary retention
qs.x: Urinary retention is a known anticholinergic effect of ipratropium, especially with an enlarged prostate, so further doses are held and the finding reported. Furosemide or fluids add volume to a bladder that cannot empty.
w: Give another ipratropium dose for residual wheezing
Give furosemide IV to help him pass urine
Give an IV fluid bolus to increase urine output

qs.q: A 25-year-old with anaphylaxis improved after IM epinephrine: airway clear, no wheeze, BP 118/74, but she still has itchy hives. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Give diphenhydramine as an adjunct and keep monitoring
qs.x: With airway and BP restored, diphenhydramine is a reasonable adjunct for the hives. More epinephrine is not needed for isolated skin symptoms, and she still needs transport because symptoms can return.
w: Give a third IM epinephrine dose to clear the remaining hives
Discontinue care since the anaphylaxis has resolved
Give diphenhydramine and cancel transport

qs.q: A 62-year-old with septic shock needs RSI for worsening hypoxia. His BP is 78/42 and HR 128 after one fluid bolus. What is the best action before giving etomidate?
qs.a: Correct the hypotension first, per protocol
qs.x: Induction and positive pressure ventilation can cause hypotensive arrest in a patient already in shock, and significant hypotension is a hold point for etomidate. Resuscitate first; paralysis without sedation is never appropriate.
w: Give the induction dose quickly to finish the airway
Give the paralytic before etomidate to avoid hypotension
Skip induction and give the paralytic only

qs.q: A patient was intubated using etomidate and rocuronium 12 minutes ago. The ETT is secure, HR has risen from 92 to 128, BP from 130/80 to 176/102, and tears are running from his eyes. No sedative has been given since induction. What is the best plan?
qs.a: Start a post-intubation sedative and analgesic per protocol
qs.x: Etomidate wears off within minutes while rocuronium lasts much longer, so this patient is likely aware under paralysis. He needs ongoing sedation and analgesia; repeat etomidate is avoided because of adrenal suppression.
w: Give a second etomidate dose and repeat it as needed during transport
Give more rocuronium to stop the hemodynamic response
Give labetalol for the hypertension and recheck

qs.q: A 45-year-old motorcyclist has an open femur fracture, pain 10/10, BP 84/50 and HR 126. Which analgesic is most appropriate?
qs.a: Ketamine 0.1-0.3 mg/kg IV
qs.x: Ketamine provides strong analgesia without lowering blood pressure, making it the best choice in the hypotensive trauma patient. Opioids can worsen hypotension, and ketorolac is contraindicated in trauma with possible hemorrhage.
w: Morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV slowly
Ketorolac 30 mg IV
Fentanyl 1 mcg/kg IV

qs.q: An 84-year-old woman weighing 45 kg has a hip fracture and no liver disease. Medical direction orders IV acetaminophen, and your partner has drawn up the standard 1,000 mg adult dose. What is the best action?
qs.a: Use a weight-based dose since she is under 50 kg
qs.x: The 1,000 mg IV dose applies to patients 50 kg or more; lighter patients need weight-based dosing to avoid exceeding safe limits. Ketorolac is not safer in an elderly trauma patient because of its bleeding and kidney risks.
w: Give the full 1,000 mg since she is an adult
Give ketorolac instead as a safer choice
Give 2,000 mg because her pain is severe

qs.q: After a dissociative ketamine dose, a 28-year-old is calm with nystagmus, but you hear gurgling and see copious oral secretions. SpO2 is 95%. What is the best action?
qs.a: Suction the airway and position to protect it
qs.x: Hypersalivation and increased secretions are known ketamine effects; suctioning and positioning maintain the airway. With adequate SpO2, this does not require intubation.
w: Give naloxone for possible opioid co-ingestion
Intubate immediately with a paralytic
Give a second ketamine dose to control him

qs.q: Four patients need analgesia. For which one is ketamine least appropriate?
qs.a: A 66-year-old with BP 224/126 and tearing chest pain
qs.x: Ketamine raises BP and HR, and severe hypertension is a stop point; in a possible aortic dissection that rise could be dangerous. The hypotensive and opioid-tolerant patients are often good ketamine candidates.
w: A 40-year-old with a tibia fracture and BP 96/60
A 25-year-old with burns who is opioid-tolerant
A 55-year-old with a dislocated shoulder and BP 138/86

qs.q: A 300-lb man with severe facial burns, a short neck and stridor is combative. The crew has no supraglottic airway or surgical airway kit, and it is a 5-minute transport to a trauma center. A partner suggests rocuronium so he can be intubated. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Do not paralyze without a rescue plan; support and transport
qs.x: Inability to manage the airway is a contraindication to paralytics; a predicted difficult airway with no rescue option can turn into a fatal cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate event. A smaller dose does not preserve safe breathing.
w: Give rocuronium, since paralysis makes intubation easier
Give rocuronium at half dose to keep some breathing
Give rocuronium now, then decide on a backup plan only if he desaturates

qs.q: After RSI with rocuronium, two intubation attempts fail. SpO2 drops to 85%, and BVM ventilation with two providers and an OPA is difficult. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Place a supraglottic airway and ventilate
qs.x: Rocuronium paralysis lasts a long time, so spontaneous breathing will not return soon; oxygenation through a supraglottic airway is the priority. Repeated attempts during desaturation worsen hypoxia.
w: Wait for the rocuronium to wear off
Keep attempting intubation until successful
Give naloxone to restore breathing

qs.q: A 58-year-old dialysis patient missed two sessions and is now obtunded with vomiting. The monitor shows peaked T waves and a wide QRS. You are preparing for RSI. Which paralytic decision is best?
qs.a: Use rocuronium instead of succinylcholine
qs.x: Known or suspected hyperkalemia contraindicates succinylcholine, which raises potassium and can trigger arrest. Rocuronium does not raise potassium; a smaller succinylcholine dose does not remove the risk.
w: Use succinylcholine at the usual RSI dose
Use succinylcholine at a reduced dose
Give succinylcholine IM to slow absorption

qs.q: A 77-year-old was hospitalized for a stroke 3 weeks ago, has been bedbound since, and now has aspiration pneumonia with worsening hypoxia that requires RSI. Which finding most affects your paralytic choice?
qs.a: Immobility since the stroke weeks ago
qs.x: Stroke with immobilization for more than 48-72 hours contraindicates succinylcholine because of the risk of severe hyperkalemia. Age and pneumonia do not change the paralytic choice.
w: Age over 75 years
Pneumonia as the underlying cause of his hypoxia
Prior use of aspirin for stroke

qs.q: Before RSI, a 24-year-old's mother tells you that her brother developed a dangerously high fever and stiffness during surgery under general anesthesia. What is the best decision about succinylcholine?
qs.a: Avoid it because of possible malignant hyperthermia risk
qs.x: A family history of malignant hyperthermia is a contraindication to succinylcholine. Antipyretics and dose reduction do not prevent a malignant hyperthermia reaction.
w: Give it as planned, since the reaction occurred in another relative
Give it but pre-treat with acetaminophen
Give a smaller dose and watch the temperature

qs.q: During transport, a patient intubated and paralyzed with vecuronium suddenly loses the EtCO2 waveform, SpO2 falls from 98% to 86%, and HR drops from 96 to 58. Sedation is running and the next vecuronium dose is due. What is the best action?
qs.a: Hold the dose and check the tube and circuit now
qs.x: Loss of the EtCO2 waveform with falling SpO2 and bradycardia suggests a dislodged tube or disconnection, and a paralyzed patient cannot breathe on his own. Redosing vecuronium or adjusting sedation ignores the airway emergency.
w: Give the vecuronium dose on schedule
Increase the sedation infusion rate
Give atropine and continue as planned

qs.q: After midazolam and fentanyl for procedural sedation, a 52-year-old's RR drops to 6, SpO2 to 87%, and EtCO2 rises to 62. What is the first action?
qs.a: Open the airway and assist ventilation with BVM
qs.x: Combined benzodiazepine and opioid sedation can cause respiratory depression; airway support and ventilation come first. Reversal agents may follow, but they do not replace immediate ventilation.
w: Give flumazenil IV to reverse the midazolam effect right away
Give naloxone IN and wait for the response
Increase oxygen by nonrebreather and observe

qs.q: An intubated trauma patient needs post-intubation sedation. His BP is 76/40 and HR 132 despite fluids. Which sedation plan is best?
qs.a: Ketamine per protocol rather than a midazolam bolus
qs.x: Midazolam can cause hypotension and shock is a relative contraindication, so ketamine is a better sedative in the hypotensive patient. Withholding sedation risks awareness, especially if the patient is paralyzed.
w: A midazolam bolus followed by a continuous midazolam infusion
No sedation until the BP is normal
A midazolam bolus plus fentanyl for analgesia

qs.q: After ketamine for a painful dislocation reduction, a 34-year-old is frightened, crying and describing terrifying visions. Vitals are stable and airway is patent. What is the best management?
qs.a: Reduce stimulation; small benzodiazepine dose per protocol
qs.x: This is a ketamine emergence reaction; a calm environment and, if needed, a small benzodiazepine dose per protocol can help. Naloxone has no effect on ketamine.
w: Give naloxone to reverse the ketamine effect
Give a repeat ketamine dose to deepen sedation
Physically restrain the patient and give haloperidol IV

qs.q: A 66-year-old COPD patient on CPAP was given lorazepam for anxiety. He is now drowsy with RR 9, EtCO2 70 and SpO2 86%. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Remove CPAP and ventilate with BVM
qs.x: CPAP requires a spontaneously breathing, alert patient; with hypoventilation and rising EtCO2, he needs assisted ventilation. Increasing the CPAP pressure does not fix hypoventilation from respiratory depression.
w: Increase the CPAP pressure to improve ventilation
Give a second lorazepam dose
Switch to a nonrebreather

qs.q: A 40-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis has a dislocated shoulder with severe muscle spasm. A partner suggests diazepam to relax the muscles. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Avoid diazepam because of her myasthenia gravis
qs.x: Myasthenia gravis is a contraindication to diazepam, which can worsen muscle weakness and breathing. IM diazepam is absorbed erratically and does not avoid the problem.
w: Give diazepam because it relaxes skeletal muscle
Give diazepam IM since IM is safer
Give diazepam with fentanyl for synergy

qs.q: After a rapid IV push of a large fentanyl dose, a patient becomes apneic. You cannot ventilate with the BVM, and the chest wall is stiff. What is the best action?
qs.a: Chest wall rigidity: naloxone or a paralytic per protocol
qs.x: Chest wall rigidity is a known serious effect of fentanyl; it is treated with naloxone or a paralytic per protocol along with continued ventilation. It is not a dystonic reaction.
w: Push harder on the BVM until the chest rises
Give more fentanyl to relax the muscles
Give IV diphenhydramine for a presumed dystonic reaction

qs.q: A 6-year-old (22 kg) with an obvious forearm deformity is screaming and has no IV access; two IV attempts have failed. What is the best analgesia plan?
qs.a: Intranasal fentanyl per protocol
qs.x: Intranasal fentanyl gives fast analgesia without IV access and avoids a painful IO for an isolated limb injury. Delaying analgesia for IV access is unnecessary.
w: Wait until IV access is obtained
IO fentanyl through a tibial needle
IM morphine 10 mg

qs.q: A 48-year-old with a tibia fracture received two doses of fentanyl. Pain is now 6/10, but she is drowsy though rousable, with RR 10 and SpO2 92%. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Withhold more fentanyl, stimulate her and monitor EtCO2
qs.x: RR around 10 with oversedation is a stop point for fentanyl, so hold doses and watch ventilation closely. Full-dose naloxone is not needed while she is breathing and rousable.
w: Give a third fentanyl dose since pain persists
Give naloxone 2 mg IV for full and rapid reversal of the opioid
Switch to morphine and give a full dose

qs.q: Four patients each need fentanyl for pain. Which patient needs the most caution?
qs.a: An 82-year-old on home O2 for COPD who takes a nightly benzodiazepine
qs.x: An older patient with chronic lung disease who also takes a benzodiazepine is at highest risk of opioid respiratory depression. The healthy patients with normal vitals carry much less risk.
w: A 30-year-old with a kidney stone and normal vital signs
A 25-year-old with an ankle fracture and BP 130/82
A 45-year-old with a shoulder dislocation and no medical history

qs.q: A 29-year-old with three rib fractures is in an acute asthma attack with diffuse wheezing and SpO2 90%. He asks for pain relief. Which plan is best?
qs.a: Avoid morphine; fentanyl per protocol and treat the asthma
qs.x: Acute or severe asthma is a contraindication to morphine without airway support, and histamine release can worsen bronchospasm. Fentanyl with close monitoring and treatment of the asthma is a safer plan.
w: Give morphine since it also reduces air hunger
Give morphine and diphenhydramine together
Give a full morphine dose so he can take deep, effective breaths

qs.q: After morphine for a hip fracture, an 81-year-old's BP falls from 124/80 to 86/58. RR is 16, SpO2 96%, and she is alert. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop morphine, position supine and give fluid per protocol
qs.x: Hypotension is a stop point for morphine; manage with positioning and fluids. With normal breathing and alertness, naloxone is not indicated and would remove her analgesia.
w: Give naloxone IV to reverse the hypotension from the morphine
Give the next morphine dose for pain control
Give epinephrine IM for possible anaphylaxis

qs.q: During an interfacility transfer, a patient's next hydromorphone dose is due. She is hard to arouse, with RR 11 and SpO2 91%. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Hold the dose and notify the sending provider
qs.x: RR below 12 and excessive sedation are hold criteria for hydromorphone. A scheduled order does not override clear signs of opioid toxicity.
w: Give the dose since it is ordered on schedule
Give half the dose and recheck in 30 minutes
Give the dose and add naloxone at the same time

qs.q: A 6-year-old weighing 20 kg improved after nebulizers for an asthma attack. Medical direction orders dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, but she has vomited twice and has no IV access. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give 12 mg IM
qs.x: 0.6 mg/kg for 20 kg is 12 mg, and the IM route avoids losing an oral dose to vomiting. A 1.2 mg dose is a tenfold error, and waiting delays a drug that already takes hours to work.
w: Give 12 mg PO now
Give 1.2 mg IM
Wait for IV access at the hospital

qs.q: After 0.4 mg naloxone IV, an opioid overdose patient now has RR 14, SpO2 96%, and responds to voice but is drowsy. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Monitor; no more naloxone is needed now
qs.x: Naloxone is titrated to adequate ventilation, not full wakefulness. Extra doses risk acute withdrawal, vomiting and agitation without improving safety.
w: Give more naloxone until he is fully awake
Give 2 mg IV to prevent relapse
Give naloxone IM to extend the effect

qs.q: After 2 mg naloxone IV, an opioid overdose patient vomits, becomes agitated, and has crackles with SpO2 84% and pink frothy sputum. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Support oxygenation and ventilation; give no more naloxone
qs.x: Pulmonary edema is a serious naloxone effect; oxygenation and ventilation support are the priority, and more naloxone is not indicated. The low SpO2 is from pulmonary edema, not recurrent opioid toxicity.
w: Give another 2 mg naloxone IV for recurrent opioid toxicity
Give midazolam to control the agitation
Give furosemide and repeat the naloxone

qs.q: A 40-year-old was intubated using succinylcholine 8 minutes ago and faces a 60-minute transport. Tube placement is confirmed and sedation and analgesia have been given, but he is starting to move against the ventilator. Medical direction orders ongoing paralysis. Which is best?
qs.a: Rocuronium per protocol
qs.x: A longer-acting nondepolarizing agent such as rocuronium maintains paralysis once placement and sedation are assured. Repeated succinylcholine can cause bradycardia and hyperkalemia, and etomidate is a sedative, not a paralytic.
w: Repeat succinylcholine every 5 minutes
An etomidate infusion for paralysis
Naloxone to reduce the movement

qs.q: A 72-year-old with renal colic has normal renal function, no bleeding history, and takes no NSAIDs. Medical direction approves ketorolac. Which single IV dose is appropriate?
qs.a: 15 mg IV
qs.x: Patients 65 and older get a reduced single dose of 15 mg IV. Higher doses are for younger adults and raise the risk of renal and GI harm.
w: 30 mg IV push
60 mg IV
60 mg IM

qs.q: A 54-year-old with renal colic takes daily aspirin for a heart stent and had a bleeding ulcer last year. Which analgesic decision is best?
qs.a: Withhold ketorolac and consider an alternative
qs.x: History of GI bleeding and concurrent aspirin use are contraindications to ketorolac. A reduced dose does not remove the bleeding risk.
w: Give ketorolac since renal colic responds well to NSAIDs
Give ketorolac at a reduced dose
Give ketorolac with ondansetron

qs.q: A 68-year-old on warfarin fell and has a wrist fracture and a mild headache. She asks for something other than opioids. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Avoid ketorolac due to bleeding risk and possible head bleed
qs.x: Coagulopathy and possible intracranial bleeding are contraindications to ketorolac. The IM route does not reduce bleeding risk.
w: Give ketorolac since she clearly wants to avoid opioids
Give ketorolac IM to reduce bleeding risk
Give ketorolac and recheck her neuro status

qs.q: A 34-year-old with an ankle sprain asks for ibuprofen. She has asthma that previously worsened after taking aspirin. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Withhold ibuprofen because of NSAID-sensitive asthma
qs.x: Aspirin- or NSAID-induced asthma is a contraindication to ibuprofen because of cross-reactivity. Having albuterol ready does not make the drug safe.
w: Give ibuprofen since it is a different drug from aspirin
Give ibuprofen with albuterol on standby
Give a smaller ibuprofen dose

qs.q: A 32-year-old at 34 weeks of pregnancy has severe back pain after a fall. She has no allergies. Which pain medication decision is best?
qs.a: Avoid ibuprofen; consider acetaminophen per protocol
qs.x: Ibuprofen is contraindicated in the third trimester of pregnancy. Acetaminophen is a safer option, and changing the route does not remove the fetal risk.
w: Give ibuprofen since she has no allergies
Give ibuprofen IV to bypass the GI tract
Give a double dose of ibuprofen for a faster, stronger effect

qs.q: A 55-year-old with known cirrhosis and jaundice has a painful wrist fracture. Which analgesic decision is best?
qs.a: Avoid acetaminophen because of his active liver disease
qs.x: Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease contraindicates acetaminophen. The IV route does not bypass liver metabolism.
w: Give acetaminophen since it is gentle on the stomach lining
Give IV acetaminophen to bypass the liver
Give acetaminophen with a reduced interval

qs.q: A 24-year-old with a sprained knee asks for IV acetaminophen. She says she took several OTC cold remedies today and is unsure how much acetaminophen they contained. What is the best decision?
qs.a: Hold acetaminophen until the total dose is known
qs.x: Many OTC products contain acetaminophen, and reaching the daily max is a stop point. Hold until the total is known; changing the route or halving the dose does not prevent exceeding it.
w: Give the full IV dose for her pain
Give half the IV dose as a precaution
Give acetaminophen PO instead of IV to be safer

qs.q: Medical direction orders promethazine for a 40-year-old woman with severe motion sickness and repeated vomiting. Her only IV is a small catheter in the back of her hand. What is the best route?
qs.a: Deep IM injection into a large muscle
qs.x: IM is the preferred route for promethazine; IV use, especially through small hand veins, risks severe tissue injury, and SQ injection is contraindicated. If given IV it must be diluted and slow.
w: Undiluted IV push through the hand IV
SQ injection in the back of the upper arm
Rapid IV push followed by a fast flush

qs.q: A 34-year-old man is found in a bathroom with a syringe nearby. He is unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, RR 4, SpO2 78% and HR 112. Your partner is preparing naloxone. What should you do right now?
qs.a: Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen while naloxone is prepared
qs.x: Hypoxia is the immediate threat, so ventilation comes first and continues while naloxone is drawn up. Waiting for naloxone to work while he stays apneic and hypoxic wastes critical minutes.
w: Give naloxone first and wait for him to breathe on his own
Intubate him before any naloxone is given so the airway is secure
Place him in the recovery position and apply a nonrebreather mask

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman who takes methadone was found with RR 6. After titrated IV naloxone she has RR 14, SpO2 96% and is awake. She now wants to refuse transport. What is your main concern?
qs.a: Methadone can outlast naloxone, so breathing may slow again
qs.x: Methadone has a long duration while naloxone wears off much sooner, so respiratory depression can return after the crew leaves. Withdrawal from naloxone is unpleasant but short-lived and is not the main danger.
w: Naloxone will cause several days of severe opioid withdrawal
Naloxone often causes a delayed hypertensive crisis at home
She must receive a full second dose before she can refuse

qs.q: A 2-year-old weighing 12 kg got into a grandparent's oxycodone. He is limp with RR 6 and pinpoint pupils. You are ventilating with a BVM. Using the PALS full-reversal dose, how much naloxone do you give?
qs.a: 1.2 mg IV, IO, IM or IN
qs.x: The PALS full-reversal dose is 0.1 mg/kg (max 2 mg), so 12 kg x 0.1 mg = 1.2 mg. A flat adult dose ignores the weight-based calculation, and ventilation continues until breathing is adequate.
w: 0.12 mg IV and wait 30 minutes
2 mg IV regardless of weight
4 mg IN as for an adult

qs.q: A 26-year-old woman took an unknown amount of amitriptyline. She had one brief seizure. HR 128, BP 84/50, QRS 148 ms, and she is ventilating adequately on a BVM. What is the best next medication?
qs.a: Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV push
qs.x: A wide QRS with hypotension after a tricyclic overdose reflects sodium channel blockade, and bicarbonate is the antidote. Procainamide and amiodarone can worsen sodium channel or QT toxicity in this setting.
w: Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes
Procainamide infusion for the wide QRS
Physostigmine to reverse anticholinergic signs

qs.q: A 40-year-old man with a tricyclic overdose has a QRS of 138 ms. He is unresponsive with RR 6 and SpO2 88%. Before you give sodium bicarbonate, what is the priority?
qs.a: Secure ventilation, because bicarbonate creates CO2 that must be exhaled
qs.x: Inadequate ventilation is a contraindication to bicarbonate: the CO2 produced by bicarbonate builds up and worsens acidosis unless the patient is ventilated. Giving it to a hypoventilating patient undercuts the treatment.
w: Give the bicarbonate first, since the wide QRS is the bigger and more urgent threat
Give midazolam first to prevent seizures during the infusion
Obtain an ABG on arrival before deciding on any bicarbonate

qs.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has Kussmaul breathing, a glucometer reading of HI, HR 124 and BP 98/60. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. Your partner suggests sodium bicarbonate for the acidosis. What is best?
qs.a: Withhold bicarbonate and give an isotonic fluid bolus per protocol
qs.x: DKA is treated with fluids and later insulin, and routine bicarbonate is not indicated without a specific reason such as hyperkalemic ECG changes or arrest. Rapid breathing here is compensation, not a reason to give bicarbonate.
w: Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg IV to correct the acidosis
Give bicarbonate only if the respiratory rate keeps increasing
Give bicarbonate first and then start IV fluids once the blood pH improves

qs.q: After IV glucagon for a propranolol overdose, a 58-year-old man's HR rises from 38 to 58 and BP improves, but he becomes drowsy and starts vomiting. What is the best action?
qs.a: Position him and suction to protect the airway; consider an antiemetic
qs.x: Nausea and vomiting are common glucagon effects, and a drowsy patient is at risk of aspiration, so airway protection comes first. Vomiting is not an allergy, and charcoal is contraindicated with altered mental status.
w: Stop all glucagon since vomiting means he is allergic to it
Give atropine to treat the vagal response that is causing all the vomiting
Give activated charcoal now that his heart rate has improved

qs.q: A 62-year-old woman with insulin-dependent diabetes was unresponsive with BG 32 and no IV access. Fifteen minutes after glucagon 1 mg IM she is awake, alert and swallowing, with BG 88. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Give oral carbohydrates now that she can swallow safely
qs.x: Glucagon raises glucose briefly by releasing stored glycogen, so an awake patient who can swallow should get oral carbohydrates to keep the glucose up. A repeat dose is not needed when she can eat.
w: Give a second glucagon dose to prevent recurrence
Withhold food because glucagon causes vomiting
Leave her at home since her glucose is now normal

qs.q: A 62-year-old dialysis patient has missed two treatments. He is weak, HR 48, BP 88/50, and the ECG shows a very wide QRS with peaked T waves. What is the first medication?
qs.a: Calcium chloride 1 g IV slow push
qs.x: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes calls for calcium first to stabilize the heart muscle. Atropine and amiodarone do not address the cause, and albuterol shifts potassium but does not protect the heart quickly enough by itself.
w: Atropine 1 mg IV for the bradycardia
Amiodarone 150 mg IV for the wide QRS
Albuterol nebulizer as the only treatment

qs.q: You are giving calcium chloride slowly through a hand IV for a verapamil overdose. The patient reports severe burning, and the site is swollen and pale. What should you do?
qs.a: Stop giving it at that site because of extravasation
qs.x: Calcium chloride can cause tissue necrosis when it extravasates, and extravasation is a reason to stop. Finish the dose through a new large, secure line such as a large vein or IO.
w: Speed up the push so the dose finishes sooner
Flush the line hard and continue at the same site
Finish the dose, then elevate the hand on arrival

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman with hyperkalemia had a wide QRS and peaked T waves. After calcium gluconate IV the QRS narrows. What is the best interpretation and plan?
qs.a: The heart is stabilized, but potassium is unchanged; add shifting therapy
qs.x: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes but does not lower serum potassium. The patient still needs treatments that move potassium into cells, such as albuterol per protocol, with continuous monitoring.
w: The potassium is now corrected, so no further treatment is needed
The improvement means the diagnosis was wrong and the calcium was not actually needed
Calcium has lowered potassium, so stop cardiac monitoring

qs.q: A patient with hyperkalemic ECG changes is receiving calcium gluconate IV. Midway through the dose, the heart rate drops from 72 to 46 and she feels lightheaded. What should you do?
qs.a: Stop the calcium and reassess the rhythm and blood pressure
qs.x: Bradycardia is a serious calcium side effect and a reason to stop, often from pushing it too fast. Speeding it up or switching to the stronger chloride salt would make the problem worse.
w: Push the rest of the calcium quickly to finish the dose
Give atropine and keep giving calcium at the same rate
Switch to calcium chloride and push it faster

qs.q: A farmworker sprayed with pesticide has drooling, wheezing, copious bronchial secretions, SpO2 86% and HR 52. After the first IV atropine dose, HR is 118 but the lungs are still wet with secretions. What next?
qs.a: Give more atropine, doubling the dose, until secretions dry
qs.x: In organophosphate poisoning the goal of atropine is drying of the airway secretions, not heart rate. Tachycardia is expected and is not a reason to stop while the lungs are still wet.
w: Stop atropine because the heart rate is now over 100
Switch to albuterol to dry the bronchial secretions
Give atropine only if the heart rate falls below 60

qs.q: You are first on scene where two field workers are vomiting and drooling after a crop-spraying accident. Their clothes are soaked with chemical. What do you do first?
qs.a: Put on PPE and decontaminate the patients before treating
qs.x: Organophosphates are absorbed through the skin, so unprotected rescuers can be poisoned too. Responder safety and decontamination come before atropine, which is given as soon as it is safe.
w: Give each patient atropine IM right away, before anything else
Start IVs in both patients inside the ambulance at once
Assist ventilation first, then remove the clothing later

qs.q: An organophosphate-poisoned patient has dry lungs after repeated atropine doses, but he has muscle twitching, increasing weakness and shallow breaths. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Give pralidoxime to treat the nicotinic muscle weakness
qs.x: Atropine treats muscarinic effects such as secretions but does nothing for nicotinic muscle weakness. Pralidoxime reactivates cholinesterase and can improve muscle strength, while ventilation is supported as needed.
w: Give more atropine until the twitching stops completely
Give midazolam, because the twitching is a seizure
Give calcium chloride for the muscle cramps and twitching

qs.q: A 20-kg child has organophosphate poisoning with weakness and fasciculations after atropine. Medical control orders IV pralidoxime. Which order fits the dosing range?
qs.a: 400-1,000 mg IV infused over 15-30 minutes
qs.x: Pediatric IV dosing is 20-50 mg/kg (max 2 g) infused over 15-30 minutes, so 20 kg gives 400-1,000 mg. A rapid push of a full adult dose exceeds the weight-based range and the administration time.
w: 2 g IV as a rapid push over 1 minute
100 mg IV infused slowly over about 2 full hours
1,800 mg IV push every 5 minutes

qs.q: A 44-year-old electroplating worker suddenly collapsed at work after a chemical spill. He had a seizure, BP is 80/50, he is gasping, and SpO2 reads 99%. Coworkers mention a bitter almond odor. What is the priority antidote?
qs.a: Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes
qs.x: Sudden collapse, seizure and shock with a normal SpO2 after an industrial exposure suggests cyanide, which blocks oxygen use in the cells. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide; naloxone and atropine do not treat cellular poisoning.
w: Naloxone 2 mg IN for possible opioid use
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg IV push
Atropine 2 mg IV for the collapse

qs.q: After hydroxocobalamin for smoke inhalation, a patient's skin and urine turn red and BP rises from 96/60 to 148/88. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: Expected effects of the drug; continue care and monitoring
qs.x: Red skin and urine and a rise in blood pressure are common effects of hydroxocobalamin. They are not signs of allergy or treatment failure, though the color can interfere with some monitors and labs.
w: A severe allergy that needs epinephrine IM right away
Worsening carbon monoxide levels that need a second 5 g dose of the drug
Kidney failure, so stop all IV fluids immediately

qs.q: A 24-year-old man used methamphetamine. He is agitated and paranoid, HR 150, BP 190/110, temp 40.2 C (104.4 F). He has IV access. What is the best first medication?
qs.a: Midazolam per protocol to reduce agitation and sympathetic drive
qs.x: Benzodiazepines are first-line for stimulant toxicity: they calm the patient and lower heart rate, blood pressure and heat production. Beta blockers are avoided as initial therapy in stimulant toxicity.
w: Metoprolol IV to slow the heart rate and lower his blood pressure quickly
Labetalol IV to bring the blood pressure down to normal
Haloperidol alone to control the paranoia and the agitation

qs.q: A 35-year-old man received midazolam 5 mg IM for violent agitation. Ten minutes later he is calm but snoring, with RR 8 and SpO2 89%. What is the next step?
qs.a: Open the airway, assist with a BVM and monitor EtCO2
qs.x: Respiratory depression is the main danger of sedation, so airway support and capnography come first. Flumazenil is generally avoided in the field because it can trigger seizures, and more sedation would make things worse.
w: Give a second midazolam dose since the first one worked
Leave him supine in restraints and recheck at the hospital
Give flumazenil IV to completely reverse the midazolam

qs.q: A 4-year-old weighing 16 kg with a fever has been having a generalized seizure for 7 minutes. There is no IV access yet. What is the best action?
qs.a: Give midazolam IN or IM using weight-based dosing
qs.x: A seizure longer than 5 minutes needs a benzodiazepine whatever the cause, and IN or IM midazolam avoids the delay of IV access. Antipyretics do not stop an active seizure.
w: Wait for it to stop, since febrile seizures are harmless
Give rectal acetaminophen first to treat the fever
Start an IV before giving any seizure medication

qs.q: A 38-year-old man in status epilepticus received lorazepam 4 mg IV. After 10-15 minutes of observation he is still having a generalized seizure, SpO2 94% with assisted ventilation and BP 142/88. What is next?
qs.a: Repeat lorazepam 4 mg IV once
qs.x: The lorazepam label allows one repeat 4 mg dose after a 10-15 minute observation period if seizures continue. Waiting longer lets status epilepticus cause more injury.
w: Wait another 30 minutes before any further dose
Give naloxone in case this is an opioid overdose
Give a fluid bolus before any more anticonvulsant

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with severe COPD is restless and anxious. SpO2 84%, RR 8, EtCO2 68. His family asks you to give him something to calm him. What is best?
qs.a: Withhold lorazepam and assist ventilation for the hypercapnia
qs.x: His restlessness comes from hypercapnic respiratory failure, and severe respiratory insufficiency without airway support is a contraindication to lorazepam. A sedative could cause respiratory arrest; he needs ventilatory support.
w: Give lorazepam IV so that he can better tolerate the oxygen mask and calm down
Give lorazepam IM since the IM route is less sedating
Give lorazepam and recheck the EtCO2 in 30 minutes

qs.q: A 52-year-old man stopped drinking alcohol 2 days ago. He has tremors, visual hallucinations, diaphoresis, HR 128, BP 172/100 and temp 38.3 C (100.9 F). What is the best medication?
qs.a: Diazepam IV, then reassess and repeat per protocol
qs.x: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam treat alcohol withdrawal and prevent seizures. Haloperidol alone lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat the withdrawal itself.
w: Haloperidol IM as the only agent for hallucinations
Metoprolol IV to slow the heart rate and lower BP
Naloxone IN in case he took opioids along with alcohol

qs.q: An 8-year-old weighing 25 kg has been seizing for 6 minutes, and there is no IV access. Your service carries diazepam rectal gel. Which dose matches the label for this age?
qs.a: 7.5 mg PR (0.3 mg/kg)
qs.x: Rectal gel dosing is 0.3 mg/kg for ages 6-11 years, so 25 kg x 0.3 = 7.5 mg. The 0.5 mg/kg dose is for ages 2-5, and 0.2 mg/kg is for age 12 and older.
w: 12.5 mg PR (0.5 mg/kg)
5 mg PR (0.2 mg/kg)
25 mg PR (1 mg/kg)

qs.q: A 55-year-old malnourished man with heavy alcohol use is confused, with BG 42 mg/dL. You have thiamine and D50 ready. What is the best approach?
