qs.q: A resident on amoxicillin suddenly has hives, wheezing, and a swollen face. The CNA should:
qs.a: Call for the nurse immediately
qs.x: These are signs of a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), which is an emergency.
w: Give the resident cold water to drink
Help the resident walk to the shower
Wait to see if it goes away on its own

qs.q: A resident on ciprofloxacin complains of new pain in the back of the ankle. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report the ankle pain to the nurse
qs.x: This antibiotic can rarely damage tendons. New tendon pain should be reported.
w: Have the resident walk on it more
Rub the area hard with a lotion
Wait to report it until the antibiotic is done

qs.q: A resident on clindamycin has had several watery, foul smelling stools. Which action by the CNA matters most for keeping it from spreading?
qs.a: Washing hands with soap and water after each contact
qs.x: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol does not kill, so physical removal by washing with soap and running water is what stops transmission. The organism is not spread through the air.
w: Using the alcohol hand rub between each resident contact
Wearing a surgical mask while in the room
Changing gloves only when they look soiled

qs.q: After caring for a resident with C. diff, the CNA should clean hands with:
qs.a: Soap and water
qs.x: Alcohol rubs do not kill C. diff spores. Washing with soap and water removes them.
w: Alcohol hand rub only
A dry paper towel
Lotion and a clean cloth

qs.q: Nystatin is used to treat:
qs.a: Yeast (fungal) infections such as thrush
qs.x: Nystatin is an antifungal used for thrush and yeast infections of the skin.
w: High blood pressure
Low potassium
Bacterial infections of the bladder and kidney

qs.q: The nurse has just given a resident nystatin oral suspension for thrush. What should the CNA do next?
qs.a: Hold food and fluids for about 30 minutes afterward
qs.x: Nystatin works by touching the fungus directly, so it is swished and held in the mouth and food and drink are kept back for about 30 minutes to keep from washing it away.
w: Offer a large glass of water to rinse it down
Give mouth care with mouthwash right after
Serve the meal tray while the mouth is still wet with it

qs.q: A resident takes alendronate (Fosamax). The CNA should help the resident:
qs.a: Stay upright for 30 minutes after the pill
qs.x: Alendronate can irritate the esophagus. Staying upright helps it go down and reduces irritation.
w: Lie flat right after taking the pill
Eat breakfast right before the pill
Lie on the left side for an hour after the dose

qs.q: Alendronate is used to treat:
qs.a: Weak, thin bones (osteoporosis)
qs.x: Alendronate helps strengthen bones and lowers fracture risk.
w: Seasonal allergies
Heart failure
Infections that cause a high fever

qs.q: Calcium carbonate (Tums) may be given for bones or heartburn. A common side effect is:
qs.a: Constipation
qs.x: Calcium carbonate often causes constipation, so bowel movements should be tracked.
w: Diarrhea
Very low blood pressure
A dry, hacking cough at night

qs.q: A resident on ferrous sulfate (iron) has dark green-black stools. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report the stool color to the nurse
qs.x: Iron often turns stools dark, but black stools can also mean bleeding. The CNA reports it so the nurse can decide.
w: Give extra laxatives from the supply room
Stop the resident's breakfast
Tell the resident iron pills cause no change

qs.q: Ferrous sulfate is given to treat:
qs.a: Low iron (anemia)
qs.x: Iron tablets help the body make red blood cells.
w: High blood sugar
Insomnia
Bladder spasms that cause leaking urine

qs.q: Allopurinol is used to prevent:
qs.a: Gout attacks
qs.x: Allopurinol lowers uric acid levels to prevent gout flares.
w: Seizures
Heart attacks
Infections of the skin after surgery

qs.q: Meloxicam is an anti-inflammatory pain medicine. The CNA should report:
qs.a: Stomach pain or black stools
qs.x: Anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can cause stomach bleeding, so pain or black stools should be reported.
w: Better movement in the knees
A better appetite
That the resident walked to the dining room with help

qs.q: Clopidogrel (Plavix) increases the risk of:
qs.a: Bleeding
qs.x: Clopidogrel keeps platelets from sticking, so watch for bruising and bleeding.
w: Low blood sugar
Constipation
High blood pressure with headache and blurred vision

qs.q: A CNA finds a tablet on the floor by a resident's bed. Besides handing it to the nurse, what information is most useful to give?
qs.a: Which resident's room it was in and when it was found
qs.x: The nurse needs to know whose dose may have been missed and roughly when, so the right medication record can be checked. Appearance alone does not identify a tablet reliably.
w: That the tablet is white and oval in shape
That the floor had been mopped earlier in the same shift
That the resident says she took all her pills

qs.q: A CNA finds several pills tucked inside a resident's pillowcase. Which detail is most important for the nurse to hear?
qs.a: Pills from more than one medication pass are present
qs.x: Pills from several passes means doses have been missed repeatedly, which changes what the nurse checks: a blood pressure that has drifted up, a missed anticoagulant, a skipped antibiotic course.
w: That the pillowcase had been changed the day before that
The resident has a private room on the unit
The resident takes her pills with applesauce

qs.q: A resident refuses her morning pills. Which part of the refusal is most important for the CNA to pass along?
qs.a: Which pills she refused and the reason she gave
qs.x: Residents may refuse, and the nurse needs to know which drug was missed and why: a skipped levothyroxine matters differently from a skipped stool softener, and nausea or trouble swallowing can be fixed.
w: That she refused at about the usual time
That she has refused once before earlier this month
That she was polite about refusing them

qs.q: In most states, giving residents their medicines is the job of the:
qs.a: Licensed nurse or certified medication aide
qs.x: CNAs do not give medicines unless they are certified as medication aides under state rules.
w: CNA on duty in the room
Dietary aide who serves trays
Housekeeper who cleans the room

qs.q: A nurse asks the CNA to give a resident their pills while the nurse is busy. The CNA is not a medication aide. The CNA should:
qs.a: Politely refuse and explain it is outside the CNA role
qs.x: Giving medicines is outside the CNA scope of practice unless the CNA is certified to do so.
w: Give the pills since the nurse asked
Give only the vitamins and leave the rest
Ask the resident whether they want to take them now

qs.q: A CNA finds a full pill cup on a resident's overbed table an hour after the medication pass. Why does the nurse need to know?
qs.a: The dose is recorded as given but was not taken
qs.x: Medications are charted when they are handed over, so an untouched cup means the record and reality no longer match. The nurse has to find out which drugs were missed before the next dose is due.
w: The pills will have gone bad sitting in the open air
The cup should have been returned to the cart
The resident may want them later in the day

qs.q: A CNA should never crush a resident's pills because:
qs.a: CNAs do not handle medicines, and some pills must not be crushed
qs.x: Crushing is medication administration, and long-acting or coated pills can become unsafe if crushed.
w: Crushed pills always taste better
It makes the medicine work too slowly
Crushing is only allowed for vitamins and herbal supplements

qs.q: Which sign of an allergic reaction should the CNA report to the nurse right away?
qs.a: Hives and trouble breathing
qs.x: Hives, swelling, and trouble breathing can mean a dangerous allergic reaction.
w: A normal temperature of 98.6°F
Steady, easy breathing at rest
Asking for a second dessert

qs.q: A resident is on fall precautions because of a new blood pressure medicine. The CNA should:
qs.a: Keep the bed low and help the resident stand slowly
qs.x: Medicines that lower blood pressure can cause dizziness. Fall precautions keep the resident safe.
w: Leave the walker out of reach so they stay in bed
Turn off all the lights at night
Use restraints so the resident cannot get up alone

qs.q: A CNA notices a new side effect after a resident's medicine changes. The CNA should:
qs.a: Report it to the nurse and document as directed
qs.x: The CNA observes and reports. The nurse and prescriber decide what to do.
w: Tell the resident to stop taking the medicine
Look up the drug and change the dose
Wait a week to see if it goes away

qs.q: A nurse delegates several tasks to a CNA. Which one is within the CNA role?
qs.a: Recording a blood pressure before an antihypertensive dose
qs.x: CNAs measure, observe, record and report. Interpreting the reading, holding a dose and teaching about medication are nursing judgment; the CNA's number is what the nurse acts on.
w: Judging whether that blood pressure is safe for the next dose
Deciding to hold the dose when the reading is low
Teaching the resident why the dose was held today

qs.q: A resident on several medicines is suddenly confused this afternoon after being clear at breakfast. Which quick check is within the CNA role and most useful to the nurse?
qs.a: A set of vital signs and a delegated blood glucose
qs.x: An abrupt change over hours is delirium rather than dementia, and low blood sugar, fever and low oxygen are the fast reversible causes. Reading the record and judging the cause belong to the nurse.
w: A review of the medication record for new drugs
A judgment about whether this is dementia worsening
A call to the family to ask about her usual behavior

qs.q: The best way for a CNA to help prevent constipation in a resident on pain medicine is to:
qs.a: Offer fluids and high-fiber foods as allowed
qs.x: Fluids, fiber, and activity help prevent opioid constipation. The CNA does not give laxatives.
w: Limit fluids so the resident does not need the bathroom
Keep the resident in bed as much as possible
Give a laxative from the cart every morning

qs.q: Before and after helping with any care, including care near medicines, the CNA should:
qs.a: Perform hand hygiene
qs.x: Hand hygiene is the most important way to prevent the spread of infection.
w: Put on a gown and face shield
Wipe hands on the uniform
Count the pills in the medicine cart

qs.q: A resident takes several medicines that can cause dizziness. Before walking, the CNA should first have the resident:
qs.a: Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment
qs.x: Dangling before standing lets blood pressure adjust and helps prevent falls.
w: Stand up as fast as possible
Drink a cup of strong coffee
Lie flat for 10 minutes with the legs raised

qs.q: A resident's daughter asks the CNA what her mother's new pill is for. The CNA should:
qs.a: Refer the question to the nurse
qs.x: Questions about medicines are answered by the nurse. The CNA also protects the resident's privacy.
w: Guess based on the pill's color
Read the chart aloud in the hallway
Tell her it is none of her business

qs.q: A resident who just got a new medicine has trouble breathing and a swollen throat. The CNA's first action is to:
qs.a: Call for help and stay with the resident
qs.x: Possible anaphylaxis is an emergency. The CNA should call for help and stay with the resident.
w: Leave to find the medicine label
Give the resident water to swallow
Write down the time and continue rounds

qs.q: A resident receiving medicines through a feeding tube should be positioned:
qs.a: With the head of the bed raised
qs.x: Raising the head of the bed helps prevent aspiration during and after tube feeding.
w: Flat on the back
On the stomach
With the feet higher than the head

qs.q: A resident coughs and chokes on her pills every morning. Which observation would be most useful for the nurse deciding on a safer plan?
qs.a: She coughs on thin liquids but not on pureed food
qs.x: Coughing on thin liquids and not on thicker textures points to the kind of swallowing problem a speech evaluation can confirm, and it tells the nurse whether a liquid form or thickened liquids would help.
w: She prefers to take her pills just before breakfast
She takes seven tablets at the morning pass
She drinks from a cup rather than a straw

qs.q: A resident refuses the bedtime snack ordered to prevent low blood sugar overnight. What should the CNA record and report?
qs.a: The refusal, the time, and what she did eat
qs.x: The nurse uses the time and the actual intake to judge the risk of a low glucose during the night, which may mean a glucose check or a change in the evening insulin.
w: That the snack was offered as the order states
That the resident said she was not hungry
That the snack was left at the bedside

qs.q: A client is due for both digoxin and metoprolol, and the apical pulse is 56. Which statement about the hold parameters is correct?
qs.a: Both drugs are commonly held below 60 beats per minute
qs.x: Both a cardiac glycoside and a beta blocker slow conduction through the AV node, so a rate under 60 is the usual threshold for holding either drug and reporting. A rate of 56 crosses it for both.
w: Digoxin is held below 60 beats per minute and metoprolol below 40
Metoprolol is held below 60 and digoxin below 50
Neither drug has a heart rate hold parameter

qs.q: A client taking digoxin reports nausea, poor appetite, and seeing yellow-green halos around lights. The nurse recognizes these as:
qs.a: Possible signs of digoxin toxicity
qs.x: GI upset and visual changes such as yellow-green halos are classic early signs of digoxin toxicity; hold the dose and report the findings.
w: Expected effects that will fade in a week
Signs of an allergic reaction to digoxin
Symptoms of low blood glucose from digoxin

qs.q: Which lab result places a client taking digoxin at greatest risk for toxicity?
qs.a: Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
qs.x: Hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity and dysrhythmias.
w: Sodium 138 mEq/L
Glucose 104 mg/dL
Hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL

qs.q: A client with heart failure and atrial fibrillation has taken digoxin for a week. Which finding best shows the drug is doing its job?
qs.a: A resting rate of 78 and easier breathing when flat
qs.x: Digoxin slows conduction through the AV node and improves contractility, so the rate comes down and heart failure symptoms ease. It is not a blood pressure drug and does not change potassium.
w: A blood pressure that fell from 140/88 to 118/74
A weight that has gone up two pounds since admission
A potassium that rose from 3.4 to 4.0 mEq/L

qs.q: A client with severe digoxin toxicity and a dangerous dysrhythmia is expected to receive which antidote?
qs.a: Digoxin immune Fab
qs.x: Digoxin immune Fab binds digoxin and reverses life-threatening toxicity.
w: Protamine sulfate
Flumazenil
Naloxone hydrochloride

qs.q: The nurse sees an order for potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push. The nurse should:
qs.a: Question the order, because potassium is never given IV push
qs.x: Potassium given by IV push can cause fatal cardiac arrest; it must be diluted and infused by pump per policy.
w: Give it slowly over 2 minutes through the existing IV line
Dilute it in 10 mL of saline and give it over 5 minutes
Give it IV push only if the client is on a continuous cardiac monitor

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking oral potassium chloride liquid?
qs.a: Dilute it in juice or water and take it with food
qs.x: Liquid potassium irritates the GI tract; dilute it and take it with or after meals.
w: Take it on an empty stomach with no other fluids
Take it at bedtime with a salt substitute for taste
Mix it with an antacid to prevent stomach upset

qs.q: Four clients have an order for oral potassium chloride. Which one should the nurse ask about before giving the dose?
qs.a: The client on spironolactone with a potassium of 5.2 mEq/L
qs.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing, so a supplement on top of it pushes an already high level toward dangerous hyperkalemia. The other three are losing potassium, which is why the supplement is ordered.
w: The client on furosemide today with a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L
The client with vomiting and a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L
The client on a thiazide with a potassium of 3.4 mEq/L

qs.q: A client is ordered IV furosemide 80 mg. Over how long should the nurse plan to give it, and why?
qs.a: About 20 minutes, because a fast push can damage hearing
qs.x: The usual limit is 4 mg per minute, so 80 mg runs over about 20 minutes. Rapid IV administration causes tinnitus and hearing loss, and the risk rises with aminoglycosides or kidney impairment.
w: About 10 seconds, because a fast push works better
About 4 hours, because the drug irritates the vein
Over 2 minutes, because a slower rate reduces urine output

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking furosemide indicates the need for more teaching?
qs.a: I will take my water pill right before I go to bed.
qs.x: Loop diuretics are taken in the morning to avoid nighttime urination and lost sleep.
w: I will weigh myself every morning before breakfast.
I will get up slowly when I stand from the chair.
I will eat foods like bananas and oranges each day.

qs.q: A client receiving furosemide should report which finding to the nurse immediately?
qs.a: Leg cramps and muscle weakness
qs.x: Muscle cramps and weakness may signal hypokalemia.
w: Increased urine output after doses
Mild thirst during the afternoon
Needing to urinate more in the morning

qs.q: A client with diabetes is started on hydrochlorothiazide. The nurse should reinforce closer monitoring of:
qs.a: Blood glucose, because thiazides can raise it
qs.x: Thiazides can cause hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, and increased uric acid.
w: Blood glucose, because thiazides can lower it sharply
Hearing, because thiazides often cause deafness
Urine color, because thiazides turn urine orange

qs.q: A client taking spironolactone asks about using a salt substitute. The nurse should advise the client to:
qs.a: Avoid salt substitutes, because most contain potassium
qs.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing; potassium-based salt substitutes can cause hyperkalemia.
w: Use salt substitutes freely, because they contain no sodium
Use salt substitutes only with meals to protect the stomach
Use salt substitutes to replace lost potassium

qs.q: A client taking lisinopril reports a persistent dry, tickling cough. The nurse should:
qs.a: Report it, because it is a common ACE inhibitor effect
qs.x: ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough from bradykinin buildup; the provider may switch to an ARB.
w: Tell the client it means a lung infection is starting
Advise the client to stop the drug right away at home
Tell the client to double the dose to control it

qs.q: A client who started lisinopril three days ago has swelling of the lips and tongue, with no hives and no wheeze. Which feature points to drug-induced angioedema rather than an allergic reaction?
qs.a: Swelling without hives or itching
qs.x: ACE inhibitor angioedema comes from bradykinin rather than histamine, so it causes deep non-itchy swelling with no urticaria and responds poorly to antihistamines. It can appear days to months after starting.
w: Swelling that came on within minutes
Swelling with a widespread red rash
Swelling that improves with an antihistamine

qs.q: A client took the first dose of lisinopril this morning. When is the blood pressure most likely to fall the furthest?
qs.a: Within about 1 to 6 hours after the dose
qs.x: Oral lisinopril starts working in about an hour and peaks around 6 hours, so first-dose hypotension shows up the same day. The drop is largest in clients who are volume depleted or already on a diuretic.
w: About 3 days after the first dose is given
Only after two weeks of daily therapy
Within about five minutes of swallowing it

qs.q: A client taking enalapril tells the nurse she has just learned she is pregnant. The nurse should:
qs.a: Notify the provider, because ACE inhibitors can harm the fetus
qs.x: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal kidney toxicity.
w: Tell her to keep taking it, because it is safe in pregnancy
Tell her to take it every other day until delivery
Tell her to stop it and take an herbal remedy until she delivers

qs.q: Which lab value is most important to monitor for a client taking losartan?
qs.a: Serum potassium
qs.x: ARBs can cause hyperkalemia, especially with kidney impairment or potassium supplements.
w: Serum amylase
Serum calcium
White blood cell count

qs.q: A client is switched from metoprolol tartrate twice daily to metoprolol succinate once daily. What should the nurse reinforce about the new tablet?
qs.a: Swallow it whole or split it only on the score line
qs.x: Metoprolol succinate is an extended-release tablet, so chewing or crushing it releases the whole day of drug at once. Scored succinate tablets may be split in half but not crushed.
w: Chew it so that it starts working more quickly
Dissolve it in water before each of the morning doses
Take it only on days when the pulse is above 80

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking metoprolol indicates that teaching was effective?
qs.a: I will not stop this medicine suddenly.
qs.x: Abruptly stopping beta blockers can cause rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and angina.
w: I will stop the pills if my pulse goes up.
I will take an extra pill if I feel dizzy.
I can skip doses on days I feel fine.

qs.q: A client with diabetes takes atenolol. The nurse reinforces that this drug may:
qs.a: Hide the fast heartbeat that warns of low blood sugar
qs.x: Beta blockers can mask tachycardia and tremor from hypoglycemia; sweating usually remains.
w: Cause blood glucose to rise sharply after meals
Make insulin injections more painful
Cause the client to feel very thirsty at night

qs.q: The nurse reviews the history of a client with a new order for propranolol. Which condition should the nurse report before giving the drug?
qs.a: Asthma
qs.x: Nonselective beta blockers can cause bronchospasm in clients with asthma.
w: Migraine
Anxiety
Tremor

qs.q: A client starting carvedilol should be taught to:
qs.a: Rise slowly from lying or sitting
qs.x: Carvedilol can cause orthostatic hypotension; it is taken with food.
w: Take it on an empty stomach only
Stop it if the ankles swell at all
Avoid all dairy products while on it

qs.q: A client on amlodipine 10 mg has ankle edema. Which finding tells the nurse this is the drug rather than fluid overload?
qs.a: Clear lungs and no weight gain
qs.x: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers dilate arterioles and raise capillary pressure in the legs, so fluid leaks locally without any rise in total body fluid. Overload brings weight gain, crackles and neck vein distention.
w: Crackles at both lung bases
A 6 pound gain over four days
Jugular veins that are distended

qs.q: The nurse should help a client taking verapamil prevent which common side effect?
qs.a: Constipation
qs.x: Verapamil commonly causes constipation; encourage fluids and fiber.
w: Diarrhea
Hair loss
Weight loss

qs.q: A client has trouble swallowing tablets. Which of these ordered drugs may the nurse crush?
qs.a: Plain lisinopril tablets
qs.x: Immediate-release tablets such as plain lisinopril can be crushed. Crushing an extended-release nifedipine tablet delivers a whole day of drug at once and can cause severe hypotension and reflex tachycardia.
w: Nifedipine extended-release tablets
Enteric-coated aspirin tablets
Sublingual nitroglycerin tablets

qs.q: A client who has taken clonidine twice daily for a year ran out of the prescription two days ago. Which finding should the nurse expect and report?
qs.a: Blood pressure 190/110 with headache and agitation
qs.x: Stopping a central alpha-2 agonist abruptly releases a surge of catecholamines, so pressure and heart rate rebound above baseline within 18 to 36 hours. Drowsiness, dry mouth and bradycardia are effects of taking the drug.
w: Blood pressure 92/58 with lightheadedness on standing
A heart rate of 48 with a very dry mouth
Drowsiness with pinpoint pupils and nausea

qs.q: Which statement by a client shows correct use of sublingual nitroglycerin?
qs.a: If one tablet does not help in 5 minutes, I will call 911.
qs.x: Pain unrelieved 5 minutes after the first dose may be an infarction rather than angina, so emergency care is called; up to three doses may be taken 5 minutes apart while help is on the way.
w: I will take all three of the tablets at once for severe pain.
I will swallow the tablet with a full glass of water.
I will wait 30 minutes before taking a second tablet.

qs.q: How should the nurse teach a client to store sublingual nitroglycerin tablets?
qs.a: In the original dark glass bottle, tightly capped
qs.x: Light, heat, moisture, and air reduce potency; keep tablets in the original amber glass container.
w: In a weekly plastic pill organizer with the other pills
In the refrigerator next to the milk
In a shirt pocket close to the body

qs.q: A client using a nitroglycerin transdermal patch asks why it is removed at bedtime. The nurse explains that:
qs.a: A patch-free period helps prevent tolerance to the drug
qs.x: A daily nitrate-free interval of 10 to 12 hours prevents tolerance.
w: The patch can cause nightmares if worn while sleeping
Nitroglycerin only works while the client is awake
The skin absorbs too much of the drug at night

qs.q: A client who uses nitroglycerin asks if he can take sildenafil. The nurse reinforces that the combination can cause:
qs.a: Severe, dangerous low blood pressure
qs.x: PDE-5 inhibitors with nitrates can cause profound hypotension.
w: Severe, dangerous high blood pressure
A rapid rise in blood glucose levels
Loss of the effect of both drugs

qs.q: A client starting isosorbide mononitrate reports a headache. The nurse should explain that:
qs.a: Headache is common and often eases with time
qs.x: Vasodilation causes headache; acetaminophen may be used if approved.
w: Headache means the drug must be stopped now
Headache is a sign of a stroke from the drug
Headache means the dose is too low to work

qs.q: A client on atorvastatin reports aching weakness in both thighs. Which lab should the nurse expect the provider to order?
qs.a: Creatine kinase
qs.x: Creatine kinase leaks from injured muscle and is the test that separates ordinary aches from statin myopathy. Levels many times the upper limit, especially with dark urine, point to rhabdomyolysis.
w: Serum amylase
Serum calcium
Prothrombin time

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking simvastatin?
qs.a: Take it in the evening and avoid grapefruit juice
qs.x: Cholesterol synthesis peaks at night; grapefruit raises simvastatin levels and myopathy risk.
w: Take it in the morning with a glass of grapefruit juice
Take it only on days when you eat fatty foods
Take it with an antacid to protect the stomach

qs.q: A client takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Which INR result should the nurse report as outside the usual goal?
qs.a: An INR of 1.3
qs.x: The usual target for atrial fibrillation is an INR of 2 to 3. An INR of 1.3 leaves the client unprotected against stroke, which is as much of a problem as a high INR.
w: An INR of 2.1
An INR of 2.6
An INR of 2.9

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking warfarin indicates that teaching was effective?
qs.a: I will keep the amount of green leafy vegetables I eat about the same.
qs.x: Consistent vitamin K intake keeps the INR stable; NSAIDs increase bleeding risk.
w: I will stop eating all green vegetables for as long as I take this drug.
I can take ibuprofen for my headaches while on this drug.
I will use a straight razor so I do not cut myself.

qs.q: A client on warfarin has an elevated INR and minor bleeding. The nurse anticipates an order for which antidote?
qs.a: Vitamin K (phytonadione)
qs.x: Vitamin K reverses warfarin; protamine reverses heparin.
w: Protamine sulfate injection
Naloxone
Flumazenil

qs.q: When giving heparin subcutaneously, the nurse should:
qs.a: Not aspirate and not massage the site afterward
qs.x: Aspirating and massaging increase bruising and hematoma formation.
w: Aspirate first and massage the site for one minute
Use the deltoid muscle with a 1-inch needle
Rub the site briskly to speed absorption

qs.q: A client receiving heparin shows signs of serious bleeding. Which antidote should the nurse expect?
qs.a: Protamine sulfate
qs.x: Protamine sulfate neutralizes heparin.
w: Vitamin K (phytonadione)
Naloxone
Atropine

qs.q: A client on heparin for five days has a platelet count that fell from 240,000 to 90,000. What is the main danger of this reaction?
qs.a: Clotting rather than bleeding
qs.x: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is an antibody reaction that activates the remaining platelets, so despite the low count the risk is arterial and venous thrombosis. It appears 5 to 10 days after heparin is started.
w: Bleeding that will not stop
A severe drop in blood pressure
An airway reaction with swelling

qs.q: When giving enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe, the nurse should:
qs.a: Leave the air bubble in and inject into the abdomen
qs.x: The air bubble ensures the full dose is given; inject into the abdomen at least 2 inches from the umbilicus without aspirating or rubbing.
w: Expel the air bubble and inject into the deltoid
Aspirate before injecting to check for blood
Massage the site well after injecting the dose

qs.q: A client receiving enoxaparin after hip surgery should report which finding?
qs.a: Black, tarry stools
qs.x: Tarry stools suggest GI bleeding. Small bruises at injection sites are common.
w: Mild soreness at the injection site
A small bruise at the injection site
Feeling tired after physical therapy

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking apixaban indicates a need for more teaching?
qs.a: I will stop it a few days before my dental work on my own.
qs.x: Stopping anticoagulants without provider direction increases clot and stroke risk.
w: I will tell my dentist that I take a blood thinner.
I will use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor.
I will report pink urine or bleeding gums right away.

qs.q: A client taking clopidogrel is scheduled for elective surgery. The nurse should:
qs.a: Make sure the surgeon knows the client takes clopidogrel
qs.x: Antiplatelet therapy is usually held about 5 to 7 days before elective surgery per the provider.
w: Tell the client to double the dose the day before surgery
Tell the client to take it with aspirin on the morning of surgery
Give it with vitamin K to prevent bleeding in surgery

qs.q: A parent asks if aspirin can be given to a 10-year-old with chickenpox and fever. The nurse should explain that:
qs.a: Aspirin should be avoided because of the risk of Reye syndrome
qs.x: Aspirin in children and teens with viral illness is linked to Reye syndrome.
w: Aspirin is the preferred fever reducer for chickenpox
Aspirin is safe if it is given with milk or food
Aspirin is safe if the child is over 40 pounds

qs.q: A client who takes high-dose aspirin for arthritis reports ringing in the ears. The nurse recognizes this as a sign of:
qs.a: Salicylate toxicity
qs.x: Tinnitus is an early sign of aspirin toxicity.
w: An inner ear infection
Low blood pressure
Normal aging

qs.q: The nurse gives insulin lispro at 0730. When should the client's breakfast be served?
qs.a: Within 15 minutes
qs.x: Rapid-acting insulin starts working in about 15 minutes; give it with or just before the meal.
w: About 60 minutes later
In 2 to 3 hours
At lunchtime

qs.q: The nurse gives regular insulin subcutaneously at 0700. The client is most at risk for hypoglycemia at about:
qs.x: Regular insulin peaks about 2 to 4 hours after an SQ dose.

qs.q: The nurse gives NPH insulin at 0800. The nurse should watch most closely for hypoglycemia:
qs.a: In the afternoon, about 4 to 12 hours later
qs.x: NPH is intermediate-acting with a peak around 4 to 12 hours.
w: Within the first 15 to 30 minutes
Only during the following night
At no particular time, because NPH has no peak

qs.q: Before drawing up NPH insulin from a vial, the nurse should:
qs.a: Gently roll the vial between the hands
qs.x: NPH is a cloudy suspension; roll gently to mix without making bubbles.
w: Shake the vial hard for 30 seconds
Warm the vial in the microwave briefly
Check that the insulin is completely clear

qs.q: When mixing regular and NPH insulin in one syringe, the nurse should:
qs.a: Draw up the clear regular insulin first
qs.x: Clear before cloudy keeps NPH from contaminating the regular insulin vial.
w: Draw up the cloudy NPH insulin first
Draw them up in either order
Shake both vials before drawing up

qs.q: Which instruction about insulin glargine is correct?
qs.a: Do not mix it with any other insulin in a syringe
qs.x: Glargine is a clear long-acting basal insulin that should not be mixed.
w: Mix it with regular insulin to reduce the number of injections
Shake it well until it turns cloudy before use
Give it only when the blood glucose is above 300

qs.q: How should a client store an opened insulin aspart pen?
qs.a: At room temperature and discard it after 28 days
qs.x: Opened insulin aspart pens are kept at room temperature and discarded after 28 days.
w: In the freezer between doses to keep it fresh
In the glove box of the car for easy access
In the refrigerator and use it for one year

qs.q: A client with diabetes is shaky and sweaty with a fingerstick glucose of 58 mg/dL. The client is alert and can swallow. The nurse should first:
qs.a: Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate
qs.x: Treat conscious hypoglycemia with 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate such as 4 oz of juice, then recheck in 15 minutes.
w: Give the scheduled insulin dose with breakfast
Have the client lie down and recheck in an hour
Call the provider for an order for IV dextrose

qs.q: Which statement by a client about insulin injections indicates that teaching was effective?
qs.a: I will rotate sites within the same body area.
qs.x: Rotating within one area prevents lipohypertrophy and keeps absorption consistent.
w: I will inject in the exact same spot each time.
I will rub the site hard after each injection.
I will inject through my clothes to save time.

qs.q: A client taking metformin who has an eGFR of 25 mL/min/1.73 m2 is scheduled for a CT scan with iodinated contrast. The nurse anticipates that metformin will be:
qs.a: Held at the time of the test and for 48 hours after
qs.x: For clients with an eGFR below 30 or acute kidney injury, metformin is held at the time of contrast and for 48 hours afterward, and kidney function is rechecked before restarting. Clients with stable, normal kidney function usually do not need to stop metformin; follow facility policy.
w: Given with extra water right before the dye is given
Doubled the day after the test to prevent high glucose
Continued without change on the day of the scan

qs.q: A client new to metformin reports nausea and loose stools. The nurse should suggest:
qs.a: Taking it with meals
qs.x: GI upset is common early in therapy; taking metformin with food reduces it. Persistent symptoms should be reported.
w: Taking it at bedtime only
Skipping doses on bad days
Taking it with grapefruit

qs.q: The nurse reinforces teaching for a client taking glipizide. Which side effect is most important to recognize?
qs.a: Low blood sugar
qs.x: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release and can cause hypoglycemia, especially with skipped meals.
w: Hair loss
Dry cough
Ringing in the ears

qs.q: Which client history should the nurse report before the first dose of semaglutide?
qs.a: Family history of medullary thyroid cancer
qs.x: GLP-1 agonists are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2.
w: Family history of seasonal allergies
Personal history of a broken wrist
Personal history of tension headaches

qs.q: A family member is taught to give glucagon to an unconscious client with diabetes. After giving it, the family member should:
qs.a: Turn the client onto the side
qs.x: Glucagon often causes vomiting; side-lying prevents aspiration. Give oral carbohydrate once the client is awake.
w: Give the client water by mouth
Give a second dose right away
Lay the client flat on the back

qs.q: Which instruction about levothyroxine should the nurse reinforce?
qs.a: Take it on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast
qs.x: Food, calcium, and iron reduce absorption; take it at the same time daily with water.
w: Take it with your breakfast and your daily calcium and iron supplements
Take it at bedtime with a glass of milk and a snack
Take it only on days when you feel tired or cold

qs.q: A client taking levothyroxine reports a racing heart, nervousness, and trouble sleeping. These findings suggest that:
qs.a: The dose may be too high
qs.x: Signs of hyperthyroidism suggest excess dosing and should be reported.
w: The dose may be too low
The client is in an expected adjustment phase
The client is allergic to the tablet dye

qs.q: A client taking methimazole calls about a fever of 101.5 F and a sore throat. Which test does the nurse expect to be ordered first?
qs.a: A white cell count with differential
qs.x: Methimazole can cause agranulocytosis, so the neutrophil count is what decides whether this is an ordinary sore throat or a drug reaction requiring the drug to be stopped and the infection treated.
w: A thyroid stimulating hormone level now
A throat culture for strep only
A liver panel and bilirubin level

qs.q: A client taking prednisone for several weeks asks if he can stop when he feels better. The nurse explains:
qs.a: The dose must be tapered as ordered by the provider
qs.x: Sudden withdrawal after long-term use can cause adrenal insufficiency.
w: He can stop as soon as his symptoms are gone
He should stop if his blood sugar goes up
He can stop and restart it as he needs it

qs.q: A client with diabetes starts prednisone. The nurse should expect:
qs.a: Higher blood glucose readings
qs.x: Corticosteroids raise blood glucose; insulin needs may increase.
w: Lower blood glucose readings
No change in glucose readings
A reduced need for insulin

qs.q: After using a fluticasone inhaler, the client should:
qs.a: Rinse the mouth with water and spit
qs.x: Rinsing reduces the risk of oral thrush and hoarseness.
w: Swallow a glass of milk right away
Hold the breath for two full minutes
Use the inhaler again right away

qs.q: A client is ordered albuterol and fluticasone inhalers at the same time. The nurse should instruct the client to use:
qs.a: Albuterol first, then wait before using fluticasone
qs.x: The bronchodilator opens the airways so that the steroid can reach deeper into the lungs.
w: Fluticasone first, then wait before using albuterol
Both at the same time, mixed in one spacer
Only one of them on any single day

qs.q: A client reports feeling shaky with a fast heartbeat after using albuterol. The nurse recognizes this as:
qs.a: A common side effect of the drug
qs.x: Beta-2 agonists commonly cause tremor and tachycardia.
w: An allergic reaction requiring epinephrine
A sign that the dose was too small
A sign that the inhaler is empty

qs.q: Which client action shows correct use of a metered-dose inhaler without a spacer?
qs.a: Breathes out fully, then inhales slowly while pressing the canister
qs.x: After exhaling, press the canister at the start of a slow, deep breath and hold the breath for about 10 seconds.
w: Inhales quickly and deeply, then presses the canister afterward
Presses the canister twice, then takes one quick shallow breath
Breathes in through the nose while pressing down on the canister

qs.q: Which statement indicates that a client understands teaching about tiotropium?
qs.a: I use it once a day to keep my airways open.
qs.x: Tiotropium is a long-acting maintenance bronchodilator, not a rescue drug; capsules are inhaled, not swallowed.
w: I use it when I suddenly cannot breathe.
I swallow the capsule with a glass of water.
I use it only when my asthma flares up badly.

qs.q: A client asks if salmeterol can be used during a sudden asthma attack. The nurse's best response is:
qs.a: No, it is a long-acting maintenance drug, not a rescue inhaler
qs.x: Salmeterol is a long-acting beta agonist; a short-acting drug such as albuterol is used for rescue.
w: Yes, it works within seconds and is the best choice for a sudden attack
Yes, but only if the client uses two puffs at once
No, it should only be used with a nebulizer

qs.q: The nurse reinforces that the family of a child taking montelukast should report:
qs.a: Changes in mood, behavior, or sleep
qs.x: Montelukast has a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events.
w: A dry mouth after doses
Mild thirst after school
Increased appetite and thirst at dinnertime

qs.q: A client taking amoxicillin for strep throat feels better after 3 days. Which statement indicates the need for more teaching?
qs.a: I will save the rest of the pills for next time.
qs.x: Stopping antibiotics early promotes resistance and relapse.
w: I will take every pill until the bottle is empty.
I will call if I get a rash or trouble breathing.
I will call if I have many watery stools a day.

qs.q: Before giving the first dose of amoxicillin, which question is most important for the nurse to ask?
qs.a: Have you ever had a reaction to penicillin?
qs.x: Amoxicillin is a penicillin; a penicillin allergy can cause anaphylaxis.
w: Have you eaten anything in the last hour?
Do you have trouble swallowing large pills?
Have you had a flu shot this year?

qs.q: A client on clindamycin has had many watery stools and tests positive for C. difficile. Which order should the nurse question?
qs.a: An order for loperamide to slow the stools
qs.x: Slowing the bowel keeps the toxin in contact with the colon and raises the risk of ileus and toxic megacolon. Oral vancomycin, contact precautions and fluid replacement are the expected orders.
w: An order for oral vancomycin given by mouth
An order to use contact precautions
An order for IV fluids with potassium

qs.q: A client takes ciprofloxacin, calcium carbonate, ferrous sulfate and levothyroxine. How should the nurse schedule the ciprofloxacin?
qs.a: At least 2 hours before the calcium and iron
qs.x: Calcium, iron and other metal ions bind fluoroquinolones in the gut and can cut absorption enough to cause treatment failure, so doses are separated by about 2 hours before or 6 hours after.
w: At the same time as the calcium and iron
With a large glass of milk at each dose
Only after an antacid to protect the stomach lining

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking doxycycline?
qs.a: Use sunscreen and stay upright after each dose
qs.x: Doxycycline causes photosensitivity and esophageal ulceration; dairy and antacids reduce absorption.
w: Take it with milk to protect the stomach lining
Take it lying down at bedtime with little water
Take it with an antacid to prevent heartburn

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking metronidazole indicates understanding of the teaching?
qs.a: I will not drink any alcohol while taking this.
qs.x: Alcohol can cause a disulfiram-like reaction; avoid it during therapy and for at least 3 days after.
w: I will take this pill with a glass of wine.
I can drink beer once I finish half the pills.
I should avoid all dairy products while on this.

qs.q: A client taking nitrofurantoin for a UTI reports dark brown urine. The nurse should explain that:
qs.a: This is a harmless, expected color change
qs.x: Nitrofurantoin can turn urine rust-yellow to brown. Report cough, chest pain, or numbness.
w: This means the infection has spread to the kidney
This is a sign of liver damage, so stop the drug
This means the client is very dehydrated

qs.q: How should the nurse teach a client to take nitrofurantoin?
qs.a: With food or milk to reduce stomach upset
qs.x: Food improves absorption and reduces GI upset.
w: On an empty stomach with an antacid
Only at bedtime with very little water
Only on days with urinary burning

qs.q: A client on gentamicin reports ringing in the ears and feels unsteady when walking. Which statement about this effect is correct?
qs.a: Hearing and balance damage is often permanent
qs.x: Aminoglycosides accumulate in the hair cells of the inner ear and destroy them, so hearing and balance loss may not recover, while kidney injury from the same drugs usually does.
w: It clears within a day of the last dose
It is prevented by giving the dose along with food
It is a sign that the dose is too low

qs.q: A client on gentamicin has a rising serum creatinine and decreasing urine output. The nurse recognizes possible:
qs.a: Nephrotoxicity
qs.x: Aminoglycosides are toxic to the kidneys; monitor creatinine, BUN, and urine output.
w: Hepatotoxicity
Cardiotoxicity
Neurotoxicity

qs.q: A trough level is ordered for a client receiving gentamicin. When should the blood be drawn?
qs.a: Just before the next scheduled dose
qs.x: The trough is the lowest level, drawn just before the next dose.
w: Right after the dose finishes infusing
One hour after the dose is started
At any time on the same day

qs.q: A client flushes bright red over the face and chest 10 minutes into a vancomycin infusion. What explains this reaction?
qs.a: A direct release of histamine from a fast infusion
qs.x: Vancomycin flushing reaction is a rate-related, non-immune release of histamine from mast cells, so it is managed by slowing the infusion to at least 60 minutes per gram rather than by labeling the client allergic.
w: An antibody reaction to a previous exposure
A sudden fall in platelets caused by the drug
An irritant effect on the lining of the vein being used

qs.q: How should the nurse teach a client to use nystatin oral suspension for thrush?
qs.a: Swish it in the mouth, then swallow it
qs.x: Holding the suspension in the mouth provides the contact time needed to treat oral candidiasis.
w: Swallow it quickly with a glass of milk
Spit it out right after it is measured
Mix it in juice and drink it with meals

qs.q: A client asks how soon oseltamivir should be started for the flu. The nurse explains it works best when started:
qs.a: Within 48 hours of symptom onset
qs.x: Oseltamivir is most effective when started early; early treatment shortens the illness.
w: After a fever lasts more than a week
Only once pneumonia has developed
When the cough begins to improve

qs.q: Which instruction about ferrous sulfate tablets should the nurse reinforce?
qs.a: Take it with orange juice and expect dark stools
qs.x: Vitamin C improves absorption; dark green-black stools are expected.
w: Take it with milk and expect light gray stools
Take it with antacids to prevent stomach upset
Take it with tea and report any black stools

qs.q: A child is prescribed liquid ferrous sulfate. The nurse teaches the parent to:
qs.a: Give it through a straw and brush the teeth afterward
qs.x: Liquid iron can stain the teeth.
w: Mix it into a full bottle of formula
Give it with a glass of milk to mask the taste
Give it only when the child is not eating

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking alendronate indicates that teaching was effective?
qs.a: I will sit or stand upright for 30 minutes after I take it.
qs.x: Alendronate is taken with a full glass of plain water on an empty stomach, and the client stays upright for 30 minutes to prevent esophagitis.
w: I will take it at bedtime so I can lie down right after.
I will take it with my breakfast and morning coffee.
I will take it with a glass of milk for the calcium.

qs.q: A client takes calcium carbonate and levothyroxine. The nurse should instruct the client to:
qs.a: Take them at least 4 hours apart
qs.x: Calcium binds levothyroxine and lowers its absorption.
w: Take them together to save time
Take them both with a glass of milk
Take the calcium first, then the levothyroxine right after

qs.q: Magnesium hydroxide should be used cautiously in a client with:
qs.a: Kidney failure
qs.x: Impaired kidneys cannot excrete magnesium, leading to toxicity.
w: Occasional heartburn
Constipation
Low back pain

qs.q: A client starting oxycodone for pain is also prescribed docusate. The nurse explains that docusate is given to:
qs.a: Soften stools and prevent opioid constipation
qs.x: Opioids cause constipation; stool softeners and stimulant laxatives are given preventively.
w: Increase the pain relief provided by the oxycodone
Prevent nausea from the opioid medication
Reduce the risk of respiratory depression

qs.q: A client asks how sennosides work. The nurse explains that sennosides:
qs.a: Stimulate the bowel to move stool along
qs.x: Senna is a stimulant laxative; it may cause cramping.
w: Draw water into the stool by osmosis only
Coat the bowel to slow down diarrhea
Neutralize stomach acid to stop heartburn

qs.q: The provider orders metoprolol tartrate 25 mg PO. Scored 50 mg tablets are available. How many tablets should the nurse give?
qs.a: 0.5 tablet
qs.x: 25 mg divided by 50 mg per tablet equals 0.5 tablet.
w: 2 tablets
1 tablet
1.5 tablets

qs.q: Amoxicillin 375 mg PO is ordered. The suspension is 250 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 7.5 mL
qs.x: 375 mg divided by 250 mg, times 5 mL, equals 7.5 mL.
w: 5 mL
15 mL

qs.q: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SQ every 12 hours is ordered for a client who weighs 80 kg. What is each dose?
qs.a: 80 mg
qs.x: 1 mg times 80 kg equals 80 mg per dose.
w: 40 mg
160 mg
8 mg

qs.q: Heparin 5,000 units SQ is ordered. The vial contains 10,000 units per mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 0.5 mL
qs.x: 5,000 units divided by 10,000 units per mL equals 0.5 mL.
w: 5 mL
2 mL

qs.q: Digoxin 0.125 mg PO is ordered. The tablets on hand are 0.25 mg. How many tablets should the nurse give?
qs.a: 0.5 tablet
qs.x: 0.125 mg divided by 0.25 mg equals 0.5 tablet. Count the apical pulse first.
w: 2 tablets
1 tablet
0.25 tablet

qs.q: Levothyroxine 0.1 mg is ordered. The available tablets are 50 mcg. How many tablets should the nurse give?
qs.a: 2 tablets
qs.x: 0.1 mg equals 100 mcg; 100 divided by 50 equals 2 tablets.
w: 0.5 tablet
1 tablet
20 tablets

qs.q: A child weighing 16 kg is ordered acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO. The liquid is 160 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 7.5 mL
qs.x: 15 mg times 16 kg equals 240 mg; 240 divided by 160, times 5 mL, equals 7.5 mL.
w: 5 mL
10 mL
2.5 mL

qs.q: A client on a stable lithium dose now has a level of 1.9 mEq/L and a coarse tremor. Which recent change best explains the rise?
qs.a: Starting hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure
qs.x: Thiazides make the kidney reabsorb lithium along with sodium, which raises the level above the usual maintenance range of 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L. NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors do the same; acetaminophen does not.
w: Starting a daily multivitamin with iron
Adding a second and third cup of coffee each morning
Starting acetaminophen for knee pain

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking lithium indicates teaching was effective?
qs.a: I will keep my salt intake steady and drink plenty of fluids.
qs.x: Low sodium intake or dehydration raises lithium levels; 2 to 3 L of fluid daily is commonly recommended.
w: I will cut all salt out of my diet to stay well.
I will drink very little water to avoid swelling.
I will take extra pills whenever I exercise outside in hot weather.

qs.q: A client taking phenytoin has a level of 28 mcg/mL and is unsteady with nystagmus. The nurse recognizes these findings as:
qs.a: Signs of phenytoin toxicity
qs.x: The usual total phenytoin range is 10 to 20 mcg/mL.
w: An expected therapeutic effect
Evidence of a subtherapeutic level
Signs of a new ear infection

qs.q: Which teaching should the nurse reinforce for a client taking phenytoin long term?
qs.a: Brush and floss well and see a dentist regularly
qs.x: Gingival hyperplasia is common; good oral hygiene helps reduce it.
w: Expect the urine to turn bright orange
Avoid all foods that contain vitamin K, such as spinach
Take it only when a seizure begins, then stop again

qs.q: A client taking carbamazepine should report which symptom right away?
qs.a: Fever, sore throat, or a blistering rash
qs.x: Carbamazepine can cause blood dyscrasias and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
w: Mild drowsiness during the first week
Slight dizziness when first starting it
Feeling more thirsty than usual

qs.q: A woman of childbearing age is starting valproic acid. The nurse reinforces that she should:
qs.a: Use reliable birth control, since it can cause birth defects
qs.x: Valproate is a major teratogen (neural tube defects); pregnancy plans must be discussed with the provider.
w: Stop taking it on her own as soon as she misses a period
Take extra iron daily to protect any future pregnancy from harm
Avoid all exercise while on this medication

qs.q: A client taking levetiracetam should be taught to report:
qs.a: New mood changes, irritability, or depression
qs.x: Levetiracetam can cause behavior changes and suicidal thoughts.
w: Mild tiredness during the first few weeks of treatment
A slightly increased appetite at meals
Occasional mild headaches in the morning

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for an older adult taking gabapentin?
qs.a: Rise slowly and use caution; it can cause dizziness
qs.x: Gabapentin causes dizziness and sedation that raise fall risk; antacids reduce absorption, and it is tapered to stop.
w: Take it with antacids to improve how well it is absorbed
Stop it abruptly if the pain goes away
Drink alcohol only in small amounts with it

qs.q: A client taking sertraline and tramadol becomes agitated, sweaty, and feverish, with muscle twitching. The nurse suspects:
qs.a: Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Combining serotonergic drugs can cause serotonin syndrome; report it immediately.
w: Opioid withdrawal
Hypoglycemia
Heat exhaustion

qs.q: A teenager is starting fluoxetine for depression. The nurse reinforces that the family should watch for:
qs.a: New or worse thoughts of suicide
qs.x: Antidepressants carry a boxed warning for suicidality in children and young adults.
w: Mild weight gain in the first week
Lighter-colored stools
Increased hunger at bedtime

qs.q: A client taking an MAO inhibitor, such as high-dose selegiline, should avoid which food?
qs.a: Aged cheddar cheese
qs.x: Tyramine-rich foods such as aged cheese and cured meats can cause hypertensive crisis with MAOIs.
w: Fresh green apples
Steamed white rice
Baked chicken breast

qs.q: An older adult taking amitriptyline is at increased risk for:
qs.a: Confusion, urinary retention, and falls
qs.x: Tricyclics are strongly anticholinergic and are on the Beers list for older adults.
w: Diarrhea, excess saliva, and small pupils
Weight loss, insomnia, and hyperactivity
High blood glucose and frequent thirst

qs.q: An 82-year-old client asks for diphenhydramine to help with sleep. The nurse recognizes that this drug may cause:
qs.a: Confusion and urinary retention in older adults
qs.x: Its anticholinergic effects place it on the Beers list for older adults.
w: Diarrhea and increased saliva in older adults
Low potassium and muscle cramping
Improved memory and alertness the next day

qs.q: Which side effect should the nurse expect in a client taking oxybutynin?
qs.a: Dry mouth and constipation
qs.x: Anticholinergic effects are common; older adults are also at risk for confusion.
w: Excess salivation
Frequent loose stools
Increased sweating and tearing

qs.q: A client taking haloperidol develops neck stiffness and upward deviation of the eyes. The nurse recognizes this as:
qs.a: An acute dystonic reaction
qs.x: Dystonia is an extrapyramidal effect; report promptly, as diphenhydramine or benztropine may be ordered.
w: A seizure from low blood sugar
An allergic reaction to the dye
A normal sign of improving psychosis

qs.q: A client taking risperidone develops a high fever, severe muscle rigidity, and confusion. The nurse should suspect:
qs.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
qs.x: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a medical emergency; report it immediately.
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Akathisia
An acute anticholinergic reaction

qs.q: The nurse should reinforce monitoring of which values for a client taking olanzapine long term?
qs.a: Weight, blood glucose, and lipids
qs.x: Second-generation antipsychotics can cause weight gain and metabolic syndrome.
w: Hearing and vision every week
Urine color and liver size
Bone density and serum calcium levels

qs.q: A client on clozapine has an absolute neutrophil count of 900 per microliter. What does the nurse expect to happen?
qs.a: The drug is held and the count is rechecked
qs.x: Clozapine causes severe neutropenia, so counts are monitored on a set schedule. An ANC under 1000 per microliter means the drug is interrupted, and below 500 it is usually stopped for good.
w: The dose is doubled in order to finish the course
The count is rechecked in three months
The drug is continued with a fever check

qs.q: A client receiving lorazepam is very drowsy with a respiratory rate of 8. The nurse anticipates which reversal agent?
qs.a: Flumazenil
qs.x: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation; support the airway first.
w: Naloxone
Atropine
Protamine

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking alprazolam indicates a need for more teaching?
qs.a: A glass of wine at night will help it work better.
qs.x: Alcohol adds to CNS and respiratory depression.
w: I will not drive until I know how it affects me.
I will not stop this drug suddenly on my own.
I will tell my provider if I feel very sleepy during the day.

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking zolpidem?
qs.a: Take it just before bed if 7 to 8 hours of sleep are possible
qs.x: Complex sleep behaviors and next-day impairment can occur; food delays onset.
w: Take it after dinner and then finish the evening chores
Take it with a large meal to make it work faster
Take it in the morning so it will prevent any daytime drowsiness

qs.q: Which client history should the nurse report before giving bupropion?
qs.a: Seizures or an eating disorder
qs.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated with bulimia or anorexia.
w: Seasonal allergies and hay fever
Osteoarthritis
Mild hypertension

qs.q: A male client taking trazodone should report which side effect immediately?
qs.a: A painful erection lasting more than 4 hours
qs.x: Priapism is a medical emergency.
w: Mild drowsiness the next morning
A dry mouth during the day
Mild dizziness when standing up quickly from bed

qs.q: The nurse should check which vital sign before giving donepezil to an older adult?
qs.a: Heart rate, because it can cause bradycardia
qs.x: Cholinesterase inhibitors increase vagal tone and can cause bradycardia and syncope.
w: Temperature, because it often causes fever
Oxygen saturation, because it often lowers it
Respiratory rate, because it causes apnea

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking carbidopa-levodopa?
qs.a: Avoid high-protein meals at the time of doses
qs.x: Protein competes with levodopa for absorption; urine or sweat may darken. The drug should never be stopped abruptly.
w: Take it with a high-protein meal each time
Expect the urine to turn bright blue or green
Stop it suddenly if dizziness occurs

qs.q: Which change in a client receiving scheduled morphine appears earliest and warns of respiratory depression?
qs.a: Increasing sedation and difficulty staying awake
qs.x: Sedation comes before respiratory depression, which is why a sedation scale is checked with every opioid dose. By the time the rate is 8 or the saturation has fallen, the problem is already advanced.
w: A respiratory rate that has fallen to 8
Pinpoint pupils on close examination
A drop in the oxygen saturation down to 88 percent

qs.q: After naloxone is given for an opioid overdose, the nurse should monitor closely because:
qs.a: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid does
qs.x: Respiratory depression can return; repeat doses may be needed.
w: Naloxone causes long periods of deep sleep
Naloxone causes the blood glucose to drop fast
Naloxone often causes a severe allergic rash

qs.q: Which teaching is most important for a client going home on oxycodone?
qs.a: Avoid alcohol and other sedatives
qs.x: Combining CNS depressants increases the risk of respiratory depression.
w: Always take it on an empty stomach
Drink very little fluid with each dose
Take an extra dose if pain is moderate

qs.q: A client takes hydrocodone-acetaminophen and asks about adding over-the-counter acetaminophen (Tylenol) for a headache. The nurse explains that:
qs.a: Total acetaminophen from all sources must stay under the daily limit
qs.x: Combination products contain acetaminophen; adults generally should not exceed 4 g daily, and a limit of 3 g is often advised.
w: Tylenol is safe as often as needed, because it is a completely different drug
Tylenol will reverse the effects of the hydrocodone
Tylenol should be taken with alcohol for best effect

qs.q: A client using a fentanyl transdermal patch should be taught to:
qs.a: Avoid heating pads and hot tubs over the patch
qs.x: Heat increases absorption and can cause overdose; fold used patches sticky sides together and dispose per instructions.
w: Cut the patch in half when a lower dose is needed
Apply a heating pad to speed up pain relief
Throw used patches in the open trash can

qs.q: Which client history should the nurse report before giving tramadol?
qs.a: Seizures
qs.x: Tramadol lowers the seizure threshold.
w: Gout
Glaucoma
Psoriasis

qs.q: A toddler swallowed a large amount of acetaminophen. The nurse anticipates which antidote?
qs.a: Acetylcysteine
qs.x: Acetylcysteine protects the liver after acetaminophen overdose.
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Protamine sulfate

qs.q: A client with osteoarthritis takes lisinopril, furosemide and warfarin. Why does the nurse question a standing order for ibuprofen?
qs.a: It raises bleeding risk and can worsen kidney function
qs.x: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that maintain renal blood flow, so with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic this is a well-known cause of acute kidney injury. Ibuprofen also impairs platelets on top of warfarin.
w: It makes the furosemide work too strongly
It blocks the absorption of both the lisinopril and the warfarin
It raises the blood level of the warfarin

qs.q: Celecoxib should be questioned in a client with an allergy to:
qs.a: Sulfonamides
qs.x: Celecoxib contains a sulfonamide group.
w: Penicillins
Shellfish
Latex

qs.q: A client taking methadone is at risk for which cardiac problem that may need ECG monitoring?
qs.a: QT prolongation
qs.x: Methadone prolongs the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes.
w: Heart block from high potassium
Valve damage
Pericarditis

qs.q: When should the nurse give a once-daily dose of omeprazole?
qs.a: 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast
qs.x: Proton pump inhibitors work best before the first meal.
w: With the evening meal and a snack
Right after the largest meal
At bedtime with a glass of milk

qs.q: A client takes sucralfate and several other oral drugs. The nurse should:
qs.a: Give sucralfate on an empty stomach; space other drugs 2 hours apart
qs.x: Sucralfate binds other drugs; give it 1 hour before meals and separate it from other drugs.
w: Give all of the drugs together with sucralfate at breakfast
Mix sucralfate with an antacid and give it along with the other drugs
Give sucralfate only after meals with the other drugs

qs.q: An older adult on famotidine has become confused. Which value best explains why the drug is involved?
qs.a: A creatinine clearance of 22 mL/min
qs.x: Famotidine is cleared by the kidney, so with a clearance under about 50 mL/min the drug accumulates and crosses into the brain and causes confusion. The dose is reduced or the interval lengthened.
w: A hemoglobin of 11.8 g per deciliter
A serum sodium level of 139 mEq/L
A fasting glucose of 108 mg/dL

qs.q: Before giving ondansetron, which client history should the nurse report?
qs.a: Long QT syndrome
qs.x: Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval.
w: Seasonal allergies
Lactose intolerance
Mild osteoarthritis

qs.q: A client taking metoclopramide develops lip smacking and tongue thrusting. The nurse should:
qs.a: Report it; it may be tardive dyskinesia
qs.x: Metoclopramide has a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible.
w: Give the next dose early to stop it
Document it as a sign of anxiety
Offer gum to chew and continue the drug as ordered

qs.q: Promethazine should not be given to:
qs.a: A child under 2 years of age
qs.x: Promethazine can cause fatal respiratory depression in children under 2.
w: An adult with mild nausea
A client with motion sickness
A client before outpatient surgery

qs.q: A client with bloody diarrhea and fever asks for loperamide. The nurse should:
qs.a: Report the symptoms before giving any antidiarrheal
qs.x: Antidiarrheals may worsen infectious diarrhea such as C. difficile infection.
w: Give it right away to stop the diarrhea quickly
Give double the dose because the stools are bloody
Give it with a laxative to balance the effect

qs.q: Which instruction about bisacodyl tablets is correct?
qs.a: Swallow them whole and avoid milk or antacids within 1 hour
qs.x: The enteric coating prevents stomach irritation; milk and antacids can dissolve it too early.
w: Chew them well before swallowing for faster bowel relief
Take them with a glass of milk to protect the stomach
Crush the tablets and mix them into applesauce or pudding

qs.q: A client with cirrhosis is taking lactulose. Which finding shows the drug is working?
qs.a: Two to three soft stools daily and clearer thinking
qs.x: Lactulose lowers ammonia by trapping it in the bowel and causing soft stools.
w: No bowel movement for three days and less confusion
Hard stools once a week and better appetite
Darker yellow skin and more sleepiness each day

qs.q: How should the nurse teach a client to take polyethylene glycol powder for constipation?
qs.a: Dissolve it in 4 to 8 ounces of a beverage
qs.x: The usual 17 g dose is dissolved in 4 to 8 ounces of liquid.
w: Swallow the dry powder, then drink a glass of water
Sprinkle it on food without any liquid
Mix it with a tablespoon of water only

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking allopurinol?
qs.a: Drink plenty of fluids and report any skin rash
qs.x: Fluids help prevent kidney stones; a rash may precede a severe reaction.
w: Limit fluids to less than 1 liter a day
Take it only during an acute gout attack, then stop
Take it with aspirin for better results

qs.q: A client starting colchicine for a gout flare asks how much to take. The nurse reinforces that the dose:
qs.a: Stops when diarrhea or vomiting begins
qs.x: Diarrhea and vomiting are the signal that the cumulative colchicine dose has been reached, and going past that point causes marrow suppression and neuropathy. Flare dosing is 1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg an hour later.
w: Continues until the joint pain is gone
Is doubled on the first day of the flare
Is taken every two hours until relief

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking tamsulosin?
qs.a: Rise slowly, especially after the first dose
qs.x: Orthostatic hypotension can occur; it is taken 30 minutes after the same meal each day.
w: Take it on an empty stomach at bedtime only
Expect the urine to turn reddish-orange
Avoid all dairy products while on it

qs.q: The pregnant wife of a client taking finasteride asks about the drug. The nurse reinforces that she should:
qs.a: Not handle crushed or broken tablets
qs.x: Finasteride can harm a male fetus if absorbed.
w: Take one tablet each day for her hair
Avoid sitting in the same room as him
Store the tablets in the refrigerator

qs.q: A client taking empagliflozin should be taught to report:
qs.a: Genital itching, painful urination, or burning
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors increase genital yeast and urinary infections; also report signs of ketoacidosis.
w: Increased appetite and gradual weight gain over time
Mild constipation and bloating after meals
Slight improvement in energy

qs.q: Which finding should the nurse report for a client taking pioglitazone?
qs.a: Weight gain of 2 kg in 3 days with ankle swelling
qs.x: Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and can worsen heart failure.
w: Fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL in the morning
Mild hunger before meals during the day and evening
Increased energy with daily walking

qs.q: A client taking acarbose and glipizide has hypoglycemia. The nurse should give:
qs.a: Glucose tablets or gel
qs.x: Acarbose blocks breakdown of sucrose and complex carbohydrates, so glucose is needed.
w: Table sugar dissolved in water
A slice of cake
Crackers with milk

qs.q: A client asks why insulin detemir is not mixed with rapid-acting insulin in the same syringe. The nurse explains:
qs.a: Mixing can change how each insulin works
qs.x: Long-acting insulins such as detemir and glargine are not mixed with other insulins.
w: It turns cloudy and loses all its effect
It must be mixed only with NPH insulin
It can be mixed if both are cold

qs.q: A client takes sitagliptin alone for type 2 diabetes. What should the nurse teach about low blood sugar on this drug?
qs.a: It is uncommon unless another diabetes drug is added
qs.x: DPP-4 inhibitors prolong incretin hormones that act only while glucose is rising, so they rarely cause hypoglycemia alone. The risk appears when they are combined with a sulfonylurea or insulin.
w: It happens most mornings and needs a bedtime snack
It is prevented by taking the dose with a large full meal
It is the most common side effect of this drug

qs.q: A parent is learning to use an epinephrine auto-injector on a child. Which part of the technique does the nurse reinforce?
qs.a: Hold it against the outer thigh for about 3 seconds
qs.x: The device needs a few seconds of contact for the full dose to leave the spring-loaded syringe. It goes into the anterolateral thigh and works through clothing, which is why it can be used right away.
w: Rub the thigh briskly for a minute afterward
Aim for the fleshy part of the upper arm
Give it only through bare skin and not through clothing

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking amiodarone long term?
qs.a: Use sunscreen; report any new cough or shortness of breath
qs.x: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary toxicity, photosensitivity, and thyroid and liver problems.
w: Drink grapefruit juice daily to improve the drug's absorption
Expect a new cough as a harmless side effect
Stop the drug if the skin looks bluish-gray

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking rivaroxaban indicates the need for more teaching?
qs.a: I can take naproxen when my back hurts.
qs.x: NSAIDs raise bleeding risk; the 15 and 20 mg doses are taken with food.
w: I will take it with my evening meal.
I will tell my dentist about this drug.
I will report red or black stools.

qs.q: How should a client store and take dabigatran capsules?
qs.a: Keep them in the original bottle and swallow them whole
qs.x: Opening capsules increases absorption and bleeding; moisture degrades the drug.
w: Open the capsules and sprinkle the beads on soft food
Move them to a weekly pill organizer to keep track of doses
Chew the capsules for faster absorption

qs.q: A client taking valsartan reports lightheadedness when getting out of bed. The nurse should teach the client to:
qs.a: Sit at the edge of the bed before standing
qs.x: Orthostatic hypotension is reduced by changing positions slowly.
w: Get up quickly to raise the blood pressure
Skip doses on days with dizziness
Take the dose with a high-salt snack

qs.q: Which lab value should the nurse report for a client taking ramipril?
qs.a: Potassium 5.8 mEq/L
qs.x: ACE inhibitors can cause hyperkalemia.
w: Sodium 140 mEq/L
Glucose 96 mg/dL
Calcium 9.4 mg/dL

qs.q: A client taking desmopressin reports headache, nausea, and confusion. The nurse suspects:
qs.a: Low sodium from water retention
qs.x: Desmopressin can cause hyponatremia.
w: High sodium from mild dehydration
Low glucose from the drug
High calcium from the drug

qs.q: A client with chronic alcohol use is ordered thiamine and IV dextrose. The nurse understands that thiamine is usually given:
qs.a: Before or with glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
qs.x: Glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
w: Only after the dextrose infusion has been completely finished
Only if the client has a seizure
Only after the client eats a full meal

qs.q: A client taking patiromer also takes other oral medications. The nurse should:
qs.a: Separate other oral drugs from patiromer by at least 3 hours
qs.x: Patiromer binds other drugs in the gut.
w: Give all the drugs together with patiromer
Mix the other drugs into the patiromer suspension before giving it
Give patiromer only at night on an empty stomach

qs.q: Before giving epoetin alfa, the nurse should check:
qs.a: Blood pressure and latest hemoglobin
qs.x: Epoetin raises blood pressure, and a high hemoglobin increases clot risk.
w: Blood glucose level and urine ketones
Temperature and pupil size
Weight, height, and head circumference

qs.q: A transplant client taking tacrolimus should be taught to:
qs.a: Avoid grapefruit and take doses at the same times daily
qs.x: Grapefruit raises tacrolimus levels; consistent timing keeps levels steady.
w: Stop it after feeling well for a month
Double the dose after missing one
Take each dose with grapefruit juice to improve absorption

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking mycophenolate indicates a need for more teaching?
qs.a: I do not need birth control while on this drug.
qs.x: Mycophenolate causes birth defects and requires effective contraception.
w: I will avoid people who are sick when I can.
I will report fever or sore throat quickly.
I will keep all of my scheduled blood test appointments.

qs.q: A client taking baclofen asks about stopping it. The nurse explains:
qs.a: It must be tapered, as sudden stopping can cause seizures
qs.x: Abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures and hallucinations.
w: It can be stopped at any time without any withdrawal problems
It should be stopped if drowsiness occurs
It should be held before each meal

qs.q: An older adult taking cyclobenzaprine should be monitored most closely for:
qs.a: Drowsiness, confusion, and falls
qs.x: Cyclobenzaprine is sedating and anticholinergic and is on the Beers list.
w: Hyperactivity and weight loss
Excess salivation and diarrhea
Increased appetite and thirst at night

qs.q: A client has a lidocaine 5% patch ordered for back pain. The nurse should:
qs.a: Apply it for up to 12 hours, then remove it for 12 hours
qs.x: The usual schedule is 12 hours on and 12 hours off on intact skin.
w: Leave it on for 3 full days before changing it
Apply it over broken skin for faster relief
Use a heating pad over the patch to improve its numbing effect

qs.q: An older adult taking levofloxacin and prednisone is at increased risk for:
qs.a: Tendon rupture
qs.x: Age over 60 and corticosteroids increase fluoroquinolone tendon rupture risk.
w: Hearing loss
Permanent hair loss
Weight gain

qs.q: A client taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole should be taught to:
qs.a: Drink plenty of fluids and report any rash
qs.x: Fluids prevent crystalluria; a rash can signal Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
w: Limit fluids to avoid frequent urination
Take it with antacids to prevent nausea
Stop it as soon as the burning with urination stops

qs.q: Furosemide 40 mg PO is ordered. The oral solution is 10 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 4 mL
qs.x: 40 mg divided by 10 mg per mL equals 4 mL.
w: 0.4 mL
40 mL
2.5 mL

qs.q: A client is to receive 6 units of regular insulin and 14 units of NPH insulin mixed in one syringe. What total dose will be in the syringe?
qs.a: 20 units
qs.x: 6 plus 14 equals 20 units; draw up the clear regular insulin first.
w: 14 units
8 units
24 units

qs.q: Potassium chloride oral solution 40 mEq is ordered. The solution is 20 mEq per 15 mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 30 mL
qs.x: 40 mEq divided by 20 mEq, times 15 mL, equals 30 mL. Dilute before giving.
w: 15 mL
45 mL
20 mL

qs.q: Morphine 4 mg SQ is ordered. The vial is 10 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 0.4 mL
qs.x: 4 mg divided by 10 mg per mL equals 0.4 mL.
w: 4 mL
2.5 mL

qs.q: Before giving any medication, the nurse identifies the client using:
qs.a: Two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth
qs.x: Two identifiers are required; a room number is never an identifier.
w: The room and bed numbers posted on the door
The name on the chart hanging at the bedside
A question asking whether the client is the right person

qs.q: A client asks the nurse to crush an extended-release tablet because it is hard to swallow. The nurse should:
qs.a: Do not crush it; ask the provider or pharmacist about another form
qs.x: Crushing extended-release, enteric-coated, or sublingual products alters release and can cause toxicity or loss of effect.
w: Crush it and mix it with a small amount of applesauce
Crush it and dissolve it in warm water before giving it to the client
Cut it in half and have the client take both halves

qs.q: To measure a liquid medication in a medicine cup, the nurse should read the dose:
qs.a: At eye level at the bottom of the meniscus
qs.x: Set the cup on a flat surface and read at eye level at the lowest point of the curve.
w: Looking down at the top of the meniscus
While holding the cup up toward the light
At the highest point the liquid touches the cup

qs.q: A parent plans to give a child's liquid medicine with a kitchen teaspoon. The nurse should recommend:
qs.a: An oral dosing syringe or marked dosing cup
qs.x: Household spoons vary in size and cause dosing errors.
w: A larger soup spoon for more accurate dosing
Pouring the dose into the child's bottle
Mixing the dose into a full cup of juice

qs.q: The nurse discovers that she gave a client the wrong medication. After checking the client, the nurse should:
qs.a: Notify the RN or provider and file an incident report per policy
qs.x: Client safety comes first, followed by notification and reporting; the incident report is not mentioned in the client's chart.
w: Document the error in the client's chart in the form of an incident report
Wait to see whether the client develops any side effects
Tell no one if the client shows no signs of a problem

qs.q: A client refuses a scheduled medication. The nurse should first:
qs.a: Ask the client about the reason for refusing
qs.x: Explore the reason, reinforce teaching, then document and report the refusal. Clients have the right to refuse.
w: Hide the medication in the client's food
Tell the client the provider will be upset if it is not taken
Leave the pill at the bedside for later

qs.q: Before giving a rectal suppository to an adult, the nurse should position the client:
qs.a: On the left side with the upper knee bent
qs.x: The left Sims position follows the natural curve of the rectum and sigmoid colon.
w: On the right side with both legs straight
Flat on the back with the knees raised
Sitting upright on the toilet or commode

qs.q: When applying a new transdermal medication patch, the nurse should:
qs.a: Remove the old patch; apply the new one to a clean, hairless site
qs.x: Remove old patches to prevent overdose, and rotate sites to prevent irritation.
w: Apply the new patch on top of the old one
Shave the site closely and apply a layer of lotion before the patch
Apply the new patch to the exact same site each time

qs.q: Prednisone 60 mg PO is ordered. Tablets on hand are 20 mg. How many tablets should the nurse give?
qs.a: 3 tablets
qs.x: 60 mg divided by 20 mg per tablet equals 3 tablets.
w: 2 tablets
4 tablets
6 tablets
