qs.q: A child weighs 22 lb. Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO is ordered. The suspension is 100 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 5 mL
qs.x: 22 lb divided by 2.2 equals 10 kg; 10 mg times 10 kg equals 100 mg, which is 5 mL.
w: 10 mL
11 mL
2.5 mL

qs.q: Cephalexin 500 mg PO is ordered. Capsules on hand are 250 mg. How many capsules should the nurse give?
qs.a: 2 capsules
qs.x: 500 mg divided by 250 mg equals 2 capsules.
w: 1 capsule
0.5 capsule
4 capsules

qs.q: Ondansetron 8 mg PO is ordered. Orally disintegrating tablets on hand are 4 mg. How many tablets should the nurse give?
qs.a: 2 tablets
qs.x: 8 mg divided by 4 mg equals 2 tablets; place them on the tongue to dissolve.
w: 1 tablet
0.5 tablet
4 tablets

qs.q: Hydromorphone 1 mg SQ is ordered. The vial is 2 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 0.5 mL
qs.x: 1 mg divided by 2 mg per mL equals 0.5 mL.
w: 2 mL
0.2 mL
1 mL

qs.q: Lithium carbonate 600 mg PO is ordered. Capsules on hand are 300 mg. How many capsules should the nurse give?
qs.a: 2 capsules
qs.x: 600 mg divided by 300 mg equals 2 capsules.
w: 3 capsules
1 capsule
0.5 capsule

qs.q: Guaifenesin 200 mg PO is ordered. The syrup is 100 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 10 mL
qs.x: 200 mg divided by 100 mg, times 5 mL, equals 10 mL.
w: 5 mL
20 mL
2.5 mL

qs.q: Warfarin 7.5 mg PO is ordered. Scored tablets on hand are 5 mg. How many tablets should the nurse give?
qs.a: 1.5 tablets
qs.x: 7.5 mg divided by 5 mg equals 1.5 tablets.
w: 2 tablets
0.5 tablet
1 tablet

qs.q: Insulin glargine 0.2 units/kg SQ daily is ordered for a client who weighs 90 kg. How many units should the client receive?
qs.a: 18 units
qs.x: 0.2 units times 90 kg equals 18 units.
w: 20 units
9 units
45 units

qs.q: A 15 kg child is ordered amoxicillin 40 mg/kg/day PO divided every 12 hours. How many mg should the child receive per dose?
qs.a: 300 mg
qs.x: 40 mg times 15 kg equals 600 mg per day; divided into 2 doses, this equals 300 mg per dose.
w: 600 mg
150 mg
400 mg

qs.q: A client weighs 154 lb. What is the client's weight in kilograms?
qs.a: 70 kg
qs.x: 154 lb divided by 2.2 equals 70 kg.
w: 77 kg
339 kg
64 kg

qs.q: While preparing medications, the nurse drops a tablet on the floor. The nurse should:
qs.a: Discard it per policy and obtain a new dose
qs.x: A contaminated dose is discarded per policy; controlled substances need a witnessed waste.
w: Wipe it off and give it to the client
Put it back in the stock bottle
Give it only if the floor was recently cleaned

qs.q: When instilling eye drops, the nurse should:
qs.a: Drop the medication into the lower conjunctival sac
qs.x: Afterward, gentle pressure on the inner corner of the eye limits systemic absorption.
w: Drop the medication directly onto the center of the cornea
Touch the dropper tip to the eyelid to steady it
Have the client blink hard right after the drop

qs.q: To give ear drops to a 2-year-old, the nurse should pull the pinna:
qs.a: Down and back
qs.x: In children under 3, pulling the pinna down and back straightens the ear canal.
w: Up and back
Straight up and forward
Forward

qs.q: When giving an IM injection using the Z-track method, the nurse should:
qs.a: Pull the skin aside, inject, and release it after removing the needle
qs.x: Z-track seals the drug in the muscle and prevents leakage into the subcutaneous tissue.
w: Massage the site firmly after injecting
Inject the drug into the subcutaneous fat layer of the abdomen instead
Use the same needle that was used to draw up the drug

qs.q: Which site is preferred for an IM injection in most adults?
qs.a: Ventrogluteal
qs.x: The ventrogluteal site is away from major nerves and blood vessels.
w: Dorsogluteal (upper outer buttock)
Abdomen
Forearm

qs.q: A pregnant client asks which over-the-counter drug is generally preferred for a mild headache. The nurse reinforces that it is usually:
qs.a: Acetaminophen
qs.x: NSAIDs are generally avoided in pregnancy, especially after 20 weeks.
w: Ibuprofen
Naproxen
Aspirin

qs.q: A nurse is titrating a continuous heparin infusion by protocol. Which result shows the infusion is in the usual therapeutic range?
qs.a: aPTT 68 seconds
qs.x: Heparin is titrated to an aPTT about 1.5 to 2.5 times control, roughly 60 to 90 seconds in most labs. The INR tracks warfarin rather than heparin, and a normal platelet count says nothing about whether the dose is therapeutic.
w: aPTT 26 seconds
INR 2.4
Platelet count 310,000/mm3

qs.q: Heparin 25,000 units in 250 mL D5W is ordered to infuse at 1,000 units/hr. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
qs.a: 10 mL/hr
qs.x: 25,000 units / 250 mL = 100 units/mL; 1,000 units/hr divided by 100 units/mL = 10 mL/hr.
w: 25 mL/hr
100 mL/hr
4 mL/hr

qs.q: A heparin protocol calls for 18 units/kg/hr for a client weighing 80 kg. The bag contains 25,000 units in 500 mL. What rate should the nurse program?
qs.a: 28.8 mL/hr
w: 14.4 mL/hr
57.6 mL/hr
36 mL/hr

qs.q: A heparin bolus of 80 units/kg is ordered for a client who weighs 80 kg. The vial contains 5,000 units/mL. How many mL should the nurse draw up?
qs.x: 80 units x 80 kg = 6,400 units; 6,400 divided by 5,000 units/mL = 1.28 mL.
w: 6.4 mL

qs.q: The nurse prepares protamine sulfate for a client with a heparin overdose. Which administration technique is correct?
qs.a: Give it slowly IV, no faster than 5 mg per minute
qs.x: Rapid protamine can cause severe hypotension, bradycardia, and anaphylactoid reactions; it is given slowly IV.
w: Give it rapidly IV push so it binds heparin quickly
Add it to the running heparin bag so the two drugs neutralize
Give it deep IM in the ventrogluteal site to avoid hypotension

qs.q: The nurse teaches a client to self-inject enoxaparin at home. Which statement indicates that the client understands the teaching?
qs.a: I will leave the air bubble in the prefilled syringe.
qs.x: The air bubble is left in to keep all the drug in the tissue; rubbing and aspirating increase bruising.
w: I will rub the site well afterward to spread the drug.
I will inject it into my thigh muscle at a 90-degree angle.
I will pull back on the plunger to check for blood first.

qs.q: A client receiving enoxaparin for 7 days has new lab results. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?
qs.a: Platelets fell from 240,000 to 90,000/mm3
qs.x: A platelet drop of more than 50% suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which needs prompt evaluation.
w: aPTT of 34 seconds compared with 31 seconds at baseline
Hemoglobin of 13.2 g/dL, unchanged from admission
Serum creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL

qs.q: A client received enoxaparin and had an epidural catheter removed earlier today. Which finding requires immediate action?
qs.a: New numbness and weakness in both legs
qs.x: Neuraxial anesthesia with low-molecular-weight heparin can cause a spinal or epidural hematoma; new neurologic deficits are an emergency.
w: Mild soreness at the former catheter site
A small bruise at the abdominal injection site
Pain rated 3 out of 10 on the incision

qs.q: A client is started on warfarin while the heparin infusion continues. Why is heparin kept running for about five more days?
qs.a: Warfarin needs days to deplete circulating clotting factors
qs.x: Warfarin blocks new synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X, but factor II already in the blood has a half-life near 60 hours, so full effect takes about 5 days. The INR can look therapeutic from loss of factor VII before the client is truly anticoagulated.
w: Warfarin cannot be absorbed until all heparin is fully cleared
Heparin raises the INR so the warfarin dose can be set
Heparin protects the stomach from warfarin irritation

qs.q: A client on warfarin has an intracranial hemorrhage and an INR of 4.5. Which treatment should the nurse prepare to give?
qs.a: Four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K
qs.x: Life-threatening warfarin bleeding is reversed rapidly with prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K for sustained effect.
w: Protamine sulfate IV and hold the next dose
Oral vitamin K alone, then recheck the INR in 24 hours
Idarucizumab 5 g IV with a platelet transfusion

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking warfarin indicates a need for further teaching?
qs.a: I can take ibuprofen when my arthritis flares up.
qs.x: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen increase bleeding risk with warfarin and should be avoided.
w: I will keep my intake of green leafy vegetables about the same.
I will use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor.
I will tell my dentist that I take a blood thinner.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing IV phytonadione for a client with a high INR. Which action is correct?
qs.a: Dilute it and infuse slowly while watching for anaphylaxis
qs.x: IV vitamin K can cause severe anaphylactoid reactions, so it is diluted and infused slowly.
w: Give it undiluted by rapid IV push over 30 seconds
Mix it into the client's heparin infusion bag
Give it with protamine to speed the reversal

qs.q: A client taking dabigatran has a life-threatening GI bleed. Which reversal agent should the nurse expect to give?
qs.a: Idarucizumab
qs.x: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that specifically binds and reverses dabigatran.
w: Protamine sulfate
Phytonadione
Andexanet given with vitamin K

qs.q: Which statement by a client starting apixaban shows correct understanding?
qs.a: I will not need routine INR blood tests.
qs.x: Apixaban does not require INR monitoring; stopping abruptly, doubling doses, or adding aspirin increase the risk of clotting or bleeding.
w: I can stop it a day before dental work on my own.
If I miss a dose I will take two doses the next time.
I should add a daily aspirin for extra clot protection.

qs.q: A client is prescribed rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for atrial fibrillation. What should the nurse include in teaching?
qs.a: Take it with your evening meal
qs.x: The 15 mg and 20 mg doses are taken with food, usually the evening meal, for proper absorption.
w: Take it on an empty stomach at bedtime
Have your INR checked weekly for the first month
Eat the same amount of vitamin K every day

qs.q: A client in DKA has a glucose of 540 mg/dL and a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L. Which order should the nurse implement first?
qs.a: Potassium replacement before starting insulin
qs.x: Insulin drives potassium into cells; starting it with a potassium below 3.3 mEq/L can cause fatal dysrhythmias.
w: Regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr right away
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mEq IV push for acidosis
Insulin glargine 20 units subcutaneously now

qs.q: A client with DKA on an insulin infusion now has a glucose of 240 mg/dL, but the anion gap is still open. What should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue insulin
qs.x: Insulin is continued until the gap closes; dextrose is added to prevent hypoglycemia.
w: Stop the insulin infusion and switch to sliding scale
Increase the insulin rate to close the gap faster
Give 50% dextrose IV push and hold the insulin

qs.q: An insulin infusion of 100 units of regular insulin in 100 mL NS is ordered at 0.1 units/kg/hr for a 70 kg client. What rate should the nurse set?
qs.a: 7 mL/hr
qs.x: 0.1 x 70 = 7 units/hr; the concentration is 1 unit/mL, so 7 mL/hr.
w: 0.7 mL/hr
70 mL/hr
14 mL/hr

qs.q: Which insulin can the nurse give as a continuous IV infusion?
qs.a: Regular human insulin
qs.x: Regular insulin is the standard IV insulin; long-acting and cloudy insulins are never given IV.
w: Insulin glargine
Insulin NPH (isophane suspension)
Insulin detemir

qs.q: A client's fingerstick glucose is 52 mg/dL. The client is alert and able to swallow. What should the nurse do first?
qs.a: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
qs.x: An alert client who can swallow gets 15 g of simple carbohydrate, then a recheck in 15 minutes.
w: Give glucagon 1 mg IM in the thigh
Start D50 IV push through the hand vein
Provide a full meal tray with a protein snack

qs.q: A client with diabetes is unresponsive with a glucose of 38 mg/dL and has no IV access. Which action is best?
qs.a: Give glucagon 1 mg IM and turn the client to the side
qs.x: Glucagon works without IV access; vomiting is common, so the client is placed on the side.
w: Place glucose gel in the cheek and recheck in 15 minutes
Give regular insulin subcutaneously and recheck in an hour
Start an IV and wait for a repeat glucose before treating

qs.q: The nurse is giving 50% dextrose IV for severe hypoglycemia. Which action is most important?
qs.a: Confirm a patent, free-flowing IV before pushing
qs.x: D50 is hypertonic and a vesicant; extravasation can cause tissue necrosis.
w: Give it IM if the IV site looks slightly puffy
Push it through the smallest available hand vein
Mix it with regular insulin in the same syringe

qs.q: A client with hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state has a glucose of 960 mg/dL and dry mucous membranes. What is the priority intervention?
qs.a: Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride as ordered
qs.x: Severe dehydration is the main problem in HHS; isotonic fluid replacement comes first.
w: Give regular insulin 20 units IV push
Start oral fluids at 120 mL per hour
Give sodium bicarbonate for the acidosis

qs.q: An order reads potassium chloride 40 mEq in 100 mL NS over 1 hour through a peripheral IV. What should the nurse do?
qs.a: Clarify the order because the rate is unsafe
qs.x: Peripheral potassium is usually limited to about 10 mEq/hr; 40 mEq/hr is unsafe without central access and cardiac monitoring.
w: Give it as ordered on an infusion pump
Run it over 30 minutes to finish it sooner
Give it as ordered but check the site every hour

qs.q: Before starting IV potassium chloride, which assessment is most important?
qs.a: Urine output of at least 30 mL/hr
qs.x: Potassium is excreted by the kidneys; giving it with poor urine output can cause hyperkalemia.
w: Serum calcium level from yesterday
Blood glucose within normal limits
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants

qs.q: Potassium chloride 20 mEq in 100 mL is ordered to infuse over 2 hours. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
qs.a: 50 mL/hr
qs.x: 100 mL over 2 hours = 50 mL/hr, which delivers 10 mEq/hr.
w: 100 mL/hr
20 mL/hr
25 mL/hr

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client taking oral potassium chloride tablets?
qs.a: Take it with a full glass of water after meals
qs.x: Oral potassium irritates the GI tract; taking it with fluid and food reduces ulceration.
w: Take it on an empty stomach first thing in the morning
Crush the extended-release tablet into pudding
Take it with a salt substitute to boost the effect

qs.q: A client with preeclampsia is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which finding requires immediate action?
qs.a: Respirations 10/min and absent patellar reflexes
qs.x: Absent reflexes and respiratory depression signal magnesium toxicity.
w: Blood pressure 146/94 mm Hg and mild headache
Patellar reflexes 2+ and urine output 50 mL/hr
Facial flushing and a feeling of warmth

qs.q: A client on a magnesium sulfate infusion becomes lethargic with a respiratory rate of 8/min. After stopping the infusion, which drug should the nurse prepare?
qs.a: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV given slowly
qs.x: Calcium gluconate antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction.
w: Naloxone 0.4 mg IV push
Potassium chloride 20 mEq IV
Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV over 30 seconds

qs.q: Which finding in a client receiving magnesium sulfate increases the risk of toxicity?
qs.a: Urine output of 80 mL over 4 hours
qs.x: Magnesium is cleared by the kidneys; output under 30 mL/hr allows it to accumulate.
w: Deep tendon reflexes of 2+ bilaterally
Respiratory rate of 16/min
Serum magnesium of 5.5 mg/dL

qs.q: A 4 g magnesium sulfate loading dose is ordered over 20 minutes. The bag contains 40 g in 1,000 mL. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
qs.a: 300 mL/hr
qs.x: 40 g/1,000 mL = 0.04 g/mL; 4 g = 100 mL; 100 mL over 20 minutes = 300 mL/hr.
w: 100 mL/hr
200 mL/hr
400 mL/hr

qs.q: After the loading dose, magnesium sulfate is ordered at 2 g/hr. The bag is 40 g in 1,000 mL. What rate should the nurse program?
qs.a: 50 mL/hr
qs.x: 2 g divided by 0.04 g/mL = 50 mL/hr.
w: 20 mL/hr
80 mL/hr
25 mL/hr

qs.q: The nurse is monitoring an oxytocin induction. Which contraction pattern meets the definition of tachysystole?
qs.a: More than 5 contractions in 10 minutes over 30 minutes
qs.x: Tachysystole is more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over a 30-minute window, and it is the reason oxytocin is titrated down or stopped. Contractions every 3 minutes is only 3 to 4 per 10 minutes, the usual goal in active labor.
w: Contractions every 3 minutes lasting 60 seconds
Contractions lasting 70 seconds with full relaxation between
A 20-minute stretch with no contractions recorded at all

qs.q: A postpartum client has received high-dose oxytocin for 12 hours. She reports headache and confusion, and urine output has dropped. Which laboratory value should the nurse check?
qs.a: Serum sodium
qs.x: Oxytocin has an antidiuretic effect and can cause water intoxication with hyponatremia.
w: Serum magnesium
Platelet count
Liver enzymes

qs.q: A client is receiving terbutaline for preterm labor. Which finding should cause the nurse to hold the next dose?
qs.a: Maternal heart rate of 132/min
qs.x: Terbutaline is a beta-agonist; maternal tachycardia over about 120/min warrants holding it.
w: Maternal heart rate of 96/min
Mild tremor of both hands
Blood glucose of 118 mg/dL

qs.q: Which statement by a client in preterm labor shows understanding of betamethasone?
qs.a: This shot helps my baby's lungs mature before birth.
qs.x: Antenatal corticosteroids speed fetal lung maturity and reduce respiratory distress syndrome.
w: This shot will stop my contractions within an hour.
This medicine prevents my baby from getting an infection.
This shot lowers my blood pressure during labor.

qs.q: Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM is ordered for postpartum hemorrhage. Which charted finding should the nurse question before giving it?
qs.a: A blood pressure of 162/98 mm Hg
qs.x: Methylergonovine is an ergot vasoconstrictor, so it is avoided in hypertension and preeclampsia because of stroke and severe hypertension. Asthma is the limit on carboprost, not on this drug, and anemia with heavy blood loss is the reason it was ordered.
w: A hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL
A history of well-controlled asthma
An estimated blood loss of 900 mL

qs.q: A postpartum client with hemorrhage has a history of asthma. Which uterotonic order should the nurse question?
qs.a: Carboprost tromethamine IM
qs.x: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha that can cause bronchospasm and is avoided in asthma.
w: Oxytocin IV infusion
Misoprostol rectally
Tranexamic acid IV

qs.q: A client has a dinoprostone vaginal insert for cervical ripening and now has contractions every 90 seconds. What should the nurse do first?
qs.a: Remove the vaginal insert
qs.x: Tachysystole with dinoprostone is managed by removing the insert.
w: Start an oxytocin infusion at 2 milliunits/min
Give a second insert to finish ripening
Have the client walk to promote dilation

qs.q: A peripheral norepinephrine infusion has infiltrated and the hand is pale, cool, and mottled. Which drug is infiltrated into the site to limit tissue loss?
qs.a: Phentolamine
qs.x: Phentolamine is an alpha blocker, so it reverses the intense alpha-mediated vasoconstriction causing the ischemia. Hyaluronidase disperses other extravasations but does not relieve vasospasm, and protamine and calcium reverse heparin and calcium channel blockers.
w: Protamine sulfate
Hyaluronidase
Calcium gluconate

qs.q: Norepinephrine 4 mg in 250 mL is ordered at 8 mcg/min. What rate should the nurse program?
qs.a: 30 mL/hr
qs.x: 4 mg/250 mL = 16 mcg/mL; 8 mcg/min divided by 16 mcg/mL = 0.5 mL/min; 0.5 mL/min x 60 = 30 mL/hr.
w: 15 mL/hr
60 mL/hr
0.5 mL/hr

qs.q: Dopamine 400 mg in 250 mL is ordered at 5 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg client. What rate should the nurse set?
qs.a: 15 mL/hr
w: 24 mL/hr
30 mL/hr
7.5 mL/hr

qs.q: Dobutamine 500 mg in 250 mL is ordered at 10 mcg/kg/min for a 60 kg client. What rate should the nurse set?
qs.a: 18 mL/hr
w: 36 mL/hr
30 mL/hr
9 mL/hr

qs.q: A client with cardiogenic shock is started on dobutamine. Which finding best shows the drug is working?
qs.a: Urine output rises from 15 to 45 mL/hr
qs.x: Dobutamine increases contractility and cardiac output, which improves kidney perfusion.
w: Heart rate rises from 90 to 135/min
Lung crackles extend higher on the posterior chest
Skin becomes cooler and more mottled at the knees

qs.q: Vasopressin 20 units in 100 mL is ordered at 0.03 units/min for septic shock. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
qs.a: 9 mL/hr
qs.x: 20 units/100 mL = 0.2 units/mL; 0.03 x 60 = 1.8 units/hr; 1.8 divided by 0.2 = 9 mL/hr.
w: 1.8 mL/hr
15 mL/hr
6 mL/hr

qs.q: After an IV phenylephrine bolus for hypotension, which finding should the nurse expect and monitor?
qs.a: Reflex bradycardia
qs.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-agonist; the rise in BP can trigger a reflex drop in heart rate.
w: Rebound tachycardia
Bronchospasm
Hypoglycemia

qs.q: A client has anaphylaxis after an IV antibiotic. Which epinephrine order should the nurse anticipate first?
qs.a: 0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL solution IM in the lateral thigh
qs.x: IM epinephrine 1 mg/mL (0.3 to 0.5 mg) in the thigh is first-line for anaphylaxis; the cardiac arrest dose is not used.
w: 1 mg of 0.1 mg/mL solution by rapid IV push
0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL solution subcutaneously in the arm
0.1 mg of 1 mg/mL solution IV push undiluted

qs.q: Adenosine 6 mg is ordered for a client with stable SVT. Which technique is correct?
qs.a: Rapid IV push followed by a 20 mL saline flush
qs.x: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds, so it must reach the heart quickly via rapid push and flush.
w: Slow IV push over 2 minutes into a hand vein
Dilute in 50 mL and infuse over 10 minutes
Give IM in the deltoid and repeat in 5 minutes

qs.q: Right after adenosine, the monitor shows a 4-second pause and the client reports chest heaviness and flushing. What should the nurse do?
qs.a: Continue monitoring; these effects are expected and brief
qs.x: Transient asystole, flushing, and chest pressure are expected and resolve within seconds.
w: Start chest compressions and call a code
Give atropine 1 mg IV push right away
Give a second dose of adenosine immediately

qs.q: A client taking oral amiodarone for 6 months reports a new dry cough and shortness of breath. What should the nurse do?
qs.a: Report it as possible pulmonary toxicity
qs.x: Pulmonary fibrosis is a serious amiodarone toxicity and requires prompt evaluation.
w: Tell the client it is a common cold symptom
Advise doubling fluids and using a humidifier
Hold the drug for 2 days and then restart it

qs.q: A client on warfarin is started on amiodarone. Which effect should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: INR increases
qs.x: Amiodarone inhibits warfarin metabolism and raises the INR; the warfarin dose often must be reduced.
w: INR decreases
Serum potassium rises sharply
Serum glucose falls sharply

qs.q: A client in atrial fibrillation with RVR is ordered a diltiazem infusion. Which finding requires the nurse to hold the infusion?
qs.a: Blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg
qs.x: Diltiazem lowers BP; hypotension is an indication to stop and notify the provider.
w: Heart rate of 108/min
Blood pressure of 112/70 mm Hg
Mild headache and flushing

qs.q: Diltiazem 125 mg in 125 mL is ordered at 10 mg/hr. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
qs.a: 10 mL/hr
qs.x: 125 mg/125 mL = 1 mg/mL, so 10 mg/hr = 10 mL/hr.
w: 12.5 mL/hr
1 mL/hr
5 mL/hr

qs.q: Which serum digoxin level falls within the usual therapeutic range for an adult treated for heart failure?
qs.a: 0.8 ng/mL
qs.x: The target for heart failure is about 0.5 to 0.9 ng/mL, and levels above 2.0 ng/mL are associated with toxicity. The window is narrow, which is why hypokalemia and falling renal function matter so much with this drug.
w: 2.4 ng/mL
4.0 ng/mL
0.1 ng/mL

qs.q: A client taking digoxin and furosemide reports nausea and seeing yellow halos. Which lab result is most important for the nurse to check?
qs.a: Serum potassium
qs.x: Hypokalemia from loop diuretics increases digoxin toxicity.
w: Serum sodium
Serum albumin
Serum phosphorus

qs.q: After a client receives digoxin immune Fab for toxicity, which finding should the nurse monitor closely?
qs.a: Hypokalemia
qs.x: As digoxin is bound and the Na-K pump recovers, potassium shifts back into cells and can drop.
w: Hypernatremia
Hyperglycemia
Hypercalcemia

qs.q: An infant is ordered digoxin 0.04 mg PO. The elixir contains 50 mcg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 0.8 mL
qs.x: 0.04 mg = 40 mcg; 40 divided by 50 mcg/mL = 0.8 mL.
w: 0.4 mL
8 mL

qs.q: Which action is correct when giving a nitroprusside infusion?
qs.a: Cover the bag with an opaque sleeve
qs.x: Nitroprusside breaks down in light; it is protected and given on a pump with arterial BP monitoring.
w: Infuse it by gravity without a pump
Mix it in a bag with dobutamine
Give it as a bolus before each titration

qs.q: A client has been on nitroprusside for 3 days. Which finding suggests cyanide toxicity?
qs.a: Rising lactate with metabolic acidosis
qs.x: Cyanide blocks cellular oxygen use, causing lactic acidosis, confusion, and hemodynamic instability.
w: Low blood glucose with shakiness
Bradycardia with peaked T waves
Rising hemoglobin with ruddy skin

qs.q: A client with chest pain took tadalafil about 30 hours ago. How does this change the plan for sublingual nitroglycerin?
qs.a: Nitrates are avoided for 48 hours after tadalafil
qs.x: Tadalafil is the long-acting PDE-5 inhibitor, so nitrates are held 48 hours, while sildenafil and vardenafil require 24 hours. Both drug classes act on the nitric oxide pathway, and together they cause profound hypotension.
w: Nitrates are safe once 12 hours have fully passed
Tadalafil has no meaningful interaction with nitrates
Nitrates may be given at half the usual dose

qs.q: A client is taught to use sublingual nitroglycerin at home. Which statement shows correct understanding?
qs.a: I can take one tablet every 5 minutes for up to three doses
qs.x: Up to three doses 5 minutes apart is the standard home regimen, with 911 called if pain persists after the first dose. Taking the tablets together or driving oneself both risk syncope from the abrupt fall in blood pressure.
w: I can take three tablets at once for faster relief
I should wait 15 minutes between tablets so my pressure holds
I should take one tablet and then drive myself to the hospital

qs.q: A client using a nitroglycerin transdermal patch asks why it must be removed at night. What is the best response?
qs.a: A daily patch-free period helps prevent tolerance
qs.x: A nitrate-free interval of 10 to 12 hours prevents tolerance to nitrates.
w: It keeps your blood sugar from dropping overnight
It stops the patch from causing nightmares
Your heart does not need oxygen while you sleep

qs.q: After receiving furosemide 120 mg IV push, a client reports ringing in the ears. What does the nurse suspect?
qs.a: Ototoxicity from overly rapid administration
qs.x: High-dose IV furosemide given too fast can cause ototoxicity; rates are generally no faster than 4 mg/min.
w: An expected sign that the diuretic is working
An allergic reaction to sulfa components
Hyperkalemia from the large single dose

qs.q: Two clients receive diuretics for heart failure. Which pairing of drug and expected potassium change is correct?
qs.a: Furosemide lowers potassium and spironolactone raises it
qs.x: Furosemide blocks the sodium-potassium-2-chloride transporter in the loop, so potassium is lost in the urine. Spironolactone blocks aldosterone in the distal tubule and spares potassium, which is why hyperkalemia is its major risk.
w: Furosemide raises potassium and spironolactone lowers it
Both furosemide and spironolactone lower potassium
Neither drug changes potassium when renal function is normal

qs.q: Which finding best shows IV furosemide is effective for a client with heart failure?
qs.a: Fewer crackles and a 1.5 kg weight loss
qs.x: Reduced fluid overload is shown by weight loss and improved lung sounds.
w: Blood pressure rising from 110 to 140 systolic
Serum potassium falling from 4.2 to 3.4
Heart rate increasing from 76 to 98/min

qs.q: A client taking lisinopril is started on spironolactone. Which instruction is most important?
qs.a: Avoid salt substitutes that contain potassium
qs.x: Both drugs raise potassium; potassium salt substitutes can cause dangerous hyperkalemia.
w: Increase your intake of bananas and oranges
Take a potassium supplement each morning
Expect your potassium level to fall

qs.q: A client who started lisinopril 3 days ago has a swollen tongue and lips and a hoarse voice. What is the priority action?
qs.a: Assess the airway and call the rapid response team
qs.x: Angioedema can obstruct the airway; airway protection comes first and the ACE inhibitor is stopped.
w: Give the next lisinopril dose with diphenhydramine
Apply ice packs to the lips and recheck in 1 hour
Document the finding and notify the provider in the morning

qs.q: A client taking lisinopril reports a persistent dry cough. Which change should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker
qs.x: ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, causing cough; ARBs do not affect bradykinin.
w: Adding a cough suppressant and continuing lisinopril
Doubling the lisinopril dose at bedtime
Switching to a different ACE inhibitor

qs.q: Which statement by a woman taking losartan requires follow-up by the nurse?
qs.a: We are planning to get pregnant in a few months.
qs.x: ARBs and ACE inhibitors cause fetal harm; pregnancy plans require a medication change.
w: I check my blood pressure at home every morning.
I stand up slowly when I get out of bed.
I avoid potassium-rich salt substitutes.

qs.q: Which medication order should the nurse question for a client with asthma?
qs.a: Propranolol 40 mg PO twice daily
qs.x: Nonselective beta blockers block beta-2 receptors in the lungs and can trigger bronchospasm.
w: Amlodipine 5 mg PO daily
Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily
Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg PO daily

qs.q: A client with type 1 diabetes is starting metoprolol. Which statement shows understanding?
qs.a: My shakiness and racing heart may not warn me of low sugar.
qs.x: Beta blockers mask adrenergic signs of hypoglycemia such as tremor and tachycardia; sweating may still occur.
w: Metoprolol will lower my blood sugar so I need less insulin.
I should stop insulin on days I take metoprolol.
I need to eat extra sugar with every metoprolol dose.

qs.q: After IV labetalol for severe hypertension, which action is most important before the client gets up?
qs.a: Check for orthostatic hypotension
qs.x: Labetalol has alpha-blocking effects that cause orthostatic hypotension and fall risk.
w: Check the blood glucose level
Auscultate bowel sounds
Measure the urine specific gravity

qs.q: When should the nurse draw a vancomycin trough level?
qs.a: Within 30 minutes before the next dose
qs.x: A trough reflects the lowest level and is drawn just before the next dose, usually before the fourth dose. Many hospitals now dose vancomycin by AUC monitoring instead of troughs alone, so follow facility protocol.
w: Exactly 1 hour after the infusion ends
Halfway through the infusion
Any time during the day shift

qs.q: Ten minutes into a vancomycin infusion a client has flushing of the face and neck with a stable blood pressure. What explains this reaction?
qs.a: Direct mast cell histamine release from the infusion rate
qs.x: Vancomycin infusion reaction is a direct, non-immune mast cell release tied to how fast the drug is given, so it can be resumed over at least 60 minutes after an antihistamine. Because it is not IgE-mediated it is not a true allergy.
w: An IgE-mediated allergy that bars vancomycin for his life
Bacterial endotoxin released as organisms are killed
Vasodilation caused by the sodium in the diluent

qs.q: Gentamicin is infused over 30 minutes. When should the nurse draw the peak level?
qs.a: 30 minutes after the infusion ends
qs.x: The peak for an IV aminoglycoside is drawn about 30 minutes after a 30-minute infusion is complete.
w: Right before the infusion starts
4 hours after the infusion ends
Halfway through the 30-minute infusion

qs.q: A client has received gentamicin for 6 days. Which finding is most important to report?
qs.a: Creatinine rising from 0.8 to 1.9 mg/dL
qs.x: Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic; a rising creatinine requires dose adjustment or a different drug.
w: Mild nausea after meals
Temperature down from 38.9 to 37.2 C (102-99 F)
White blood cell count down to 9,000/mm3

qs.q: A client says penicillin gave him a flat itchy rash as a child, with no swelling or trouble breathing. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is ordered. What does this history mean?
qs.a: A rash alone is low-risk and the drug is often given
qs.x: A childhood maculopapular rash without urticaria, angioedema or airway involvement is a low-risk label, and most such clients tolerate penicillins; documented anaphylaxis is what bars the class. Clavulanate is a beta-lactamase inhibitor and does not change allergy risk.
w: Any penicillin history rules out every beta-lactam antibiotic
The clavulanate component removes the risk of a reaction
A test dose will confirm whether he can tolerate the drug

qs.q: A client with a creatinine clearance of 22 mL/min is ordered ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours. Which order should the nurse question?
qs.a: The cefepime, which requires a renal dose adjustment
qs.x: Ceftriaxone is largely eliminated in bile, so its dose is not routinely adjusted for renal function. Cefepime is renally cleared, and at this clearance it accumulates and causes encephalopathy and myoclonus; most other cephalosporins also need adjustment.
w: The ceftriaxone, which requires a renal dose adjustment
Both orders, since neither drug is used in renal failure
Neither order, since cephalosporins are cleared by the liver

qs.q: A client takes ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO twice daily along with calcium carbonate, a multivitamin with iron, and a stool softener. How should the nurse schedule them?
qs.a: Give the ciprofloxacin 2 hours before the calcium and iron
qs.x: Divalent and trivalent cations such as calcium, iron, magnesium and zinc chelate fluoroquinolones in the gut and can cut absorption by more than half. The usual spacing is 2 hours before or 6 hours after the cation.
w: Give all of the medications together with a full glass of milk
Crush the ciprofloxacin and mix it in applesauce with the iron
Give the ciprofloxacin with the antacid to protect the stomach

qs.q: A client on clindamycin for 8 days has had 6 watery stools today. Which result would confirm the suspected cause?
qs.a: Stool positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin
qs.x: Clindamycin strips anaerobic gut flora and carries one of the highest risks of C. difficile colitis, which is diagnosed by stool toxin or toxin-gene testing. A normal white count and a negative occult blood test do not rule it out.
w: Stool culture growing only normal gut flora organisms
A white blood cell count of 9,000/mm3
A stool sample negative for occult blood

qs.q: Which statement indicates that the client understands teaching about metronidazole?
qs.a: I will avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 days after.
qs.x: Metronidazole with alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction.
w: I can have a glass of wine with dinner once in a while.
I will take it on an empty stomach with milk.
I will stop it once the diarrhea starts to improve.

qs.q: A client who takes valproic acid for seizures is started on meropenem. What should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: A large drop in the valproic acid level
qs.x: Carbapenems sharply lower valproic acid levels and can lead to breakthrough seizures.
w: A rise in valproic acid to toxic levels
No interaction between the two drugs
Increased risk of meropenem allergy

qs.q: A client on a morphine PCA is difficult to arouse, has pinpoint pupils, and a respiratory rate of 7/min. What is the nurse's first action?
qs.a: Stop the PCA and prepare naloxone
qs.x: Opioid-induced respiratory depression requires stopping the opioid and reversing it with naloxone while supporting breathing.
w: Lower the PCA dose and recheck in 1 hour
Raise the head of bed and apply oxygen
Notify the provider and document findings

qs.q: A family member is seen pressing the PCA button while the client sleeps. What should the nurse do?
qs.a: Explain that only the client should press it
qs.x: PCA by proxy bypasses the built-in safety of sedation (a sedated client cannot press the button) and can cause overdose and respiratory depression.
w: Thank them for helping control the pain
Ask them to press it only every 2 hours
Increase the lockout interval to be safe

qs.q: A client's respirations improved after naloxone for opioid overdose. Which is the priority ongoing assessment?
qs.a: Watch for respiratory depression returning
qs.x: Naloxone's duration is shorter than many opioids, so sedation and respiratory depression can return.
w: Watch for hypoglycemia over the next hour
Watch for urinary retention
Watch for a rash at the IV site

qs.q: Hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV is ordered. The vial contains 2 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.x: 0.5 mg divided by 2 mg/mL = 0.25 mL.
w: 0.5 mL
2.5 mL
0.4 mL

qs.q: A client with a fentanyl transdermal patch now has a fever of 39.4°C. What is the nurse's primary concern?
qs.a: Increased drug absorption and oversedation
qs.x: Heat increases skin blood flow and fentanyl absorption, raising the risk of respiratory depression.
w: Decreased drug absorption and increased pain
Loss of patch adhesion and detachment
Conversion of fentanyl to an inactive form

qs.q: A client on methadone maintenance is admitted. Which finding requires the nurse to notify the provider before the next dose?
qs.a: QTc interval of 520 milliseconds
qs.x: Methadone prolongs the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes.
w: Constipation for the past 2 days despite docusate
Pupils 3 mm and reactive to light
Respiratory rate of 16/min

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client discharged on scheduled oxycodone?
qs.a: Take a stool softener and a stimulant laxative daily
qs.x: Opioid-induced constipation does not resolve over time, so a bowel regimen is started along with the opioid.
w: Take it with a glass of wine to help you relax
Stop taking it abruptly once the pain is gone
Drive as usual once the first dose takes effect

qs.q: A client taking sertraline is prescribed tramadol. Which findings should the nurse teach the client to report?
qs.a: Agitation, sweating, and muscle twitching
qs.x: Tramadol combined with an SSRI can cause serotonin syndrome; tramadol also lowers the seizure threshold.
w: Drowsiness and dry mouth during the first few days
Mild constipation and nausea
Itching without a rash

qs.q: Flumazenil is ordered for a client oversedated with lorazepam who has taken benzodiazepines daily for 10 years. What is the nurse's primary concern?
qs.a: It may precipitate seizures
qs.x: Flumazenil can trigger abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal and seizures in clients who use benzodiazepines chronically.
w: It may cause respiratory depression
It may increase sedation
It may cause severe hypertension

qs.q: During moderate sedation with midazolam and fentanyl, which finding requires immediate intervention?
qs.a: EtCO2 rising from 38 to 58 mm Hg with an RR of 6/min
qs.x: A rising end-tidal CO2 with a low respiratory rate indicates hypoventilation, often before SpO2 falls.
w: Responding to voice and following commands
SpO2 of 96% on 2 L via nasal cannula
Heart rate decreasing from 92 to 80/min

qs.q: Which action is correct when maintaining a propofol infusion?
qs.a: Change the tubing and bottle every 12 hours
qs.x: Propofol is a lipid emulsion that supports bacterial growth, so strict aseptic technique and hang-time limits apply.
w: Mix it with the client's antibiotic infusion
Keep an opened vial at the bedside for 24 hours
Use it as the client's only pain medication

qs.q: A ventilated client on propofol is grimacing and has a heart rate of 118/min after turning. What should the nurse do?
qs.a: Assess for pain and give the ordered analgesic
qs.x: Propofol has no analgesic properties, so pain must be treated separately.
w: Increase the propofol because it relieves pain
Document it as an expected response to turning
Give a paralytic to stop the grimacing

qs.q: A client is sedated on a dexmedetomidine infusion in the ICU. How does this drug differ from a propofol or midazolam infusion?
qs.a: It sedates with little respiratory depression
qs.x: Dexmedetomidine is a central alpha-2 agonist, so clients stay rousable and keep their respiratory drive, which is why it is used during ventilator weaning. Its hallmark adverse effects are bradycardia and hypotension, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines instead.
w: It raises both the heart rate and blood pressure
It gives deep sedation with full amnesia
It can be reversed with flumazenil

qs.q: A client sedated with ketamine in the ED is emerging from sedation, appears frightened, and is hallucinating. What should the nurse do?
qs.a: Reduce stimulation and prepare a benzodiazepine
qs.x: Emergence reactions are managed with a calm, quiet environment and, if needed, a benzodiazepine.
w: Turn on bright lights and speak loudly to reorient the client
Give a second full dose of ketamine by IV push
Restrain all four limbs and leave the room

qs.q: After rapid sequence intubation with etomidate, a client with sepsis remains hypotensive. Which effect of etomidate may be contributing?
qs.a: Adrenal suppression
qs.x: Etomidate inhibits cortisol synthesis, which may worsen hypotension in septic shock.
w: Histamine release
Malignant hyperthermia
Hyperkalemia

qs.q: For which client should the nurse question an order for succinylcholine for intubation?
qs.a: A client with a potassium level of 6.1 after a crush injury
qs.x: Succinylcholine raises serum potassium and can cause cardiac arrest in clients with hyperkalemia or with crush or burn injuries after the first day.
w: A client with pneumonia and a potassium level of 4.0
A client with an overdose and a normal potassium level
A client with an acute asthma attack and normal labs

qs.q: Shortly after receiving succinylcholine, a surgical client develops jaw rigidity, a sharp rise in EtCO2, and tachycardia. What should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Stopping triggering agents and giving dantrolene
qs.x: These are early signs of malignant hyperthermia; dantrolene is the antidote.
w: Giving more succinylcholine to relieve the rigidity
Giving acetaminophen and using cooling blankets only
Giving naloxone to reverse the sedation

qs.q: A client is intubated and receiving a continuous rocuronium infusion. What is the nurse's priority?
qs.a: Ensuring ongoing sedation and analgesia
qs.x: Paralytics provide no sedation or analgesia; a paralyzed client must be sedated to prevent awareness.
w: Checking for intact cough and gag reflexes
Encouraging deep-breathing exercises
Keeping the client NPO because of aspiration risk

qs.q: Which teaching is essential for a female client who received sugammadex at the end of surgery?
qs.a: Use a backup birth control method for 7 days
qs.x: Sugammadex binds progestogens and reduces hormonal contraceptive effectiveness, similar to a missed dose.
w: Avoid dairy products and leafy greens for 48 hours
Expect your urine to turn orange for a day
Take your birth control pill twice tomorrow

qs.q: A train-of-four test is performed on a client receiving vecuronium. Which result typically reflects the target level of blockade?
qs.a: 1 to 2 twitches out of 4
qs.x: One or two twitches usually reflect adequate blockade without excessive paralysis.
w: 0 twitches out of 4
4 strong twitches out of 4
3 to 4 twitches with fade

qs.q: Neostigmine is given to reverse neuromuscular blockade. Why is glycopyrrolate given with it?
qs.a: To prevent bradycardia
qs.x: Neostigmine also increases acetylcholine at muscarinic sites; an anticholinergic prevents bradycardia and excess secretions.
w: To prevent hypertension
To speed reversal
To prevent hypoglycemia

qs.q: Which action is correct when giving IV phenytoin?
qs.a: Dilute in normal saline; give no faster than 50 mg/min
qs.x: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions and causes hypotension and dysrhythmias if given too fast.
w: Mix in D5W and infuse as fast as the client tolerates
Give it IM in the deltoid if the IV is not patent
Dilute it in lactated Ringer's and push over 1 minute

qs.q: A client with a serum albumin of 2.1 g/dL has a total phenytoin level reported as 9 mcg/mL. Why may this level be misleading?
qs.a: Low albumin lowers the total while free drug is therapeutic
qs.x: Phenytoin is about 90 percent albumin bound and only the free fraction is active. With low albumin, less drug is carried in the bound pool, so the total reads low while the free level may be in range; the quoted 10 to 20 mcg/mL range assumes normal albumin.
w: Low albumin raises the total level and hides a low free level
Phenytoin is not protein bound, so albumin has no effect
Phenytoin levels are only valid when drawn after a meal

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking long-term phenytoin indicates correct understanding?
qs.a: "I will brush and floss carefully every day."
qs.x: Gingival hyperplasia is common; switching brands or stopping abruptly can change drug levels or cause seizures.
w: "I can switch brands whenever one is cheaper."
"I can stop it once I have been seizure-free for a month."
"I will take an antacid with each dose."

qs.q: What is an advantage of fosphenytoin over IV phenytoin?
qs.a: It can be infused faster with less tissue injury
qs.x: Fosphenytoin is water-soluble, causes less purple glove syndrome, and can be infused at up to 150 mg PE/min.
w: It never requires blood level monitoring
It can be mixed with any IV fluid in the line
It cannot cause hypotension or dysrhythmias

qs.q: Which report from a client taking levetiracetam should the nurse follow up on?
qs.a: "I have been feeling angry and hopeless."
qs.x: Levetiracetam can cause irritability, depression, and suicidal thoughts.
w: "I feel a little sleepy in the afternoon."
"I have had a slight headache this week."
"I am a bit dizzy when I first stand up."

qs.q: A client taking valproic acid reports severe abdominal pain radiating to the back and vomiting. What does the nurse suspect?
qs.a: Pancreatitis
qs.x: Valproic acid carries boxed warnings for pancreatitis and hepatotoxicity.
w: Viral gastroenteritis
An expected adjustment effect
Drug-induced kidney stones

qs.q: Which finding in a client taking carbamazepine should the nurse report immediately?
qs.a: Fever, sore throat, and a blistering rash
qs.x: Carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
w: Mild drowsiness during the first week
Slight dizziness when standing
Mild nausea when a dose is taken on an empty stomach

qs.q: A client starts lamotrigine on a schedule that raises the dose slowly over about 6 weeks. What is the reason for the slow titration?
qs.a: It lowers the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome
qs.x: The risk of serious rash, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, rises with rapid dose escalation, so the manufacturer's schedule takes about 6 weeks to reach maintenance. Adding valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine levels, so the starting dose is halved.
w: It lets the kidneys adapt to clearing the drug
It prevents withdrawal seizures between doses
It allows a blood level to be checked each week

qs.q: A client on maintenance lithium has a level of 1.6 mEq/L. Which finding fits this level?
qs.a: Coarse hand tremor and nausea
qs.x: Maintenance levels run about 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L, and 1.5 to 2.0 mEq/L brings coarse tremor, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. A fine tremor and polyuria occur at therapeutic levels, while seizures and stupor appear above roughly 2.5 mEq/L.
w: A fine tremor present since the first week
Seizures and a decreased level of consciousness
Polyuria and thirst since the drug was started

qs.q: Which statement by a client taking lithium indicates a need for further teaching?
qs.a: "I am going to start a low-salt diet."
qs.x: Low sodium intake causes lithium retention and toxicity.
w: "I will drink about 2 to 3 liters of fluid daily."
"I will have my blood level checked as ordered."
"I will call if I have vomiting or diarrhea."

qs.q: A client taking lithium has several new orders. Which order should the nurse question?
qs.a: Ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours
qs.x: NSAIDs decrease lithium clearance and raise lithium levels.
w: Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours
Docusate 100 mg twice daily
Famotidine 20 mg twice daily

qs.q: A client taking clozapine reports a sore throat and a fever of 38.6°C. What should the nurse do first?
qs.a: Check the most recent absolute neutrophil count
qs.x: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia; signs of infection require an urgent ANC.
w: Give acetaminophen and recheck the temperature in 4 hours
Encourage warm saltwater gargles
Hold fluids to reduce secretions

qs.q: A client on haloperidol has a temperature of 104 F, lead-pipe rigidity, and a creatine kinase of 4,200 units/L. Which syndrome do these findings fit?
qs.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
qs.x: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome brings fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability and a high creatine kinase from muscle breakdown, and it builds over days. Serotonin syndrome instead causes hyperreflexia, clonus and diarrhea and appears within hours.
w: Serotonin syndrome from an SSRI
An acute dystonic reaction
Tardive dyskinesia of the tongue

qs.q: A client given haloperidol develops sudden twisting of the neck and upward rolling of the eyes. Which order should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV or IM
qs.x: Acute dystonia is treated with an anticholinergic such as diphenhydramine or benztropine.
w: Haloperidol 5 mg IM now
Lorazepam 0.5 mg PO at bedtime
Naloxone 0.4 mg IV push

qs.q: Which monitoring is most important for a client taking olanzapine long-term?
qs.a: Weight, fasting glucose, and lipids
qs.x: Second-generation antipsychotics such as olanzapine cause weight gain, diabetes, and dyslipidemia.
w: Monthly serum lithium levels
Daily peak flow readings
Hearing tests and eye exams every 6 months

qs.q: An 80-year-old client is started on quetiapine. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give?
qs.a: Rise slowly from a lying or sitting position
qs.x: Quetiapine causes orthostatic hypotension and sedation, which increase the risk of falls in older adults.
w: Take it with grapefruit juice
Avoid all dairy products
Expect reddish-orange urine for a few days

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse give about ziprasidone?
qs.a: Take it with a meal
qs.x: Ziprasidone absorption roughly doubles with food; the drug also prolongs the QT interval.
w: Take it on an empty stomach
Take it with an antacid
Crush it in applesauce

qs.q: A client recently started on sertraline along with another serotonergic drug has agitation, diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, and leg clonus. What does the nurse suspect?
qs.a: Serotonin syndrome
qs.x: Clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome; NMS causes lead-pipe rigidity and slowed reflexes.
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Acute dystonic reaction
Anticholinergic toxicity

qs.q: Which statement by a client starting fluoxetine indicates a need for further teaching?
qs.a: "I can stop it as soon as I feel better."
qs.x: Antidepressants should not be stopped abruptly, and their full effect takes several weeks.
w: "It may take several weeks to feel the full effect."
"I will report any thoughts of hurting myself."
"I will take it in the morning if it keeps me awake."

qs.q: A client taking phenelzine ate aged cheese and salami and now has a severe occipital headache and a BP of 210/120 mm Hg. What does the nurse suspect?
qs.a: Hypertensive crisis
qs.x: MAOIs taken with tyramine-rich foods can cause a hypertensive crisis.
w: Serotonin syndrome
Orthostatic hypotension
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

qs.q: A client taking fluoxetine is to be switched to an MAOI. What should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: A washout period of about 5 weeks
qs.x: Because of fluoxetine's long half-life, about 5 weeks must pass before an MAOI is started to prevent serotonin syndrome.
w: Starting the MAOI the next morning
Taking both drugs together for 1 week
A washout period of 24 hours

qs.q: For which client should the nurse question an order for bupropion?
qs.a: A client with bulimia nervosa
qs.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in clients with eating disorders or seizure disorders.
w: A client trying to quit smoking
A client with seasonal depression
A client taking an SSRI who has low sexual desire

qs.q: Which adverse effect of trazodone should the nurse teach a male client to report immediately?
qs.a: An erection lasting more than 4 hours
qs.x: Priapism is a rare but serious emergency with trazodone.
w: Mild morning drowsiness
Dry mouth during the day
Mild dizziness when standing up quickly

qs.q: Which parameter should the nurse monitor in a client taking high doses of venlafaxine?
qs.a: Blood pressure
qs.x: Venlafaxine can cause sustained, dose-related hypertension.
w: Serum potassium
Blood glucose
Hearing acuity

qs.q: Which order should the nurse question for an 84-year-old client?
qs.a: Diphenhydramine 50 mg at bedtime for sleep
qs.x: Diphenhydramine is on the Beers list because of anticholinergic effects such as confusion, falls, and urinary retention.
w: Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours for pain
Melatonin 3 mg at bedtime for sleep
Polyethylene glycol 17 g daily for constipation

qs.q: A newly admitted 82-year-old client takes glyburide. Why should the nurse discuss this drug with the provider?
qs.a: It causes prolonged hypoglycemia
qs.x: Glyburide is on the Beers list because of prolonged hypoglycemia in older adults.
w: It causes severe hyperkalemia
It raises the risk of lactic acidosis
It often causes severe weight loss

qs.q: An 88-year-old client asks for temazepam for sleep. Which risk should the nurse discuss with the provider?
qs.a: Falls and confusion
qs.x: In older adults, benzodiazepines increase the risk of falls, fractures, and delirium.
w: Hypertensive crisis
Severe hyperglycemia
Excessive daytime energy

qs.q: Which statement indicates that the client understands teaching about zolpidem?
qs.a: "I will take it right before bed when I can sleep 7 to 8 hours."
qs.x: Zolpidem can cause next-day impairment and complex sleep behaviors; it is taken only at bedtime.
w: "I will take it with a glass of wine to help it work."
"I can drive to work 2 hours after taking it."
"I will take an extra tablet if I wake up at 3 AM."

qs.q: A client has taken prednisone 40 mg daily for 4 months and asks why the dose is being stepped down over weeks. What is the best response?
qs.a: Your adrenal glands need time to make cortisol again
qs.x: Daily steroids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis after about 2 to 3 weeks, so an abrupt stop can cause adrenal crisis with hypotension, weakness and hypoglycemia. The taper gives endogenous cortisol production time to recover.
w: The drug must clear slowly to protect your kidneys
Stopping quickly would make your blood sugar drop fast
A slow taper keeps the medicine from upsetting you

qs.q: A client on long-term prednisone has been NPO for 2 days and is now confused with a BP of 78/40 mm Hg. Which drug should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV
qs.x: Missed steroid doses can cause adrenal crisis, which is treated with IV hydrocortisone and fluids.
w: Dexamethasone 4 mg PO
Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg PO
Prednisone 5 mg PO

qs.q: A client without diabetes is receiving high-dose IV methylprednisolone. Which finding is most important to monitor?
qs.a: Blood glucose
qs.x: Corticosteroids cause hyperglycemia that may require insulin coverage.
w: Serum calcium
Hearing acuity
Serum ammonia

qs.q: A client on high-dose dexamethasone for cerebral edema is also started on pantoprazole. What is the reason for the second drug?
qs.a: Steroids raise the risk of gastric ulceration and bleeding
qs.x: Glucocorticoids reduce mucosal prostaglandins and impair healing, so ulcer and GI bleeding risk rises, particularly at high dose or alongside an NSAID. Acid suppression is added for that reason, not to change absorption or glucose.
w: Pantoprazole improves the absorption of dexamethasone tablets
Pantoprazole prevents the steroid from raising glucose
Steroids cause reflux by relaxing the lower esophagus

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client taking levothyroxine?
qs.a: Take it on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast
qs.x: Food, calcium, and iron reduce levothyroxine absorption.
w: Take it with your calcium and iron to improve absorption
Take it at bedtime with a full meal and milk
Skip doses on days you feel full of energy

qs.q: An older adult with coronary artery disease recently started levothyroxine. Which finding requires immediate action?
qs.a: Chest pain and a heart rate of 118/min
qs.x: Levothyroxine increases cardiac oxygen demand and can trigger angina or dysrhythmias.
w: Mild fatigue and feeling cold in the first week
Weight loss of 0.5 kg in a month
Feeling less cold than before

qs.q: Which finding should the nurse teach a client taking propylthiouracil to report immediately?
qs.a: Dark urine and yellowing of the skin
qs.x: PTU carries a boxed warning for severe liver injury.
w: Mild itching of the arms without a rash
Feeling warm in a hot room
A metallic taste in the mouth

qs.q: A client taking methimazole develops a sore throat and fever. Which lab should the nurse expect to be ordered?
qs.a: Complete blood count with differential
qs.x: Methimazole can cause agranulocytosis.
w: Thyroid-stimulating hormone level
Serum calcium level
Hemoglobin A1C

qs.q: A client in thyroid storm has orders for propylthiouracil and an iodine solution. Which sequence is correct?
qs.a: Give PTU at least 1 hour before the iodine
qs.x: The thionamide is given first so that the iodine cannot be used to synthesize new thyroid hormone.
w: Give the iodine first, then PTU 1 hour later
Give both at the same time to speed recovery
Give the iodine only, and hold PTU until stable

qs.q: A client receiving desmopressin reports a headache and nausea and has new confusion. Which laboratory value is most important to check?
qs.a: Serum sodium
qs.x: Desmopressin causes water retention and dilutional hyponatremia.
w: Serum potassium
Serum glucose
Serum calcium

qs.q: A client with bleeding esophageal varices is on an octreotide infusion. Which finding best indicates that it is effective?
qs.a: Stable hemoglobin and no further hematemesis
qs.x: Octreotide reduces portal blood flow and bleeding from varices.
w: Blood glucose falling below 70 mg/dL during the infusion
Heart rate rising from 88 to 118/min
Recurrence of black, tarry stools

qs.q: Two clients react during a transfusion. Which finding points to an acute hemolytic reaction rather than a febrile nonhemolytic one?
qs.a: Flank pain with dark red-brown urine
qs.x: An acute hemolytic reaction is ABO incompatibility: free hemoglobin from lysed cells reaches the urine and causes flank pain and renal failure. Fever with chills alone is the far more common febrile reaction from donor leukocyte cytokines, and hives suggest a mild allergic reaction.
w: A temperature rise of 1.5 C with chills
Mild headache during the first 20 minutes
Hives on the chest that fade with an antihistamine

qs.q: After stopping a transfusion for a suspected reaction, which solution should the nurse use to keep the vein open?
qs.a: 0.9% sodium chloride with new tubing
qs.x: New tubing prevents infusion of more blood; normal saline is the only IV fluid compatible with blood products.
w: D5W through the blood tubing
Lactated Ringer's through the blood tubing
0.9% sodium chloride through the blood tubing

qs.q: A client develops dyspnea and bilateral infiltrates an hour into a transfusion. Which finding separates circulatory overload from acute lung injury?
qs.a: A rising blood pressure with distended neck veins
qs.x: Circulatory overload is a volume problem, so venous and arterial pressures rise and the client improves with a diuretic. Transfusion-related acute lung injury is capillary leak with a normal or low blood pressure, and hypoxemia with crackles occurs in both.
w: A temperature of 38.5 C with shaking chills
An oxygen saturation that falls below 90 percent on air
Crackles heard through both lung fields

qs.q: Which task can the RN delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) during a blood transfusion?
qs.a: Taking vital signs at intervals set by the RN
qs.x: UAP may take vital signs; verification, assessment, and administration remain with licensed nurses.
w: Checking the blood unit with another nurse
Assessing the client for a transfusion reaction
Starting the transfusion after the first 15 minutes

qs.q: A client receiving chemotherapy has a WBC of 2,000/mm3 with 25% segmented neutrophils and 5% bands. What is the absolute neutrophil count?
qs.x: ANC = WBC x (segs + bands); 2,000 x 0.30 = 600.

qs.q: A client receiving filgrastim reports several symptoms. Which one requires immediate follow-up?
qs.a: Left upper abdominal pain radiating to the shoulder
qs.x: Left upper quadrant or shoulder pain may signal splenic rupture; bone pain is expected.
w: Aching bones in the lower back and hips
Mild redness at the subcutaneous injection site
A low-grade headache relieved by acetaminophen

qs.q: What should the nurse wear when hanging an IV chemotherapy drug?
qs.a: Two pairs of chemotherapy gloves and a disposable gown
qs.x: Hazardous drug handling requires double chemotherapy-tested gloves and an impermeable gown.
w: One pair of sterile gloves and a cloth gown
A surgical mask and one pair of exam gloves
A face shield and no gloves, for a better grip

qs.q: A vesicant chemotherapy drug has extravasated at a peripheral IV site. Which step comes before the catheter is removed?
qs.a: Aspirate residual drug back through the catheter
qs.x: The catheter stays in place so residual drug can be aspirated and any antidote given along the same path; flushing or diluting drives more vesicant into the tissue. Cold is applied for most vesicants, with heat reserved for the vinca alkaloids.
w: Flush the catheter with 10 mL of normal saline
Infuse warm saline to dilute the drug in the tissue
Inject lidocaine around the site to relieve pain

qs.q: A client with neutropenia has a new temperature of 38.4°C. Which action is the priority?
qs.a: Draw blood cultures and start antibiotics within 1 hour
qs.x: Neutropenic fever is an emergency; empiric antibiotics such as cefepime are started within 60 minutes, after cultures are drawn.
w: Recheck the temperature in 4 hours before acting
Give acetaminophen and encourage fluids only
Wait for the ANC result before starting antibiotics

qs.q: A client with chronic kidney disease is due for epoetin alfa. Which finding should cause the nurse to hold the dose?
qs.a: Hemoglobin of 12.4 g/dL and BP of 168/100
qs.x: Epoetin is held when hemoglobin exceeds the target or hypertension is uncontrolled because of the risk of thrombosis.
w: Hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL and BP of 128/78
Ferritin level within the normal range
Serum potassium of 4.6 mEq/L

qs.q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client taking oral ferrous sulfate?
qs.a: Take it with orange juice and expect dark stools
qs.x: Vitamin C enhances iron absorption; dark green or black stools are expected.
w: Take it with milk to protect your stomach
Take it at the same time as your antacid
Stop taking it if your stools become dark

qs.q: A kidney transplant client taking tacrolimus asks what to avoid. Which item raises the tacrolimus level enough to risk toxicity?
qs.a: Grapefruit juice
qs.x: Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, the enzyme that metabolizes tacrolimus, so blood levels can climb sharply and bring tremor, nephrotoxicity and hyperglycemia. Levels are followed with trough samples drawn just before a dose.
w: A high-potassium banana
Acetaminophen 650 mg
A calcium carbonate antacid

qs.q: Which statement indicates that a transplant client understands teaching about cyclosporine?
qs.a: "I will have my blood drawn before my morning dose."
qs.x: Trough levels are drawn before the dose; grapefruit increases cyclosporine levels.
w: "I will drink grapefruit juice with each dose."
"I can skip doses if I feel well."
"I will have my level drawn 2 hours after my dose."

qs.q: Which teaching is most important for a female client of childbearing age taking mycophenolate?
qs.a: Use two reliable methods of birth control
qs.x: Mycophenolate can cause pregnancy loss and birth defects.
w: Take it with a high-fat meal to improve absorption
Avoid all green leafy vegetables
Expect your urine to turn orange

qs.q: A client taking azathioprine is prescribed allopurinol for gout. Why should the nurse clarify the order?
qs.a: Allopurinol greatly increases azathioprine toxicity
qs.x: Allopurinol blocks azathioprine breakdown, which can cause severe bone marrow suppression.
w: Allopurinol makes azathioprine less effective
Azathioprine prevents allopurinol absorption
No interaction exists, so the order is safe to give

qs.q: A client ingested a large amount of acetaminophen 6 hours ago and has no symptoms. What should the nurse anticipate?
qs.a: Starting acetylcysteine without waiting for symptoms
qs.x: Acetylcysteine is most effective when started within 8 hours; early overdose is often asymptomatic.
w: Discharge after 4 hours of observation
Giving naloxone and observing for 2 hours
Waiting for liver enzymes to rise before treating

qs.q: A client takes oxycodone-acetaminophen 5/325 mg, 2 tablets every 4 hours (6 doses daily), plus an additional 1,000 mg of acetaminophen daily. What is the client's total daily acetaminophen intake?
qs.a: 4,900 mg, which exceeds the usual maximum
qs.x: 650 mg x 6 = 3,900 mg plus 1,000 mg = 4,900 mg; the usual adult maximum is 4 g per day.
w: 3,900 mg, which is within the usual maximum
1,950 mg, which is within the usual maximum
2,950 mg, which is within the usual maximum

qs.q: Amoxicillin 40 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours is ordered for a child weighing 22 lb. The suspension is 250 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give per dose?
qs.a: 4 mL
qs.x: 22 lb = 10 kg; 400 mg/day divided by 2 = 200 mg per dose; 200 divided by 50 mg/mL = 4 mL.
w: 8 mL
2 mL

qs.q: Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg is ordered for a child weighing 18 kg. The liquid is 160 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
qs.a: 8.4 mL
qs.x: 15 x 18 = 270 mg; 160 mg/5 mL = 32 mg/mL; 270 divided by 32 = 8.4 mL.

2.7 mL

qs.q: A loading dose of phenytoin 20 mg/kg is ordered for a 70 kg adult. At the maximum adult rate of 50 mg/min, what is the shortest safe infusion time?
qs.a: 28 minutes
qs.x: 20 x 70 = 1,400 mg; 1,400 divided by 50 mg/min = 28 minutes.
w: 14 minutes
40 minutes
7 minutes

qs.q: The nurse receives report on four clients on a psychiatric unit. Which client should the nurse see first?
qs.a: A client on clozapine with a fever and sore throat
qs.x: Fever and sore throat with clozapine may signal severe neutropenia and life-threatening infection.
w: A client on lithium with a level of 0.9 mEq/L and mild thirst
A client on sertraline who reports trouble falling asleep
A client on haloperidol who asks for a snack

qs.q: Which medication task is appropriate for the RN to assign to an LPN?
qs.a: Reinforcing warfarin diet teaching provided by the RN
qs.x: LPNs can reinforce teaching; initial teaching, assessment of new changes, and clinical decisions belong to the RN.
w: Assessing a client on warfarin who has new confusion
Planning discharge teaching for a new warfarin user
Deciding whether to hold warfarin based on today's INR

qs.q: Which instruction should the RN give to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) caring for a client receiving IV furosemide?
qs.a: Measure and record all urine output this shift
qs.x: UAP can measure intake and output; assessment and medication decisions remain with the nurse.
w: Decide whether to give the next dose based on output
Assess the client's lung sounds every 4 hours
Check the potassium result and adjust the diet

qs.q: Four clients are receiving antibiotics. Which client should the nurse see first?
qs.a: A client on vancomycin with wheezing and throat tightness
qs.x: Wheezing and throat tightness suggest anaphylaxis, which threatens the airway.
w: A client on vancomycin with a trough due at 0600
A client on cephalexin with mild nausea after breakfast
A client on amoxicillin who asks for an extra pillow

qs.q: Which client should the nurse assess first?
qs.a: A client on a morphine PCA with a sedation score of 3 and an RR of 9/min
qs.x: Increasing sedation and a low respiratory rate precede opioid-induced respiratory arrest.
w: A client on oxycodone reporting pain of 5 out of 10 before a dose
A client on hydrocodone asking when the next dose is due
A client on morphine who has had constipation for 2 days

qs.q: Four clients are receiving potassium replacement. Which client should the nurse see first?
qs.a: A client receiving IV potassium chloride with new burning and swelling at the site
qs.x: Potassium infiltration can cause tissue damage; the infusion must be stopped immediately.
w: A client on oral potassium who asks for juice to take it with
A client whose potassium is now 4.0 mEq/L after two rounds of replacement
A client due for a potassium level recheck at 1000

qs.q: Four clients with diabetes are on the nurse's assignment. Which client should the nurse see first?
qs.a: A client who received lispro 20 minutes ago and refuses breakfast
qs.x: Rapid-acting insulin without food will soon cause hypoglycemia.
w: A client on glargine with a fasting glucose of 132 mg/dL
A client on metformin asking about tonight's dinner
A client on NPH who needs foot care teaching today

qs.q: Which task can the RN assign to an LPN on a postpartum unit?
qs.a: Giving scheduled oral ibuprofen to a stable client
qs.x: LPNs give routine oral medications to stable clients; titration and assessment of unstable clients remain with the RN.
w: Titrating the oxytocin infusion for a client with heavy bleeding
Assessing a client on magnesium sulfate with new blurred vision
Providing initial teaching about methylergonovine side effects

qs.q: Before giving metoprolol succinate 50 mg PO to a client with heart failure, which assessment is most important?
qs.a: Apical pulse and blood pressure
qs.x: Beta blockers slow the heart rate and lower blood pressure; check both before each dose and hold the dose according to the ordered parameters.
w: Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Pupil size and reaction to light
Skin turgor over the sternum and forearms

qs.q: Before the morning dose of levothyroxine, the nurse should first confirm that:
qs.a: The client has not yet eaten breakfast
qs.x: Levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast and at least 4 hours apart from calcium or iron.
w: The client has already taken the morning calcium dose
The client has had a glass of milk or juice
The client's bedtime glucose was normal

qs.q: Which result is most important to review before giving spironolactone to a client with heart failure?
qs.a: Most recent serum potassium level
qs.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing; hyperkalemia is its major risk, so check potassium and renal function before giving.
w: Most recent serum calcium level
Most recent hemoglobin A1c result
Number of bowel movements since yesterday

qs.q: Before giving metformin to a client admitted with vomiting and dehydration, which data should the nurse review?
qs.a: Recent serum creatinine and eGFR
qs.x: Metformin is cleared by the kidneys; dehydration and a low eGFR raise the risk of lactic acidosis.
w: Recent TSH and free T4 levels
Recent lipid panel results
Recent serum amylase and lipase levels

qs.q: Before and after albuterol is given by nebulizer, which assessment best shows the drug's effect?
qs.a: Breath sounds and work of breathing
qs.x: Albuterol is a bronchodilator; assess lung sounds, respiratory effort, SpO2, and heart rate before and after the treatment.
w: Capillary refill in the fingertips
Bowel sounds and abdominal girth
Blood glucose and level of consciousness

qs.q: Before giving insulin lispro with a meal, the nurse should first check:
qs.a: The fingerstick glucose and that the meal tray is present
qs.x: Rapid-acting insulin starts working in about 15 minutes; confirm the glucose and that food is available before giving it.
w: The serum sodium and that the client is sitting upright
The blood pressure and that the client has voided
The temperature and that the IV line is patent

qs.q: Before giving the evening dose of warfarin, which assessment is most important?
qs.a: Today's INR result and any signs of bleeding
qs.x: The INR guides warfarin dosing; the nurse also assesses for bleeding before each dose.
w: Today's potassium result and any muscle cramps
Today's glucose result and any shakiness
Today's sodium result and any new ankle swelling

qs.q: A client with gout is prescribed hydrochlorothiazide. Which data should the nurse review before the first dose?
qs.a: Recent uric acid level and gout flares
qs.x: Thiazides raise uric acid levels and can trigger gout attacks.
w: Recent amylase level and alcohol use
Recent vitamin B12 level and diet
Recent TSH level and weight changes

qs.q: Before starting oral amiodarone, which baseline studies should the nurse confirm have been done?
qs.a: Thyroid, liver, and pulmonary function tests
qs.x: Amiodarone can cause thyroid disease, liver injury, and pulmonary toxicity; baselines are needed along with an ECG and eye exam.
w: Serum amylase, lipase, and a lipid panel
Complete blood count and blood cultures
Hemoglobin A1c and urine microalbumin

qs.q: Before giving diltiazem 20 mg IV push for atrial fibrillation with RVR, which assessment is most important?
qs.a: Blood pressure and the ECG rhythm
qs.x: IV diltiazem can cause hypotension, bradycardia, and heart block; check BP and confirm the rhythm on a continuous monitor.
w: Serum glucose and urine output
Temperature and white blood cell count
Pupil response and level of consciousness

qs.q: Before starting a weight-based heparin infusion, which baseline data should the nurse verify?
qs.a: Current weight, aPTT or anti-Xa, platelets, and hemoglobin
qs.x: Dosing depends on an accurate weight; baseline coagulation tests and a CBC with platelets are needed to monitor bleeding and HIT.
w: Current weight, serum sodium, potassium, chloride, and glucose levels
Height, lipid panel, and liver enzymes
Temperature, blood cultures, and white blood cell count

qs.q: A client with hypomagnesemia is to receive IV magnesium sulfate. Which assessment should the nurse perform before and during the infusion?
qs.a: Deep tendon reflexes, respirations, and urine output
qs.x: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is an early sign of magnesium toxicity; monitor respirations and urine output because magnesium is renally excreted.
w: Pupil size, bowel sounds, and skin turgor
Capillary glucose, temperature, and pain score
Peripheral pulses, edema, and daily weight

qs.q: Before starting an IV nitroglycerin infusion for unstable angina, which question is most important to ask the client?
qs.a: Have you taken sildenafil or tadalafil in the past 48 hours?
qs.x: Nitrates with PDE-5 inhibitors can cause severe, refractory hypotension (avoid within 24 hours of sildenafil and 48 hours of tadalafil).
w: Have you had any recent changes in your bowel habits?
Do you have an allergy to shellfish or iodine dye?
Have you ever had a reaction to latex gloves or IV tubing in the past?

qs.q: Before giving insulin glargine to a client who is NPO for surgery, the nurse should first:
qs.a: Check the glucose and clarify the dose with the provider
qs.x: Basal insulin is usually continued, often at a reduced dose, when NPO; check glucose and confirm the dose rather than omitting it.
w: Hold the dose entirely until the client is able to eat again
Give the dose mixed with a rapid-acting insulin
Give double the dose to cover the stress of surgery

qs.q: Before increasing the theophylline dose for a client with poorly controlled asthma, which data should the nurse review?
qs.a: Serum theophylline level and heart rate
qs.x: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range (about 5 to 15 mcg/mL); toxicity causes tachycardia, dysrhythmias, and seizures.
w: Serum potassium level and urine output
Serum calcium level and bone density
Hemoglobin and peripheral pulses

qs.q: Four clients are due for oral digoxin. Which apical pulse, counted for a full minute, meets the usual parameter to hold the dose in an adult?
qs.a: 52 beats per minute
qs.x: The standard adult parameter is to hold digoxin and report an apical pulse below 60 beats per minute, because digoxin slows conduction through the AV node. A fast rate is not a reason to hold it, since digoxin is given to slow the rate.
w: 64 beats per minute
78 beats per minute
96 beats per minute

qs.q: A client takes metoprolol and amlodipine each morning. The pulse is 48 beats per minute and the blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Which action fits these findings?
qs.a: Hold the metoprolol and report the pulse, and give the amlodipine
qs.x: Metoprolol is the drug that slows the heart rate, so a pulse of 48 is the reason to hold it and report. Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that dilates arteries without slowing the AV node, and it may raise the rate slightly.
w: Hold both drugs, because each one slows the heart rate
Give both drugs, because the blood pressure is acceptable
Hold the amlodipine and report the pulse, and give the metoprolol

qs.q: A client on lisinopril is also ordered spironolactone and a potassium-containing salt substitute. The morning potassium is 5.4 mEq/L. What should the nurse report?
qs.a: That three sources are all raising potassium at once
qs.x: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone, spironolactone blocks aldosterone at the tubule, and salt substitutes are potassium chloride, so all three push potassium up. Normal potassium is 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L, and this combination is a common cause of hyperkalemia.
w: That lisinopril itself has no effect on potassium
That the salt substitute will actually lower the potassium
That spironolactone offsets the lisinopril effect

qs.q: A client takes glipizide before breakfast and metformin with dinner. At 1100 the client is shaky and diaphoretic with a glucose of 54 mg/dL. Which drug best explains this?
qs.a: Glipizide, because it makes the pancreas release insulin
qs.x: Sulfonylureas such as glipizide stimulate insulin secretion whether or not the client has eaten, so they do cause hypoglycemia. Metformin lowers hepatic glucose output and improves insulin sensitivity, and it rarely causes hypoglycemia used alone.
w: Metformin, because it blocks glucose absorption from food
Both equally, since each one lowers glucose the same way
Neither one, since oral agents do not cause low glucose

qs.q: A client started on amlodipine 10 mg daily 3 weeks ago now has pitting edema of both ankles, clear lung sounds, and no weight gain. What should the nurse report?
qs.a: Ankle edema that is a known dose-related effect
qs.x: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers dilate arterioles more than veins, so fluid is driven into the tissue at the ankles. The edema is dose-related rather than volume overload, which is why the clear lungs and stable weight matter here.
