qs.x: Ivabradine is indicated in symptomatic HFrEF with EF 35 percent or less, sinus rhythm, and resting heart rate 70/min or higher despite a maximally tolerated beta blocker.
w: Dronedarone
Ranolazine
Diltiazem

qs.q: A 76-year-old woman has dyspnea on exertion and edema. Echocardiogram shows an EF of 60 percent with diastolic dysfunction, and BNP is elevated. After diuresis she remains NYHA class II. Which medication is most likely to reduce HF hospitalization?
qs.a: Empagliflozin
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors have a class 2a recommendation in HFpEF because they reduce HF hospitalization and cardiovascular death.
w: Digoxin
Carvedilol
Isosorbide mononitrate

qs.q: A 67-year-old woman has palpitations for 6 hours. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 142/min. BP is 132/80 mm Hg. Echocardiogram 1 year ago showed normal EF. Which is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
qs.a: Intravenous diltiazem
qs.x: In stable AF with rapid ventricular response and preserved EF, IV diltiazem or a beta blocker is first-line for rate control. Adenosine does not treat AF.
w: Intravenous adenosine
Oral flecainide without an AV nodal blocker
Intravenous procainamide followed by oral quinidine

qs.q: A 71-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 20 percent) has atrial fibrillation at 150/min. BP is 98/64 mm Hg and he is mentating normally with mild dyspnea. Which medication is most appropriate for acute rate control?
qs.a: Intravenous amiodarone
qs.x: Nondihydropyridine CCBs are avoided in decompensated HFrEF. IV amiodarone or digoxin can control rate when blood pressure is borderline.
w: Intravenous diltiazem
Intravenous verapamil
Oral dronedarone

qs.q: A 69-year-old man with atrial fibrillation at 168/min becomes confused. BP is 72/40 mm Hg and he is diaphoretic. Which is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Synchronized electrical cardioversion
qs.x: Hemodynamically unstable AF requires immediate synchronized cardioversion; rate-slowing drugs worsen hypotension.
w: Intravenous diltiazem bolus followed by infusion
Oral amiodarone loading dose
Intravenous metoprolol 5 mg

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman with hypertension has newly diagnosed nonvalvular atrial fibrillation. Creatinine clearance is 70 mL/min and she has no bleeding history. Which is the most appropriate stroke prevention therapy?
qs.a: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily
qs.x: CHA2DS2-VASc is 3 (female, age 65 to 74, hypertension). Oral anticoagulation is indicated, and a DOAC is preferred over warfarin for nonvalvular AF.
w: Aspirin 81 mg daily alone
Aspirin plus clopidogrel daily
No antithrombotic therapy at this time

qs.q: A 54-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease has moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis and new atrial fibrillation. Which anticoagulant is most appropriate?
qs.a: Warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3
qs.x: DOACs are not recommended in AF with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or mechanical valves; warfarin remains the anticoagulant of choice.
w: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily
Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily

qs.q: A 45-year-old man has an episode of atrial fibrillation that converted spontaneously. He has no hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, vascular disease, or prior stroke. Which is the most appropriate long-term antithrombotic therapy?
qs.a: No antithrombotic therapy
qs.x: With a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 0 in a man, neither anticoagulation nor aspirin is recommended for stroke prevention.
w: Aspirin 81 mg daily
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily
Warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3 for one year

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman with no structural heart disease has infrequent symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation lasting a few hours. Echocardiogram and stress test are normal. She wants a pill-in-the-pocket strategy. Which regimen is most appropriate?
qs.a: Flecainide taken with a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine CCB
qs.x: Class IC agents are safe without structural or ischemic heart disease; an AV nodal blocker is co-administered to prevent 1:1 conduction of atrial flutter.
w: Amiodarone 400 mg taken at the onset of each episode
Digoxin 0.25 mg taken at symptom onset
Flecainide alone without any AV nodal blocking agent

qs.q: A 70-year-old man has taken amiodarone for 2 years for atrial fibrillation. He now reports fatigue, cold intolerance, and weight gain. Which laboratory abnormality is most likely?
qs.a: Elevated TSH with low free T4
qs.x: Amiodarone is iodine-rich and commonly causes hypothyroidism; TSH and LFTs should be monitored every 6 months, with a baseline chest x-ray and PFTs.
w: Low TSH with elevated free T3
Elevated serum calcium
Low serum potassium

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with persistent AF and an EF of 30 percent is selected for rhythm control with dofetilide. Creatinine clearance is 65 mL/min and baseline QTc is 430 ms. Which is required when starting this drug?
qs.a: Inpatient initiation with continuous ECG monitoring for 3 days
qs.x: Dofetilide can cause torsades de pointes, so it must be started in the hospital with creatinine clearance-based dosing and QTc monitoring.
w: Outpatient start with a single follow-up ECG at 3 months
Baseline pulmonary function tests and chest x-ray
Monthly liver function testing for the first 6 months

qs.q: A 78-year-old man taking dabigatran for atrial fibrillation is brought in after a fall with an acute subdural hematoma. His last dose was 3 hours ago. Which is the most appropriate reversal agent?
qs.a: Idarucizumab
qs.x: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that specifically binds and reverses dabigatran within minutes.
w: Protamine sulfate
Andexanet alfa
Intravenous vitamin K

qs.q: A 74-year-old woman taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation presents with a large intracerebral hemorrhage. Her last dose was 4 hours ago. Which is the most appropriate reversal therapy?
qs.a: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
qs.x: With andexanet alfa withdrawn from the US market in 2025, factor Xa inhibitor-associated life-threatening bleeding is treated with 4-factor PCC. Idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran.
w: Protamine sulfate intravenously
Idarucizumab 5 g intravenously
Fresh frozen plasma with vitamin K and platelets

qs.q: A man on warfarin is given oral vitamin K 2.5 mg for an INR of 11.2 without bleeding. Four hours later the INR is still 7.4. Why?
qs.a: New clotting factors must be synthesized by the liver
qs.x: Vitamin K restores the reduced cofactor needed for gamma-carboxylation, but the INR falls only as the liver makes new factors II, VII, IX and X; oral vitamin K takes about 24 hours for full effect. That lag is why 4-factor PCC is used when correction is needed in minutes.
w: Oral vitamin K is destroyed by gastric acid
Vitamin K acts only on factor VIII and von Willebrand factor
Warfarin blocks the vitamin K receptor on the platelet

qs.q: A 77-year-old woman on warfarin presents with sudden headache and left hemiparesis. CT shows an intraparenchymal hemorrhage. INR is 3.4. Which is the most appropriate immediate therapy?
qs.a: 4-factor PCC plus intravenous vitamin K 10 mg
qs.x: Warfarin-associated major bleeding is reversed with 4-factor PCC for rapid correction plus IV vitamin K to sustain it.
w: Oral vitamin K 5 mg and hold warfarin
Protamine sulfate 50 mg intravenously
Platelet transfusion and desmopressin

qs.q: A 64-year-old man receiving an IV unfractionated heparin infusion for PE develops brisk hematemesis. aPTT is 140 seconds. After stopping the infusion, which agent is most appropriate?
qs.a: Protamine sulfate
qs.x: Protamine binds heparin and fully reverses unfractionated heparin (and partially reverses LMWH).
w: Intravenous vitamin K
Idarucizumab
Tranexamic acid alone without other reversal

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis has received heparin for 6 days. Platelets fall from 230,000 to 80,000/mm3 and the PF4 antibody is strongly positive. Which anticoagulant is most appropriate?
qs.a: Argatroban infusion
qs.x: In HIT, stop all heparins and start a non-heparin anticoagulant. Argatroban is hepatically cleared, so it is preferred in renal failure; fondaparinux is renally cleared.
w: Daily fondaparinux injections
Weight-based enoxaparin
Warfarin 5 mg daily, started now

qs.q: A 47-year-old man has a right femoral DVT 2 weeks after a long-haul flight. He has no cancer, normal renal function, and no bleeding risk. Which is the most appropriate outpatient treatment?
qs.a: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily
qs.x: CHEST guidelines prefer DOACs over warfarin for VTE without cancer. Apixaban needs no parenteral lead-in; warfarin requires heparin overlap.
w: Warfarin alone starting at 10 mg daily without bridging
Aspirin 325 mg daily for 3 months
Unfractionated heparin infusion for 5 days, then stop

qs.q: A 59-year-old woman has sudden dyspnea. BP is 78/46 mm Hg despite 1 L of fluid, and pulse is 128/min. CT angiography shows a saddle pulmonary embolus with RV dilation. She has no bleeding contraindications. Which is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase
qs.x: Massive (high-risk) PE with sustained hypotension warrants systemic thrombolysis unless contraindicated, in addition to heparin.
w: Start apixaban 10 mg twice daily
Place an IVC filter and observe
Subcutaneous enoxaparin and admit to telemetry

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks gestation has a left iliofemoral DVT confirmed by ultrasound. Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
qs.a: Weight-based enoxaparin twice daily
qs.x: LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta; warfarin is teratogenic and DOACs are not recommended.
w: Warfarin titrated to an INR of 2 to 3
Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily

qs.q: A 34-year-old woman has her second unprovoked DVT. Testing shows lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies on two occasions. Which long-term anticoagulant is preferred?
qs.a: Warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3
qs.x: In antiphospholipid syndrome, especially triple-positive disease, DOACs have higher rates of thrombosis than warfarin; warfarin is preferred.
w: Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily
Aspirin 81 mg daily

qs.q: A 55-year-old man develops a calf-to-popliteal DVT 3 weeks after knee replacement surgery. Rivaroxaban is started. He has no other risk factors. What is the recommended duration of anticoagulation?
qs.a: 3 months
qs.x: A first VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor such as surgery is treated for 3 months; extended therapy is for unprovoked or persistent risk factors.
w: 2 weeks
12 months
Lifelong

qs.q: A 50-year-old Black man has BP readings of 152/96 mm Hg and 154/98 mm Hg at two visits. He has no diabetes, no CKD, and no albuminuria. Which is the most appropriate initial antihypertensive?
qs.a: Amlodipine
qs.x: In Black adults without CKD or HF, a thiazide diuretic or calcium channel blocker is preferred initial therapy because they lower BP more effectively than ACE inhibitors.
w: Lisinopril
Metoprolol
Doxazosin

qs.q: A 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a BP of 146/90 mm Hg on repeated measurements. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 420 mg/g and eGFR is 70 mL/min. Which antihypertensive is most appropriate?
qs.a: Lisinopril
qs.x: With diabetes and albuminuria, an ACE inhibitor or ARB is first-line because it slows progression of kidney disease.
w: Amlodipine
Chlorthalidone
Atenolol

qs.q: A 61-year-old man started lisinopril 3 months ago for hypertension and has developed a persistent dry cough. Lung exam and chest x-ray are normal. Which is the most appropriate change?
qs.a: Switch to losartan
qs.x: ACE inhibitor cough is bradykinin mediated; ARBs do not raise bradykinin and are an appropriate substitute.
w: Add benzonatate and continue lisinopril
Switch to enalapril
Switch to sacubitril-valsartan

qs.q: A 62-year-old man has tearing chest pain radiating to the back. BP is 190/110 mm Hg in the right arm and 150/90 mm Hg in the left; pulse is 104/min. CT shows a type B aortic dissection. Which is the most appropriate initial medication?
qs.a: Intravenous esmolol
qs.x: In aortic dissection, give an IV beta blocker first to reduce heart rate and shear stress, then add a vasodilator if needed, targeting SBP near 120 mm Hg.
w: Intravenous hydralazine
Intravenous nitroprusside without other drugs
Sublingual nifedipine

qs.q: A 55-year-old man presents with headache, confusion, and papilledema. BP is 236/138 mm Hg. CT head shows no hemorrhage. Which is the most appropriate goal of pharmacotherapy in the first hour?
qs.a: Lower mean arterial pressure by no more than 25 percent with IV nicardipine
qs.x: In hypertensive emergency without dissection or eclampsia, reduce MAP by no more than 25 percent in the first hour, then toward 160/100 mm Hg over the next 2 to 6 hours.
w: Lower blood pressure to below 120/80 mm Hg with IV nitroprusside
Give oral lisinopril and recheck BP in 24 hours
Give sublingual immediate-release nifedipine

qs.q: A 31-year-old woman with chronic hypertension taking lisinopril has a positive pregnancy test at 7 weeks. BP is 138/88 mm Hg. Which is the most appropriate management?
qs.a: Stop lisinopril and start labetalol
qs.x: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic; labetalol and nifedipine are preferred antihypertensives in pregnancy.
w: Continue lisinopril throughout pregnancy
Switch lisinopril to losartan
Stop lisinopril and start hydrochlorothiazide plus spironolactone

qs.q: A 27-year-old woman at 35 weeks gestation has a BP of 168/112 mm Hg on two readings 15 minutes apart. She has a headache. She has no asthma. Which is the most appropriate antihypertensive?
qs.a: Intravenous labetalol
qs.x: Severe-range BP in pregnancy (160/110 or higher) should be treated within 30 to 60 minutes with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or immediate-release oral nifedipine.
w: Intravenous nitroprusside
Oral lisinopril
Intravenous enalaprilat

qs.q: A 44-year-old woman has resistant hypertension and a potassium level of 3.1 mEq/L. Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio is elevated, and adrenal CT shows bilateral hyperplasia. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Spironolactone
qs.x: Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is treated medically with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; surgery is for unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma.
w: Hydrochlorothiazide
Laparoscopic unilateral adrenalectomy
Clonidine

qs.q: A 55-year-old woman has type 2 diabetes and hypertension and smokes cigarettes. LDL cholesterol is 124 mg/dL. She has no known ASCVD. Which is the most appropriate lipid-lowering therapy?
qs.a: Rosuvastatin 20 mg daily
qs.x: Adults aged 40 to 75 years with diabetes and additional ASCVD risk factors should receive high-intensity statin therapy.
w: Rosuvastatin 5 mg every other day
Ezetimibe 10 mg daily alone
Fenofibrate 145 mg daily

qs.q: A 48-year-old man has fasting triglycerides of 1,250 mg/dL. He had acute pancreatitis 1 year ago. He already follows a low-fat diet and has stopped alcohol. Which medication is most appropriate to reduce his immediate risk?
qs.a: Fenofibrate
qs.x: Triglycerides above 1,000 mg/dL carry a risk of pancreatitis; fibrates are first-line. Bile acid sequestrants can raise triglycerides.
w: Ezetimibe
Colesevelam
Evolocumab

qs.q: A 67-year-old man taking simvastatin 40 mg was started on clarithromycin 5 days ago for pneumonia. He now has diffuse muscle pain and dark urine. CK is 18,000 U/L. Which medication should be discontinued first?
qs.a: Simvastatin
qs.x: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor that raises simvastatin levels, causing rhabdomyolysis; the statin must be stopped.
w: Lisinopril
Metformin
Aspirin

qs.q: A 49-year-old man has a hemoglobin A1c of 7.6 percent on two occasions. BMI is 31 kg/m2, eGFR is 90 mL/min, and he has no ASCVD, heart failure, or CKD. Which is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
qs.a: Metformin
qs.x: Metformin plus lifestyle changes is first-line for type 2 diabetes without compelling indications for other agents.
w: Glipizide
Insulin glargine
Pioglitazone

qs.q: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes had an MI 2 years ago. She takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. A1c is 7.9 percent, BMI 34 kg/m2, and eGFR 80 mL/min. Which addition is most appropriate?
qs.a: Semaglutide
qs.x: With established ASCVD, ADA recommends a GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit independent of A1c; GLP-1 RAs also promote weight loss.
w: Glipizide
Sitagliptin
Pioglitazone

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 40 mL/min and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 600 mg/g on maximal lisinopril. A1c is 7.4 percent on metformin. Which addition best slows kidney disease progression?
qs.a: Empagliflozin
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended in diabetic CKD with an eGFR of 20 mL/min or higher to reduce CKD progression and cardiovascular events.
w: Glyburide
Saxagliptin
Pioglitazone

qs.q: A woman on metformin with an eGFR of 26 mL/min presents with a lactate of 8.4 mmol/L. Which action of metformin best explains the lactate?
qs.a: It inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis from lactate
qs.x: Metformin inhibits mitochondrial complex I and hepatic gluconeogenesis, so lactate is no longer consumed through the Cori cycle. The drug is cleared unchanged by tubular secretion via OCT2 and MATE, so an eGFR under 30 lets levels and lactate rise.
w: It uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in muscle
It blocks renal tubular secretion of hydrogen ion
It is converted directly into lactate in the gut wall

qs.q: A 45-year-old man has polyuria, polydipsia, and a 7-kg weight loss. Glucose is 380 mg/dL and A1c is 12.1 percent. Urine ketones are trace positive, pH is normal, and the anion gap is normal. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?
qs.a: Basal insulin such as glargine in addition to metformin
qs.x: Symptomatic catabolic hyperglycemia or A1c above 10 percent calls for early insulin therapy.
w: Sitagliptin monotherapy titrated over 3 months
Acarbose with each meal plus a low-carbohydrate diet
Lifestyle changes alone and recheck A1c in 3 months

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman started semaglutide 3 months ago. She now has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. Lipase is 900 U/L. Which is the most appropriate action regarding this medication?
qs.a: Discontinue semaglutide permanently
qs.x: GLP-1 receptor agonists are associated with acute pancreatitis; stop the drug and do not restart a GLP-1 RA if pancreatitis is confirmed.
w: Continue semaglutide at a lower dose
Switch to dulaglutide after recovery
Hold semaglutide for 1 week, then resume

qs.q: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin has nausea and vomiting after 2 days of poor oral intake. Glucose is 210 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, and anion gap 22. Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is high. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis from the SGLT2 inhibitor
qs.x: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose, especially with illness, fasting, or surgery; hold the drug and treat as DKA with insulin and dextrose.
w: Lactic acidosis from metformin accumulation
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Starvation ketosis that needs no treatment

qs.q: An 81-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and eGFR 35 mL/min is found confused. Fingerstick glucose is 38 mg/dL. Her medications include glyburide, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. After glucose correction, which medication change is most appropriate?
qs.a: Stop glyburide
qs.x: Glyburide has active renally cleared metabolites and causes prolonged hypoglycemia in older adults and CKD; it should be avoided (Beers criteria).
w: Stop lisinopril
Stop atorvastatin
Increase glyburide

qs.q: A 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and BMI 39 kg/m2 takes metformin. A1c is 8.2 percent. She wants a medication that maximizes both glucose lowering and weight loss. She has no personal or family history of thyroid cancer. Which is most appropriate?
qs.a: Tirzepatide
qs.x: Dual GIP and GLP-1 agonist therapy with tirzepatide provides very high glucose-lowering efficacy and the greatest weight loss among diabetes agents.
w: Glimepiride
Pioglitazone
Insulin detemir

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes metformin and insulin glargine 20 units at bedtime. Fasting glucose readings over the past week are 170 to 190 mg/dL with no hypoglycemia. Which is the most appropriate adjustment?
qs.a: Increase glargine by 2 units every 3 days until fasting glucose is at goal
qs.x: Basal insulin is titrated to fasting glucose (goal 80 to 130 mg/dL) by about 2 units every 3 days when there is no hypoglycemia.
w: Add prandial insulin lispro with every meal right away
Decrease glargine to 16 units at bedtime
Switch glargine to NPH insulin twice daily at the same dose

qs.q: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has vomiting and abdominal pain. Glucose is 520 mg/dL, pH 7.12, bicarbonate 9 mEq/L, potassium 4.8 mEq/L, and serum ketones are high. BP is 94/58 mm Hg. Which is the best initial step?
qs.a: Intravenous 0.9 percent saline bolus
qs.x: Fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline is the first step in DKA; insulin follows once potassium is known to be at least 3.3 mEq/L.
w: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion
Subcutaneous insulin lispro every 2 hours
Intravenous 5 percent dextrose in water

qs.q: A 24-year-old man in DKA has glucose 460 mg/dL, pH 7.10, and serum potassium 3.0 mEq/L. He has received 1 L of normal saline. Which is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Give IV potassium and delay insulin until potassium is at least 3.3 mEq/L
qs.x: Insulin drives potassium into cells and can cause fatal hypokalemia; hold insulin and replace potassium when it is below 3.3 mEq/L.
w: Start an insulin infusion at 0.14 units/kg/h immediately
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Give an IV insulin bolus and recheck potassium in 4 hours

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman with DKA is on an IV regular insulin infusion. Her glucose falls to 220 mg/dL, but the anion gap is still 18. Which is the most appropriate adjustment?
qs.a: Add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue the insulin infusion
qs.x: Insulin must continue until the anion gap closes; dextrose is added when glucose falls to about 200 to 250 mg/dL to prevent hypoglycemia.
w: Stop the insulin infusion and switch to oral fluids
Stop insulin and give subcutaneous glargine only
Double the insulin infusion rate and stop IV fluids

qs.q: A 78-year-old nursing home resident is lethargic. Glucose is 980 mg/dL, serum osmolality 352 mOsm/kg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and ketones are negative. BP is 92/50 mm Hg. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?
qs.a: Intravenous 0.9 percent saline at about 1 L per hour
qs.x: HHS is driven by profound volume depletion; aggressive isotonic fluid is the first priority, followed by insulin.
w: Intravenous insulin bolus before any fluids
Intravenous 3 percent hypertonic saline
Oral water and subcutaneous insulin glargine

qs.q: A 34-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, and a diffuse goiter with proptosis. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated. TSH receptor antibodies are positive. Pulse is 112/min. She is not pregnant. Which is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
qs.a: Methimazole plus propranolol
qs.x: Methimazole is the preferred thionamide outside the first trimester; a beta blocker controls adrenergic symptoms.
w: Propylthiouracil plus propranolol
Levothyroxine plus propranolol
Potassium iodide alone

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman at 8 weeks gestation has Graves disease with free T4 twice the upper limit of normal. Which is the most appropriate antithyroid medication?
qs.a: Propylthiouracil
qs.x: PTU is preferred in the first trimester because methimazole is associated with embryopathy; switch to methimazole in the second trimester.
w: Methimazole
Radioactive iodine
Levothyroxine

qs.q: A 42-year-old woman with Graves disease has a fever of 40 C (104 F), agitation, vomiting, and atrial fibrillation at 160/min after an appendectomy. Propranolol has been started. Regarding iodine therapy, which sequence is correct?
qs.a: Give propylthiouracil, then give iodine at least 1 hour later
qs.x: In thyroid storm, a thionamide must be given before iodine so that iodine is not used as substrate for new hormone synthesis. Steroids are also given.
w: Give iodine immediately, then propylthiouracil 1 hour later
Give iodine alone and avoid thionamides
Give radioactive iodine as soon as she is stable

qs.q: A woman with Graves disease in her first trimester needs a thionamide. Which fact guides the choice between methimazole and propylthiouracil?
qs.a: Methimazole is linked to aplasia cutis and choanal atresia
qs.x: Methimazole embryopathy, including aplasia cutis and choanal or esophageal atresia, follows first-trimester exposure, so PTU is preferred then despite its own risk of fulminant hepatic failure. PTU, not methimazole, is the one that blocks peripheral deiodination.
w: Methimazole causes more hepatocellular failure than PTU does
Methimazole crosses the placenta far less than PTU does
Methimazole also blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion

qs.q: A 78-year-old man with stable coronary artery disease has fatigue and constipation. TSH is 24 mU/L and free T4 is low. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?
qs.a: Levothyroxine 25 mcg daily, titrated slowly
qs.x: Older patients and those with CAD start levothyroxine at a low dose to avoid precipitating angina or arrhythmia.
w: Levothyroxine 1.6 mcg/kg daily as a full dose
Liothyronine 25 mcg twice daily
Intravenous levothyroxine loading dose

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis on levothyroxine 100 mcg daily has a positive home pregnancy test. TSH was normal 2 months ago. Which is the most appropriate step?
qs.a: Increase levothyroxine by about 30 percent now
qs.x: Thyroid hormone needs rise early in pregnancy; increase the dose by about 2 extra tablets weekly (about 30 percent) and check TSH every 4 weeks.
w: Continue the same dose until the second trimester
Stop levothyroxine for the first trimester
Switch levothyroxine to liothyronine

qs.q: A 65-year-old woman on a stable levothyroxine dose now has a TSH of 9.8 mU/L. Three months ago she began taking calcium carbonate and ferrous sulfate with her levothyroxine every morning. Which is the most appropriate step?
qs.a: Separate levothyroxine from calcium and iron by at least 4 hours
qs.x: Calcium, iron, and PPIs reduce levothyroxine absorption; take levothyroxine on an empty stomach separated from these products.
w: Double the levothyroxine dose and keep timing the same
Add liothyronine to her morning regimen
Stop levothyroxine and recheck TSH in 6 weeks

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman with known Addison disease has vomiting and diarrhea. BP is 72/40 mm Hg, sodium 126 mEq/L, potassium 5.9 mEq/L, and glucose 58 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate immediate therapy?
qs.a: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV plus normal saline with dextrose
qs.x: Adrenal crisis needs immediate high-dose IV hydrocortisone (which also provides mineralocorticoid activity) plus fluids and dextrose; never delay steroids for testing.
w: Dexamethasone 1 mg orally and recheck cortisol in the morning
Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg orally alone
Norepinephrine infusion before any steroid is given

qs.q: A 40-year-old man is newly diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency. He has salt craving, hyperkalemia, and orthostatic hypotension. Which maintenance regimen is most appropriate?
qs.a: Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone
qs.x: Primary adrenal insufficiency lacks both cortisol and aldosterone, so glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement are needed.
w: Hydrocortisone alone
Dexamethasone alone
Prednisone plus spironolactone

qs.q: A 16-year-old girl has asthma symptoms twice a month with no nighttime awakenings and normal spirometry between episodes. Which reliever regimen is preferred by current GINA recommendations?
qs.a: As-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol
qs.x: GINA Track 1 prefers as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol for mild asthma because it reduces severe exacerbations compared with SABA-only therapy.
w: As-needed albuterol alone for symptom relief
Daily montelukast plus as-needed albuterol
Daily salmeterol alone with as-needed albuterol

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman with asthma uses low-dose budesonide-formoterol as maintenance and reliever therapy. She still has symptoms most days and woke at night twice last week. Inhaler technique and adherence are good. Which is the most appropriate step?
qs.a: Increase to medium-dose budesonide-formoterol maintenance and reliever
qs.x: Step up within the ICS-formoterol track to medium-dose maintenance-and-reliever therapy after confirming technique and adherence.
w: Add a long-acting beta agonist alone as a separate inhaler
Stop the inhaled steroid and start daily montelukast instead
Start a 30-day course of oral prednisone at 40 mg daily

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman with a severe asthma exacerbation has received three back-to-back albuterol-ipratropium nebulizers and IV methylprednisolone. She still speaks in words only, and peak flow is 30 percent of predicted. Which is the most appropriate next medication?
qs.a: Intravenous magnesium sulfate
qs.x: IV magnesium sulfate is recommended for severe exacerbations not responding to initial bronchodilators and steroids.
w: Oral montelukast
Inhaled fluticasone
Intravenous theophylline

qs.q: A 34-year-old man has severe allergic asthma with 3 prednisone bursts in the past year despite high-dose ICS-LABA and good technique. Total IgE is 420 IU/mL with sensitization to dust mite. Which add-on therapy is most appropriate?
qs.a: Omalizumab
qs.x: Anti-IgE therapy is indicated for severe allergic asthma with elevated IgE uncontrolled on step 4 to 5 therapy.
w: Daily oral theophylline
Long-term oral prednisone
Inhaled cromolyn

qs.q: Montelukast is added for a boy with asthma and allergic rhinitis. Which receptor action produces its effect?
qs.a: Blockade of the cysteinyl leukotriene type 1 receptor
qs.x: Montelukast is a competitive antagonist at the CysLT1 receptor, blocking the bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion and eosinophil recruitment driven by LTD4. Zileuton is the 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor and roflumilast the PDE4 inhibitor, so each acts at a different point.
w: Inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase in the leukotriene pathway
Blockade of thromboxane A2 receptors on bronchial muscle
Inhibition of phosphodiesterase 4 inside airway cells

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 55 percent predicted) has an mMRC dyspnea score of 2 and no exacerbations in the past year. Blood eosinophils are 120/microL. Which is the most appropriate maintenance therapy?
qs.a: LAMA plus LABA such as tiotropium-olodaterol
qs.x: GOLD recommends LABA plus LAMA for symptomatic patients (group B); ICS monotherapy is not recommended in COPD.
w: Inhaled corticosteroid alone such as fluticasone
Albuterol as needed only, with pulmonary rehab
Daily low-dose oral prednisone plus albuterol

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman with COPD on LAMA plus LABA has had 2 exacerbations requiring prednisone in the past year. Blood eosinophils are 380/microL. Which is the most appropriate change?
qs.a: Add an inhaled corticosteroid to make triple therapy
qs.x: GOLD recommends escalating to LABA, LAMA, and ICS for exacerbations when eosinophils are 100/microL or higher, with the strongest benefit at 300/microL or higher.
w: Stop the LAMA and continue the LABA alone
Add daily low-dose oral prednisone long term
Switch to as-needed albuterol only for symptoms

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with COPD has 3 days of worsening dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and green sputum. SpO2 is 91 percent and he is not in respiratory distress. In addition to bronchodilators and an antibiotic, which is the most appropriate therapy?
qs.a: Prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days
qs.x: A short course of prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days is as effective as longer courses for COPD exacerbations and has less toxicity.
w: Prednisone 60 mg daily tapered over 6 weeks
Inhaled cromolyn four times daily
Intravenous theophylline infusion

qs.q: A 32-year-old man has 3 days of fever, productive cough, and right lower lobe consolidation. He has no comorbidities and has not taken antibiotics recently. Pulse is 96/min and SpO2 96 percent. Which is the most appropriate outpatient antibiotic?
qs.a: Amoxicillin 1 g three times daily
qs.x: ATS/IDSA recommends high-dose amoxicillin (or doxycycline or a macrolide where resistance is low) for healthy outpatients with CAP.
w: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily
Cephalexin 500 mg four times daily
Clindamycin 300 mg four times daily

qs.q: A 64-year-old woman with COPD and type 2 diabetes has CAP. She is stable for outpatient treatment and has no recent antibiotic use. Which is the most appropriate regimen?
qs.a: Amoxicillin-clavulanate plus azithromycin
qs.x: Outpatients with comorbidities receive a beta-lactam plus a macrolide or doxycycline, or monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone.
w: Azithromycin alone
Amoxicillin alone
Cephalexin plus metronidazole

qs.q: A 70-year-old man is admitted to a medical ward with CAP. He is not in the ICU, has no MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors, and has no drug allergies. Which is the most appropriate empiric therapy?
qs.a: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
qs.x: Non-severe inpatient CAP is treated with a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone.
w: Vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam
Azithromycin alone
Oral amoxicillin alone

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with prior MRSA pneumonia is admitted to the ICU with severe CAP requiring norepinephrine. Which is the most appropriate empiric regimen?
qs.a: Ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and vancomycin
qs.x: Severe CAP with prior respiratory MRSA isolation warrants empiric MRSA coverage with vancomycin or linezolid added to standard therapy.
w: Ceftriaxone and azithromycin only
Levofloxacin alone
Doxycycline plus amoxicillin

qs.q: A 55-year-old woman with a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin is admitted to a medical ward with CAP. Which is the most appropriate empiric therapy?
qs.a: Levofloxacin monotherapy
qs.x: A respiratory fluoroquinolone covers typical and atypical pathogens and avoids beta-lactams in severe penicillin allergy.
w: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
Ampicillin-sulbactam plus azithromycin
Amoxicillin plus doxycycline

qs.q: A 26-year-old nonpregnant woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency without fever or flank pain. Urinalysis shows pyuria and nitrites. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Nitrofurantoin for 5 days
qs.x: IDSA first-line options for uncomplicated cystitis are nitrofurantoin for 5 days (Macrobid label: 7 days), TMP-SMX for 3 days (if resistance is low), or a single dose of fosfomycin.
w: Ciprofloxacin for 14 days
Amoxicillin for 3 days
Intravenous ceftriaxone for 7 days

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman has a fever of 38.6 C (101.5 F), flank pain, and costovertebral tenderness. She is tolerating oral intake and is not pregnant. Local fluoroquinolone resistance is below 10 percent. Which is the most appropriate outpatient treatment?
qs.a: Ciprofloxacin for 7 days
qs.x: Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin do not achieve adequate renal tissue levels; oral fluoroquinolones for 7 days are first-line for pyelonephritis.
w: Nitrofurantoin for 5 days
Fosfomycin as a single dose
Amoxicillin for 3 days

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman at 26 weeks gestation has fever, rigors, and right flank pain. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Which is the most appropriate management?
qs.a: Admit and give IV ceftriaxone
qs.x: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy is treated as an inpatient with IV beta-lactam therapy; fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines are avoided.
w: Outpatient oral nitrofurantoin
Outpatient oral ciprofloxacin
Admit and give IV gentamicin plus doxycycline

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman at 12 weeks gestation has a urine culture with more than 100,000 CFU/mL of E. coli. She has no symptoms. The organism is susceptible to all tested agents. Which is the most appropriate management?
qs.a: Cephalexin for 5 to 7 days
qs.x: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated to prevent pyelonephritis; beta-lactams are preferred in the first trimester.
w: No treatment because she is asymptomatic
Ciprofloxacin for 3 days
Doxycycline for 7 days

qs.q: A 22-year-old college student has fever, headache, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash. CSF shows neutrophilic pleocytosis and low glucose. Which is the most appropriate empiric regimen?
qs.a: Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone plus dexamethasone
qs.x: Empiric adult bacterial meningitis coverage is vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin, with dexamethasone given before or with the first dose.
w: Ampicillin plus gentamicin
Ceftriaxone alone without adjunctive steroids
Acyclovir plus doxycycline

qs.q: A 68-year-old man has fever, confusion, and nuchal rigidity. CSF shows 1,800 WBC/mm3 with neutrophils and low glucose. Which is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?
qs.a: Vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and ampicillin
qs.x: Adults older than 50 need ampicillin added for Listeria monocytogenes coverage, along with dexamethasone.
w: Vancomycin and ceftriaxone only
Ampicillin and gentamicin only
Cefazolin and metronidazole

qs.q: A 35-year-old man with suspected pneumococcal meningitis is about to receive vancomycin and ceftriaxone. When should dexamethasone be given?
qs.a: Shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose
qs.x: Dexamethasone reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis when given before or with the first antibiotic dose.
w: Only after CSF culture confirms pneumococcus
24 hours after antibiotics have started
Only if the patient develops seizures

qs.q: A 45-year-old man has a 2-day history of a spreading, warm, erythematous area on the lower leg without purulence or abscess. He is afebrile with normal vital signs. Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
qs.a: Cephalexin
qs.x: Nonpurulent cellulitis is usually streptococcal; oral beta-lactams such as cephalexin are first-line. TMP-SMX alone covers streptococci poorly.
w: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone
Ciprofloxacin
Intravenous vancomycin

qs.q: A 28-year-old man has a 4-cm fluctuant abscess on the thigh with surrounding erythema and a temperature of 38.3 C (100.9 F). Incision and drainage is performed. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
qs.a: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
qs.x: Purulent infections with systemic signs warrant drainage plus MRSA coverage such as TMP-SMX or doxycycline.
w: Penicillin V potassium
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Cefuroxime axetil

qs.q: A 52-year-old man with diabetes has rapidly spreading thigh erythema, severe pain out of proportion to exam, crepitus, and BP 84/50 mm Hg. Along with emergency surgical debridement, which regimen is most appropriate?
qs.a: Vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and clindamycin
qs.x: Necrotizing soft tissue infection requires broad coverage including MRSA and gram-negatives, plus clindamycin to suppress toxin production.
w: Cephalexin plus oral doxycycline twice daily
Penicillin G alone at high intravenous doses
Nafcillin alone, then oral dicloxacillin step-down

qs.q: A 50-year-old woman receiving IV vancomycin over 20 minutes develops flushing and an erythematous rash on the face, neck, and upper trunk. BP is 118/76 mm Hg and there is no wheezing or angioedema. Which is the most appropriate management?
qs.a: Slow the infusion rate and give an antihistamine
qs.x: Vancomycin infusion reaction is non-IgE histamine release from rapid infusion; infuse over at least 60 minutes and premedicate with an antihistamine.
w: Stop vancomycin permanently and record an allergy
Give intramuscular epinephrine immediately
Switch to cefazolin plus clindamycin indefinitely

qs.q: A 63-year-old man has MRSA pneumonia confirmed by sputum culture. Which antibiotic should not be used for this infection?
qs.a: Daptomycin
qs.x: Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and is not used for pneumonia, although it is effective for MRSA bacteremia and endocarditis.
w: Vancomycin
Linezolid
Ceftaroline

qs.q: A 23-year-old man has urethral discharge and dysuria. NAAT is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and negative for Chlamydia. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once
qs.x: CDC recommends a single 500-mg IM ceftriaxone dose for uncomplicated gonorrhea (1 g if 150 kg or more); add doxycycline only if chlamydia is not excluded.
w: Azithromycin 1 g orally once
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally once
Cefixime 400 mg orally plus azithromycin

qs.q: A 20-year-old nonpregnant woman has a positive NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis on routine screening. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
qs.x: CDC now prefers doxycycline for 7 days over single-dose azithromycin for chlamydia in nonpregnant patients.
w: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once
Metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days
Penicillin G benzathine once

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman has 6 weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, early morning awakening, poor concentration, and excessive guilt. She has no suicidal ideation, no history of mania, and no medical illness. PHQ-9 score is 17 and she prefers medication. Which is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
qs.a: Sertraline 50 mg daily
qs.x: An SSRI such as sertraline is first-line for moderate major depression because of efficacy, tolerability, and safety in overdose. TCAs are more toxic in overdose, and benzodiazepines do not treat depression.
w: Alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily
Lithium carbonate 300 mg twice daily
Amitriptyline 75 mg at bedtime, titrated over 2 weeks

qs.q: A 44-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium for 5 years. He now has coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting, and confusion. Lithium level is 2.4 mEq/L (previously 0.8). Two weeks ago a new antihypertensive was started. Which medication most likely precipitated this?
qs.a: Hydrochlorothiazide
qs.x: Thiazides increase proximal tubular sodium and lithium reabsorption and can raise lithium levels 25 percent or more. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and NSAIDs also raise levels; calcium channel blockers and alpha blockers do not meaningfully affect levels.
w: Amlodipine
Doxazosin
Metoprolol succinate extended-release

qs.q: A man has been on clozapine for 5 weeks. Which laboratory result requires the drug to be interrupted under its REMS program?
qs.a: Absolute neutrophil count of 900 per microliter
qs.x: Clozapine is interrupted when the ANC falls below 1,000 per microliter, and the ANC rather than the total WBC is the monitored value, weekly for the first 6 months. The eosinophil and platelet values shown here are not treatment-limiting.
w: White blood cell count of 6,200 per microliter
Absolute eosinophil count of 720 cells per microliter
Platelet count of 141,000 per microliter

qs.q: A man on IV haloperidol has fever, rigidity and a CK of 18,000 U/L. Which additional finding would instead point to serotonin syndrome?
qs.a: Inducible ankle clonus with brisk reflexes
qs.x: Clonus and hyperreflexia are characteristic of serotonin syndrome and are absent in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, where rigidity is lead-pipe and reflexes are normal or reduced. Fever, diaphoresis and autonomic instability occur in both, so they do not separate them.
w: Lead-pipe rigidity of the arms and legs
Diaphoresis with a labile blood pressure reading
A temperature above 40 C with confusion

qs.q: A 40-year-old woman taking sertraline was started on tramadol for back pain. She now has agitation, a temperature of 39.0 C (102.2 F), diaphoresis, diarrhea, mydriasis, hyperreflexia, and inducible clonus most prominent in the legs. Both drugs are stopped and IV benzodiazepines are given, but symptoms persist. Which medication is indicated next?
qs.a: Cyproheptadine
qs.x: Serotonin syndrome features clonus and hyperreflexia. After stopping serotonergic drugs and giving benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine, a 5-HT2A antagonist, is used. Bromocriptine worsens serotonin toxicity, and dantrolene is for NMS or malignant hyperthermia.
w: Dantrolene
Bromocriptine
Physostigmine

qs.q: A 34-year-old woman with schizophrenia well controlled on olanzapine 20 mg daily has gained 14 kg in 9 months. Fasting glucose is 118 mg/dL and triglycerides are 290 mg/dL. Which antipsychotic is the best alternative to minimize metabolic risk?
qs.a: Aripiprazole
qs.x: Aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone have the lowest metabolic liability. Clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest risk, and quetiapine and low-potency typicals also cause substantial weight gain.
w: Clozapine
Quetiapine
Chlorpromazine

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa (self-induced vomiting until 1 year ago) wants help quitting her 1-pack-per-day smoking habit. Which smoking cessation medication is contraindicated?
qs.a: Bupropion sustained-release
qs.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in seizure disorders and in bulimia or anorexia nervosa, in which electrolyte disturbances further increase seizure risk.
w: Varenicline
Nicotine patch plus nicotine gum
Nicotine lozenge as needed

qs.q: A 56-year-old man with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis (ascites, INR 2.0, albumin 2.4 g/dL) is admitted. Thirty hours after his last drink he has tremor, diaphoresis, pulse 118/min, BP 162/96 mm Hg, and visual hallucinations. CIWA-Ar score is 22. Which is the most appropriate medication?
qs.a: Lorazepam
qs.x: Benzodiazepines are first-line for alcohol withdrawal. In severe liver disease, agents metabolized only by glucuronidation without active metabolites (lorazepam, oxazepam) are preferred over long-acting chlordiazepoxide or diazepam.
w: Chlordiazepoxide
Haloperidol
Clonidine

qs.q: A 48-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has completed detoxification and wants medication to help maintain abstinence. He has decompensated cirrhosis with bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL and an elevated INR. Creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate medication?
qs.a: Acamprosate
qs.x: Acamprosate is renally cleared without hepatic metabolism, making it suitable in advanced liver disease. Naltrexone is avoided in acute hepatitis or liver failure, and disulfiram is hepatotoxic.
w: Naltrexone
Disulfiram
Chlordiazepoxide taper continued for 3 months

qs.q: A 4-year-old boy has had hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention at home and in preschool for 9 months, causing significant impairment. Hearing, vision, and development are otherwise normal. Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
qs.a: Parent training in behavior management
qs.x: For preschool children ages 4 to 5, the AAP recommends evidence-based parent training in behavior management first; methylphenidate may be considered if behavioral therapy is insufficient.
w: Methylphenidate immediate-release 5 mg twice daily
Atomoxetine 0.5 mg/kg daily
Guanfacine extended-release 1 mg daily

qs.q: A 17-year-old girl has morning myoclonic jerks and had one generalized tonic-clonic seizure after a sleepless night. EEG shows 4- to 6-Hz generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges. Which is the most appropriate initial medication?
qs.a: Levetiracetam
qs.x: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy responds to broad-spectrum agents. Valproate is effective but is avoided in people who may become pregnant because of neural tube defects and lower offspring IQ. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen myoclonic seizures.
w: Valproic acid
Carbamazepine
Phenytoin

qs.q: A 61-year-old woman has taken haloperidol for 8 years for stable schizophrenia. She has developed involuntary lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and choreiform finger movements. Which medication is most appropriate to treat this movement disorder?
qs.a: Valbenazine
qs.x: Tardive dyskinesia is treated with a VMAT2 inhibitor such as valbenazine or deutetrabenazine. Anticholinergics such as benztropine do not help and may worsen TD.
w: Benztropine
Amantadine
Propranolol

qs.q: A 32-year-old veteran has PTSD with intrusive memories, nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance. He is starting trauma-focused psychotherapy and asks about medication. Which medication should be avoided for PTSD?
qs.a: Alprazolam
qs.x: Guidelines recommend against benzodiazepines in PTSD because they may worsen outcomes and impede extinction learning. Sertraline, paroxetine, and venlafaxine are recommended pharmacotherapies.
w: Sertraline
Paroxetine
Venlafaxine extended-release

qs.q: An 84-year-old man becomes acutely confused 2 days after hip fracture surgery. His attention fluctuates and is worse at night. He picks at the sheets but is not a danger to himself or staff. Infection and metabolic causes are being addressed. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
qs.a: Reorientation, sleep promotion, mobilization, and family presence
qs.x: Delirium is managed by treating underlying causes and using multicomponent nonpharmacologic measures. Antipsychotics are reserved for severe distress or danger, and benzodiazepines and anticholinergics worsen delirium.
w: Lorazepam 1 mg IV at night as needed
Scheduled oral haloperidol 2 mg every 6 hours for the rest of the stay
Diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime for sleep

qs.q: An older woman taking nightly diphenhydramine has urinary retention, constipation and worsening memory. Which receptor action explains these?
qs.a: Antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
qs.x: First-generation antihistamines are nonselective and block muscarinic receptors, producing retention, constipation, dry mouth and cognitive impairment, which is why they sit on the Beers list. H1 blockade in the brain explains the sedation but not the anticholinergic findings.
w: Antagonism at central histamine H1 receptors
Antagonism at peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic receptors
Inverse agonism at central 5-HT2A receptors

qs.q: An 82-year-old man with Alzheimer disease on donepezil has urge urinary incontinence. Oxybutynin was started 3 weeks ago and his confusion has worsened. Which is the best alternative for his bladder symptoms?
qs.a: Mirabegron
qs.x: Antimuscarinics worsen cognition and oppose cholinesterase inhibitors. A beta-3 agonist such as mirabegron treats overactive bladder without anticholinergic effects.
w: Tolterodine
Hyoscyamine
Imipramine

qs.q: A 34-year-old man is having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that began 12 minutes ago. He has received IV lorazepam 4 mg twice without cessation. Glucose is 104 mg/dL and the airway is supported. Which is the most appropriate next medication?
qs.a: Intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg
qs.x: After benzodiazepines fail, a second-line IV agent is given: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate, which had similar efficacy in ESETT. Further benzodiazepine doses add respiratory risk without benefit.
w: A third dose of IV lorazepam 4 mg
Oral phenytoin 1 g loading dose by nasogastric tube
Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg

qs.q: A 7-year-old girl has many brief staring spells daily, lasting about 10 seconds with eyelid fluttering and no postictal confusion. Hyperventilation provokes an episode. EEG shows 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges. Which is the most appropriate initial medication?
qs.a: Ethosuximide
qs.x: Ethosuximide is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy, with better tolerability than valproate. Carbamazepine, phenytoin, and gabapentin can worsen absence seizures.
w: Carbamazepine
Phenytoin
Gabapentin

qs.q: A 32-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry has brief electric-shock pains in the right cheek triggered by chewing and brushing his teeth. Exam and MRI are normal. Carbamazepine is planned. Which test should be performed before starting it?
qs.a: HLA-B*1502 genotyping
qs.x: HLA-B*1502, common in people of Asian ancestry, strongly predicts carbamazepine-induced SJS and TEN. HLA-B*5701 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity and TPMT guides thiopurine dosing.
w: HLA-B*5701 genotyping
Thiopurine methyltransferase activity
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level

qs.q: A 54-year-old woman with migraine without aura had an MI with a coronary stent placed 1 year ago. She asks for an acute treatment for her migraine attacks. Which medication should be avoided?
qs.a: Sumatriptan
qs.x: Triptans cause vasoconstriction and are contraindicated in coronary artery disease, stroke, and uncontrolled hypertension. Gepants such as ubrogepant do not vasoconstrict and are an option.
w: Acetaminophen
Ubrogepant
Metoclopramide

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman has migraine with 7 headache days per month despite trigger avoidance. She has moderate persistent asthma and a BMI of 33 kg/m2. She uses a levonorgestrel IUD. Which is the most appropriate preventive medication?
qs.a: Topiramate
qs.x: Topiramate is an effective migraine preventive that tends to cause weight loss. Propranolol is avoided in asthma, amitriptyline and valproate cause weight gain, and valproate is teratogenic. Topiramate also needs reliable contraception.
w: Propranolol
Amitriptyline
Valproic acid

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine has dysuria and frequency without fever. Urinalysis shows pyuria. Which antibiotic should be avoided?
qs.a: Ciprofloxacin
qs.x: Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for exacerbating myasthenia gravis. Aminoglycosides, macrolides, and magnesium also impair neuromuscular transmission.
w: Nitrofurantoin
Cephalexin
Fosfomycin

qs.q: A 63-year-old woman has a minor ischemic stroke (NIHSS 2) and is not a thrombolysis candidate. ECG and telemetry show sinus rhythm. Which antithrombotic regimen is most appropriate?
qs.a: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, then single antiplatelet
qs.x: Short-term DAPT started within 24 hours reduces recurrent stroke after minor stroke or high-risk TIA (CHANCE, POINT). Prolonged DAPT increases bleeding without added benefit, and anticoagulation is not indicated without AF.
w: Aspirin plus clopidogrel continued indefinitely for secondary prevention
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily
Warfarin with an INR goal of 2 to 3

qs.q: A 79-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease started donepezil 6 weeks ago. She has now had two episodes of syncope. Pulse is 44/min and ECG shows sinus bradycardia. Which is the most likely mechanism?
qs.a: Increased vagal tone from cholinesterase inhibition
qs.x: Cholinesterase inhibitors increase acetylcholine at cardiac muscarinic receptors, causing bradycardia, heart block, and syncope. They should be used cautiously with conduction disease.
w: Orthostatic hypotension from alpha-1 adrenergic blockade
QT prolongation with torsades de pointes
Hyperkalemia caused by drug-induced hypoaldosteronism

qs.q: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease has distressing visual hallucinations. Anticholinergics and amantadine have been stopped and levodopa reduced as far as tolerated. Which antipsychotic is most appropriate?
qs.a: Quetiapine
qs.x: Parkinson disease psychosis is treated with quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin, which have minimal D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway. Haloperidol, risperidone, and olanzapine worsen motor symptoms.
w: Haloperidol
Risperidone
Olanzapine

qs.q: A 55-year-old woman has an urge to move her legs in the evening, relieved by walking, that disrupts sleep. Exam is normal. Serum ferritin is 32 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is 18 percent. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
qs.a: Iron supplementation
qs.x: Iron is recommended in restless legs syndrome when ferritin is 75 ng/mL or lower or TSAT is below 20 percent. Dopamine agonists and levodopa cause augmentation, and antihistamines worsen symptoms.
w: Pramipexole 0.125 mg nightly
Carbidopa-levodopa at bedtime
Diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime

qs.q: A 46-year-old man with heavy alcohol use is brought in confused. He has horizontal nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus weakness, and a wide-based gait. Fingerstick glucose is 82 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Intravenous thiamine
qs.x: Wernicke encephalopathy requires high-dose IV thiamine immediately, given before or with glucose. Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in alcohol use disorder and inadequate for acute treatment.
w: Intravenous 50 percent dextrose followed by oral thiamine
Oral thiamine 100 mg daily
Intravenous lorazepam 2 mg

qs.q: A 3-year-old boy has 2 days of ear pain and fever of 39.2 C (102.6 F). The right tympanic membrane is bulging and erythematous. He has not received antibiotics in the past month and has no drug allergies. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: High-dose amoxicillin 80 to 90 mg/kg/day
qs.x: High-dose amoxicillin is first-line for acute otitis media in the absence of recent amoxicillin use, concurrent conjunctivitis, or penicillin allergy. Severe symptoms such as fever of 39 C (102.2 F) or higher warrant immediate antibiotics.
w: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 45 mg/kg/day
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg on day 1, then 5 mg/kg daily
Cefdinir 14 mg/kg/day

qs.q: A 10-year-old girl has fever, sore throat, tonsillar exudates, and tender anterior cervical nodes. Rapid strep test is positive. She had anaphylaxis to amoxicillin at age 5. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Azithromycin for 5 days
qs.x: With immediate-type penicillin allergy, IDSA recommends clindamycin, azithromycin, or clarithromycin. First-generation cephalosporins are acceptable only for non-anaphylactic allergy.
w: Cephalexin for 10 days
Amoxicillin for 10 days
Ciprofloxacin for 7 days

qs.q: A 4-month-old girl has 3 days of rhinorrhea, cough, and wheeze. Respiratory rate is 52/min, SpO2 is 93 percent on room air, and she is feeding adequately. Which is the most appropriate management?
qs.a: Nasal suctioning, hydration, and observation
qs.x: AAP guidelines recommend supportive care for bronchiolitis. Albuterol, epinephrine, glucocorticoids, and antibiotics are not routinely recommended; oxygen is given if SpO2 stays below 90 percent.
w: Scheduled nebulized albuterol every 4 hours
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 5 days
Nebulized hypertonic saline and oral azithromycin in the clinic

qs.q: A 3-year-old boy has had fever for 6 days with bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, and swollen hands. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Intravenous immune globulin plus aspirin
qs.x: Kawasaki disease is treated with IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysms. Ibuprofen antagonizes aspirin's antiplatelet effect.
w: Ibuprofen and oral prednisolone
Intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin
Aspirin alone with echocardiography in 6 weeks

qs.q: A 12-day-old girl has a temperature of 38.4 C (101.1 F) and is feeding less than usual. CSF shows pleocytosis and Gram stain is pending. Which is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?
qs.a: Ampicillin plus ceftazidime
qs.x: Febrile neonates need coverage for GBS, E. coli, and Listeria. Ampicillin plus ceftazidime or cefepime is used when meningitis is suspected. Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because it displaces bilirubin and precipitates with calcium.
w: Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin
Ampicillin alone
Oral amoxicillin and outpatient follow-up

qs.q: A 3-year-old boy living in an older home has a venous blood lead level of 52 mcg/dL on repeat testing. He is asymptomatic with a normal neurologic exam. Which is the most appropriate management besides removing the lead source?
qs.a: Oral succimer chelation
qs.x: Oral succimer is used for lead levels of 45 to 69 mcg/dL. Levels of 70 or higher or encephalopathy require hospitalization with dimercaprol plus CaNa2EDTA.
w: Intramuscular dimercaprol plus calcium disodium EDTA
Repeat lead level in 3 months without chelation
Intravenous deferoxamine infusion

qs.q: A 2-year-old girl ingested her mother's prenatal iron tablets 4 hours ago. She has vomiting, hematemesis, and lethargy. Serum bicarbonate is 12 mEq/L and serum iron is 620 mcg/dL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Intravenous deferoxamine
qs.x: Severe iron poisoning with acidosis, shock, or a level above 500 mcg/dL is treated with IV deferoxamine. Activated charcoal does not bind iron.
w: Activated charcoal 1 g/kg
Oral sodium bicarbonate solution
Intravenous N-acetylcysteine

qs.q: A 31-year-old woman at 36 weeks gestation has BP 166/110 mm Hg, a severe headache, and platelets of 88,000/mm3. Antihypertensive therapy has been given and delivery is planned. Which medication should be given to prevent seizures?
qs.a: Magnesium sulfate
qs.x: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures and is superior to phenytoin and diazepam.
w: Levetiracetam
Phenytoin
Lorazepam

qs.q: A 27-year-old woman receiving magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia with severe features becomes drowsy. Patellar reflexes are absent and respiratory rate is 8/min. Which is the most appropriate treatment after stopping the infusion?
qs.a: Intravenous calcium gluconate
qs.x: Magnesium toxicity causes loss of deep tendon reflexes, then respiratory depression and cardiac arrest. Calcium gluconate antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction.
w: Intravenous naloxone
Intravenous furosemide
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with moderate persistent asthma has uterine atony and heavy bleeding after vaginal delivery despite uterine massage and oxytocin infusion. BP is 118/72 mm Hg. Which uterotonic is contraindicated?
qs.a: Carboprost tromethamine
qs.x: Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2-alpha) causes bronchoconstriction and is contraindicated in asthma. Methylergonovine is acceptable in normotensive patients.
w: Methylergonovine
Misoprostol
Additional oxytocin

qs.q: A 33-year-old woman with preeclampsia delivered vaginally and has uterine atony with 1,000 mL of blood loss despite oxytocin. BP is 158/102 mm Hg. She has no asthma. Which uterotonic should be avoided?
qs.a: Methylergonovine
qs.x: Methylergonovine, an ergot alkaloid, causes vasoconstriction and is contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia.
w: Carboprost tromethamine
Misoprostol
Additional oxytocin

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman at 9 weeks gestation has daily nausea with occasional vomiting. She is tolerating fluids, has no ketonuria, and dietary changes and ginger did not help. Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?
qs.a: Pyridoxine with or without doxylamine
qs.x: ACOG recommends vitamin B6 alone or with doxylamine as first-line pharmacotherapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy. Ondansetron and other antiemetics are later options, and steroids are for refractory hyperemesis.
w: Ondansetron 8 mg every 8 hours
Oral methylprednisolone taper
Intravenous metoclopramide every 6 hours at home

qs.q: A 26-year-old woman with a BMI of 36 kg/m2 had unprotected intercourse 4 days ago. She wants to avoid pregnancy and would like long-term contraception. Which is the most effective option?
qs.a: Copper intrauterine device
qs.x: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception up to 5 days after intercourse, is unaffected by body weight, and provides ongoing contraception. Oral levonorgestrel loses efficacy after 72 hours and with obesity.
w: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally once
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally once
Two doses of combined oral contraceptive pills 12 hours apart

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome and BMI 31 kg/m2 has oligomenorrhea and has been trying to conceive for 14 months. Her partner's semen analysis is normal and tubes are patent. Which is the most appropriate first-line ovulation induction agent?
qs.a: Letrozole
qs.x: Letrozole produces higher live birth rates than clomiphene in PCOS and is first-line per ACOG and ASRM. Metformin alone is less effective, and oral contraceptives prevent pregnancy.
w: Clomiphene citrate
Metformin alone
Combined oral contraceptive pills

qs.q: A 51-year-old woman has frequent severe hot flashes and night sweats that disrupt sleep. Her last period was 14 months ago and she has an intact uterus. She has no history of breast cancer, VTE, or cardiovascular disease. Which is the most effective treatment?
qs.a: Estrogen plus a progestogen
qs.x: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms. With an intact uterus, a progestogen must be added to estrogen to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer.
w: Transdermal estradiol alone
Black cohosh extract twice daily
Gabapentin 300 mg nightly

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman at 30 weeks gestation has gestational diabetes. Despite 2 weeks of medical nutrition therapy, fasting glucose values are 104 to 112 mg/dL, while postprandial values are at goal. Which is the preferred pharmacotherapy?
qs.a: Bedtime NPH insulin
qs.x: Insulin is preferred for gestational diabetes because it does not cross the placenta. Glyburide and metformin cross the placenta, and DPP-4 inhibitors are not used in pregnancy. Bedtime NPH targets fasting hyperglycemia.
w: Glyburide 2.5 mg daily
Metformin 500 mg twice daily
Sitagliptin 100 mg daily

qs.q: A 23-year-old nonpregnant woman has a frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge and vulvar itching. Wet mount shows motile flagellated organisms and vaginal pH is 6.0. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days
qs.x: CDC recommends the 7-day metronidazole regimen for trichomoniasis in women because it is more effective than single-dose therapy. Sex partners should also be treated.
w: Metronidazole 2 g orally as a single dose
Fluconazole 150 mg orally once
Clindamycin 2 percent vaginal cream for 7 days

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman at 18 weeks gestation has vulvar itching and thick white discharge. KOH prep shows pseudohyphae. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Topical clotrimazole for 7 days
qs.x: Topical azoles for 7 days are recommended for vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy. Oral fluconazole has been linked to miscarriage and birth defects.
w: Oral fluconazole 150 mg once
Oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months
Vaginal boric acid capsules for 14 days

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman received benzathine penicillin G for secondary syphilis 4 hours ago. She now has fever of 38.7 C (101.7 F), myalgias, headache, and a more prominent rash. BP is 118/74 mm Hg. Which is the most appropriate management?
qs.a: Antipyretics and reassurance
qs.x: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute febrile response to treponemal lysis within 24 hours of treatment. It is self-limited, is not an allergy, and is treated supportively.
w: Intramuscular epinephrine and admission for anaphylaxis
Switch to doxycycline for penicillin allergy
Give a second dose of penicillin for treatment failure

qs.q: A 30-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. CD4 count is 420 cells/mm3 and viral load is 60,000 copies/mL. HLA-B*5701 is negative, hepatitis B serologies are negative, and creatinine is normal. Which is the most appropriate approach?
qs.a: Start dolutegravir plus tenofovir-emtricitabine now
qs.x: Guidelines recommend starting ART at diagnosis regardless of CD4 count, ideally the same day. Initial regimens are based on an integrase inhibitor such as dolutegravir or bictegravir with two NRTIs.
w: Defer ART until the CD4 count falls below 350
Start efavirenz-tenofovir-emtricitabine after resistance testing returns in 4 weeks
Start lopinavir-ritonavir plus zidovudine-lamivudine

qs.q: A 26-year-old nurse sustained a deep needlestick injury 3 hours ago from a patient with known HIV and a detectable viral load. Her baseline HIV test is pending. Which is the most appropriate management?
qs.a: Start a 3-drug PEP regimen now for 28 days
qs.x: Post-exposure prophylaxis should begin as soon as possible, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours, with a 3-drug regimen such as bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide for 28 days.
w: Wait for the source viral load before deciding on PEP
Tenofovir-emtricitabine alone for 7 days
Start PEP only if her baseline HIV test is positive

qs.q: A 39-year-old man with untreated HIV (CD4 60 cells/mm3) has progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. PaO2 is 62 mm Hg on room air. Induced sputum confirms Pneumocystis. TMP-SMX is started. Which medication should be added?
qs.a: Prednisone for 21 days
qs.x: Adjunctive glucocorticoids reduce mortality in moderate to severe Pneumocystis pneumonia with PaO2 below 70 mm Hg or an A-a gradient of 35 or more, and should start within 72 hours.
w: Intravenous caspofungin
Inhaled fluticasone-salmeterol
Azithromycin plus ethambutol daily

qs.q: A 34-year-old man with HIV (CD4 30 cells/mm3) has 2 weeks of headache and fever. CSF opening pressure is 32 cm H2O and cryptococcal antigen is positive. Which is the most appropriate induction therapy?
qs.a: Liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine
qs.x: Induction for cryptococcal meningitis is liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine, with serial LPs for elevated pressure. ART is delayed 4 to 6 weeks to reduce fatal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
w: Fluconazole 400 mg daily alone
Voriconazole plus caspofungin
Amphotericin B plus immediate initiation of antiretroviral therapy

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman from Vietnam has a positive interferon-gamma release assay during employment screening. She has no symptoms and chest x-ray is normal. HIV is negative and she takes no other medications. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Rifampin daily for 4 months
qs.x: Rifamycin-based short regimens (4 months of rifampin, 3 months of weekly isoniazid-rifapentine, or 3 months of daily isoniazid-rifampin) are preferred for latent TB because of better completion and less hepatotoxicity.
w: Rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months
No treatment unless symptoms develop
Isoniazid daily for 3 months

qs.q: A 27-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive is starting rifampin for latent TB. Which is the most appropriate contraceptive advice?
qs.a: Use a copper IUD or other nonhormonal method during therapy
qs.x: Rifampin strongly induces CYP3A4 and reduces levels of oral hormonal contraceptives and implants. A copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUD, or DMPA injection is recommended.
w: No change, since the interaction is not clinically significant
Double the daily dose of the oral contraceptive pill
Switch to the etonogestrel implant

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation must travel for work to rural Ghana, where chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum is widespread. Which malaria chemoprophylaxis is most appropriate?
qs.a: Mefloquine weekly
qs.x: Mefloquine is the recommended chemoprophylaxis in pregnancy for chloroquine-resistant areas. Doxycycline is contraindicated, primaquine risks hemolysis in a G6PD-deficient fetus, and chloroquine resistance is widespread in Africa.
w: Doxycycline daily
Primaquine daily
Chloroquine weekly

qs.q: A 26-year-old man traveling in Thailand develops fever of 38.8 C (101.8 F), abdominal cramps, and bloody diarrhea. Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
qs.a: Azithromycin
qs.x: Azithromycin is preferred for dysentery and for travelers' diarrhea in Southeast Asia because of high fluoroquinolone resistance in Campylobacter. Rifaximin is not used for invasive disease.
w: Ciprofloxacin
Rifaximin
Loperamide alone

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, headache, and confusion with an episode of olfactory hallucinations. MRI shows right temporal lobe hyperintensity and CSF has lymphocytic pleocytosis with red cells. Which is the most appropriate treatment while awaiting PCR?
qs.a: Intravenous acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours
qs.x: Suspected HSV encephalitis requires empiric IV acyclovir immediately because delay increases mortality and neurologic sequelae. Oral agents do not achieve adequate CNS levels.
w: Oral valacyclovir 1 g three times daily
Intravenous ganciclovir 5 mg/kg every 12 hours
Withhold antivirals until the HSV PCR result returns

qs.q: A 30-year-old man from Connecticut had an expanding red rash after a camping trip and now, 3 weeks after the trip, has a left facial droop involving the forehead. Lyme serology is positive. He has no headache or meningismus. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Oral doxycycline for 14 days
qs.x: Lyme facial palsy without meningitis can be treated with oral doxycycline for 14 days. IV ceftriaxone is reserved for meningitis, high-grade AV block, or inability to take oral therapy.
w: Intravenous ceftriaxone for 28 days
Oral prednisone alone
Oral amoxicillin for 5 days

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman has 8 watery stools daily after a course of clindamycin. WBC is 11,000/mm3 and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Stool testing confirms C. difficile infection. This is her first episode. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Oral fidaxomicin for 10 days
qs.x: IDSA prefers fidaxomicin for an initial episode because of lower recurrence, with oral vancomycin as an acceptable alternative. Metronidazole is only an option for nonsevere disease when the others are unavailable.
w: Oral metronidazole for 14 days
Intravenous metronidazole alone
Oral rifaximin for 7 days

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with lung cancer will receive cisplatin-based chemotherapy. Which antiemetic regimen is most appropriate before the first cycle?
qs.a: NK1 antagonist, 5-HT3 antagonist, dexamethasone, and olanzapine
qs.x: Highly emetogenic chemotherapy such as cisplatin warrants four-drug prophylaxis per ASCO and NCCN: an NK1 antagonist, a 5-HT3 antagonist, dexamethasone, and olanzapine.
w: Ondansetron alone before each cycle
Prochlorperazine and lorazepam as needed after each chemotherapy infusion
Ondansetron and dexamethasone only

qs.q: A 54-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer has a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F). ANC is 200/mm3. BP is 122/76 mm Hg, she has no catheter site infection, and lungs are clear. Which is the most appropriate empiric therapy?
qs.a: Intravenous cefepime
qs.x: High-risk febrile neutropenia requires prompt IV monotherapy with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam. Vancomycin is added only for specific indications such as instability or catheter infection.
w: Intravenous vancomycin plus ceftriaxone
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate at home
Intravenous ceftriaxone plus fluconazole

qs.q: A 16-year-old boy with osteosarcoma receives high-dose methotrexate. Which medication is given 24 hours later to protect normal cells?
qs.a: Leucovorin
qs.x: Leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses dihydrofolate reductase to rescue normal cells after high-dose methotrexate. Hydration, urine alkalinization, and level monitoring are also used.
w: Mesna
Dexrazoxane
Folic acid

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with lupus nephritis is receiving IV cyclophosphamide. Which medication reduces her risk of hemorrhagic cystitis?
qs.a: Mesna
qs.x: Acrolein, a cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide metabolite, injures the bladder. Mesna binds acrolein in the urine; hydration also helps.
w: Leucovorin
Amifostine
Dexrazoxane

qs.q: A 64-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has new back pain, bilateral leg weakness, and urinary retention. Which is the most appropriate immediate step while arranging urgent MRI of the spine?
qs.a: Intravenous dexamethasone
qs.x: Suspected malignant spinal cord compression is treated with high-dose dexamethasone immediately, then urgent MRI of the whole spine and radiation or surgery.
w: Intravenous morphine and observation
Start leuprolide
Oral ibuprofen and physical therapy

qs.q: A 72-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer starts scheduled oxycodone for pain. Which is the most appropriate bowel regimen to start at the same time?
qs.a: Scheduled senna
qs.x: Opioid-induced constipation should be prevented when opioids are started, using a stimulant laxative such as senna, with or without an osmotic laxative. Fiber can worsen it, and docusate alone is ineffective.
w: Psyllium fiber twice daily
Loperamide as needed
Docusate alone

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 22 mL/min) has an acutely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint aspiration shows negatively birefringent crystals. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Oral prednisone 30 to 40 mg daily for 5 days
qs.x: Glucocorticoids are preferred for acute gout in advanced CKD. NSAIDs worsen kidney function, and colchicine requires dose reduction in CKD; hourly high-dose colchicine is no longer used.
w: Indomethacin 50 mg three times daily
Colchicine 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg every hour until diarrhea
Start allopurinol 300 mg daily alone

qs.q: A 58-year-old man of Korean descent with CKD stage 3 has recurrent gout and tophi. Urate-lowering therapy is planned. Which test is recommended before starting allopurinol?
qs.a: HLA-B*5801 testing
qs.x: ACR recommends HLA-B*5801 testing before allopurinol in people of Korean descent with CKD 3 or worse and in those of Han Chinese, Thai, or African ancestry, because the allele predicts severe cutaneous reactions.
w: HLA-B*1502 testing
Thiopurine methyltransferase activity
24-hour urinary uric acid excretion

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman has newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis with high disease activity. Liver enzymes, creatinine, and CBC are normal. She does not drink alcohol. Which is the most appropriate initial DMARD?
qs.a: Methotrexate with folic acid
qs.x: ACR recommends methotrexate monotherapy as the first DMARD in RA with moderate to high disease activity, with folic acid to reduce adverse effects. Long-term glucocorticoids should be avoided.
w: Long-term prednisone monotherapy
Adalimumab monotherapy
Hydroxychloroquine plus prednisone 20 mg daily

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman has new temporal headache, jaw claudication, and 1 day of blurred vision in the left eye. ESR is 98 mm/h. Temporal artery biopsy is scheduled for next week. Which is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Start high-dose glucocorticoids now, before biopsy
qs.x: Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms requires immediate high-dose glucocorticoids (often IV methylprednisolone) to prevent permanent vision loss. Biopsy remains diagnostic for 2 weeks or more.
w: Wait for biopsy results before starting any therapy
Start low-dose prednisone 10 mg daily
Start aspirin 81 mg daily alone

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman has 2 months of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching with morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. ESR is 62 mm/h and CK is normal. She has no headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Prednisone 12.5 to 25 mg daily
qs.x: Polymyalgia rheumatica responds rapidly to low-dose prednisone 12.5 to 25 mg daily with a slow taper. High doses are used for giant cell arteritis.
w: Prednisone 60 mg daily
Methotrexate monotherapy
Oral naproxen 500 mg twice daily alone

qs.q: A 26-year-old woman with SLE has hematuria, proteinuria of 2.5 g/day, and rising creatinine. Kidney biopsy shows class IV lupus nephritis. Which is the most appropriate induction therapy with glucocorticoids?
qs.a: Mycophenolate mofetil
qs.x: Mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids is used to induce remission in proliferative lupus nephritis. Belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor may be added.
w: Hydroxychloroquine alone
Methotrexate
Azathioprine plus NSAID

qs.q: A 48-year-old woman has a duodenal ulcer and a positive H. pylori stool antigen. She received clarithromycin for sinusitis last year. She has no drug allergies. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days
qs.x: ACG prefers bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) for 14 days for treatment-naive H. pylori infection, especially with prior macrolide exposure, because clarithromycin resistance is common.
w: PPI, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin for 7 days
PPI and amoxicillin for 5 days
Levofloxacin alone for 10 days
