qs.x: Nesiritide is recombinant BNP; NPR-A is a membrane-bound guanylate cyclase that raises cGMP, relaxing vascular smooth muscle.
w: Increased cyclic AMP from Gs-coupled adenylyl cyclase
Increased IP3 and calcium release from Gq signaling
Decreased cyclic GMP from phosphodiesterase activation

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman with acute decompensated heart failure is started on nesiritide. Which adverse effect is most common and most likely to limit the infusion?
qs.a: Hypotension
qs.x: Hypotension is the most frequent adverse effect of nesiritide; it is contraindicated in cardiogenic shock and when SBP is below 100 mmHg.
w: Hyperkalemia
Bronchospasm
Hyperglycemia

qs.q: A client is to begin a nesiritide bolus and infusion. Current vital signs are BP 94/58 mmHg, HR 92/min, and RR 24/min. What is the nurse's best action?
qs.a: Withhold the drug and notify the provider of the BP
qs.x: Nesiritide should not be started when systolic BP is below 100 mmHg because it can cause significant, prolonged hypotension.
w: Give the bolus and begin the infusion as ordered
Give the bolus only and hold the infusion for 1 hour
Begin the infusion at a double rate to skip the bolus

qs.q: A patient with a hypertensive emergency and acute kidney injury receives an IV agent that dilates renal arterioles and increases sodium excretion. Which receptor does this drug activate?
qs.a: Peripheral dopamine D1 receptor
qs.x: Fenoldopam is a selective peripheral D1 agonist that raises cAMP in vascular smooth muscle, dilating renal and mesenteric arterioles.
w: Central alpha-2 adrenergic receptor
Vascular beta-2 adrenergic receptor
Presynaptic dopamine D2 receptor

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with a hypertensive emergency is treated with a fenoldopam infusion. Which adverse effect is a recognized dose-related consequence of this drug?
qs.a: Increased intraocular pressure
qs.x: Fenoldopam can raise intraocular pressure and cause hypokalemia and reflex tachycardia; cyanide toxicity is associated with nitroprusside.
w: Cyanide accumulation
Bronchospasm
Hyperkalemia

qs.q: A client has been receiving a fenoldopam infusion for 6 hours for severe hypertension. Which laboratory value is most important for the nurse to monitor?
qs.a: Serum potassium
qs.x: Fenoldopam commonly lowers serum potassium, often within the first 6 hours, so potassium should be checked and replaced as ordered.
w: Serum calcium
Serum amylase
Platelet count

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and an LVOT gradient of 80 mmHg is started on a drug that reduces actin-myosin cross-bridge formation. What is its molecular target?
qs.a: Cardiac myosin ATPase
qs.x: Mavacamten is an allosteric, reversible inhibitor of cardiac myosin ATPase that reduces hypercontractility and LVOT obstruction.
w: Cardiac troponin C
L-type calcium channel
Phospholamban protein

qs.q: A patient with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is being considered for mavacamten. Which finding must be confirmed before therapy begins?
qs.a: Left ventricular ejection fraction of at least 55%
qs.x: The boxed warning requires echocardiographic LVEF of at least 55% before starting because mavacamten can cause HF from systolic dysfunction.
w: Resting heart rate of at least 70/min in sinus rhythm
Serum potassium above 5.0 mEq/L before the first dose
Absence of prior septal myectomy on surgical history

qs.q: A client on mavacamten for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes for the scheduled echocardiogram. Which result requires the drug to be interrupted?
qs.a: An LVEF of 45 percent
qs.x: Mavacamten reduces contractility by inhibiting cardiac myosin ATPase, so its REMS program requires serial echocardiograms and the drug is interrupted when LVEF falls below 50 percent. Atrial size and septal thickness are features of the disease, not stopping rules.
w: An LVEF of 62 percent
A left atrial size of 42 mm
A septal thickness of 18 mm

qs.q: An oral heart failure drug increases cyclic GMP by directly stimulating the nitric oxide receptor, even when nitric oxide levels are low. Which enzyme does it act on?
qs.a: Soluble guanylate cyclase
qs.x: Vericiguat stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase independently of NO and sensitizes it to endogenous NO, increasing cGMP.
w: Phosphodiesterase type 5
Neutral endopeptidase
Membrane adenylyl cyclase

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with HFrEF who was recently hospitalized is being started on vericiguat. Which of his current medications is contraindicated with it?
qs.a: Riociguat for pulmonary hypertension
qs.x: Vericiguat is contraindicated with other soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat because of additive hypotension.
w: Atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia
Empagliflozin for heart failure
Metformin for type 2 diabetes

qs.q: A woman of reproductive age is starting vericiguat. Which teaching point is the priority for the nurse to include?
qs.a: Avoid pregnancy and use effective contraception
qs.x: Vericiguat carries a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, so pregnancy must be excluded and effective contraception used.
w: Take each dose on an empty stomach at bedtime
Avoid foods high in potassium such as bananas
Expect orange urine during the first week of use

qs.q: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis and ascites develops hepatorenal syndrome with acute kidney injury. He is treated with albumin plus a vasopressin analog. Which receptor mediates the main therapeutic effect of this drug?
qs.a: V1 receptor on splanchnic vascular smooth muscle
qs.x: Terlipressin is a V1-selective vasopressin analog; splanchnic vasoconstriction raises effective arterial volume and improves renal perfusion in hepatorenal syndrome.
w: V2 receptor on renal collecting duct principal cells
Alpha-1 receptor on systemic arteriolar smooth muscle
SSTR2 receptor on splanchnic endothelial cells

qs.q: A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis and hepatorenal syndrome-AKI is being considered for terlipressin. Which finding is a contraindication to starting it?
qs.a: Oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
qs.x: Terlipressin carries a boxed warning for serious or fatal respiratory failure and should not be started in patients with SpO2 below 90% or worsening respiratory symptoms.
w: Serum sodium of 131 mEq/L
Urine sodium below 10 mEq/L
Large-volume ascites on ultrasound

qs.q: A client is starting terlipressin for hepatorenal syndrome. Which baseline assessment does the boxed warning drive?
qs.a: Oxygen saturation and volume status
qs.x: Terlipressin carries a boxed warning for serious or fatal respiratory failure, so oxygenation and volume status are assessed before the first dose and the drug is avoided in patients who are hypoxic or fluid overloaded. Its V1 receptor action causes ischemic complications rather than QT change.
w: Serum potassium and magnesium
A twelve-lead ECG with QT interval
A fasting lipid panel with an A1c and TSH

qs.q: A 68-year-old hospitalized woman with SIADH and a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L is started on an IV drug that blocks vasopressin receptors. What is the mechanism by which this drug raises the serum sodium?
qs.a: Reduced aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct
qs.x: Conivaptan blocks V2 receptors, preventing cAMP-driven aquaporin-2 insertion and producing free water excretion (aquaresis); it also blocks V1a receptors.
w: Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop
Increased aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex
Blockade of the epithelial sodium channel in the tubule

qs.q: A 72-year-old man is admitted with a serum sodium of 121 mEq/L. Which clinical situation is a contraindication to treatment with IV conivaptan?
qs.a: Vomiting with dry mucosa and orthostasis
qs.x: Conivaptan is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia; it is used for euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia.
w: Small-cell lung cancer with euvolemia
Heart failure with peripheral edema
Postoperative nausea with normal volume

qs.q: A client with euvolemic hyponatremia receives an IV conivaptan infusion. Which effect accounts for the rise in serum sodium?
qs.a: Loss of free water without loss of sodium
qs.x: Conivaptan blocks the V2 receptor in the collecting duct, so aquaporin-2 channels are withdrawn and solute-free water is excreted. That is an aquaresis rather than a diuresis, which is why fluid restriction is relaxed during the infusion to keep the sodium from climbing too fast.
w: Loss of sodium and water in about equal amounts
Increased renal reabsorption of sodium
Movement of sodium out of the cells

qs.q: A 47-year-old man with acromegaly has persistent elevation of IGF-1 after transsphenoidal surgery. He is started on a monthly deep subcutaneous injection that inhibits growth hormone release. Which receptor does this drug activate?
qs.a: Somatostatin receptor subtype 2
qs.x: Lanreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analog that acts mainly at SSTR2 and SSTR5, a Gi-coupled receptor that suppresses GH secretion.
w: Growth hormone receptor on hepatocytes
Dopamine D2 receptor on somatotrophs
GHRH receptor on anterior pituitary cells

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic small bowel neuroendocrine tumor and carcinoid syndrome has received lanreotide every 4 weeks for 1 year. Which adverse effect is most likely to develop with long-term use?
qs.a: Cholelithiasis
qs.x: Somatostatin analogs reduce gallbladder contractility and cholecystokinin release, causing gallbladder sludge and gallstones.
w: Hypercalcemia
Pulmonary fibrosis
Hyperkalemia

qs.q: A nurse is preparing to give lanreotide 120 mg to a client with a neuroendocrine tumor. Which administration technique is correct?
qs.a: Deep subcutaneous injection in the upper outer buttock
qs.x: Lanreotide is given by deep subcutaneous injection in the superior external quadrant of the buttock, alternating sides; the site is not massaged.
w: IV push over 2 minutes through a saline lock
Intramuscular injection into the deltoid muscle
Subcutaneous injection into the abdomen with massage

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman has fasting hypoglycemia with inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide levels from an unresectable insulinoma. She is started on an oral drug that prevents insulin release. Which action describes this drug?
qs.a: Opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells
qs.x: Diazoxide binds the SUR1 subunit and opens K-ATP channels, hyperpolarizing beta cells and blocking insulin release, the opposite of sulfonylureas.
w: Closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells
Blocks GLP-1 receptors on pancreatic beta cells
Activates SSTR5 receptors on pancreatic delta cells

qs.q: A 6-month-old infant with congenital hyperinsulinism has been treated with oral diazoxide for 4 months. Which adverse effect is most characteristic of this therapy?
qs.a: Hypertrichosis
qs.x: Diazoxide commonly causes hypertrichosis and also fluid retention; infants are at risk for pulmonary hypertension.
w: Gingival hyperplasia
Hypokalemic alkalosis
Lactic acidosis

qs.q: A nurse is teaching the parents of an infant started on diazoxide oral suspension for congenital hyperinsulinism. Which statement by a parent shows correct understanding?
qs.a: I will report fast breathing or swelling right away
qs.x: Diazoxide can cause fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension in infants; respiratory distress or swelling must be reported promptly, and doses are measured with the dropper on a schedule.
w: I will stop it if my baby grows extra body hair
I can measure the dose with a kitchen teaspoon
I will give it only when the sugar reading is low

qs.q: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting, muscle weakness, and cardiomyopathy. Plasma carnitine is very low. Supplementation corrects his defect in which process?
qs.a: Transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria
qs.x: Carnitine is required to carry long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation; deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia and myopathy.
w: Transport of pyruvate into the mitochondrial matrix
Conversion of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA in cytosol
Transfer of reducing equivalents by the malate shuttle

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman with epilepsy takes a large intentional overdose of valproic acid. She is lethargic, and her ammonia level is markedly elevated. Which therapy is most appropriate for the hyperammonemia?
qs.a: IV levocarnitine
qs.x: Valproate depletes carnitine and impairs urea cycle function; IV levocarnitine is used for valproate-induced hyperammonemia and hepatotoxicity.
w: IV physostigmine
Oral lactulose alone
IV fomepizole

qs.q: A client on hemodialysis is prescribed IV levocarnitine. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
qs.a: Give it as a slow IV bolus after the dialysis session
qs.x: In end-stage renal disease, levocarnitine is given as a slow IV bolus over 2-3 minutes at the end of each dialysis session, since dialysis removes carnitine.
w: Give it before dialysis so the filter clears the excess
Mix it with the client's oral phosphate binder dose
Give it by rapid IV push during the first hour of dialysis

qs.q: A 16-year-old with osteosarcoma develops acute kidney injury after high-dose methotrexate and has a markedly elevated plasma methotrexate level. He receives an IV enzyme. What is the mechanism of this drug?
qs.a: Cleaves the terminal glutamate from methotrexate
qs.x: Glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase G2) hydrolyzes methotrexate to inactive DAMPA and glutamate; leucovorin, by contrast, bypasses the DHFR block.
w: Bypasses dihydrofolate reductase by providing folate
Enhances renal tubular secretion of methotrexate
Inhibits thymidylate synthase in normal tissues

qs.q: A 45-year-old man with lymphoma receives glucarpidase for toxic methotrexate levels and impaired renal function. Which statement about subsequent management is correct?
qs.a: Leucovorin is continued but not within 2 hours of the dose
qs.x: Glucarpidase degrades leucovorin, so leucovorin is separated by 2 hours but continued; immunoassays overestimate methotrexate for 48 hours due to DAMPA.
w: Leucovorin should be stopped once glucarpidase is given
Immunoassay methotrexate levels are reliable right away
Hemodialysis should be started at the same time as dosing

qs.q: A nurse is giving glucarpidase to a client with methotrexate toxicity. The client is also scheduled for IV leucovorin. When should the leucovorin be given?
qs.a: At least 2 hours after the glucarpidase dose
qs.x: Leucovorin is a substrate for glucarpidase, so it should not be given within 2 hours before or after the glucarpidase dose.
w: Mixed with glucarpidase in the same syringe
Immediately before glucarpidase in the same line
Only after levels are undetectable on immunoassay

qs.q: A 64-year-old man on a continuous 5-fluorouracil infusion receives the full 4-day dose in 4 hours due to a pump error. He is given an oral antidote. What is its mechanism?
qs.a: Uridine competes with fluorouridine triphosphate for RNA
qs.x: Uridine triacetate is converted to uridine, and the resulting UTP competitively limits incorporation of the 5-FU metabolite FUTP into RNA of normal cells.
w: It restores thymidylate synthase activity by binding 5-FU
It supplies reduced folate to stabilize thymidylate synthase
It increases dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity

qs.q: A 59-year-old woman taking capecitabine develops severe diarrhea, mucositis, and neutropenia within 2 days of starting therapy. Genetic testing later shows dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency. Which is the most appropriate antidote?
qs.a: Uridine triacetate
qs.x: Uridine triacetate treats early-onset severe toxicity from 5-FU or capecitabine within 96 hours; leucovorin potentiates 5-FU, and glucarpidase is for methotrexate.
w: Leucovorin
Glucarpidase
Mesna

qs.q: A client receiving uridine triacetate every 6 hours vomits 45 minutes after taking a dose. What should the nurse do?
qs.a: Give another full dose as soon as possible
qs.x: The label directs that if vomiting occurs within 2 hours of a dose, a complete dose should be repeated as soon as possible, then the schedule continues.
w: Wait and give the next dose on schedule
Give half a dose mixed with water instead
Hold all remaining doses and notify pharmacy

qs.q: A 78-year-old woman taking apixaban has a large intracerebral hemorrhage. She receives a recombinant protein that lacks the Gla domain and has an inactivated active site. How does this agent restore hemostasis?
qs.a: It acts as a decoy that binds and sequesters the factor Xa inhibitor
qs.x: Andexanet alfa is a catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy that binds apixaban and rivaroxaban, freeing native factor Xa to function.
w: It directly activates factor X to generate thrombin at the bleeding site
It replaces vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X in plasma
It binds the drug with a monoclonal antibody fragment and is renally cleared

qs.q: A 70-year-old man on rivaroxaban receives andexanet alfa for a life-threatening GI bleed and hemostasis is achieved. Which complication carries a boxed warning for this agent?
qs.a: Thromboembolic events, ischemic events and cardiac arrest
qs.x: Andexanet alfa has a boxed warning for thromboembolic and ischemic events, cardiac arrest and sudden death; anticoagulation should resume when appropriate.
w: Severe hypoglycemia and ventricular arrhythmia
Acute interstitial nephritis progressing to renal failure
Hepatic necrosis with marked transaminase elevation

qs.q: A 60-year-old man has persistent oozing after cardiac surgery with laboratory evidence of hyperfibrinolysis. He is given a lysine analog. What is its mechanism?
qs.a: Blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin, preventing plasmin formation
qs.x: Aminocaproic acid occupies the lysine-binding sites of plasminogen, preventing its binding to fibrin and its activation to plasmin.
w: Directly inhibits thrombin and fibrin-bound thrombin
Replaces fibrinogen and factor XIII consumed during bypass surgery
Activates glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors on platelets

qs.q: A patient with severe hemophilia A is treated with aminocaproic acid for a prolonged dental bleed. Which condition is a contraindication to this drug unless heparin is also given?
qs.a: Disseminated intravascular coagulation with active clotting
qs.x: Antifibrinolytics can cause dangerous thrombosis in active intravascular clotting such as DIC unless heparin is given concurrently.
w: Mild iron deficiency anemia
Stable stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a normal serum potassium
A history of seasonal allergic rhinitis and asthma

qs.q: A patient has received continuous aminocaproic acid for several days. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor for a characteristic adverse effect?
qs.a: Creatine kinase
qs.x: Prolonged aminocaproic acid can cause skeletal muscle weakness with necrosis and rhabdomyolysis, so CK should be monitored.
w: Serum amylase
Thyroid stimulating hormone
Serum ammonia

qs.q: During PCI, a patient receives an IV antiplatelet agent with a half-life of 3 to 6 minutes that does not need hepatic activation. Which statement best describes this drug?
qs.a: A direct, reversible antagonist of the platelet P2Y12 receptor
qs.x: Cangrelor is an ATP analog that directly and reversibly blocks P2Y12 without metabolic activation, so platelet function returns within about 1 hour.
w: An irreversible prodrug inhibitor of the platelet P2Y12 receptor
A reversible antagonist of the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor
An irreversible inhibitor of platelet cyclooxygenase-1

qs.q: A patient finishing PCI on a cangrelor infusion needs to start oral clopidogrel. When should the clopidogrel 600 mg load be given to achieve platelet inhibition?
qs.a: Immediately after the cangrelor infusion is stopped
qs.x: Cangrelor blocks binding of the clopidogrel and prasugrel active metabolites, so those loads are given right after the infusion ends; ticagrelor may be given during it.
w: Thirty minutes before the cangrelor bolus is given
Halfway through the cangrelor infusion
Only after a 24-hour washout of cangrelor

qs.q: A nurse is caring for a patient receiving a cangrelor infusion after femoral PCI. Which assessment finding requires immediate notification of the provider?
qs.a: A rapidly expanding hematoma at the groin access site
qs.x: Bleeding is the main adverse effect of cangrelor; an expanding hematoma suggests significant access site bleeding and needs urgent evaluation.
w: Mild bruising near a peripheral IV site in the forearm
Heart rate of 78 beats per minute and regular rhythm
Blood pressure of 128/76 mmHg with no symptoms

qs.q: A 6-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A has high-titer factor VIII inhibitors. He starts a SC antibody that prevents bleeding. What is its mechanism?
qs.a: Bridges factors IXa and X to replace the cofactor role of factor VIIIa
qs.x: Emicizumab is a bispecific antibody that binds factor IXa and factor X, mimicking factor VIIIa; it is not affected by factor VIII inhibitors.
w: Directly activates prothrombin to thrombin at sites of tissue injury
Inhibits tissue factor pathway inhibitor to increase thrombin generation
Binds and neutralizes the factor VIII inhibitor antibodies in plasma

qs.q: A patient with hemophilia A and inhibitors on emicizumab prophylaxis has a breakthrough joint bleed. Which treatment carries a boxed warning in combination with emicizumab?
qs.a: Activated prothrombin complex concentrate at high cumulative doses
qs.x: Thrombotic microangiopathy and thromboembolism occurred when aPCC averaging more than 100 U/kg per 24 hours was given for 24 hours or more.
w: Recombinant activated factor VII given at standard labeled doses
Tranexamic acid given orally for a mucosal bleed
Acetaminophen for joint pain after the bleed

qs.q: A patient on emicizumab has a preoperative aPTT that is shorter than normal. What is the best interpretation by the nurse?
qs.a: The drug interferes with aPTT, so the result does not reflect hemostasis
qs.x: Emicizumab falsely shortens the aPTT and affects one-stage factor VIII assays; chromogenic assays with bovine reagents are used instead.
w: The patient has developed a clot and needs heparin started
The patient no longer has hemophilia and needs no further factor therapy
The specimen was hemolyzed and must be redrawn at once

qs.q: A patient in refractory septic shock is started on a synthetic peptide vasopressor. Which receptor mediates its pressor effect?
qs.a: Angiotensin II type 1 receptor on vascular smooth muscle
qs.x: Angiotensin II activates Gq-coupled AT1 receptors, causing vasoconstriction and aldosterone release, a mechanism distinct from catecholamines and vasopressin.
w: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor on vascular smooth muscle
Vasopressin V1a receptor on vascular smooth muscle
Beta-1 adrenergic receptor on cardiac myocytes

qs.q: A 64-year-old man in septic shock remains hypotensive despite norepinephrine and vasopressin and is started on angiotensin II. Which order should accompany this drug?
qs.a: Pharmacologic venous thromboembolism prophylaxis
qs.x: Thrombosis occurred more often with angiotensin II than placebo, so the label requires concurrent VTE prophylaxis.
w: Daily scheduled IV loop diuretic therapy to prevent edema
Routine oral potassium chloride replacement
Continuous IV insulin regardless of glucose

qs.q: A nurse is titrating an angiotensin II infusion for distributive shock. Which finding is most important to report as a drug-related adverse effect?
qs.a: Cool, mottled fingers with weak radial pulses
qs.x: Angiotensin II can cause peripheral ischemia and thrombosis; signs of poor distal perfusion must be reported promptly.
w: Mean arterial pressure of 68 mmHg on the infusion
Urine output of 45 mL per hour for 2 hours
Heart rate of 92 beats per minute and regular rhythm

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension starts a continuous SC infusion. Which intracellular change mediates the drug's vasodilation?
qs.a: Increased cAMP after prostacyclin IP receptor activation
qs.x: Treprostinil is a prostacyclin analog that activates Gs-coupled IP receptors, raising cAMP to cause vasodilation and platelet inhibition.
w: Increased cGMP after soluble guanylate cyclase stimulation
Decreased endothelin-1 binding at ETA receptors
Decreased cGMP breakdown by phosphodiesterase-5

qs.q: A patient with PAH on continuous IV treprostinil arrives with a disconnected pump that stopped 2 hours ago. What is the most important risk?
qs.a: Rebound pulmonary hypertension with acute right heart failure
qs.x: Abrupt withdrawal or interruption of prostacyclin therapy can cause rebound PAH and right ventricular failure; the infusion should be restored promptly.
w: Severe systemic hypertensive crisis from unopposed vasoconstriction
Acute hypoglycemia from loss of prostacyclin effect
Delayed allergic reaction once the infusion is restarted

qs.q: A nurse is caring for a patient receiving SC treprostinil by home pump. Which teaching point is most accurate?
qs.a: Pain and redness at the infusion site are common and should be reported
qs.x: Infusion site pain is the most common adverse effect of SC treprostinil; the infusion must never be interrupted, flushed or bolused.
w: The pump may be turned off overnight to rest the infusion site
The catheter should be flushed rapidly whenever the alarm sounds
Missed doses should be made up by doubling the next pump rate

qs.q: A 55-year-old man with inoperable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension starts an oral drug that works even when nitric oxide is low. What is its target?
qs.a: Soluble guanylate cyclase
qs.x: Riociguat sensitizes soluble guanylate cyclase to NO and stimulates it directly, increasing cGMP; it is approved for CTEPH and PAH.
w: Phosphodiesterase type 5
Endothelin receptor type A
Prostacyclin IP receptor

qs.q: A woman with CTEPH is stable on riociguat. Which medication is contraindicated with riociguat because of severe hypotension?
qs.a: Sildenafil
qs.x: Riociguat is contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors and nitrates because combined cGMP elevation causes profound hypotension.
w: Warfarin
Furosemide
Atorvastatin

qs.q: A nurse reviews the plan for a 30-year-old woman starting riociguat. Which action must be confirmed before the first dose?
qs.a: A negative pregnancy test
qs.x: Riociguat has a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity; pregnancy must be excluded before starting and effective contraception used.
w: A normal serum potassium
A normal hemoglobin A1c
A baseline chest x-ray

qs.q: A 41-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension begins an oral once-daily agent that selectively blocks one receptor subtype for a potent vasoconstrictor peptide. Which receptor is targeted?
qs.a: Endothelin type A receptor
qs.x: Ambrisentan is ETA-selective, blocking endothelin-1 mediated vasoconstriction and proliferation while largely sparing ETB.
w: Endothelin type B receptor
Prostacyclin IP receptor
Angiotensin II type 1 receptor

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has pulmonary hypertension on right heart catheterization. Which drug is contraindicated in this patient?
qs.a: Ambrisentan
qs.x: Ambrisentan is contraindicated in IPF, including IPF with pulmonary hypertension, because it increased disease progression and hospitalization in a trial.
w: Supplemental oxygen
Pirfenidone
Inhaled treprostinil

qs.q: A client with pulmonary arterial hypertension started ambrisentan 2 weeks ago. Which finding is most important for the nurse to report?
qs.a: Bilateral ankle edema with a 2-kg weight gain
qs.x: Peripheral edema and fluid retention are common with ambrisentan and may signal heart failure or pulmonary edema requiring evaluation.
w: Mild nasal congestion since starting the drug
Occasional flushing after taking the tablet
Fatigue that improves after a short afternoon rest period

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension starts a once-daily dual endothelin receptor antagonist. Which enzyme converts it to its active metabolite and mediates its key drug interactions?
qs.a: CYP3A4
qs.x: Macitentan is metabolized by CYP3A4 to an active metabolite, so strong CYP3A4 inducers and inhibitors should be avoided.
w: CYP2D6
Carboxylesterase 1
UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1

qs.q: A 34-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension is starting macitentan. Which laboratory test must be obtained before the first dose?
qs.a: Serum pregnancy test
qs.x: Macitentan carries a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, so pregnancy must be excluded before starting therapy.
w: Serum uric acid level
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Serum lipase level

qs.q: A client taking macitentan for pulmonary arterial hypertension is prescribed rifampin for latent tuberculosis. What is the nurse's best action?
qs.a: Contact the prescriber about the interaction
qs.x: Rifampin is a strong CYP3A4 inducer that markedly lowers macitentan levels, and the combination should be avoided.
w: Give both drugs at least 2 hours apart
Give rifampin and hold macitentan for the next week
Administer both drugs as ordered with food

qs.q: A 47-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension on an endothelin receptor antagonist and a PDE-5 inhibitor starts an oral nonprostanoid agent. Which intracellular change mediates its vasodilator effect?
qs.a: Increased cAMP via a Gs-coupled IP receptor
qs.x: Selexipag activates the Gs-coupled prostacyclin IP receptor, raising cAMP in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle.
w: Increased cGMP via soluble guanylate cyclase
Decreased IP3 via Gq-coupled receptor blockade
Decreased calcium entry via L-type channel block

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with pulmonary arterial hypertension takes selexipag. His physician plans to treat his hypertriglyceridemia. Which drug is contraindicated with selexipag?
qs.a: Gemfibrozil
qs.x: Gemfibrozil is a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor that greatly increases exposure to the active selexipag metabolite.
w: Fenofibrate
Atorvastatin
Icosapent ethyl

qs.q: A client on selexipag for pulmonary arterial hypertension is prescribed gemfibrozil for high triglycerides. What does the selexipag label say?
qs.a: The combination is contraindicated
qs.x: Gemfibrozil is a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor and roughly doubles selexipag exposure while raising the active metabolite several-fold, so the label contraindicates concomitant use. Selexipag is an oral agonist at the prostacyclin IP receptor, not a prostacyclin analog.
w: The selexipag dose should be doubled
The two should be given 2 hours apart
No change is needed with this pair

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with coronary artery disease receives a subcutaneous drug every 6 months that is taken up by hepatocytes via the asialoglycoprotein receptor. What is its mechanism?
qs.a: RNA interference that degrades PCSK9 mRNA
qs.x: Inclisiran is a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA that directs RISC-mediated cleavage of PCSK9 mRNA in hepatocytes.
w: Antibody binding to circulating PCSK9
Inhibition of ATP-citrate lyase
Inhibition of NPC1L1 sterol transport

qs.q: A 59-year-old woman with prior MI has an LDL of 104 mg/dL on maximally tolerated statin and ezetimibe. She prefers the fewest injections. Which regimen fits best?
qs.a: Inclisiran at day 0, month 3, then every 6 months
qs.x: After the initial doses, inclisiran is given every 6 months, the least frequent schedule among LDL-lowering injectables.
w: Alirocumab every 2 weeks indefinitely by self-injection
Evolocumab every 2 weeks or monthly by self-injection
Icosapent ethyl capsules twice daily

qs.q: A client received the first dose of inclisiran today. When should the nurse schedule the next dose?
qs.a: In 3 months
qs.x: Inclisiran is given at day 0, again at 3 months, and then every 6 months.
w: In 2 weeks
In 1 month
In 12 months

qs.q: A 45-year-old man with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia starts alirocumab. By which mechanism does it lower LDL?
qs.a: Prevents degradation of hepatic LDL receptors
qs.x: Alirocumab binds PCSK9 so LDL receptors recycle to the hepatocyte surface instead of being degraded.
w: Inhibits hepatic HMG-CoA reductase activity
Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption
Activates lipoprotein lipase via PPAR-alpha

qs.q: A 64-year-old man is evaluated 2 months after an acute coronary syndrome. His LDL is 92 mg/dL on high-intensity statin and ezetimibe. Which addition has been shown to reduce cardiovascular events after recent ACS?
qs.a: Alirocumab
qs.x: ODYSSEY OUTCOMES showed alirocumab reduced major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with recent ACS on statins.
w: Niacin
Fenofibrate
Colesevelam

qs.q: A client is learning to self-inject alirocumab with a prefilled pen stored in the refrigerator. Which instruction is correct?
qs.a: Let it warm to room temperature for 30 to 40 minutes
qs.x: Allowing the pen to reach room temperature reduces injection discomfort; it should not be shaken or heated, and sites should be rotated.
w: Shake the pen well to mix it before each injection
Warm the pen in the microwave for a few seconds
Inject into the same spot each time for consistency

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman develops myalgias on several statins and starts an oral lipid-lowering prodrug. Its activating enzyme is absent in skeletal muscle. Which enzyme does the active drug inhibit?
qs.a: ATP-citrate lyase
qs.x: Bempedoic acid is activated by ACSVL1 in liver and inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, upstream of HMG-CoA reductase.
w: HMG-CoA reductase
Acyl-CoA cholesterol acyltransferase
Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with statin intolerance starts bempedoic acid. Three months later he has an acutely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Drug-induced hyperuricemia
qs.x: Bempedoic acid inhibits renal OAT2 and raises serum uric acid, which can precipitate gout.
w: Drug-induced rhabdomyolysis
Drug-induced septic arthritis
Drug-induced hypercalcemia

qs.q: A client who stopped statins because of muscle aches is started on bempedoic acid. Why is muscle pain less likely with it?
qs.a: The prodrug is activated only in the liver
qs.x: Bempedoic acid is a prodrug activated by ACSVL1, an enzyme present in liver but not in skeletal muscle, so no active drug forms in muscle. It inhibits ATP-citrate lyase upstream of HMG-CoA reductase and does lower LDL, and it raises uric acid.
w: It does not lower LDL cholesterol at all
It is given every other day instead of daily
It is not absorbed from the small intestine

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with diabetes and triglycerides of 210 mg/dL on atorvastatin starts a prescription omega-3 product. Which statement describes this product?
qs.a: It contains purified EPA without DHA
qs.x: Icosapent ethyl is purified eicosapentaenoic acid ethyl ester; it lacks DHA and does not significantly raise LDL.
w: It inhibits PCSK9 messenger RNA synthesis
It activates PPAR-alpha in hepatocytes
It contains both EPA and DHA in equal amounts

qs.q: A 67-year-old woman with prior MI starts icosapent ethyl 2 g twice daily for elevated triglycerides on a statin. Which adverse effect occurred more often with this drug in its outcome trial?
qs.a: Atrial fibrillation
qs.x: In REDUCE-IT, icosapent ethyl increased hospitalization for atrial fibrillation or flutter and showed a trend toward more bleeding.
w: Severe hypoglycemia
Severe hyperkalemia
Acute cholestatic hepatitis

qs.q: A client starting icosapent ethyl also takes apixaban. Which finding should the nurse teach the client to report?
qs.a: Unusual bruising or bleeding
qs.x: Icosapent ethyl can increase bleeding risk, especially with anticoagulants, so bleeding should be reported.
w: Mild constipation after meals
Mild aching in the knees
Fishy aftertaste after a dose

qs.q: A 78-year-old woman (64 kg) has a new proximal DVT. Her creatinine clearance is 22 mL/min, and she has no active bleeding. Which enoxaparin order is correct for treatment?
qs.a: 1 mg/kg (64 mg) subcutaneously once every 24 hours
qs.x: Per the label, CrCl below 30 mL/min calls for 1 mg/kg once daily for treatment because enoxaparin accumulates. Keeping q12h dosing raises bleeding risk, and 40 mg daily is a prophylaxis dose that undertreats a DVT.
w: 1 mg/kg (64 mg) subcutaneously every 12 hours, unchanged
40 mg subcutaneously once daily, the standard prophylaxis dose
1.5 mg/kg (96 mg) subcutaneously every 12 hours for the first week

qs.q: A 74-year-old man on dabigatran for atrial fibrillation arrives with an acute subdural hematoma and a GCS of 11. His last dose was 5 hours ago and his CrCl is 48 mL/min. Which reversal order is best?
qs.a: Idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5 g IV
qs.x: Idarucizumab is an antibody fragment that binds dabigatran; the labeled dose is 5 g IV. Andexanet reverses factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban, not a direct thrombin inhibitor.
w: Andexanet alfa high-dose bolus then infusion
Protamine sulfate 50 mg slow IV push
Vitamin K 10 mg IV with fresh frozen plasma

qs.q: A 66-year-old man on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 3, CrCl 85 mL/min) is scheduled for an elective total knee replacement, a high bleeding-risk procedure. What is the best periprocedural plan?
qs.a: Hold apixaban 2 days before surgery with no heparin bridging
qs.x: Per the PAUSE approach, apixaban is held 2 days before a high bleeding-risk procedure (1 day for low risk) with normal renal function, and bridging is unnecessary given its short half-life. Bridging only adds bleeding.
w: Hold apixaban 5 days before surgery and bridge with enoxaparin
Continue apixaban without any interruption through the surgery
Hold apixaban the morning of surgery only and resume that night

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve on warfarin (INR goal 3.0) needs an elective colonoscopy with likely polypectomy. Which plan is most appropriate?
qs.a: Stop warfarin 5 days prior and bridge with therapeutic enoxaparin
qs.x: A mechanical mitral valve is a high thrombotic risk, so bridging with LMWH or UFH is indicated. BRIDGE studied atrial fibrillation, not mechanical valves, and DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves.
w: Stop warfarin 5 days prior with no bridging, as in the BRIDGE trial
Switch warfarin to apixaban for the week around the procedure
Continue warfarin and give vitamin K only if bleeding occurs

qs.q: A 71-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 6.8 on routine testing. He has no bleeding and no planned procedures. What is the best management per CHEST guidelines?
qs.a: Hold 1-2 doses, then resume at a lower dose and recheck the INR
qs.x: For INR 4.5-10 without bleeding, CHEST guidance is to hold warfarin and resume at a lower dose; routine vitamin K is not needed. IV vitamin K 10 mg overshoots and causes warfarin resistance on restarting.
w: Give vitamin K 10 mg IV now and recheck the INR in 6 hours
Give 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and hold all warfarin
Stop warfarin permanently and switch to dabigatran the same day

qs.q: An 80-year-old woman on warfarin presents with a spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage; her INR is 3.4. Which reversal strategy is best?
qs.a: 4-factor PCC plus vitamin K 10 mg by slow IV infusion
qs.x: Guidelines favor 4F-PCC for rapid factor replacement plus IV vitamin K to sustain reversal after the PCC wears off. FFP alone is slow and volume-heavy, and protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.
w: Vitamin K 10 mg orally and repeat the INR in 24 hours
Fresh frozen plasma alone, 2 units, without any vitamin K
Protamine sulfate IV followed by recombinant factor VIIa

qs.q: A 70-year-old man on prednisone starts levofloxacin and 3 days later has posterior ankle pain and cannot push off. Which drug effect is this?
qs.a: Tendinopathy from fluoroquinolone collagen damage
qs.x: Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for tendinitis and tendon rupture, most often Achilles, through degradation of collagen and the tenocyte matrix; risk is highest over age 60 and with concurrent corticosteroids. The cartilage effect is the separate pediatric concern.
w: Myopathy from direct skeletal muscle toxicity
Neuropathy from sodium channel blockade
Arthropathy from loss of cartilage glycosaminoglycan

qs.q: A man on chronic colchicine for gout is started on clarithromycin. Which toxicity is he now at risk for?
qs.a: Colchicine toxicity with pancytopenia and myopathy
qs.x: Colchicine is a substrate of both CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein and clarithromycin inhibits both, so levels climb and fatal colchicine toxicity with diarrhea, myelosuppression and myopathy has been reported. Azithromycin lacks meaningful CYP3A4 inhibition.
w: Clarithromycin toxicity with irreversible hearing loss
Colchicine failure with a rebound gout flare
Clarithromycin failure from colchicine binding

qs.q: A 55-year-old man with Child-Pugh B cirrhosis (no active drinking) has knee osteoarthritis pain. Which analgesic plan is safest?
qs.a: Acetaminophen at a reduced ceiling of about 2 g per day
qs.x: Expert guidance favors acetaminophen up to about 2 g/day in cirrhosis. NSAIDs precipitate renal failure, GI bleeding, and diuretic resistance in cirrhosis, and tramadol accumulates and lowers the seizure threshold.
w: Ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours with food
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with a daily PPI for GI protection
Tramadol 100 mg every 4 hours as needed for pain

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and HFrEF takes Jardiance. He is scheduled for an elective colectomy next week. What is the correct perioperative order?
qs.a: Hold it for at least 3 days before surgery
qs.x: The label advises stopping empagliflozin at least 3 days before scheduled surgery because of euglycemic DKA risk with fasting and surgical stress. Its low hypoglycemia risk is irrelevant; ketoacidosis is the danger.
w: Hold it only on the morning of surgery
Continue it, since it rarely causes hypoglycemia
Hold it 2 weeks before and restart once discharged

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman on metformin with an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 needs a CT with IV iodinated contrast. What is the correct metformin order?
qs.a: Hold it at the scan, recheck eGFR, and restart at 48 hours
qs.x: Per the label, metformin is held at or before iodinated contrast when eGFR is 30-60 and restarted 48 hours later if renal function is stable. An eGFR of 30-45 does not mandate permanent discontinuation.
w: Continue it without interruption, since her eGFR is above 30
Stop it permanently, since her eGFR is now below 45 mL/min
Hold it 1 week before the scan and restart it 1 week after

qs.q: A 61-year-old man had a drug-eluting stent placed 2 months ago for stable angina and takes aspirin plus Plavix. He is referred for an elective inguinal hernia repair. What is the best recommendation?
qs.a: Defer the elective surgery until DAPT can safely be interrupted
qs.x: Elective noncardiac surgery should be delayed after DES (ideally 6 months for stable disease) because stopping a P2Y12 inhibitor early markedly raises stent thrombosis risk. Heparin bridging does not protect against stent thrombosis.
w: Stop both antiplatelets 7 days before and proceed as planned
Stop clopidogrel 5 days before and bridge with enoxaparin
Switch clopidogrel to warfarin for the perioperative period

qs.q: A 72-year-old man on Tikosyn for atrial fibrillation develops cystitis. Which antibiotic is contraindicated with his antiarrhythmic?
qs.a: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
qs.x: Trimethoprim inhibits renal cationic secretion of dofetilide, raising levels and torsades risk; the label lists it as contraindicated. The other agents do not interact this way.
w: Nitrofurantoin macrocrystals
Cephalexin for 7 days
Fosfomycin as a single 3-gram dose

qs.q: On day 7 of heparin prophylaxis after hip surgery, a 68-year-old woman's platelets fall from 260,000 to 95,000 and she has a new DVT. CrCl is 20 mL/min; liver tests are normal. What is the best order?
qs.a: Stop all heparin and start an argatroban infusion
qs.x: Suspected HIT requires stopping all heparin, including LMWH, and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant; argatroban is hepatically cleared, suiting renal failure. Starting warfarin during acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene.
w: Switch to enoxaparin at a renally adjusted dose
Stop heparin and start warfarin 5 mg daily now
Continue heparin and transfuse platelets as needed

qs.q: A 52-year-old man with septic shock from a central line infection was started on vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam. Blood cultures on day 2 grow methicillin-susceptible S. aureus. What is the best antibiotic change?
qs.a: Switch to cefazolin alone
qs.x: For MSSA bacteremia, a beta-lactam such as cefazolin or nafcillin is superior to vancomycin, which kills more slowly and fails more often. Keeping broad Gram-negative coverage adds toxicity and resistance without benefit.
w: Continue vancomycin alone
Continue both current drugs
Switch to oral linezolid

qs.q: A 67-year-old woman with pyelonephritis and bacteremia is on Zosyn. Cultures grow ESBL-producing E. coli that tests susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam. What is the best definitive therapy?
qs.a: Change to meropenem
qs.x: In the MERINO trial, piperacillin-tazobactam had higher mortality than meropenem for ESBL bloodstream infection, so a carbapenem is preferred despite in-vitro susceptibility. Third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins are hydrolyzed by ESBLs.
w: Continue piperacillin-tazobactam
Change to ceftriaxone
Change to cefepime

qs.q: Twenty minutes into a vancomycin infusion a patient has flushing of the face and trunk with itching and a brief fall in BP. Which mechanism is this?
qs.a: Direct mast cell degranulation by the drug
qs.x: Vancomycin infusion reaction is a non-immune, rate-dependent release of histamine from mast cells through the MRGPRX2 receptor, so it responds to slowing the infusion and to antihistamine premedication rather than requiring avoidance. True IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to vancomycin is rare.
w: IgE antibody formed at a prior exposure
Complement activation by immune complexes
Bradykinin accumulation from ACE inhibition

qs.q: A 64-year-old woman with urosepsis has a MAP of 57 mmHg after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid; lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. She has only peripheral IV access. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Start Levophed through a proximal peripheral IV
qs.x: Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidance supports starting norepinephrine peripherally rather than delaying for central access. Dopamine causes more arrhythmias, and excess fluid beyond initial resuscitation worsens outcomes.
w: Give another 3 liters of crystalloid before any vasopressor
Delay vasopressors until a central line is placed
Start dopamine as the first-line vasopressor

qs.q: A 76-year-old woman has 9 watery stools daily, WBC 19,000, and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9) with positive C. difficile toxin. She is not hypotensive and has no ileus. Which treatment is best?
qs.a: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days
qs.x: Per IDSA, an initial severe episode (WBC above 15,000 or creatinine above 1.5) is treated with oral vancomycin 125 mg QID or fidaxomicin. IV vancomycin does not reach the colon, and 500 mg plus IV metronidazole is for fulminant disease.
w: IV vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 12 hours
Oral metronidazole 500 mg three times daily
Oral vancomycin 500 mg four times daily plus IV metronidazole

qs.q: A 64-year-old man presents with fever, neck stiffness, and confusion. CSF shows 1,800 WBC with neutrophil predominance. Besides dexamethasone, which empiric antibiotic regimen is best?
qs.a: Vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and ampicillin
qs.x: Adults over 50 need ampicillin for Listeria added to vancomycin plus ceftriaxone. Omitting vancomycin misses resistant pneumococcus, and acyclovir does not replace Listeria coverage.
w: Vancomycin and ceftriaxone only
Ceftriaxone and ampicillin only
Vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and acyclovir only

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has MRSA pneumonia with concurrent MRSA bacteremia. A colleague suggests daptomycin to cover both sites. What is the best response?
qs.a: Use linezolid or vancomycin, since daptomycin fails in the lung
qs.x: Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and should not be used for pneumonia. Cefazolin does not cover MRSA.
w: Use daptomycin, since its rapid bactericidal killing covers both sites
Use daptomycin at double the usual dose for the lung
Use cefazolin, since it covers MRSA in the lung

qs.q: A patient in DKA on an insulin drip has glucose down to 220 mg/dL but the anion gap is still 18. What is the appropriate change?
qs.a: Add dextrose to the fluids and keep the insulin drip
qs.x: The insulin infusion continues until the anion gap closes and bicarbonate recovers, because insulin is what suppresses ketogenesis; dextrose is added near a glucose of 200 mg/dL so that can happen without hypoglycemia. Stopping at a normal glucose with an open gap lets ketoacidosis return.
w: Stop the insulin drip and give subcutaneous insulin
Halve the insulin rate and recheck the gap in 6 hours
Switch to subcutaneous insulin since glucose is under 250

qs.q: A man with DKA on an insulin infusion now has a glucose of 220 mg/dL, but his anion gap remains 19. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Add dextrose to the fluids and continue the insulin infusion
qs.x: Insulin is needed to clear ketones, so once glucose reaches about 250 mg/dL, dextrose is added (often with a lower rate) while insulin continues until the gap closes. Stopping insulin early causes rebound ketosis.
w: Stop the insulin infusion and start a correction scale
Stop the infusion and give glargine subcutaneously now
Double the insulin infusion rate to close the anion gap faster

qs.q: A patient with type 1 diabetes recovering from DKA has a closed anion gap and is eating. How should the transition off the insulin infusion be ordered?
qs.a: Give subcutaneous Lantus 2 hours before stopping the drip
qs.x: Basal insulin must overlap the infusion by about 2 hours because IV regular insulin has a half-life of minutes; a gap leads to recurrent DKA. Correction scale alone is inadequate in type 1 diabetes.
w: Stop the drip and give Lantus 2 hours later
Stop the drip and use a correction scale only
Stop the drip once the glucose is below 150 mg/dL

qs.q: A 74-year-old man with HHS has glucose 1,020 mg/dL, measured sodium 131 mEq/L, and severe dehydration with BP 92/58. Which initial management is best?
qs.a: Isotonic saline first, adding insulin once fluids alone plateau
qs.x: In HHS, isotonic fluid is the priority; insulin given before volume repletion shifts water into cells and worsens hypotension. His corrected sodium is high, but hypotonic fluid is not the first choice in shock.
w: An insulin bolus of 0.1 units/kg plus an infusion before any IV fluids
Hypotonic 0.45% saline as the first liter given his sodium
Insulin infusion at 0.14 units/kg/h with free water flushes

qs.q: A 90-kg woman with type 2 diabetes (A1c 9.4%) is admitted with pneumonia, eating well, with glucoses of 250-320 mg/dL on correction insulin alone. Using about 0.5 units/kg/day per guidelines, which regimen is best?
qs.a: Glargine 22 units daily plus lispro 7 units with meals, plus correction
qs.x: A total daily dose of about 45 units is split half basal and half prandial (divided over 3 meals), plus correction insulin. Sliding scale alone is reactive and discouraged, and 90 units of NPH doubles the needed dose.
w: Lispro correction every 6 hours only, switching to a more aggressive scale
Glargine 45 units daily alone with no prandial or correction insulin
NPH 45 units twice daily before meals with no correction scale

qs.q: A 34-year-old man with type 1 diabetes on glargine 30 units nightly is NPO for an elective morning surgery. What is the best order for the night before?
qs.a: Give about 75-80% of the glargine dose (about 24 units)
qs.x: Guidelines suggest about 75-80% of basal insulin the evening before surgery. Holding basal insulin in type 1 diabetes risks DKA, since he makes no endogenous insulin.
w: Hold glargine entirely while he remains NPO
Give the full 30 units plus a dose of lispro
Switch the glargine to a correction scale only

qs.q: A 56-year-old woman on empagliflozin and metformin has vomited for 2 days. Glucose 188 mg/dL, bicarbonate 11 mEq/L, anion gap 24, beta-hydroxybutyrate 6.1 mmol/L. What is the best management?
qs.a: Insulin infusion with dextrose-containing fluids; stop empagliflozin
qs.x: This is euglycemic DKA from an SGLT2 inhibitor; insulin suppresses ketogenesis and dextrose prevents hypoglycemia. A near-normal glucose does not mean insulin is unnecessary.
w: Withhold insulin because the glucose is under 250 mg/dL
IV fluids alone without insulin until glucose exceeds 250
Sodium bicarbonate infusion, then resume empagliflozin at discharge

qs.q: An 82-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 on glyburide is found with glucose 38 mg/dL. She improves with D50 but becomes hypoglycemic twice more in 4 hours despite a dextrose infusion. What is the best addition?
qs.a: Octreotide to suppress insulin release
qs.x: Sulfonylureas drive ongoing insulin secretion that dextrose further provokes; octreotide suppresses this and prevents rebound hypoglycemia. Glucagon also stimulates insulin release and wears off quickly.
w: Glucagon 1 mg IM every hour as needed
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours
Oral diazoxide, then discharge her home

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is started on prednisone 60 mg each morning for a COPD flare. Fasting glucose is 130 mg/dL, but afternoon readings exceed 300 mg/dL. Which insulin strategy best matches the steroid effect?
qs.a: Add morning NPH dosed by weight and steroid dose
qs.x: Morning prednisone causes afternoon and evening hyperglycemia that matches the NPH profile when given with the steroid. Raising bedtime basal insulin risks overnight hypoglycemia as the steroid wears off.
w: Increase bedtime glargine by 50 percent
Add bedtime NPH titrated to target the fasting glucose
Add a correction scale at bedtime only

qs.q: An anuric 60-year-old man on hemodialysis missed two sessions. K is 7.4 mEq/L with a widened QRS. He received calcium gluconate, insulin with dextrose, and albuterol, and the QRS has narrowed. What is the definitive next step?
qs.a: Urgent hemodialysis
qs.x: Calcium stabilizes membranes and insulin and albuterol shift K into cells for only a few hours; an anuric patient needs dialysis to remove potassium. Furosemide requires urine output.
w: Furosemide 80 mg IV
Repeat calcium every 30 minutes
Sodium bicarbonate infusion

qs.q: A 46-year-old woman with Na 113 mEq/L has a generalized seizure. Which treatment is most appropriate per expert hyponatremia guidelines?
qs.a: 100 mL bolus of 3% saline, repeated up to twice if needed
qs.x: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia needs a 3% saline bolus (about 100 mL, repeatable) to raise Na 4-6 mEq/L and stop seizures. Tolvaptan acts too slowly for emergencies, and normal saline can worsen Na in SIADH.
w: Fluid restriction to 800 mL per day
Tolvaptan 15 mg orally now with hourly sodium checks
1 liter of 0.9% saline over 1 hour, then recheck the sodium

qs.q: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder and K 2.9 mEq/L had Na 112 mEq/L. Twelve hours later his Na is 123 mEq/L and he is making 400 mL/hour of dilute urine. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Give D5W and IV desmopressin to re-lower the sodium
qs.x: He has exceeded the safe correction limit (about 8 mEq/L per 24 hours in high-risk patients such as alcoholism and hypokalemia), so relowering with free water and desmopressin reduces osmotic demyelination risk. Fluid restriction accelerates the rise.
w: Continue current management and recheck in 12 hours
Start 3% saline to maintain the current trajectory
Restrict all fluids to slow the water diuresis

qs.q: A 66-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer has calcium 14.6 mg/dL and creatinine 3.4 mg/dL from AKI that persists after fluids. He has received calcitonin. Which agent is preferred for durable calcium lowering?
qs.a: Denosumab
qs.x: Bisphosphonates are nephrotoxic and need dose reduction or avoidance in severe renal dysfunction, while denosumab is not renally cleared (watch for hypocalcemia). High-dose loop diuretics are no longer recommended.
w: Zoledronic acid at full dose
Furosemide 80 mg IV every 6 hours
Pamidronate 90 mg over 2 hours

qs.q: A 71-year-old woman with SIADH (Na 121 mEq/L, asymptomatic) is started on tolvaptan in the hospital. Which order is inappropriate and should be removed?
qs.a: Fluid restriction to 1 liter per day
qs.x: The label warns against fluid restriction in the first 24 hours because it risks overly rapid correction and osmotic demyelination. Use is limited to 30 days because of hepatotoxicity.
w: Serum sodium checks every 6-8 hours
Free access to water when thirsty
Plan to stop the drug within 30 days

qs.q: A 50-year-old woman has K 3.0 mEq/L, normal renal function, and is tolerating a diet. A peripheral IV order reads KCl 40 mEq IV over 1 hour. What is the best action?
qs.a: Change to oral KCl, or IV at no more than 10 mEq/h
qs.x: Per the KCl label, when K exceeds 2.5 mEq/L the rate should generally not exceed 10 mEq/h; faster rates risk arrhythmia and peripheral vein injury. The oral route is preferred when the patient can eat.
w: Approve it, since 40 mEq/h is safe for K above 2.5
Give it as a 40 mEq IV push for faster correction
Infuse at 40 mEq/h in 50 mL via the peripheral IV

qs.q: A 77-year-old man on lisinopril and spironolactone for HFrEF is given Bactrim for a UTI. Three days later his K is 6.6 mEq/L. Which mechanism explains the antibiotic's contribution?
qs.a: Trimethoprim blocks ENaC in the collecting duct, like amiloride
qs.x: Trimethoprim acts like a potassium-sparing diuretic by blocking epithelial sodium channels, compounding ACE inhibitor and spironolactone effects. Hemolysis is not the main mechanism.
w: Sulfamethoxazole causes intravascular hemolysis
Trimethoprim inhibits aldosterone synthase in the adrenal gland
Sulfamethoxazole causes acute interstitial nephritis alone

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman 1 day after hip surgery on a morphine PCA is arousable only to sternal rub, RR 7, pinpoint pupils, SpO2 88% on 2 L. What is the best Narcan order?
qs.a: 0.1-0.2 mg IV every 2-3 minutes titrated to breathing
qs.x: For postoperative opioid depression, the label uses small IV increments (0.1-0.2 mg) titrated to ventilation to avoid abrupt pain, hypertension, arrhythmia, and pulmonary edema. A full 2 mg push reverses analgesia abruptly. Stop the PCA in any case.
w: 2 mg IV push now, repeated every 2 minutes
4 mg intranasal, then restart the PCA later
0.4 mg IM once, then resume the PCA at once

qs.q: A 72-kg man develops wheezing, hypotension, and hives 10 minutes into a cefazolin infusion. The infusion is stopped. What is the next drug to give?
qs.a: Epinephrine 0.5 mg IM into the lateral thigh
qs.x: IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg in adults) is first-line for anaphylaxis. Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway obstruction or shock, and a 1 mg IV push is a cardiac arrest dose that can cause arrhythmia.
w: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV push, then reassess
Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV with an H2 blocker
Epinephrine 1 mg IV push now

qs.q: An 81-year-old man with Parkinson disease on carbidopa-levodopa becomes agitated and hallucinating overnight, pulling at his lines. Nonpharmacologic measures fail. Which drug is safest if one is needed?
qs.a: Low-dose quetiapine
qs.x: Haloperidol and metoclopramide (Reglan) block D2 receptors and can severely worsen parkinsonism, while low-dose quetiapine has little D2 blockade. Benzodiazepines worsen delirium in the elderly.
w: Haloperidol 5 mg IM
Lorazepam 2 mg IV
Reglan 10 mg IV for nausea and sedation

qs.q: A 54-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis on day 2 of admission has tremor, diaphoresis, HR 128, and visual hallucinations from alcohol withdrawal. Which benzodiazepine is preferred?
qs.a: Lorazepam
qs.x: Lorazepam is conjugated by glucuronidation without active metabolites, so it does not accumulate in severe liver disease. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide have long-acting active metabolites that accumulate in cirrhosis.
w: Diazepam
Chlordiazepoxide
Alprazolam

qs.q: A 73-year-old woman with HFrEF (EF 20%) has new atrial fibrillation with HR 150, BP 96/58, and crackles. Cardioversion is not immediately available. Which rate-control drug is most appropriate?
qs.a: IV amiodarone
qs.x: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negatively inotropic and are avoided in decompensated HFrEF, and beta-blocker boluses can worsen acute heart failure. Amiodarone or digoxin is preferred.
w: IV Cardizem
IV verapamil
IV metoprolol in rapid boluses

qs.q: At 2 a.m. a 66-year-old man admitted for pneumonia has BP 188/104. He is asymptomatic with normal labs and no chest pain or neurologic deficits. He missed his evening amlodipine. What is the best order?
qs.a: Give his home amlodipine and recheck later
qs.x: Asymptomatic inpatient hypertension without end-organ damage is not an emergency; IV hydralazine or labetalol causes unpredictable drops and is linked to harm. Resume oral home therapy and address pain or anxiety.
w: Hydralazine 10 mg IV now, repeated as needed
Labetalol 20 mg IV now and every 10 minutes

qs.q: A 70-kg man with epilepsy is still seizing after two doses of lorazepam 4 mg IV. Which second-line order is correctly written?

qs.q: A 31-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation has an acute proximal DVT. Which anticoagulant is preferred?

qs.q: A 29-year-old at 34 weeks with preeclampsia has BP 168/112 sustained over 15 minutes. Which treatment does ACOG recommend?

Nitroprusside infusion
Furosemide 40 mg IV

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman with chronic hypertension on lisinopril has a positive pregnancy test at 6 weeks. What is the best plan?

Switch to losartan for the rest of the pregnancy

Doxycycline for 7 days
No treatment unless symptoms occur

qs.q: A patient with magnesium toxicity needs IV calcium through a peripheral line. Why is calcium gluconate 1 g chosen over calcium chloride 1 g?

It is absorbed more completely from a peripheral vein
It does not need the liver to release the free calcium

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy well controlled on Lamictal is 14 weeks pregnant and has new breakthrough seizures. What is the most likely cause and step?

Normal pregnancy change; no action is needed

qs.q: A 27-year-old at 8 weeks' gestation has Graves hyperthyroidism needing a thionamide. Which plan is preferred?

Radioactive iodine ablation in the first trimester
Propranolol alone through delivery

qs.q: A woman with severe preeclampsia and moderate persistent asthma has postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony despite oxytocin and massage. Which uterotonic is most appropriate next?

qs.q: A 12-kg toddler with fever has an order for Tylenol 1,800 mg PO every 6 hours. What is the correct dose?

450 mg twice daily
900 mg three times daily

qs.q: Which analgesic plan is best for a 6-year-old after tonsillectomy?

qs.q: A 10-day-old neonate with suspected sepsis is receiving IV calcium gluconate for hypocalcemia. Which antibiotic order is contraindicated?

Gentamicin IV
Acyclovir IV infusion

qs.q: A 15-kg child develops anaphylaxis. Which order is correct?

0.15 mg of 0.1 mg/mL epinephrine IV push

qs.q: An 83-year-old woman with two falls has taken Xanax 1 mg nightly for 12 years and asks to stop. What is the best plan?

qs.q: An older man with CKD stage 3b has prolonged nocturnal hypoglycemia on glyburide. Which property of glyburide explains that?

qs.q: A 78-year-old man with Alzheimer dementia on donepezil was started on oxybutynin for urge incontinence that began after donepezil was started. His cognition has worsened. What is the best interpretation?

The oxybutynin dose is too low

qs.q: A woman has ankle edema from amlodipine 10 mg and furosemide is added with no benefit. Why does a loop diuretic fail against this edema?

w: The edema comes from a loss of plasma oncotic pressure
Amlodipine blocks the Na-K-2Cl transporter directly
Furosemide needs an intact RAAS in order to work

qs.q: A patient on linezolid for 4 weeks for VRE osteomyelitis now has platelets of 68,000 and hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL. Which mechanism fits?

qs.q: A 35-year-old man given Haldol in the ED 3 days ago has temperature 40.1 C (104.2 F), lead-pipe rigidity, labile BP, confusion, and CK 14,000 U/L. Reflexes are diminished without clonus. Besides stopping the drug and cooling, which drug is a reasonable addition?

Physostigmine

qs.q: An 84-year-old woman on digoxin develops AKI with nausea, yellow vision, HR 38 in a junctional rhythm, and K 5.9 mEq/L. Her digoxin level is 3.6 ng/mL. What is the best treatment?

qs.q: A 72-year-old man with CrCl 18 mL/min receiving cefepime 2 g every 8 hours for pneumonia develops confusion and myoclonus on day 4. EEG shows triphasic waves with nonconvulsive features. What is the most likely cause?

qs.x: Adequate ventilation produces visible chest rise and improving oxygenation; gastric distention, mask leaks, and gurgling indicate poor technique or an airway needing repositioning or suction.
opts: Visible chest rise with each breath
Improving skin color and SpO2
Increasing distention of the upper abdomen
Air escaping loudly around the mask seal
Gurgling sounds during each ventilation
ok: Visible chest rise with each breath
Improving skin color and SpO2

qs.q: A patient in respiratory distress is being considered for CPAP. Which findings are contraindications? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Unable to follow commands or protect the airway; Suspected pneumothorax; Systolic blood pressure of 84 mmHg
qs.x: CPAP requires an alert patient who can protect the airway and an adequate blood pressure; it can worsen a pneumothorax and lower blood pressure. Tachypnea, CHF, and hypoxia are reasons to use it.
opts: Unable to follow commands or protect the airway
Suspected pneumothorax
Systolic blood pressure of 84 mmHg
Respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min
History of congestive heart failure
SpO2 of 88% on room air
ok: Unable to follow commands or protect the airway
Suspected pneumothorax
Systolic blood pressure of 84 mmHg

qs.q: Before placing a nonrebreather mask on a patient, what should you do?
qs.a: Fill the reservoir bag with oxygen
qs.x: The reservoir bag should be prefilled and stay at least partly inflated during inhalation, using 10-15 L/min; otherwise the patient may rebreathe exhaled air.
w: Set the flow rate to 4 L/min
Remove the one-way valves from the mask
Ask the patient to exhale fully first

qs.q: A 5-year-old boy has a sudden high fever, is drooling, sits leaning forward on his hands, and speaks in a muffled voice. What is the most appropriate approach?
qs.a: Keep him calm in a position of comfort and avoid looking in his throat
qs.x: These findings suggest epiglottitis; agitating the child or placing anything in the mouth can trigger complete obstruction, so give oxygen as tolerated and transport promptly.
w: Lay him supine and use a tongue depressor to inspect the throat
Insert an oropharyngeal airway to keep the swollen tissues open
Separate him from his parent so you can examine him more easily

qs.q: A 9-month-old infant is choking, cannot cry, and is turning blue but remains responsive. What should you do?
qs.a: Give 5 back slaps followed by 5 chest thrusts
qs.x: For a responsive infant with severe obstruction, alternate 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts and blind finger sweeps are not used in infants.
w: Give abdominal thrusts until the object comes out
Perform a blind finger sweep of the mouth
Give 2 rescue breaths and then check a pulse

qs.q: A woman in her third trimester of pregnancy is choking and cannot speak or cough. What maneuver should you use?
qs.a: Chest thrusts
qs.x: Chest thrusts are used in visibly pregnant or obese patients because abdominal thrusts are ineffective or may harm the fetus.
w: Abdominal thrusts
Back slaps only
Blind finger sweeps

qs.q: An adult choking patient you have been treating becomes unresponsive. After lowering him to the ground and calling for help, what should you do?
qs.a: Begin CPR, looking in the mouth for the object before each set of breaths
qs.x: An unresponsive choking victim gets CPR; compressions may dislodge the object, and you look in the mouth and remove only a visible object before ventilating.
w: Continue abdominal thrusts while he lies supine until the object is seen
Perform repeated blind finger sweeps until the obstruction is removed
Check a carotid pulse for a full 30 seconds before starting anything

qs.q: A 16-year-old with asthma was wheezing loudly 10 minutes ago. She is now drowsy, her chest is nearly silent, and air movement is minimal. What does this indicate?
qs.a: Respiratory failure; assist her ventilations
qs.x: A quiet chest with decreasing mental status means too little air is moving to produce wheezes, an ominous sign of respiratory failure that requires BVM ventilation and rapid transport.
w: The bronchospasm is resolving on its own and she can rest
She is hyperventilating from anxiety and needs coaching
Her airway is clear, so oxygen can be reduced

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with COPD is in respiratory distress, speaking in short phrases, with an SpO2 of 84%. How should you manage oxygen?
qs.a: Give oxygen and titrate to relieve hypoxia
qs.x: Oxygen should never be withheld from a hypoxic COPD patient; give it, titrate to the target saturation in your protocol, and monitor mental status and breathing.
w: Withhold oxygen because it will suppress his hypoxic drive
Give no oxygen until the hospital checks a blood gas
Only use room air and coach pursed-lip breathing

qs.q: In which situations may a pulse oximetry reading be unreliable? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Carbon monoxide poisoning; Cold extremities with poor perfusion; Constant patient movement or shivering
qs.x: CO binds hemoglobin and can produce a falsely normal reading, and poor perfusion or motion interferes with the sensor; heart rate and posture alone do not make the reading inaccurate.
opts: Carbon monoxide poisoning
Cold extremities with poor perfusion
Constant patient movement or shivering
A heart rate of 110 beats/min
A patient sitting upright on the stretcher
ok: Carbon monoxide poisoning
Cold extremities with poor perfusion
Constant patient movement or shivering

qs.q: A 6-month-old has a cough and fever. Which findings indicate increased work of breathing? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Nasal flaring; Intercostal retractions; Grunting at the end of each breath
qs.x: Flaring, retractions, and grunting are signs of respiratory distress in infants; a rate of 40 is within the normal infant range and pink mucosa is a normal finding.
opts: Nasal flaring
Intercostal retractions
Grunting at the end of each breath
Respiratory rate of 40 breaths/min
Pink oral mucous membranes
ok: Nasal flaring
Intercostal retractions
Grunting at the end of each breath

qs.q: A 3-year-old with labored breathing has been crying and agitated. Which change suggests he is progressing toward respiratory arrest?
qs.a: Sleepiness and a falling heart rate
qs.x: Decreasing level of consciousness and bradycardia are late signs of hypoxia in children and signal impending arrest; begin assisted ventilation.
w: Louder crying and kicking during your exam
A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute
Nasal flaring that started on the drive to the hospital

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman has rapid breathing, tingling hands, and numbness around her mouth after an argument. Her lung sounds are clear. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Coach her to slow her breathing while assessing for medical causes
qs.x: Hyperventilation may be anxiety-related but can also stem from serious conditions such as PE or DKA; coach slower breathing and do not use a paper bag, which can cause hypoxia.
w: Have her breathe into a paper bag to raise her carbon dioxide level
Assume it is anxiety and release her without further assessment
Restrict all oxygen because it will worsen her symptoms

qs.q: An unresponsive motorcyclist with suspected spinal injury has snoring respirations. Which technique should you use first to open the airway?
qs.a: Jaw-thrust maneuver
qs.x: The jaw thrust opens the airway with minimal neck movement; if it fails to open the airway, head-tilt chin-lift is used because the airway takes priority.
w: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
Recovery position
Tongue-jaw lift with finger sweep

qs.q: An adult patient is breathing 36 times per minute with very shallow chest movement. Why is this a concern?
qs.a: Minute volume is likely inadequate, so assist ventilations
qs.x: Minute volume equals rate times tidal volume; very shallow breaths move mostly dead-space air, so a fast shallow pattern can be inadequate and needs BVM assistance.
w: The fast rate guarantees good oxygenation, so no action is needed
Rapid breathing always means anxiety and should be coached down
Shallow breaths are normal when the respiratory rate is that high

qs.q: A 74-year-old woman with heart failure is sitting upright, coughing pink frothy sputum, with crackles in both lungs. She is alert, BP 168/98, SpO2 86%. Which treatment is most appropriate within EMT scope?
qs.a: CPAP per protocol
qs.x: This is acute pulmonary edema in an alert patient with good blood pressure, a classic indication for CPAP, which improves oxygenation and reduces work of breathing.
w: Lay her supine with legs raised
Nasal cannula at 2 L/min only
Encourage her to drink fluids

qs.q: While you ventilate an apneic patient, the upper abdomen becomes increasingly distended. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Ventilations that are too forceful or too fast
qs.x: Excess ventilation volume or rate forces air into the stomach, increasing vomiting risk; reposition the airway and give only enough volume for visible chest rise.
w: An oropharyngeal airway that is slightly too small
Supplemental oxygen flowing at 15 L/min
Chest compressions that are too shallow

qs.q: Which findings indicate an adult patient is breathing inadequately? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Use of neck and accessory muscles; Cyanosis of the lips; Able to speak only 1 or 2 words at a time
qs.x: Accessory muscle use, cyanosis, and one- or two-word dyspnea show inadequate breathing; a normal rate with equal chest rise and full sentences indicates adequate breathing.
opts: Use of neck and accessory muscles
Cyanosis of the lips
Able to speak only 1 or 2 words at a time
Rate of 16 breaths/min with equal chest rise
Speaking in full sentences without pausing
ok: Use of neck and accessory muscles
Cyanosis of the lips
Able to speak only 1 or 2 words at a time

qs.q: What compression rate should you use when performing CPR on an adult?
qs.a: 100 to 120 per minute
qs.x: AHA guidelines call for a compression rate of 100-120/min for patients of all ages; faster rates reduce depth and filling time.
w: 80 to 100 per minute
At least 140 per minute, as fast as possible
60 to 80 per minute

qs.q: What is the correct compression depth for an adult in cardiac arrest?
qs.a: At least 2 inches but not more than 2.4 inches
qs.x: Adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) and no more than about 2.4 inches (6 cm), with full recoil after each one.
w: About 1 inch, just enough to see the chest move
At least 3 inches to maximize blood flow
One-quarter of the depth of the chest

qs.q: You are performing CPR on a 3-month-old infant. How deep should compressions be?
qs.a: About 1.5 inches
qs.x: Infant compressions should be at least one-third of the chest depth, about 1.5 inches (4 cm).
w: About 2.5 inches
About 0.5 inch, using one fingertip
One-half the depth of the chest

qs.q: Two EMTs are performing CPR on a 6-year-old with no advanced airway. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
qs.x: Two-rescuer CPR for infants and children uses 15:2; single rescuers use 30:2, and 3:1 is reserved for newborns.
w: Continuous compressions with no breaths

qs.q: You are about to use an AED on a pulseless 5-year-old, but only adult pads are available. What should you do?
qs.a: Use the adult pads, placing them front and back if they would overlap
qs.x: If pediatric pads or an attenuator are not available, adult pads should be used; anterior-posterior placement prevents the pads from touching.
w: Withhold the AED until pediatric pads arrive
Cut the adult pads in half so they fit the small chest
Use one adult pad only on the center of the chest

qs.q: The AED has just delivered a shock to an adult in cardiac arrest. What should you do next?
qs.a: Resume CPR with compressions right away
qs.x: After a shock, immediately resume compressions for about 2 minutes before the next rhythm analysis; pausing for a pulse check delays perfusion.
w: Check a carotid pulse for 10 seconds
Reanalyze the rhythm immediately
Give 2 breaths and then check for breathing

qs.q: Paramedics have placed an advanced airway in an adult in cardiac arrest. How should you now provide ventilations?
qs.a: 1 breath every 6 seconds during continuous compressions
qs.x: With an advanced airway in place, compressions are continuous and ventilations are given at 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min).
w: 2 breaths after every 30 compressions with pauses
1 breath every 2 seconds without pausing compressions
1 breath every 15 seconds to avoid hyperventilation

qs.q: A 62-year-old man collapses. He is unresponsive, has no pulse, and takes occasional gasping breaths. What should you do?
qs.a: Start CPR and apply the AED
qs.x: Agonal gasps are not effective breathing and are a sign of cardiac arrest; start compressions and attach the AED immediately.
w: Give oxygen by nonrebreather
Place him in the recovery position
Assist ventilations and recheck in 2 minutes

qs.q: When checking for a pulse in an unresponsive adult, what is the maximum time you should spend?
qs.a: 10 seconds
qs.x: Pulse and breathing checks should take no more than 10 seconds so that compressions are not delayed when the patient is in arrest.
w: 30 seconds
5 seconds
However long it takes to be certain

qs.q: Which actions are part of high-quality adult CPR? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Allow full chest recoil after each compression; Switch compressors about every 2 minutes; Keep pauses in compressions under 10 seconds
qs.x: High-quality CPR includes full recoil, rotating compressors to limit fatigue, and minimal interruptions; excessive ventilation, leaning, and frequent pulse checks reduce blood flow.
opts: Allow full chest recoil after each compression
Switch compressors about every 2 minutes
Keep pauses in compressions under 10 seconds
Give large, forceful breaths to maximize oxygen
Lean on the chest between compressions to hold depth
Check a pulse after every cycle of 30 compressions
ok: Allow full chest recoil after each compression
Switch compressors about every 2 minutes
Keep pauses in compressions under 10 seconds

qs.q: A 66-year-old man has chest pain and asks you to help him take his nitroglycerin. Which findings mean you should NOT assist? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Systolic blood pressure of 84 mmHg; He took sildenafil for erectile dysfunction 6 hours ago; The nitroglycerin is prescribed to his wife
qs.x: Nitroglycerin can cause severe hypotension with a low systolic pressure or recent erectile dysfunction drug use, and EMTs assist only with the patient's own prescribed medication.
opts: Systolic blood pressure of 84 mmHg
He took sildenafil for erectile dysfunction 6 hours ago
The nitroglycerin is prescribed to his wife
His heart rate is 96 beats/min
He rates his pain 8 out of 10
He has a history of hypertension
ok: Systolic blood pressure of 84 mmHg
He took sildenafil for erectile dysfunction 6 hours ago
The nitroglycerin is prescribed to his wife
