w: Focused exam of only the chest and abdomen, guided by his chief complaint
Wait until he wakes up, then obtain a SAMPLE history from him directly
Skip the physical exam and transport, since unresponsive patients cannot be assessed

qs.q: In which patient is capillary refill time most useful as an indicator of perfusion?
qs.a: A 3-year-old in a warm room
qs.x: Capillary refill is most reliable in young children; cold exposure, age, smoking, and some medications reduce its accuracy in adults.
w: An 82-year-old found on a cold porch
A 45-year-old smoker in freezing weather
A 70-year-old taking blood pressure medication

qs.q: A 71-year-old woman with dementia is more confused than usual, has a temperature of 100.9 F, and her caregiver reports new incontinence and foul-smelling urine. What should you suspect?
qs.a: An infection that may be developing into sepsis
qs.x: Acute worsening of mental status with fever and urinary symptoms in an older adult suggests infection, such as a urinary tract infection, which can lead to sepsis.
w: Normal progression of her dementia over time
A psychiatric emergency requiring restraint
Simple dehydration from not drinking enough fluids

qs.q: A 52-year-old man smelling strongly of alcohol is confused, has slurred speech, and is staggering. What is the main danger of assuming he is simply intoxicated?
qs.a: Missing low glucose, head injury, or other serious causes
qs.x: Alcohol odor does not explain all altered mental status; hypoglycemia, head injury, stroke, infection, and other poisonings can coexist and must be considered.
w: Embarrassing him in front of bystanders and family
Delaying the police response to the scene
Failing to document the odor of alcohol on the report

qs.q: A 34-year-old man with epilepsy has two generalized seizures in a row without regaining consciousness between them. What is this condition called?
qs.a: Status epilepticus
qs.x: Continuous seizure activity, or repeated seizures without return to consciousness between them, is status epilepticus, a life-threatening emergency.
w: A postictal state
An absence seizure
A simple partial seizure

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman has been seizing continuously for 7 minutes. She is cyanotic and her mouth is full of secretions. What should you do?
qs.a: Suction, give high-flow oxygen, request ALS, and transport
qs.x: Prolonged seizures need airway clearance, oxygenation, ventilation as needed, ALS support for medications, and prompt transport; restraint and objects in the mouth cause injury.
w: Insert a bite block between her teeth to protect her tongue
Hold her arms and legs down firmly to stop the movements
Wait until the seizure stops before beginning any care

qs.q: A 25-year-old man is drowsy and confused after a witnessed seizure that has stopped. He is breathing adequately with gurgling sounds. How should you position him?
qs.a: On his side in the recovery position
qs.x: The recovery position lets secretions drain and protects the airway of a postictal patient who is breathing adequately; suction should be ready.
w: Supine with his legs elevated
Prone with his face turned to one side
Sitting upright with his head tilted back

qs.q: A 31-year-old was found on the floor after a brief loss of consciousness. Which findings suggest a seizure rather than a simple faint? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Bitten side of the tongue; Confusion lasting 20 minutes after the event; Rhythmic jerking of all limbs for about 2 minutes
qs.x: Lateral tongue biting, prolonged rhythmic activity, and a postictal period favor seizure, while warning symptoms and rapid recovery suggest syncope.
opts: Bitten side of the tongue
Confusion lasting 20 minutes after the event
Rhythmic jerking of all limbs for about 2 minutes
Lightheadedness and tunnel vision just before collapse
Full alertness within seconds of lying flat
ok: Bitten side of the tongue
Confusion lasting 20 minutes after the event
Rhythmic jerking of all limbs for about 2 minutes

qs.q: A 79-year-old man suddenly passed out while seated at dinner, with no warning symptoms. He is now alert with normal vital signs. Why is transport important?
qs.a: Sudden syncope in an older adult may indicate a dysrhythmia
qs.x: Syncope without a warning period, especially while seated or in an older adult, raises concern for a cardiac rhythm problem that may recur.
w: Syncope while seated is always caused by low blood sugar
He needs observation for a likely postictal period
Fainting in an older adult always means he has had a stroke

qs.q: A 22-year-old fainted when she saw blood during a lab draw. She is now alert, with normal vital signs. What is the most likely mechanism?
qs.a: A vagal response that slowed her heart and dilated vessels
qs.x: Vasovagal syncope occurs when a trigger such as fear or pain stimulates the vagus nerve, slowing the heart rate and dilating blood vessels so that brain blood flow briefly falls.
w: A seizure triggered by a sudden emotional shock
A sudden drop in her blood glucose level
An allergic reaction to the needle or skin cleanser

qs.q: Which features of a fainting episode raise concern for a serious underlying cause? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Fainting during exercise; Chest pain or palpitations before the event; No warning symptoms in an older adult
qs.x: Exertional syncope, associated chest pain or palpitations, and sudden collapse without warning in older adults suggest a cardiac cause; brief faints with a clear trigger are usually benign.
opts: Fainting during exercise
Chest pain or palpitations before the event
No warning symptoms in an older adult
Lightheadedness after standing for a long time in a hot room
Fainting after seeing an injury, with quick recovery
ok: Fainting during exercise
Chest pain or palpitations before the event
No warning symptoms in an older adult

qs.q: Which findings suggest hypoglycemia rather than hyperglycemia in a diabetic patient? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Cool, pale, sweaty skin; Onset over minutes; Anxiety or combativeness
qs.x: Hypoglycemia typically develops quickly with sympathetic signs such as diaphoresis and agitation, while hyperglycemia develops slowly with thirst, Kussmaul respirations, and fruity breath.
opts: Cool, pale, sweaty skin
Onset over minutes
Anxiety or combativeness
Deep, rapid respirations
Fruity odor on the breath
Increased thirst over several days
ok: Cool, pale, sweaty skin
Onset over minutes
Anxiety or combativeness

qs.q: A 16-year-old with type 1 diabetes has had flu symptoms and vomiting for 2 days. She now has abdominal pain and deep, rapid breathing. Why is she breathing this way?
qs.a: Her body is compensating for acid buildup
qs.x: In diabetic ketoacidosis, deep rapid respirations blow off carbon dioxide to offset the metabolic acidosis caused by ketones.
w: She is anxious and having a panic attack
She has inhaled vomit into her lungs
Her blood sugar has dropped dangerously low

qs.q: A 67-year-old man was hypoglycemic, received oral glucose, and is now alert. He takes a long-acting oral diabetes medication and wants to refuse transport. What is the main concern?
qs.a: His glucose may drop again
qs.x: Some diabetes medications last many hours, so hypoglycemia can recur after a temporary improvement; this should be explained during any refusal discussion.
w: Oral glucose may cause high blood sugar later
He may have an allergic reaction to the glucose
He will need insulin within the next hour

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Her blood glucose is 38 mg/dL. What should you keep in mind?
qs.a: Hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke
qs.x: Low blood glucose can cause focal weakness and speech changes that look like a stroke, so it must be identified and treated, with reassessment of the neurologic findings.
w: The low glucose confirms she has had a stroke
Glucose readings are unreliable in stroke patients
She should be given nothing and reassessed in an hour

qs.q: An 81-year-old with type 2 diabetes has become confused over the past week. She is very dehydrated, has no fruity breath odor, and breathes normally. Her glucose meter reads "HI." What condition is most likely?
qs.a: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
qs.x: Older type 2 diabetics can develop extremely high glucose and severe dehydration over days without significant ketone production, so Kussmaul breathing and fruity odor are often absent.
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Insulin shock
Acute alcohol intoxication

qs.q: A 30-year-old man has itchy hives on his arms after eating shrimp. He has no history of severe reactions, no breathing difficulty, no swelling of the face or throat, and normal vital signs. What is appropriate?
qs.a: Monitor closely for progression during transport
qs.x: Isolated skin findings without respiratory, circulatory, or other systemic signs indicate a mild allergic reaction, but it can progress, so close monitoring is essential.
w: Administer an epinephrine auto-injector right away
Insert an oral airway to prevent swelling
Place him supine with legs elevated and give nothing else

qs.q: A 10-year-old with a peanut allergy ate a cookie at a party. She has stridor, a hoarse voice, and hives, and has her prescribed epinephrine auto-injector. What is the most important action?
qs.a: Administer her epinephrine auto-injector
qs.x: Airway involvement with known allergen exposure is anaphylaxis, and early epinephrine is the treatment that reverses airway swelling and shock.
w: Have her drink water to rinse the allergen down
Give high-flow oxygen and wait to see if it resolves
Transport first and let the hospital decide on treatment

qs.q: A 26-year-old's breathing and blood pressure improved after his epinephrine auto-injector. He now feels fine and wants to go home. Why should he be transported?
qs.a: Symptoms can return as the epinephrine wears off
qs.x: Epinephrine acts for a short time, and anaphylaxis can recur or a second phase can develop hours later, so observation at a hospital is needed.
w: The epinephrine will cause a dangerously high blood sugar
He needs a second injection given at the hospital
He is at risk for low blood pressure from the injection itself

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman stung by a wasp has wheezing, facial swelling, and a BP of 78/50. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Administer epinephrine by auto-injector per protocol; Provide high-flow oxygen; Request ALS and transport promptly
qs.x: Anaphylaxis requires epinephrine, oxygen, ALS support, and rapid transport; tourniquets are not used for stings and exertion worsens shock.
opts: Administer epinephrine by auto-injector per protocol
Provide high-flow oxygen
Request ALS and transport promptly
Apply a tight tourniquet above the sting site
Have her walk to the ambulance to save time
ok: Administer epinephrine by auto-injector per protocol
Provide high-flow oxygen
Request ALS and transport promptly

qs.q: A 2-year-old swallowed liquid drain cleaner. There are burns around his mouth and he is drooling. What should you do?
qs.a: Do not induce vomiting; transport and contact poison control
qs.x: Vomiting re-exposes the esophagus and airway to a corrosive, so it is never induced; giving anything by mouth should be guided by medical direction or poison control.
w: Make him vomit to empty the stomach quickly
Give him milk to neutralize the chemical
Give him a large glass of water to dilute the chemical

qs.q: A 50-year-old man is removed from a closed garage where a car was running. He has a headache and nausea, and his SpO2 reads 99%. How should you interpret the SpO2?
qs.a: It may be falsely normal; give high-flow oxygen
qs.x: Standard pulse oximeters read carbon monoxide-bound hemoglobin as oxygenated, so the reading can be falsely high; treat suspected CO exposure with high-flow oxygen.
w: It confirms that he has no carbon monoxide exposure
It shows that he needs no supplemental oxygen
It means his headache must have another cause

qs.q: A family of three has headaches and confusion after running a generator indoors. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Remove them from the environment if it is safe to do so; Give high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask; Transport for evaluation even if they feel better
qs.x: CO patients need removal from the source, high-flow oxygen, and evaluation; symptoms improving in fresh air does not rule out significant poisoning, and routine pulse oximetry is unreliable.
opts: Remove them from the environment if it is safe to do so
Give high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask
Transport for evaluation even if they feel better
Use pulse oximetry to decide who needs oxygen
Allow them to stay home once the windows are opened
ok: Remove them from the environment if it is safe to do so
Give high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask
Transport for evaluation even if they feel better

qs.q: You arrive at a farm where two workers have collapsed inside a manure storage tank. A third worker climbed in to help and also collapsed. What should you do?
qs.a: Stay out and request specialized rescue
qs.x: Multiple collapses in a confined space suggest a toxic or oxygen-deficient atmosphere; only rescuers with proper training and supplied-air equipment should enter.
w: Enter quickly while holding your breath
Lower a rope into the tank and climb in after it
Enter wearing a surgical mask over your face

qs.q: A landscaper has a dry chemical powder on his arms and clothing. The label says it reacts with water. What should you do first?
qs.a: Brush off the powder and remove contaminated clothing
qs.x: Dry chemicals should be brushed off and contaminated clothing removed before any flushing, especially when the product reacts with water.
w: Flush the area immediately with large amounts of water
Wipe the skin with an alcohol pad to remove it
Cover the area with a dressing and leave it in place

qs.q: A worker got a liquid industrial chemical splashed in both eyes. Which action is most important?
qs.a: Flush the eyes with clean water for at least 20 minutes
qs.x: Prolonged irrigation is the key treatment for chemical eye exposure and should continue during transport when possible.
w: Patch both eyes and transport without flushing them
Rinse briefly with saline and stop when the pain eases
Have the patient rub his eyes to clear the chemical

qs.q: A 28-year-old is found unresponsive in a public restroom with drug paraphernalia nearby. Which findings are consistent with an opioid overdose? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Pinpoint pupils; Respiratory rate of 6/min; Decreased level of responsiveness
qs.x: The opioid toxidrome is respiratory depression, constricted pupils, and depressed mental status; dilated pupils and hot, dry skin suggest other toxidromes.
opts: Pinpoint pupils
Respiratory rate of 6/min
Decreased level of responsiveness
Widely dilated pupils
Hot, flushed, dry skin
Respiratory rate of 32/min
ok: Pinpoint pupils
Respiratory rate of 6/min
Decreased level of responsiveness

qs.q: After naloxone, a 33-year-old who overdosed on an opioid is awake and breathing well. He wants to leave. What is the main risk of refusal?
qs.a: The naloxone may wear off before the opioid
qs.x: Many opioids act longer than naloxone, so respiratory depression can return after the antidote wears off.
w: He will become hypoglycemic within minutes
The naloxone will cause delayed anaphylaxis
He is likely to develop dangerously high blood pressure

qs.q: A 24-year-old who used cocaine is agitated and sweating heavily, with a heart rate of 142, a temperature of 104 F, and dilated pupils. Which toxidrome does this represent?
qs.a: Sympathomimetic
qs.x: Stimulants such as cocaine and methamphetamine cause agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, and dilated pupils.
w: Opioid
Cholinergic
Sedative-hypnotic

qs.q: A 15-year-old took a large amount of an over-the-counter antihistamine. Which findings would you expect?
qs.a: Hot, dry, flushed skin with dilated pupils
qs.x: Anticholinergic poisoning causes dry, hot, red skin, dilated pupils, rapid heart rate, and confusion, the opposite of the wet cholinergic picture.
w: Cool, sweaty skin with pinpoint pupils
Heavy drooling, tearing, and frequent urination
Slow breathing with pinpoint pupils and no agitation

qs.q: A 55-year-old who drinks heavily every day stopped 2 days ago. He is tremulous, sweating, and seeing insects on the wall. Why is this serious?
qs.a: Severe alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and death
qs.x: Alcohol withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens, which carries significant mortality and needs medical care.
w: Withdrawal symptoms are mild and fade within an hour
It shows that he is intoxicated again and needs only rest
Hallucinations confirm a primary psychiatric illness

qs.q: A 72-year-old man has sudden, severe abdominal pain radiating to his back. You feel a pulsating mass above his navel. His BP is 90/58. What should you do?
qs.a: Treat for shock and transport promptly
qs.x: These findings suggest a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm; avoid vigorous palpation, treat for shock, and transport rapidly to an appropriate facility.
w: Palpate the mass firmly to estimate its size
Have him walk to the stretcher to save time
Give him water to ease his discomfort

qs.q: A 44-year-old woman has right upper quadrant abdominal pain that began after a fatty meal and spreads to her right shoulder. Which organ is most likely involved?
qs.a: Gallbladder
qs.x: Gallbladder inflammation often follows fatty meals and refers pain to the right shoulder or scapula.
w: Appendix
Spleen
Left kidney

qs.q: A 19-year-old has pain that began around his navel and over several hours moved to the right lower quadrant. He has nausea and a low-grade fever. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Appendicitis
qs.x: Pain that starts near the umbilicus and migrates to the right lower quadrant, with nausea and fever, is classic for appendicitis.
w: Gallbladder disease
Pancreatitis
Kidney stone

qs.q: A 61-year-old has had black, tarry, foul-smelling stools for 2 days and feels dizzy when standing. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Bleeding in the upper digestive tract
qs.x: Black, tarry stool (melena) is digested blood, usually from the stomach or upper intestine, and dizziness on standing suggests significant blood loss.
w: Bleeding from hemorrhoids
A bladder infection
Food poisoning from undercooked meat

qs.q: A 37-year-old has severe abdominal pain with nausea. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Allow a position of comfort; Give nothing by mouth; Watch for signs of shock; Be ready to suction or position for vomiting
qs.x: Abdominal pain care is supportive: position of comfort, nothing by mouth, monitoring for shock, and airway protection if vomiting occurs.
opts: Allow a position of comfort
Give nothing by mouth
Watch for signs of shock
Be ready to suction or position for vomiting
Give a small meal to settle the stomach
Apply a heating pad to the abdomen
ok: Allow a position of comfort
Give nothing by mouth
Watch for signs of shock
Be ready to suction or position for vomiting

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with a long history of heavy drinking is vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. What is your first priority?
qs.a: Keep the airway clear with suction and positioning
qs.x: Massive upper GI bleeding, such as from esophageal varices, threatens the airway first; position and suction to prevent aspiration while treating for shock.
w: Give him water to rinse his mouth between episodes
Lay him flat on his back and elevate his legs
Collect the vomit to measure its volume

qs.q: Which findings suggest gastrointestinal bleeding? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Vomit that looks like coffee grounds; Black, tarry stools; Dizziness or fainting on standing
qs.x: Coffee-ground emesis, melena, and orthostatic symptoms indicate GI blood loss; a stiff neck with fever and flank-to-groin pain suggest other conditions.
opts: Vomit that looks like coffee grounds
Black, tarry stools
Dizziness or fainting on standing
Fever with a stiff neck
Pain radiating from the flank to the groin
ok: Vomit that looks like coffee grounds
Black, tarry stools
Dizziness or fainting on standing

qs.q: A 66-year-old dialysis patient missed his last two treatments. He is weak, and his pulse is 46 and irregular. What is the greatest concern?
qs.a: A high potassium level causing a dangerous rhythm
qs.x: Missed dialysis allows potassium to build up, which can slow the heart and cause life-threatening dysrhythmias.
w: Low blood sugar from skipping meals
Dehydration from too much fluid removal
Infection of his dialysis access site

qs.q: A 59-year-old just left her dialysis center and is bleeding steadily from her AV fistula needle site. What should you do first?
qs.a: Apply firm direct pressure to the site
qs.x: Direct pressure controls most fistula bleeding; escalate per bleeding control guidelines if pressure fails, but avoid clamping the fistula.
w: Apply a tourniquet before trying anything else
Clamp the fistula shut with a hemostat
Elevate the arm and wait for clotting

qs.q: A 70-year-old dialysis patient who missed treatment is short of breath, with crackles in both lungs and swollen ankles. What should you do?
qs.a: Sit him upright and support his breathing
qs.x: Missed dialysis can cause fluid overload and pulmonary edema; an upright position, oxygen, ventilatory support as needed, and transport are appropriate.
w: Lay him flat with his legs raised
Give him fluids by mouth to restore volume
Apply cold packs to his chest and legs

qs.q: A 35-year-old man is pacing and cannot get comfortable. He has severe left flank pain radiating to his groin and blood in his urine. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Kidney stone
qs.x: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with restlessness and hematuria is typical of a kidney stone.
w: Appendicitis
Abdominal aortic aneurysm
Testicular infection

qs.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has a temperature of 96.2 F, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 26, BP 94/58, and new confusion. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Sepsis, even without a fever
qs.x: Older adults with serious infections may have low or normal temperatures; tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and altered mentation point to sepsis.
w: Normal aging changes in vital signs
Mild dehydration only
Hypothermia from a cold room

qs.q: A 62-year-old with a cough and fever is being assessed. Which findings raise concern for sepsis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: New confusion; Respiratory rate of 26/min; Systolic BP of 92 mmHg
qs.x: Altered mentation, a respiratory rate of 22 or more, and a systolic BP of 100 or less in a patient with infection suggest sepsis and the need for early notification.
opts: New confusion
Respiratory rate of 26/min
Systolic BP of 92 mmHg
Respiratory rate of 14/min
Clear speech and normal orientation
ok: New confusion
Respiratory rate of 26/min
Systolic BP of 92 mmHg

qs.q: You suspect sepsis in a 58-year-old woman who is hypotensive and confused. Which action most improves her care?
qs.a: Notify the hospital early of possible sepsis
qs.x: Sepsis outcomes depend on early antibiotics and fluids, so prompt transport and early hospital notification matter, along with oxygen and warmth as needed.
w: Delay transport to obtain repeated vital signs
Allow her to walk to the ambulance
Give her large amounts of water by mouth

qs.q: A 30-year-old man was extremely agitated, sweating, and fighting with police. He is now physically restrained and suddenly becomes quiet and still. What should you do?
qs.a: Immediately check his breathing and pulse
qs.x: Sudden quiet in a severely agitated, restrained patient can signal respiratory or cardiac arrest, so assess breathing and circulation immediately.
w: Assume he has calmed down and continue transport
Tighten the restraints to prevent further struggle
Leave him alone so he does not become agitated again

qs.q: A violent patient must be restrained for transport. Which practices promote safety? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Have enough trained personnel to control each limb; Keep him supine or on his side; Monitor his airway and breathing continuously; Check circulation beyond each restraint
qs.x: Restraint must never compress the chest or use prone hobble positions; adequate personnel, a safe position, and continuous monitoring reduce the risk of sudden death.
opts: Have enough trained personnel to control each limb
Keep him supine or on his side
Monitor his airway and breathing continuously
Check circulation beyond each restraint
Place him prone with wrists tied to ankles
Kneel on his back until he stops resisting
ok: Have enough trained personnel to control each limb
Keep him supine or on his side
Monitor his airway and breathing continuously
Check circulation beyond each restraint

qs.q: You are called for a 40-year-old man who is anxious and agitated but not violent. How should you position yourself while talking with him?
qs.a: With a clear path to the exit
qs.x: Keeping your exit route clear lets you leave if the situation escalates; do not let the patient come between you and the door.
w: Between him and the only door in the room
Directly face to face within arm's reach
Behind him, out of his line of sight

qs.q: A 27-year-old woman is breathing rapidly after an argument and has tingling around her mouth and in her hands. What should you do?
qs.a: Reassure her and coach her breathing
qs.x: Coaching slower breathing and reassurance help anxiety-related hyperventilation; paper bag rebreathing is unsafe because serious medical causes of rapid breathing may be missed.
w: Have her breathe into a paper bag
Tell her the symptoms are all in her head
Restrain her until her breathing slows

qs.q: A 64-year-old man says he is "tired of living." Which findings increase his risk of suicide? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A previous suicide attempt; A detailed plan with access to a firearm; Recently widowed and living alone
qs.x: Prior attempts, a specific plan with access to lethal means, and recent loss with isolation increase risk; social support and future plans are protective.
opts: A previous suicide attempt
A detailed plan with access to a firearm
Recently widowed and living alone
Strong support from friends and family
Plans for an upcoming family trip
ok: A previous suicide attempt
A detailed plan with access to a firearm
Recently widowed and living alone

qs.q: A 17-year-old is withdrawn and tearful after a breakup. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Ask her directly if she is thinking of suicide
qs.x: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and is the only way to find out whether she is in danger.
w: Avoid the topic because asking may put the idea in her head
Tell her she will feel better soon and change the subject
Ask her parents but not her about suicidal thoughts

qs.q: A 36-year-old man says he took a bottle of pills to end his life. He is alert and refuses transport. What should you do?
qs.a: Stay with him and involve law enforcement and medical direction
qs.x: A patient with a suicide attempt and possible overdose lacks capacity to refuse; do not leave him, and use law enforcement and medical direction per local protocol.
w: Have him sign a refusal form and leave
Leave a crisis hotline number and clear the scene
Wait outside until he changes his mind

qs.q: A 32-year-old hiker is shivering, alert, and talking clearly after falling into a cold stream. What is the best care?
qs.a: Remove wet clothing and warm her in a heated area
qs.x: Mild hypothermia is treated by removing wet clothing, insulating, and passive or external rewarming in a warm environment.
w: Rub her arms and legs briskly to restore circulation
Give her a drink of alcohol to warm her up
Have her walk quickly to generate body heat

qs.q: A 74-year-old was found in an unheated house. He is unresponsive, with very cold skin. How should you check his pulse?
qs.a: Feel for a pulse longer than usual
qs.x: In severe hypothermia, the pulse may be very slow and faint, so it should be checked for longer than usual before deciding on CPR.
w: Check briefly and start CPR if none is felt immediately
Skip the pulse check and begin CPR at once
Check only the radial pulse

qs.q: A 68-year-old is moderately hypothermic after a night outdoors. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Handle him gently; Remove wet clothing; Apply heat packs to the armpits and groin
qs.x: Gentle handling, removal of wet clothing, and warming of the trunk are recommended; rubbing extremities and exertion can cause tissue injury or dysrhythmias.
opts: Handle him gently
Remove wet clothing
Apply heat packs to the armpits and groin
Massage his arms and legs
Have him walk to the ambulance
ok: Handle him gently
Remove wet clothing
Apply heat packs to the armpits and groin

qs.q: A skier's cheeks are pale and numb, but the skin is soft and regains color when warmed. What condition is this?
qs.a: Frostnip
qs.x: Frostnip is superficial cold injury with blanched, numb skin that remains soft and recovers with warming.
w: Deep frostbite
Trench foot
Heat exhaustion

qs.q: A 46-year-old roofer working in the heat has painful cramps in his legs. He is alert and sweating. What should you do?
qs.a: Move him to a cool place and give electrolyte fluid by mouth
qs.x: Heat cramps from salt and fluid loss respond to rest, cooling, and oral electrolyte replacement in an alert patient.
w: Apply a tourniquet to his legs to relieve cramping
Immerse him immediately in an ice water bath
Have him continue working to stretch the muscles

qs.q: A 38-year-old is dizzy and nauseated after working in the heat. Her skin is pale and sweaty, her heart rate is 110, and she is fully alert and oriented. What is most likely?
qs.a: Heat exhaustion
qs.x: Heat exhaustion causes weakness, dizziness, sweating, and tachycardia with normal mental status; altered mental status indicates heat stroke.
w: Heat stroke
Heat cramps
Hypoglycemia

qs.q: A 21-year-old soldier collapses during a march. He is confused and his skin is hot. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Remove excess clothing; Cool rapidly, ideally with cold-water immersion; Apply cold packs to the neck, armpits, and groin
qs.x: Exertional heat stroke needs rapid cooling on scene, with cold-water immersion being the most effective method when available.
opts: Remove excess clothing
Cool rapidly, ideally with cold-water immersion
Apply cold packs to the neck, armpits, and groin
Rub his skin with alcohol
Delay cooling until arrival at the hospital
ok: Remove excess clothing
Cool rapidly, ideally with cold-water immersion
Apply cold packs to the neck, armpits, and groin

qs.q: An 11-year-old was pulled from a pool. She coughed up water and is now alert and breathing normally. Her parents want no transport. What is your concern?
qs.a: Breathing problems can develop hours later
qs.x: Aspiration of water can cause delayed respiratory compromise, so evaluation after a submersion event is important even when the patient looks well.
w: She has a high risk of hypothermia from the warm pool
She may have swallowed too much chlorine
She may become dehydrated from swallowing water

qs.q: A 16-year-old dove into the shallow end of a lake and is floating face down. What should you suspect?
qs.a: A spinal injury
qs.x: Diving into shallow water causes cervical spine injuries; remove the patient from the water with in-line stabilization while maintaining the airway.
w: Hyperthermia
Decompression sickness
Anaphylaxis from lake water

qs.q: A 9-year-old is pulled from a lake. She is unresponsive, apneic, and pulseless. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin CPR with emphasis on effective ventilations
qs.x: Drowning arrest is caused by hypoxia, so ventilations are especially important; attempts to drain water delay care.
w: Drain water from her lungs before starting CPR
Perform abdominal thrusts to remove water
Do not attempt CPR because she was submerged

qs.q: Lightning struck a group of hikers. One is screaming in pain, one is confused, and one is apneic and pulseless. Whom should you treat first?
qs.a: The apneic, pulseless hiker
qs.x: In lightning strikes, those in respiratory or cardiac arrest often survive with prompt care, so reverse triage puts them first.
w: The hiker who is screaming in pain
The confused hiker
All are equal, so treat whoever is closest

qs.q: A 39-year-old was bitten while moving wood. She now has severe abdominal cramping and a rigid abdomen. Which bite is most likely?
qs.a: Black widow spider
qs.x: Black widow venom acts on nerves and causes muscle cramping and abdominal rigidity, while brown recluse bites cause local tissue damage.
w: Brown recluse spider
Non-venomous snake
Domestic cat

qs.q: A 23-year-old was stung by a bee and the stinger is still in his skin. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove it quickly, such as by scraping with a card
qs.x: Prompt removal limits venom delivery; the method matters less than speed, and scraping is a common technique.
w: Leave it in place for removal at the hospital
Squeeze it out between your fingers slowly
Cover it with a tight dressing to trap the venom

qs.q: A 30-year-old stepped on a stingray. She has severe foot pain and a small wound. What is appropriate?
qs.a: Immerse the foot in hot water as tolerated
qs.x: Hot water immersion, without causing burns, helps relieve pain from many marine venoms.
w: Apply ice to the wound
Apply a tight tourniquet above the ankle
Rub sand into the wound to remove venom

qs.q: A 42-year-old scuba diver has joint pain and tingling in his arms 2 hours after surfacing. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Decompression sickness
qs.x: Nitrogen bubbles forming after a dive cause joint pain, skin changes, and neurologic symptoms; high-flow oxygen and transport to a facility able to provide hyperbaric care are needed.
w: Heat exhaustion
Arterial gas embolism
Carbon monoxide poisoning

qs.q: A 28-year-old diver ascended quickly and, within a minute of surfacing, became unresponsive with one-sided weakness. What is most likely?
qs.a: Arterial gas embolism
qs.x: Rapid ascent can force air into the arterial circulation, causing stroke-like signs immediately after surfacing.
w: Decompression sickness
Hypoglycemia
Heat stroke

qs.q: During a delivery, the baby's head has delivered and you have checked for a cord. What is the next step?
qs.a: Support the head and guide it gently downward to deliver the upper shoulder
qs.x: Gentle downward guidance helps the upper shoulder deliver, then upward guidance for the lower shoulder; never pull hard on the head.
w: Pull firmly on the head to deliver the body quickly
Push the head back up to slow down the delivery
Wait until the next day for the mother to deliver the shoulders

qs.q: When should you suction a newborn's mouth and nose after delivery?
qs.a: Only if secretions block the airway
qs.x: Routine suctioning is not recommended for newborns; suction the mouth before the nose only when secretions obstruct breathing or ventilation is needed.
w: Always, immediately after delivery
Only after the placenta delivers
Never, under any circumstances

qs.q: A healthy term newborn is crying with good tone. When should the umbilical cord be clamped?
qs.a: After at least 30 to 60 seconds
qs.x: Delayed cord clamping for at least 30 to 60 seconds is recommended for vigorous newborns.
w: Immediately before the baby breathes
Only after the placenta delivers
Within 5 seconds of delivery

qs.q: After delivery of the baby, the placenta has not yet delivered. What should you do?
qs.a: Allow it to deliver naturally and bring it to the hospital
qs.x: Pulling on the cord can tear it or invert the uterus; the placenta should deliver naturally and be bagged for examination.
w: Pull firmly on the cord to speed it up
Push on the uterus forcefully to expel it
Cut the cord close to the vagina and leave the placenta

qs.q: During delivery, the umbilical cord is wrapped tightly around the baby's neck and cannot be slipped over the head. What should you do?
qs.a: Clamp the cord in two places and cut between them
qs.x: A tight nuchal cord that cannot be loosened must be clamped and cut so delivery can continue safely.
w: Pull the baby out quickly to loosen the cord
Push the baby's head back in
Leave it and continue the delivery

qs.q: During a breech delivery, the body has delivered but the head has not after 3 minutes. What should you do?
qs.a: Place gloved fingers to form an airway for the baby
qs.x: Creating an airway by placing fingers alongside the baby's face allows breathing while transport continues.
w: Pull firmly on the legs to deliver the head
Push the body back into the vagina
Wait until the mother can be transported

qs.q: After the baby's head delivers, it pulls back tightly against the mother's perineum and the shoulders do not deliver. What should you do?
qs.a: Have her pull her knees back toward her chest
qs.x: This is shoulder dystocia; flexing the mother's hips by drawing her knees to her chest widens the pelvis and can free the shoulder.
w: Pull hard on the baby's head
Push on the top of the uterus
Push the head back into the vagina

qs.q: A 37-weeks-pregnant woman is having a seizure. Her BP is 172/112. What is appropriate?
qs.a: Place her on her left side, give oxygen, and transport rapidly
qs.x: Eclampsia is life-threatening; protect the airway, position on the left side, give oxygen, minimize stimulation, and transport rapidly.
w: Give her oral glucose and wait
Put her flat on her back and elevate her legs
Place a bite block in her mouth

qs.q: A woman who gave birth 10 days ago has a seizure. Her BP is 170/110. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Eclampsia after delivery
qs.x: Preeclampsia and eclampsia can occur up to several weeks after delivery, so new seizures and hypertension postpartum are concerning.
w: Epilepsy that she has always had
A simple faint
Normal changes after childbirth

qs.q: A woman 33 weeks pregnant has sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Placenta previa
qs.x: Placenta previa causes painless bright red bleeding late in pregnancy; never perform a vaginal exam.
w: Placental abruption
Ectopic pregnancy
Normal labor

qs.q: A 35-weeks-pregnant woman has sudden abdominal pain. Which findings suggest placental abruption? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Painful, rigid abdomen; Shock signs out of proportion to visible bleeding; Dark red vaginal bleeding
qs.x: Abruption causes painful, rigid uterus and concealed bleeding that leads to shock, while painless bleeding suggests previa.
opts: Painful, rigid abdomen
Shock signs out of proportion to visible bleeding
Dark red vaginal bleeding
Painless bright red bleeding
Normal soft uterus
ok: Painful, rigid abdomen
Shock signs out of proportion to visible bleeding
Dark red vaginal bleeding

qs.q: A 27-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant has heavy vaginal bleeding with cramping and has passed clots and tissue. Her pulse is 116. What should you do?
qs.a: Treat for shock and bring the passed tissue to the hospital
qs.x: A likely miscarriage with tachycardia needs shock care and transport; place a pad over the vaginal opening, never pack it, and bring tissue for examination.
w: Discard the tissue in a biohazard bag to reduce infection risk
Pack gauze into the vagina to stop the bleeding
Reassure her that early pregnancy bleeding is normal and suggest she follow up with her doctor

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman is in labor with her second child. Which findings indicate that delivery is imminent? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Crowning during contractions; A strong urge to push or move her bowels; Contractions about 2 minutes apart and lasting about a minute
qs.x: Crowning, the urge to bear down, and strong contractions about 2 minutes apart signal imminent delivery; ruptured membranes or bloody show alone do not.
opts: Crowning during contractions
A strong urge to push or move her bowels
Contractions about 2 minutes apart and lasting about a minute
Her water broke 6 hours ago, with contractions 10 minutes apart
A small amount of blood-tinged mucus with no contractions
ok: Crowning during contractions
A strong urge to push or move her bowels
Contractions about 2 minutes apart and lasting about a minute

qs.q: You have just delivered a baby at home. The mother's abdomen remains about as large as before, and strong contractions begin again a few minutes later. What should you suspect?
qs.a: A second baby is about to deliver
qs.x: A uterus that stays large with renewed contractions after the first birth suggests multiple gestation; prepare for a second delivery and additional newborn care.
w: The placenta is delivering and nothing else is expected
She has a uterine rupture and needs immediate surgery
This is normal and she can be transported without further preparation

qs.q: A term baby is born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid. He is crying vigorously with good muscle tone. What should you do?
qs.a: Provide routine newborn care
qs.x: A vigorous newborn needs routine care (warm, dry, stimulate, clear the airway only if needed) whether or not meconium is present.
w: Suction deeply below the vocal cords before stimulating him
Begin positive pressure ventilation at once
Withhold drying until the meconium is suctioned

qs.q: At 1 minute, a newborn has a pink body with blue hands and feet, a heart rate of 110/min, a grimace to stimulation, some flexion of the arms and legs, and a weak, slow cry. What is the APGAR score?
qs.x: Appearance 1, pulse 2, grimace 1, activity 1, and respiration 1 total 6.

qs.q: A newborn is limp and not breathing immediately after birth. How should the APGAR score affect your initial care?
qs.a: Do not wait for it to begin resuscitation
qs.x: The APGAR score describes the newborn's condition at 1 and 5 minutes but is not used to decide whether to start resuscitation; breathing and heart rate guide care.
w: Wait for the 1-minute score to decide whether to ventilate
Begin compressions only if the 1-minute score is below 7
Delay ventilation until both the 1-minute and 5-minute scores are known

qs.q: Despite effective ventilation, a newborn's heart rate remains below 60/min and you begin chest compressions. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should you use?
qs.x: Neonatal resuscitation uses a 3:1 ratio, giving about 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute.

qs.q: Two minutes after birth, a crying newborn has a pink trunk and lips but bluish hands and feet. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: It is a normal finding
qs.x: Acrocyanosis, bluish extremities with a pink central body, is common in the first minutes of life and does not require treatment.
w: It indicates severe hypoxia that requires chest compressions
It is a sign of shock that requires immediate fluid replacement
It suggests a heart defect and requires high-flow oxygen by mask

qs.q: Which method gives the most accurate heart rate in a newborn who needs resuscitation in the field?
qs.a: Listening over the chest
qs.x: Auscultation of the chest is more reliable than palpation in newborns, whose peripheral pulses are difficult to feel.
w: Palpating the radial pulse at the wrist
Palpating the carotid pulse in the neck
Estimating from capillary refill time

qs.q: You have dried and stimulated a newborn. Which findings indicate a need for positive pressure ventilation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Apnea; Gasping respirations; A heart rate of 80/min
qs.x: Apnea, gasping, or a heart rate below 100/min after initial steps calls for positive pressure ventilation; a crying newborn with a normal heart rate and acrocyanosis does not.
opts: Apnea
Gasping respirations
A heart rate of 80/min
Crying with a heart rate of 150/min
Bluish hands and feet with a pink trunk
ok: Apnea
Gasping respirations
A heart rate of 80/min

qs.q: You are providing positive pressure ventilation to an apneic newborn with a heart rate of 90/min. At what rate should you ventilate?
qs.a: 40 to 60 breaths per minute
qs.x: Newborn positive pressure ventilation is given at 40 to 60 breaths per minute, watching for chest rise and a rising heart rate.
w: 10 to 12 breaths per minute
20 to 30 breaths per minute
100 to 120 breaths per minute

qs.q: A 20-month-old with a fever of 103 F has had a seizure. Which findings suggest something more serious than a simple febrile seizure? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A stiff neck with a purple, non-blanching rash; Jerking limited to one side of the body; A second seizure later the same day
qs.x: Simple febrile seizures are brief, generalized, and do not recur within 24 hours; focal seizures, recurrence, or signs of meningitis suggest a more serious cause, while a quick fever rise and brief drowsiness are typical.
opts: A stiff neck with a purple, non-blanching rash
Jerking limited to one side of the body
A second seizure later the same day
A rapid rise in temperature before the seizure
Drowsiness for a few minutes afterward
ok: A stiff neck with a purple, non-blanching rash
Jerking limited to one side of the body
A second seizure later the same day

qs.q: An 8-month-old has had diarrhea for 3 days. She is lethargic, with a heart rate of 190/min, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and cool, mottled extremities. What does this indicate?
qs.a: Shock from severe dehydration
qs.x: Lethargy, marked tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, and cool, mottled skin indicate shock; give oxygen, keep her warm, and transport rapidly.
w: Mild dehydration that can be managed at home
Normal findings for an infant who has been sleeping
A fever that has broken and is resolving

qs.q: A 2-month-old is found unresponsive in his crib. He is warm, has no lividity or rigor mortis, and has no pulse. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin CPR and transport
qs.x: Without obvious signs of death, an infant in cardiac arrest should receive immediate resuscitation; questions about the cause come later.
w: Pronounce death on scene and call the medical examiner
Interview the parents in detail before touching the infant
Wait for law enforcement to photograph the scene first

qs.q: A 3-month-old briefly stopped breathing, turned blue, and went limp, then recovered within a minute. She now looks well. The parents ask whether transport is needed. What should you advise?
qs.a: Transport for evaluation
qs.x: A brief resolved unexplained event can be caused by serious problems such as infection, seizures, heart rhythm problems, or abuse, so evaluation is recommended even when the infant appears well.
w: No care is needed because she looks normal now
Watch her closely at home and call again only if it recurs
Give her a bottle and recheck her in an hour

qs.q: You are caring for an injured 2-year-old. Which findings suggest possible abuse? Select all that apply.
qs.a: An explanation that does not fit the injury; Bruises in many different stages of healing; Burns on both feet with sharp lines like a sock; A long delay before calling for help
qs.x: Inconsistent histories, multiple healing stages, immersion burn patterns, and delays in seeking care are red flags; shin bruises and forehead bumps are common accidental toddler injuries.
opts: An explanation that does not fit the injury
Bruises in many different stages of healing
Burns on both feet with sharp lines like a sock
A long delay before calling for help
Bruises on the shins of an active toddler
A single bump on the forehead from a fall while walking
ok: An explanation that does not fit the injury
Bruises in many different stages of healing
Burns on both feet with sharp lines like a sock
A long delay before calling for help

qs.q: You suspect that a 5-year-old's injuries were caused by abuse. The caregiver is present. What should you do?
qs.a: Report your concerns as required by law
qs.x: Suspected abuse must be reported according to state law and agency policy; avoid confrontation, care for the child, and document objectively.
w: Confront the caregiver about your suspicions
Leave the child at home to avoid conflict
Ask the child repeatedly until he admits what happened

qs.q: A 4-month-old is lethargic and has been vomiting, with no visible injuries. The caregiver says the baby was "fine an hour ago" and gives a vague story. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Abusive head trauma
qs.x: Unexplained lethargy and vomiting in an infant, with an inconsistent history, can be signs of abusive head trauma even without external injury.
w: Normal teething discomfort
Colic that will resolve on its own
Normal infant sleepiness after a feeding

qs.q: An 82-year-old takes nine medications. Her family says she became confused and fell twice since a new medication was added last week. What should you consider?
qs.a: An adverse drug effect or interaction
qs.x: Polypharmacy is a common cause of new confusion and falls in older adults; bring the medications or a list to the hospital.
w: Normal aging that requires no further evaluation
Long-standing dementia that has not changed
Too little sleep, with no other cause to consider

qs.q: A 78-year-old woman fell in her bathroom and has hip pain. Why is it important to ask what happened just before the fall?
qs.a: A medical problem may have caused it
qs.x: Falls in older adults are often caused by syncope, dysrhythmias, stroke, hypoglycemia, or medications, and these must be identified along with the injury.
w: To decide who is legally responsible
To determine which hospital she prefers
To confirm whether she needs a walker

qs.q: You respond to an 86-year-old woman who lives with her son. Which findings suggest possible elder abuse or neglect? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Unexplained bruises in different stages of healing; A son who answers every question and will not leave her alone; Poor hygiene with untreated pressure ulcers
qs.x: Unexplained injuries, a controlling caregiver, and signs of neglect are red flags; a well-kept home and hearing loss are not.
opts: Unexplained bruises in different stages of healing
A son who answers every question and will not leave her alone
Poor hygiene with untreated pressure ulcers
A tidy home with medications organized in a pillbox
Mild hearing loss
ok: Unexplained bruises in different stages of healing
A son who answers every question and will not leave her alone
Poor hygiene with untreated pressure ulcers

qs.q: An 85-year-old has mild abdominal discomfort, normal vital signs, and no fever. Why is transport still recommended?
qs.a: Serious problems may present subtly in older adults
qs.x: Older adults often have blunted pain, fever, and heart rate responses, so serious conditions can present with mild symptoms and normal vital signs.
w: Older adults usually exaggerate their pain
Abdominal pain in older adults is almost always minor
Normal vital signs rule out serious illness in older adults

qs.q: A 76-year-old with known dementia has become much more confused and agitated over the past day. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Delirium from an acute medical problem
qs.x: A sudden change in mental status is delirium, which often signals infection, dehydration, medication effects, or another acute medical problem.
w: Expected progression of dementia
A new psychiatric illness only
A normal change in older adults

qs.q: A 54-year-old on a home ventilator is in respiratory distress and the ventilator alarm is sounding. What should you do?
qs.a: Disconnect and ventilate with a BVM
qs.x: When a ventilator-dependent patient is in distress, remove the ventilator from the equation and ventilate manually while looking for the cause.
w: Silence the alarm and continue to watch him
Increase the ventilator rate and wait
Call the equipment company before any care

qs.q: A 10-year-old with a tracheostomy who uses a home ventilator is in respiratory distress. Which problems should you consider? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The tube has come out of position; The tube is blocked with mucus; The ventilator or tubing is malfunctioning
qs.x: Displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax, and equipment failure are common causes of distress in patients with a tracheostomy and ventilator.
opts: The tube has come out of position
The tube is blocked with mucus
The ventilator or tubing is malfunctioning
The child is breathing too deeply
The oxygen tank is too full
ok: The tube has come out of position
The tube is blocked with mucus
The ventilator or tubing is malfunctioning

qs.q: A 64-year-old with a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) is alert and talking. You cannot feel a radial pulse or hear a blood pressure. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: It may be normal with this device
qs.x: Many LVADs produce continuous flow with little or no pulse; assess mental status and skin perfusion, and contact the device coordinator listed on the equipment.
w: He is in cardiac arrest
He needs immediate CPR
The device has failed

qs.q: A 70-year-old with a gastrostomy feeding tube develops coughing and difficulty breathing right after a feeding. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Aspiration of the feeding
qs.x: Patients with feeding tubes can aspirate stomach contents; position them upright, suction as needed, and support breathing.
w: An allergic reaction to the formula
Hypoglycemia from the feeding
Dehydration from the feeding

qs.q: A 45-year-old receiving long-term treatment through a central venous catheter has a fever, chills, and a heart rate of 118. What should you suspect?
qs.a: A serious bloodstream infection
qs.x: Central lines provide a direct route for infection into the blood, so fever and tachycardia in these patients raise concern for sepsis.
w: A normal reaction to the catheter
A blood clot in the leg
Low blood sugar

qs.q: A 7-year-old with a shunt for hydrocephalus has a headache, vomiting, and increasing sleepiness. What should you suspect?
qs.a: A shunt malfunction
qs.x: Shunt blockage or infection causes rising pressure in the skull, with headache, vomiting, and decreasing mental status, and requires prompt transport.
w: A stomach virus
Seasonal influenza
A typical migraine

qs.q: A 9-year-old with autism spectrum disorder becomes very agitated in the ambulance. What should you do?
qs.a: Reduce stimulation and involve the caregiver
qs.x: Reducing noise, lights, and touch, and using the caregiver's knowledge of the child, help keep patients with autism calm.
w: Restrain the child before he becomes violent
Turn on more lights so you can see him better
Ignore the behavior and continue with your questions

qs.q: You are preparing to insert a supraglottic airway in an unresponsive adult in cardiac arrest. How should you choose the device size?
qs.a: Follow the manufacturer's height or weight guide for that device
qs.x: Supraglottic airways are sized by the manufacturer's height or weight chart for that specific product. The mouth-to-jaw and nose-to-earlobe measurements are used to size oral and nasal airways.
w: Measure from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw
Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe
Match the diameter of the patient's little finger to the outside of the tube

qs.q: A 61-year-old man with a pulse is being ventilated through a supraglottic airway. His capnography waveform has been normal at 38 mmHg, but after he is moved down a flight of stairs the waveform is a flat line, there is no chest rise and his SpO2 is falling. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: The device has become displaced
qs.x: A sudden loss of the capnography waveform with no chest rise after moving the patient points to a dislodged airway. Bronchospasm produces a sloped waveform rather than a flat line, and a loose oximeter probe would not stop chest rise.
w: He has developed bronchospasm
He is being hyperventilated
The oxygen saturation probe has slipped off

qs.q: During transport, the SpO2 of a patient ventilated through a supraglottic airway drifts from 96 to 85 percent. Chest rise is good, breath sounds are equal and the capnography waveform is unchanged. What should you check next?
qs.a: The oxygen tubing connection and the cylinder pressure
qs.x: With good chest rise, equal breath sounds and a normal waveform, the airway is working, so equipment failure such as a disconnected oxygen line or empty tank is the likely problem. Thinking through displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax and equipment keeps troubleshooting organized.
w: Whether the cuff needs an additional 20 mL of air
Whether the device should be exchanged for a larger size
Whether the ventilation rate should be doubled

qs.q: A 35-year-old crash victim with chest wall bruising is being ventilated through a supraglottic airway. Bagging becomes progressively harder, breath sounds disappear on the right, his neck veins distend and his BP falls to 74/40. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Tension pneumothorax
qs.x: Rising resistance to ventilation, unilateral absent breath sounds, distended neck veins and hypotension after chest trauma indicate tension pneumothorax, which positive pressure ventilation can worsen. Request ALS for decompression and expedite transport.
w: Displacement of the device into the esophagus
Gastric distension from the ventilations
Mucus plugging of the airway tube

qs.q: You are ventilating an adult through a supraglottic airway when frothy secretions begin bubbling up into the tube and resistance to bagging increases. Chest rise and capnography were confirmed earlier. What should you do?
qs.a: Suction the airway tube with a soft catheter, then reassess
qs.x: Secretions obstructing the airway tube should be suctioned through the device and ventilation reassessed. Overinflating the cuff or bagging faster does not clear the obstruction, and a nasal cannula cannot ventilate an apneic patient.
w: Add air to the cuff until the secretions stop rising
Increase the ventilation rate to push the secretions back down
Remove the device immediately and switch to a nasal cannula

qs.q: What is the normal end-tidal carbon dioxide range for an adult with adequate ventilation and perfusion?
qs.a: 35 to 45 mmHg
qs.x: Normal ETCO2 is about 35 to 45 mmHg. Lower values suggest hyperventilation or poor perfusion, while higher values suggest hypoventilation.
w: 10 to 20 mmHg
50 to 60 mmHg
90 to 100 mmHg

qs.q: A 57-year-old man has return of spontaneous circulation and is being ventilated through a supraglottic airway. Your partner is squeezing the bag about 24 times per minute, and the ETCO2 is 25 mmHg with a normal waveform. What should you do?
qs.a: Slow ventilations to about 1 breath every 6 seconds
qs.x: An ETCO2 of 25 mmHg with a fast bagging rate indicates hyperventilation, which lowers carbon dioxide, constricts cerebral vessels and reduces venous return. Slowing to about 10 breaths per minute brings ETCO2 back toward normal.
w: Increase the rate further to bring the ETCO2 below 20 mmHg
Remove the device because the waveform must be inaccurate
Stop ventilating because the patient now has a pulse

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman with COPD is in respiratory distress with an SpO2 of 84 percent on room air. She is alert. What oxygen saturation should you generally target?
qs.a: 88 to 92 percent
qs.x: Patients with chronic carbon dioxide retention are commonly titrated to about 88 to 92 percent, which corrects dangerous hypoxia while limiting worsening hypercapnia. Oxygen is never withheld from a hypoxic patient.
w: 100 percent
94 to 99 percent
80 to 84 percent

qs.q: A 69-year-old man with COPD in severe distress is given oxygen, and 15 minutes later he is increasingly drowsy and breathing 8 times per minute with shallow breaths. What should you do?
qs.a: Assist his ventilations with a BVM
qs.x: Drowsiness with a slow, shallow respiratory rate is inadequate breathing and requires assisted ventilation with oxygen. Removing oxygen from a hypoxic patient is dangerous, and the decline in mental status signals respiratory failure.
w: Stop all oxygen and observe for improvement
Allow him to sleep because he is finally comfortable
Switch to a nasal cannula at 1 L/min and reassess in 10 minutes

qs.q: A 77-year-old with pneumonia is breathing 38 times per minute with shallow breaths and an SpO2 of 86 percent on a nonrebreather. She was alert on arrival but now only responds to loud voice. What is the most appropriate action?
qs.a: Assist ventilations with a BVM and oxygen
qs.x: Fatigue, falling mental status and persistent hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen indicate respiratory failure, which needs assisted ventilation. CPAP requires a patient who is alert enough to protect the airway and follow commands.
w: Continue the nonrebreather and reassess in 10 minutes
Apply CPAP and coach her to breathe slowly
Increase the nonrebreather flow to 25 L/min

qs.q: You are ventilating a 3-year-old who has a pulse of 110 but is breathing only 4 times per minute. No advanced airway is in place. How often should you give breaths?
qs.a: One breath every 2 to 3 seconds
qs.x: Infants and children with a pulse and inadequate breathing receive 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds, about 20 to 30 per minute. Compressions are not indicated with a pulse of 110.
w: One breath every 6 seconds
One breath every 10 seconds
Two breaths after every 15 compressions

qs.q: A 6-year-old in cardiac arrest has a supraglottic airway in place. How should ventilations be delivered during CPR?
qs.a: 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds with continuous compressions
qs.x: With an advanced airway in a child, compressions continue without pauses and breaths are given every 2 to 3 seconds. The 15:2 ratio applies only before an advanced airway is placed.
w: 2 breaths after every 15 compressions
1 breath every 6 seconds with pauses for each breath
1 breath every 10 seconds with continuous compressions to avoid overinflating the small lungs

qs.q: A 2-month-old has a cold, is breathing 64 times per minute with nasal flaring and is struggling to feed. You hear thick congestion in the nose. What should you do first?
qs.a: Gently suction the nose with a bulb syringe
qs.x: Young infants breathe mainly through the nose, so nasal congestion can cause real distress. Gentle bulb suctioning often improves breathing and feeding without invasive interventions.
w: Insert a nasopharyngeal airway in each nostril
Insert an oropharyngeal airway
Ventilate with a BVM at 40 breaths per minute

qs.q: An 18-month-old has a barking cough, a hoarse cry and stridor while resting after several days of cold symptoms. He is alert and clinging to his mother. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Keep him with his mother, give oxygen as tolerated and transport
qs.x: A barky cough and stridor after a viral illness suggest croup. Agitation worsens airway narrowing, so keep the child calm with the caregiver and avoid unnecessary examination of the throat.
w: Lay him supine and insert an oral airway to open the airway
Look at his throat with a tongue blade to check for swelling
Separate him from his mother so you can complete a full head-to-toe assessment before transport

qs.q: A 7-month-old is choking on a piece of food. She is awake but cannot cry or cough effectively. What should you do?
qs.a: Give 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts, repeating as needed
qs.x: Responsive infants with severe airway obstruction receive alternating sets of 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts. Abdominal thrusts can injure an infant, and blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper.
w: Perform abdominal thrusts until the object comes out
Sweep the mouth with your finger to remove the object
Give 2 rescue breaths and then begin chest compressions at a ratio of 30 to 2 until help arrives

qs.q: A woman who is 32 weeks pregnant is choking in a restaurant and cannot speak. What is the correct maneuver?
qs.a: Chest thrusts
qs.x: In late pregnancy and in patients too large to encircle at the abdomen, chest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts. This avoids pressure on the uterus and still generates enough force to expel the object.
w: Abdominal thrusts
Back slaps followed by abdominal thrusts
Blind finger sweeps

qs.q: A 52-year-old choking patient becomes unresponsive as you lower him to the floor. What should you do?
qs.a: Begin CPR and look in the mouth before each set of breaths
qs.x: When a choking patient becomes unresponsive, start CPR because compressions can dislodge the object. Look in the mouth before giving breaths and remove an object only if you can see it.
w: Continue abdominal thrusts while he lies on his back
Perform blind finger sweeps until the object is found
Insert a supraglottic airway to bypass the obstruction

qs.q: A 66-year-old man who had a laryngectomy breathes through a stoma in his neck. He is apneic with a pulse. How should you ventilate him?
qs.a: Seal a small mask over the stoma and ventilate with a BVM
qs.x: After a total laryngectomy, the trachea no longer connects to the mouth, so ventilation must go through the stoma. An infant or child mask often seals well over the opening.
w: Seal a mask over his mouth and nose and pinch the stoma
Insert a supraglottic airway through the mouth and inflate the cuff to seal the pharynx
Give mouth-to-mouth breaths while closing the stoma

qs.q: A 25-year-old has just stopped a generalized seizure. He has snoring respirations, clenched teeth and a strong gag reflex. Which adjunct is most appropriate?
qs.a: Nasopharyngeal airway
qs.x: A nasal airway is tolerated by patients with a gag reflex and can be placed when the jaw is clenched. Oral airways and supraglottic devices are only for patients without a gag reflex.
w: Oropharyngeal airway
Supraglottic airway
Bite block and oral suction catheter only

qs.q: An unresponsive 20-year-old was struck in the head with a bat. He has bruising behind both ears, clear fluid draining from his nose and no gag reflex. Which airway adjunct should you avoid?
qs.a: Nasopharyngeal airway
qs.x: Bruising behind the ears and clear nasal drainage suggest a basilar skull fracture, so nasal airways are avoided. An oral airway is appropriate because the patient has no gag reflex.
w: Oropharyngeal airway
Bag-valve mask
Rigid suction catheter

qs.q: How should you insert an oropharyngeal airway in a 4-year-old?
qs.a: Use a tongue blade and insert it in its normal curved position
qs.x: In children, rotating the airway can injure the soft palate, so the tongue is held down with a tongue blade and the airway is inserted following the natural curve.
w: Insert it upside down and rotate it 180 degrees
Insert it sideways along the cheek and rotate it 90 degrees once it reaches the back of the tongue
Lubricate it and insert it through the nose

qs.q: You find a 79-year-old hypothermic woman with cold, mottled fingers. The pulse oximeter reading jumps between 70 and 92 percent and the waveform is poor. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Poor peripheral perfusion is making the reading unreliable
qs.x: Pulse oximetry needs good perfusion at the probe site, so cold or constricted extremities give erratic readings. Base decisions on your clinical assessment and move the probe to a warmer site such as the earlobe if possible.
w: She is in severe respiratory failure and needs immediate ventilation
The oximeter is accurate and shows intermittent hypoxia
Hypothermia increases the oxygen carried by hemoglobin

qs.q: A 27-year-old is breathing 34 times per minute and reports numbness around the mouth. Nasal capnography shows an ETCO2 of 22 mmHg with a square waveform. What does this reading indicate?
qs.a: Rapid breathing is blowing off carbon dioxide
qs.x: A low ETCO2 with a normal shaped waveform during rapid breathing reflects excessive carbon dioxide elimination. You should still look for serious causes such as pulmonary embolism, DKA or sepsis before assuming anxiety.
w: Carbon dioxide is building up in the blood
There is severe bronchospasm
The capnography sensor is malfunctioning

qs.q: An unresponsive overdose patient with a supraglottic airway begins coughing, gagging and reaching for the tube. What should you do?
qs.a: Deflate the cuff, remove the device and have suction ready
qs.x: A returning gag reflex means the patient no longer tolerates the device, and leaving it in risks vomiting and aspiration. Remove it with suction ready and support the airway as needed.
w: Add air to the cuff to keep the device from moving
Restrain his hands and continue ventilating at the same rate
Push the device deeper so it cannot be pulled out

qs.q: While you ventilate an unresponsive adult with a BVM, she suddenly vomits a large amount. She has no suspected spinal injury. What should you do first?
qs.a: Roll her onto her side and suction the mouth
qs.x: Turning the patient lets vomit drain and suctioning clears what remains, reducing aspiration. Ventilating through vomit forces it into the lungs.
w: Continue ventilating to push air past the vomit
Insert a supraglottic airway immediately
Give abdominal thrusts to clear the airway

qs.q: You cannot get a good mask seal while ventilating a heavily bearded 60-year-old man with a BVM. What technique will most likely improve ventilation?
qs.a: Two rescuers, one sealing the mask with both hands
qs.x: A two-person technique, with one rescuer holding the mask with both hands while the other squeezes the bag, gives a better seal and jaw lift. A nonrebreather does not ventilate an apneic patient.
w: Squeezing the bag harder and faster
Switching to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Using a smaller mask pressed firmly over the mouth only

qs.q: After a 45-year-old was moved from the floor to the stretcher, what should you do to make sure his supraglottic airway is still properly placed?
qs.a: Recheck capnography, chest rise and lung sounds
qs.x: Every patient movement can displace an advanced airway, so placement is reconfirmed after each move with the capnography waveform, chest rise and breath sounds. Continuous waveform capnography is the most reliable ongoing indicator.
w: Assume it is placed because it was confirmed before the move
Remove the device and reinsert it on the stretcher
Wait until arrival at the hospital and let staff check it

qs.q: A newborn is limp and not breathing after being dried, warmed and stimulated. The heart rate is 80. What should you do next?
qs.a: Begin positive pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths per minute
qs.x: Apnea or a heart rate below 100 after initial steps calls for positive pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths per minute. Effective ventilation is the most important step in newborn resuscitation.
w: Begin chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio
Continue drying and stimulating for another full minute before any other intervention
Give blow-by oxygen and reassess in 2 minutes

qs.q: Where should you place the pulse oximeter on a newborn who needs resuscitation?
qs.a: Right hand or wrist
qs.x: Readings from the right hand or wrist reflect preductal blood, which is what newborn oxygen saturation targets are based on.
w: Left foot
Left hand
Either earlobe, whichever gives the strongest waveform

qs.q: A woman at 36 weeks of pregnancy stops breathing after a seizure and needs ventilation. Why will her oxygen saturation fall faster than in a nonpregnant adult?
qs.a: Reduced lung reserve and higher oxygen use
qs.x: The enlarged uterus reduces functional residual capacity while the mother and fetus use more oxygen. Pregnant patients desaturate quickly, so prompt oxygenation and ventilation are critical.
w: The uterus increases her lung volume
Pregnancy lowers the body's oxygen requirements
Her heart rate is slower than normal

qs.q: A 4-month-old with bronchiolitis is grunting at the end of each breath. What does grunting indicate?
qs.a: An attempt to keep the small airways open
qs.x: Grunting is exhalation against a partly closed glottis to keep alveoli open. It signals significant respiratory distress and the need for close monitoring and support.
w: Partial obstruction of the upper airway by the tongue
A normal breathing pattern in infants
A foreign body in the right main bronchus

qs.q: A 34-year-old woman returned from a long international flight 2 days ago. She has sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain when she breathes in, a heart rate of 118, clear lung sounds and an SpO2 of 89 percent. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Pulmonary embolism
qs.x: Sudden dyspnea with pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia and clear lung sounds after prolonged immobility suggests pulmonary embolism. Give oxygen, monitor closely and transport.
w: Asthma exacerbation
Pneumonia
Spontaneous pneumothorax with tension

qs.q: A tall, thin 19-year-old man has sudden sharp left-sided chest pain and mild dyspnea while sitting at his desk. Breath sounds are diminished on the left, and his vital signs are stable. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Spontaneous pneumothorax
qs.x: Spontaneous pneumothorax commonly affects tall, thin young men and causes sudden pleuritic pain with diminished breath sounds on one side. Watch for signs of tension, especially if ventilation becomes necessary.
w: Acute myocardial infarction
Pulmonary edema
Croup

qs.q: A 23-year-old with asthma can speak only 2 or 3 words at a time, has diffuse wheezing and an SpO2 of 90 percent. She is alert. Within AEMT scope, which treatment is most appropriate?
qs.a: Inhaled beta-agonist by nebulizer with oxygen
qs.x: A nebulized bronchodilator with oxygen is the standard treatment for an alert patient with bronchospasm. Advanced airways are for unresponsive patients who cannot protect their airway.
w: Insertion of a supraglottic airway
Nasopharyngeal airway and observation
Rapid fluid bolus to thin secretions and open the narrowed airways

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman is breathing rapidly after a heated argument and has tingling hands with carpal spasm. Her SpO2 is 99 percent and she has no medical history. What is the most appropriate care?
qs.a: Coach her breathing while assessing for other causes
qs.x: Rebreathing into a bag can cause hypoxia and is not recommended. Calm coaching while you assess for serious causes such as PE or a metabolic problem is the safest approach.
w: Have her breathe into a paper bag
Apply CPAP to slow her respiratory rate
Assist her breathing with a BVM at 20 per minute

qs.q: You are using a nonrebreather mask on an adult with severe hypoxia. Which step ensures that the device delivers the highest oxygen concentration?
qs.a: Fill the reservoir bag before placing the mask
qs.x: The reservoir must be prefilled and the flow kept high enough, usually 10 to 15 L/min, so the bag does not collapse when the patient inhales. Only then does the mask deliver high oxygen concentrations.
w: Set the flow rate to 4 L/min
Remove the one-way valves from the mask
Let the reservoir bag collapse fully with each breath

qs.q: An adult ventilated through a supraglottic airway suddenly desaturates. Which problems could explain this? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The device has moved out of position; Secretions are blocking the airway tube; The oxygen tubing has come off the bag
qs.x: Displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax and equipment failure are the main causes of deterioration in a patient with an advanced airway. A rate of 1 breath every 6 seconds and a properly inflated cuff are correct practice.
opts: The device has moved out of position
Secretions are blocking the airway tube
The oxygen tubing has come off the bag
Ventilations are given once every 6 seconds
The cuff is inflated to the recommended volume
ok: The device has moved out of position
Secretions are blocking the airway tube
The oxygen tubing has come off the bag

qs.q: Which findings indicate that BVM ventilation is effective? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Visible chest rise with each breath; Rising SpO2 and improving skin color; Heart rate returning toward normal
qs.x: Chest rise, better oxygenation and improving heart rate show that ventilations are reaching the lungs. Abdominal distension means air is entering the stomach, and a flat capnography line means no gas exchange is detected.
opts: Visible chest rise with each breath
Rising SpO2 and improving skin color
Heart rate returning toward normal
Increasing abdominal distension
A flat line on waveform capnography
ok: Visible chest rise with each breath
Rising SpO2 and improving skin color
Heart rate returning toward normal

qs.q: Which are appropriate uses of waveform capnography for an AEMT? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Confirming placement of a supraglottic airway; Monitoring the quality of CPR; Detecting hypoventilation after an overdose
qs.x: Capnography measures exhaled carbon dioxide, so it confirms ventilation through a device, reflects blood flow during CPR and detects hypoventilation. Pulse oximetry measures saturation and a 12-lead ECG shows ST changes.
opts: Confirming placement of a supraglottic airway
Monitoring the quality of CPR
Detecting hypoventilation after an overdose
Measuring the oxygen saturation of hemoglobin
Identifying ST elevation in a patient with chest pain
ok: Confirming placement of a supraglottic airway
Monitoring the quality of CPR
Detecting hypoventilation after an overdose

qs.q: Which features of a young child's airway differ from an adult's? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The tongue is larger relative to the mouth; The large back of the head flexes the neck when supine; The narrow airway is more easily blocked by swelling
qs.x: A relatively large tongue, a large occiput and a narrow airway make children prone to obstruction. Their tracheas are softer and more easily kinked, and their necks are short.
opts: The tongue is larger relative to the mouth
The large back of the head flexes the neck when supine
The narrow airway is more easily blocked by swelling
The neck is longer
The trachea is more rigid
ok: The tongue is larger relative to the mouth
The large back of the head flexes the neck when supine
The narrow airway is more easily blocked by swelling

qs.q: Which patients with respiratory distress should not receive CPAP? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A patient who cannot follow commands; A patient with a suspected pneumothorax; A patient who is actively vomiting
qs.x: CPAP needs a patient who is alert, can protect the airway and has no pneumothorax. Alert patients with pulmonary edema or COPD and adequate blood pressure are typical candidates.
opts: A patient who cannot follow commands
A patient with a suspected pneumothorax
A patient who is actively vomiting
An alert patient with pulmonary edema and a normal BP
An alert patient with a COPD exacerbation
ok: A patient who cannot follow commands
A patient with a suspected pneumothorax
A patient who is actively vomiting

qs.q: Which are early signs of hypoxia in an adult? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Restlessness or anxiety; Tachycardia; Increased respiratory rate
qs.x: Early hypoxia causes restlessness, tachycardia and tachypnea as the body compensates. Bradycardia, cyanosis and unresponsiveness are late, ominous signs.
opts: Restlessness or anxiety
Tachycardia
Increased respiratory rate
Bradycardia
Central cyanosis with unresponsiveness
ok: Restlessness or anxiety
Tachycardia
Increased respiratory rate

qs.q: Which steps are part of the initial care of a newborn who is not crying after birth? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Dry, warm and stimulate the baby; Position the airway and clear secretions if needed; Begin ventilation if apneic or the heart rate is below 100
qs.x: Initial newborn steps are warming, drying, stimulating and positioning, with suction only for obstruction. Ventilation is started for apnea or a heart rate under 100, and compressions are reserved for a heart rate under 60 despite effective ventilation.
opts: Dry, warm and stimulate the baby
Position the airway and clear secretions if needed
Begin ventilation if apneic or the heart rate is below 100
Deep suction every newborn routinely
Start compressions for a heart rate of 90
ok: Dry, warm and stimulate the baby
Position the airway and clear secretions if needed
