w: The needle wobbles when gently touched
Swelling develops in the calf as you flush
The child's BP drops slightly during the flush

qs.q: An 82-year-old with heart failure who takes a diuretic has had vomiting and diarrhea for 3 days. She is dizzy when sitting up, with a pulse of 112 and a BP of 96/60. How should you give IV fluids?
qs.a: Small boluses with frequent lung checks
qs.x: Older adults with heart disease may need fluid for dehydration but are prone to pulmonary edema. Small boluses with reassessment of lung sounds and breathing balance these risks.
w: A rapid 2-liter bolus through two large-bore lines
No fluids at all
By mouth only, regardless of her vomiting

qs.q: A woman who is 32 weeks pregnant has sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Placenta previa
qs.x: Painless bright red bleeding in late pregnancy is typical of placenta previa, a placenta lying over the cervix. Do not examine inside the vagina; treat for shock and transport.
w: Placental abruption
Ectopic pregnancy
Normal bloody show of early labor

qs.q: During labor, you see the umbilical cord protruding from the vagina ahead of the baby. What should you do?
qs.a: Lift the presenting part off the cord
qs.x: The presenting part compresses a prolapsed cord and cuts off fetal oxygen. A gloved hand lifts the presenting part off the cord, the mother is positioned with hips elevated, and transport is rapid.
w: Push the cord back into the vagina
Pull gently on the cord to speed delivery
Clamp and cut the cord immediately

qs.q: During a breech delivery, the body delivers but the head does not after 3 minutes. What should you do?
qs.a: Make an airway with a V of your fingers
qs.x: Placing gloved fingers in a V on either side of the baby's nose holds the vaginal wall off the face so the baby can breathe. Keep the airway open and transport rapidly.
w: Pull on the legs
Push the baby back into the birth canal
Wait for several more contractions without intervening

qs.q: After the head delivers, the baby's shoulders become stuck. What is the first maneuver?
qs.a: Sharply flex the mother's thighs
qs.x: Shoulder dystocia is managed first by flexing the mother's thighs sharply toward her abdomen, the McRoberts maneuver, which widens the pelvic outlet. Pulling on the head or pushing on the fundus can injure the baby.
w: Pull the head firmly downward
Press hard on the top of the uterus
Tell the mother to stop pushing and wait

qs.q: A term newborn is not breathing after being warmed, dried and stimulated. What should you do next?
qs.a: Begin positive-pressure ventilation
qs.x: A newborn who stays apneic after initial steps needs positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute, at 40 to 60 breaths per minute. Term newborns start with room air.
w: Begin chest compressions
Give blow-by oxygen and observe
Continue stimulating for 2 more minutes

qs.q: You are giving PPV to a newborn whose heart rate is 80, but the chest is not rising. What should you do?
qs.a: Reposition the head and reseal the mask
qs.x: Ineffective ventilation is corrected first by checking mask seal and head position, then suctioning, opening the mouth and increasing pressure. Chest rise is the key sign that ventilation is working.
w: Begin chest compressions at a 3-to-1 ratio
Increase the ventilation rate to 80 per minute
Give blow-by oxygen

qs.q: A baby is born at about 30 weeks. How should you prevent heat loss?
qs.a: Plastic wrap without drying the body
qs.x: Very preterm newborns lose heat rapidly. Placing the body in plastic wrap or a bag without drying it, plus a hat and a warm environment, reduces heat loss.
w: Dry the baby and leave it uncovered on the mother's abdomen
Turn down the heat in the ambulance
Give a warm water bath

qs.q: At 1 minute, a newborn has a pink body with blue hands and feet, a heart rate of 110, grimaces when stimulated, some flexion of the arms and legs and a weak cry. What is the APGAR score?
qs.x: Appearance 1, pulse 2, grimace 1, activity 1 and respiration 1 total 6.

qs.q: A woman about 10 weeks pregnant has heavy vaginal bleeding and cramping. Her pulse is 118. What is the most appropriate care?
qs.a: Treat for shock and bring any passed tissue
qs.x: Early pregnancy loss can cause heavy bleeding and shock. Treat for shock, bring passed tissue to the hospital and provide emotional support.
w: Pack the vagina with gauze to stop the bleeding
Have her walk to the ambulance
Wait on scene until the bleeding stops

qs.q: After delivering a healthy baby, the placenta has not delivered after 30 minutes. What should you do?
qs.a: Transport without pulling on the cord
qs.x: Pulling on the cord can tear it or invert the uterus. The mother is transported with monitoring for bleeding.
w: Pull firmly on the cord
Reach inside the uterus to remove the placenta
Cut the cord at the vagina and push it back in

qs.q: A 67-year-old found outdoors in winter is confused and no longer shivering, with a core temperature of 29 C (84 F) and a pulse of 42. Why should you move him gently and keep him horizontal?
qs.a: Rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation
qs.x: A severely cold heart is irritable, and jarring movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Remove wet clothing, insulate him and keep him horizontal during transport.
w: Gentle handling allows his muscles to resume shivering
Moving him upright helps blood return to the brain faster
Rough handling causes the skin to rewarm too quickly

qs.q: A hiker has frozen, waxy toes and must walk out through deep snow for several more hours before reaching transport. What should you do about the toes?
qs.a: Leave them frozen until refreezing can be prevented
qs.x: Thawing followed by refreezing causes much worse tissue damage than leaving the part frozen until definitive rewarming. Protect the area, pad it and never rub frostbitten tissue.
w: Rub them vigorously with snow to restore circulation
Rewarm them beside the campfire before the hike out
Thaw them in warm water, then continue the walk out

qs.q: Lightning strikes a group of hikers. Several are down. Which patients should receive care first?
qs.a: Those who are pulseless and apneic
qs.x: Unlike standard triage, lightning patients in cardiac or respiratory arrest are treated first because they often recover with prompt CPR and ventilation. Conscious patients usually survive, so this is called reverse triage.
w: Those who are awake and talking with burns
Those with confusion and ringing in the ears
Those who are walking with minor injuries

qs.q: A 35-year-old finished a marathon after drinking water at every station. She is confused with a headache and vomiting, a normal temperature and a glucose of 94 mg/dL. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Exercise-associated hyponatremia
qs.x: Drinking excess water during endurance events dilutes blood sodium, causing headache, confusion, vomiting and seizures. Giving large volumes of fluid can make it worse, so she needs prompt hospital evaluation.
w: Heat stroke from exertion
Hypoglycemia from glycogen depletion
Dehydration from sweat loss

qs.q: A scuba diver made a rapid ascent and within 2 minutes of surfacing developed chest pain and weakness of one arm. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Arterial gas embolism
qs.x: Gas forced into the arterial circulation during rapid ascent causes stroke-like and cardiac symptoms within minutes of surfacing. Give high-concentration oxygen, keep the patient supine and transport toward recompression.
w: Nitrogen narcosis from deep diving
Hypothermia from cold water
Delayed decompression sickness from long bottom time

qs.q: A 40-year-old was bitten on the ankle by a rattlesnake 10 minutes ago. Swelling is spreading. What is appropriate care?
qs.a: Immobilize the leg and mark the swelling edge
qs.x: Pit viper bites are managed by keeping the patient calm, immobilizing the limb, removing rings or tight items and marking the advancing swelling. Tourniquets, ice, cutting and suction cause harm.
w: Apply a tight tourniquet above the bite to trap the venom
Pack the bite in ice
Make a small incision and suction out the venom

qs.q: A 31-year-old with suspected hyperactive delirium, sometimes called excited delirium, was hot, sweaty and fighting restraints. He suddenly becomes quiet and still. What should you do?
qs.a: Check breathing and pulse at once
qs.x: Sudden quiet in a severely agitated, hyperthermic patient may mean respiratory or cardiac arrest. Check immediately and start resuscitation if needed.
w: Let him rest since he has finally calmed down
Tighten the restraints before he becomes agitated again
Turn him prone so he cannot strike the crew

qs.q: How should a combative patient be positioned once physical restraint is required?
qs.a: Supine or on the side, continuously monitored
qs.x: Prone and hobble positions, and any weight on the back, can cause positional asphyxia and death. Restrained patients are placed supine or on their side with continuous monitoring of breathing and mental status.
w: Prone with wrists and ankles tied together behind him
Prone with a long backboard strapped over his back
Seated with a blanket held over his face to calm him

qs.q: You are dispatched to a man who is waving a knife and threatening his neighbors. What should you do?
qs.a: Stage until law enforcement secures the scene
qs.x: Responder safety comes first. EMS stages at a safe distance and enters only after police have secured the scene, then provides care.
w: Approach calmly and try to talk him into putting it down
Enter with your partner and restrain him together
Cancel the call because it is a law enforcement matter

qs.q: A 74-year-old with COPD is newly combative and confused. Her SpO2 is 82 percent and her glucose is 110 mg/dL. What is the most likely cause of the behavior?
qs.a: Hypoxia from her lung disease
qs.x: Hypoxia commonly causes confusion, restlessness and combativeness. Medical causes of behavior change are identified and treated before assuming a psychiatric cause.
w: A new psychiatric illness
Alcohol intoxication
Normal age-related dementia

qs.q: A 40-year-old says he feels hopeless and has been giving away his belongings. What is the best way to assess suicide risk?
qs.a: Ask directly whether he is thinking of suicide
qs.x: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts and plans does not increase risk and is the best way to identify patients who need emergency evaluation. Giving away belongings is a warning sign.
w: Avoid the topic because asking may plant the idea
Change the subject to something more positive
Reassure him that things will get better soon

qs.q: A 23-year-old has right lower abdominal pain that began near the umbilicus, with fever, nausea and pain when the ambulance hits bumps. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Appendicitis
qs.x: Appendicitis classically begins with pain around the umbilicus that moves to the right lower quadrant, often with fever, nausea and pain on movement. Transport in a position of comfort and give nothing by mouth.
w: Kidney stone
Gastroenteritis
Gallbladder disease

qs.q: Which findings are consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Rapid, deep respirations; Fruity breath odor; Excessive thirst and urination
qs.x: DKA develops over hours to days with Kussmaul breathing, a ketone odor and polyuria from high glucose. Cool, clammy skin and sudden onset point to hypoglycemia.
opts: Rapid, deep respirations
Fruity breath odor
Excessive thirst and urination
Cool, clammy, sweaty skin
Onset over a few minutes
ok: Rapid, deep respirations
Fruity breath odor
Excessive thirst and urination

qs.q: Which conditions can mimic an acute stroke? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypoglycemia; Weakness after a seizure; Complex migraine
qs.x: Hypoglycemia, postictal weakness and complex migraine can all produce focal deficits. Atrial fibrillation is a cause of stroke and elevated BP often accompanies stroke, so neither explains away the deficits.
opts: Hypoglycemia
Weakness after a seizure
Complex migraine
Atrial fibrillation
A BP of 170/90
ok: Hypoglycemia
Weakness after a seizure
Complex migraine

qs.q: A 2-year-old with vomiting received a 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus. He is still listless with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a heart rate of 170, and his lungs are clear. What should you do next?
qs.a: Repeat the isotonic bolus and reassess perfusion
qs.x: Persistent signs of poor perfusion after one bolus in a child without signs of fluid overload call for another isotonic bolus with reassessment after each one.
w: Stop fluids because one bolus is the limit for children
Switch to oral fluids now that one bolus is in
Give dextrose 50 percent for the poor perfusion

qs.q: A 38-year-old man has sudden severe left flank pain that radiates to his groin. He is restless and cannot find a comfortable position, and he has blood in his urine. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Kidney stone
qs.x: Kidney stones cause colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, restlessness and blood in the urine. In an older patient, an abdominal aortic aneurysm must also be considered.
w: Appendicitis
Pancreatitis
Small bowel obstruction

qs.q: Which findings are consistent with opioid toxicity? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Pinpoint pupils; Slow, shallow breathing; Decreased level of consciousness
qs.x: The opioid toxidrome is pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and depressed consciousness. Agitation with sweating and dilated pupils suggests a stimulant.
opts: Pinpoint pupils
Slow, shallow breathing
Decreased level of consciousness
Hot, sweaty skin with agitation
Widely dilated pupils
ok: Pinpoint pupils
Slow, shallow breathing
Decreased level of consciousness

qs.q: An 84-year-old has an infection. Which findings suggest sepsis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: New confusion; Respiratory rate of 26; A temperature below normal
qs.x: Older adults often do not mount a fever and may even be hypothermic, while new confusion and tachypnea are early signs of sepsis.
opts: New confusion
Respiratory rate of 26
A temperature below normal
A high fever is always present
Hives on the trunk
ok: New confusion
Respiratory rate of 26
A temperature below normal

qs.q: Which patients are at increased risk for hyperkalemia? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A dialysis patient who missed treatments; A man released after a prolonged crush; A patient with kidney failure and new muscle weakness
qs.x: Kidney failure and crush injuries raise serum potassium, which causes weakness, bradycardia and lethal dysrhythmias.
opts: A dialysis patient who missed treatments
A man released after a prolonged crush
A young adult hyperventilating from anxiety
A runner who has been sweating heavily
A patient with kidney failure and new muscle weakness
ok: A dialysis patient who missed treatments
A man released after a prolonged crush
A patient with kidney failure and new muscle weakness

qs.q: At which sites should IO placement be avoided? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A bone with a fracture; An area with signs of infection; A bone with a failed IO attempt earlier that day
qs.x: Fluid leaks out of a fractured or previously punctured bone, and placing a needle through infected tissue can seed the bone. Shock and cardiac arrest are indications for IO access.
opts: A bone with a fracture
An area with signs of infection
A bone with a failed IO attempt earlier that day
The proximal tibia of a hypotensive child
The humerus of an adult in cardiac arrest
ok: A bone with a fracture
An area with signs of infection
A bone with a failed IO attempt earlier that day

qs.q: A woman who is 36 weeks pregnant has vaginal bleeding. Which findings suggest placental abruption? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Constant abdominal pain; A rigid, tender uterus; Shock out of proportion to visible bleeding
qs.x: Abruption causes painful bleeding, a firm uterus and concealed hemorrhage behind the placenta. Painless bleeding with a soft uterus suggests placenta previa.
opts: Constant abdominal pain
A rigid, tender uterus
Shock out of proportion to visible bleeding
Painless bright red bleeding
A soft, nontender uterus
ok: Constant abdominal pain
A rigid, tender uterus
Shock out of proportion to visible bleeding

qs.q: Which are initial steps for a term newborn who is not vigorous at birth? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Warm the baby; Dry and stimulate; Position the airway
qs.x: NRP initial steps are to warm, dry, stimulate and position the airway, clearing secretions only if needed. Term newborns start with room air, and routine deep suctioning can cause bradycardia.
opts: Warm the baby
Dry and stimulate
Position the airway
Routine deep suctioning
Hold the baby upside down
Give 100 percent oxygen
ok: Warm the baby
Dry and stimulate
Position the airway

qs.q: Which findings are consistent with severe hypothermia? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Shivering has stopped; Bradycardia; Altered mental status
qs.x: As the core temperature falls, shivering stops, the pulse slows and mental status declines. Rapid breathing and hot skin point elsewhere.
opts: Shivering has stopped
Bradycardia
Altered mental status
Hot, dry skin
Rapid breathing with agitation
ok: Shivering has stopped
Bradycardia
Altered mental status

qs.q: Which findings are associated with hyperactive delirium with severe agitation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: High body temperature; Extreme strength with insensitivity to pain; Tachycardia
qs.x: These patients are hyperthermic, tachycardic, sweaty and violent with unusual strength. They are at high risk of sudden cardiac arrest, especially during struggle and restraint.
opts: High body temperature
Extreme strength with insensitivity to pain
Tachycardia
Bradycardia and hypothermia
Calm, cooperative behavior
ok: High body temperature
Extreme strength with insensitivity to pain
Tachycardia

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate during and after a generalized seizure? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Move objects away to protect the patient; Note how long the seizure lasts; Check the glucose once the seizure ends
qs.x: Protection from injury, timing the event and checking glucose are core seizure care. Restraint causes injury, and objects in the mouth can break teeth or obstruct the airway.
opts: Move objects away to protect the patient
Note how long the seizure lasts
Check the glucose once the seizure ends
Restrain the arms and legs
Place a bite block between the teeth
ok: Move objects away to protect the patient
Note how long the seizure lasts
Check the glucose once the seizure ends

qs.q: A farm worker collapsed after spraying a field. Which findings suggest organophosphate poisoning? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Drooling and heavy secretions; Pinpoint pupils; Wheezing
qs.x: Organophosphates cause cholinergic toxicity with excess secretions, bronchospasm and small pupils. Decontaminate the patient before care in the ambulance to protect the crew.
opts: Drooling and heavy secretions
Pinpoint pupils
Wheezing
Hot, dry, flushed skin
Dilated pupils
ok: Drooling and heavy secretions
Pinpoint pupils
Wheezing

qs.q: Which findings suggest carbon monoxide poisoning? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Headache and nausea; Several people in the home are ill; Symptoms improve after leaving the home
qs.x: Carbon monoxide causes headache, nausea and confusion in people sharing the same space, with relief after leaving it. Pulse oximetry often reads normal, and cherry red skin is a rare, late finding.
opts: Headache and nausea
Several people in the home are ill
Symptoms improve after leaving the home
A reliably low SpO2 reading
Cherry red skin in most patients
ok: Headache and nausea
Several people in the home are ill
Symptoms improve after leaving the home

qs.q: An adult has signs of septic shock. Which actions are appropriate within AEMT scope? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Give an isotonic fluid bolus; Reassess lung sounds after each bolus; Notify the hospital early of suspected sepsis
qs.x: Early fluids with frequent reassessment and hospital prealert are key in sepsis. Oxygen is given for hypoxia, and dextrose does not treat hypotension.
opts: Give an isotonic fluid bolus
Reassess lung sounds after each bolus
Notify the hospital early of suspected sepsis
Withhold oxygen to avoid hiding hypoxia
Give dextrose to raise the BP
ok: Give an isotonic fluid bolus
Reassess lung sounds after each bolus
Notify the hospital early of suspected sepsis

qs.q: Which findings in an older adult with dehydration suggest the need for IV fluids rather than oral rehydration? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Altered mental status; Persistent vomiting; Hypotension
qs.x: Patients who are confused, cannot keep fluids down or are hypotensive need IV or IO fluids. Mild thirst alone can usually be managed orally.
opts: Altered mental status
Persistent vomiting
Hypotension
Mild thirst
Dry lips after a long walk
ok: Altered mental status
Persistent vomiting
Hypotension

qs.q: You are assessing a 48-year-old man before intubation. Using the 3-3-2 approach, you find only one fingerbreadth between the hyoid bone and the top of the thyroid cartilage. What does this suggest?
qs.a: A high, anterior larynx that is hard to visualize
qs.x: Fewer than two fingerbreadths from hyoid to thyroid cartilage means the larynx sits high and anterior, so the glottis is harder to bring into the line of sight.
w: Mouth opening too narrow to insert a laryngoscope blade
Probable difficulty obtaining a bag-valve-mask seal
Restricted neck extension from cervical arthritis

qs.q: A 55-year-old woman sitting upright opens her mouth and protrudes her tongue. You can see only her hard palate; the soft palate and uvula are hidden. What does this predict?
qs.a: Difficult laryngoscopy
qs.x: Seeing only the hard palate (Mallampati class IV) predicts a poor laryngoscopic view, so a bougie, video laryngoscope, supraglottic airway and surgical backup should be ready.
w: An easy view with a curved blade
A high risk of aspiration during bag-valve-mask ventilation
A normal airway needing no special preparation

qs.q: A 62-year-old alert man needs rapid sequence intubation for worsening pneumonia. SpO2 is 95 percent on a nonrebreather mask. Which preoxygenation approach best fills his lungs with oxygen before induction?
qs.a: At least 3 minutes of high-flow oxygen with tidal breathing
qs.x: Several minutes of tidal breathing on high-flow oxygen washes nitrogen out of the lungs, creating an oxygen reservoir that lengthens safe apnea time.
w: One minute of nasal cannula oxygen at 4 L/min
Rapid bag-valve-mask ventilation at 30 breaths/min for 1 minute
Room air until induction so the oximeter shows his true baseline

qs.q: A 160-kg woman needs to be intubated. How should she be positioned to improve both preoxygenation and the laryngoscopic view?
qs.a: Ramped, ear canal level with the sternal notch
qs.x: Ramping an obese patient so the external ear canal lines up with the sternal notch improves the glottic view and reduces the abdominal pressure that speeds desaturation.
w: Flat supine with a rolled towel under her shoulders
Head-down tilt to improve venous return to the heart
Left lateral recumbent with the neck flexed forward

qs.q: During your first intubation attempt on a 50-year-old man, his SpO2 falls from 99 to 89 percent and you still cannot see the vocal cords. What should you do?
qs.a: Stop and reoxygenate with a bag-valve mask
qs.x: Falling saturation means the attempt should end; reoxygenate with a bag-valve mask and change something (position, device or operator) before the next attempt.
w: Keep going until the cords are seen, since the oximeter reading lags
Pass the tube blindly and check it with capnography
Have your partner apply cricoid pressure and continue looking

qs.q: A 67-year-old septic patient needs intubation for a worsening mental status. BP is 74/40 and HR is 128. What should be addressed before induction drugs are given?
qs.a: Hypotension, with fluids or vasopressors per protocol
qs.x: Induction drugs and positive pressure ventilation commonly drop blood pressure further, so resuscitating the hypotension first reduces the risk of peri-intubation cardiac arrest.
w: Hypothermia, by warming the patient compartment first
Hyperventilation, by bagging at a slower rate beforehand
Agitation, by applying soft restraints to both arms and legs

qs.q: A 24-year-old in severe diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply at 34/min with an ETCO2 of 16 mmHg. After he is intubated, how should his ventilation be managed?
qs.a: Match his high pre-intubation minute ventilation
qs.x: His low CO2 is compensation for a severe metabolic acidosis; ventilating at a normal rate lets CO2 rise, the pH falls sharply and cardiac arrest can follow.
w: Ventilate at 10 breaths/min to prevent barotrauma
Let the ETCO2 rise to 40 mmHg so it is normal
Ventilate only when the SpO2 falls below 90 percent

qs.q: On laryngoscopy of a 44-year-old man you can see the epiglottis but none of the glottic opening. Which device is most helpful for passing the tube?
qs.a: A tracheal tube introducer (bougie)
qs.x: With an epiglottis-only view a bougie can be steered under the epiglottis; clicks against the tracheal rings or hold-up in a small airway confirm placement before the tube is passed over it.
w: A larger endotracheal tube
An oropharyngeal airway placed first
A nasopharyngeal airway placed first

qs.q: During laryngoscopy you can see only the posterior part of the vocal cords. Which maneuver may improve your view?
qs.a: Backward, upward and rightward pressure on the thyroid cartilage
qs.x: External laryngeal manipulation, such as backward, upward and rightward pressure on the thyroid cartilage, moves the larynx into view; cricoid pressure can actually worsen the view.
w: Firm pressure on the cricoid cartilage throughout the attempt
Turning the patient's head toward the left shoulder
Pressing downward on the forehead while lifting the patient's chin

qs.q: After intubating an adult you check the endotracheal tube cuff with a manometer. Which cuff pressure range is generally recommended?
qs.a: 20 to 30 cm H2O
qs.x: A cuff pressure of about 20 to 30 cm H2O seals the airway while limiting injury to the tracheal lining; cuffs inflated by feel are often far too tight.
w: 5 to 10 cm H2O
40 to 50 cm H2O
60 to 80 cm H2O

qs.q: After intubating a 5-foot-2-inch woman, you hear breath sounds only on the right. The tube is at 27 cm at the teeth and the ETCO2 waveform is normal. What should you do?
qs.a: Deflate the cuff and pull back slightly while listening
qs.x: A normal waveform with right-only breath sounds and a deep tube suggests a right mainstem intubation; withdrawing the tube a short distance usually restores left-sided ventilation.
w: Remove the tube completely and reintubate with a smaller size
Perform needle decompression of the left side of the chest
Advance the tube 2 cm further and then reassess breath sounds

qs.q: A ventilated 30-year-old after a fall from height has rising airway pressures, absent breath sounds on the left, BP 70/40 and distended neck veins. What should you do?
qs.a: Perform needle decompression on the left
qs.x: Positive pressure ventilation can rapidly turn a pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax; hypotension with distended neck veins and absent breath sounds needs immediate decompression.
w: Increase the PEEP to reinflate the left lung
Withdraw the tube 2 cm and recheck
Increase the tidal volume to improve oxygenation

qs.q: The transport ventilator on an intubated patient sounds a low-pressure alarm and the exhaled tidal volumes have dropped sharply. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: A leak or disconnection in the circuit
qs.x: Low pressure with loss of returned volume points to a leak, such as a disconnected circuit, a deflated cuff or a tube pulled above the cords; obstruction, bronchospasm and pneumothorax raise pressures.
w: A mucus plug in the tube
Worsening bronchospasm
A tension pneumothorax

qs.q: You hear air escaping from the mouth of an intubated patient with each breath, and the pilot balloon is flat. Tube depth is unchanged and the ETCO2 waveform persists but is smaller. What is the first step?
qs.a: Reinflate the cuff and see if it holds
qs.x: A deflated cuff with the tube still in place is first managed by reinflating it; if the cuff will not hold air, the tube needs to be exchanged.
w: Remove the tube immediately and insert a supraglottic airway instead
Increase the tidal volume to make up for the lost volume
Advance the tube 3 cm so the cuff sits deeper in the trachea

qs.q: An intubated, sedated 52-year-old has a normal square ETCO2 waveform, but over 20 minutes his ETCO2 has risen from 38 to 56 mmHg. SpO2 is 97 percent and BP is stable. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
qs.a: Increase minute ventilation
qs.x: A rising ETCO2 with a normal waveform means CO2 is not being removed fast enough; increasing the rate or tidal volume increases CO2 elimination.
w: Decrease the respiratory rate
Lower the oxygen concentration
Increase the PEEP

qs.q: The capnography waveform of a patient being bagged no longer returns to zero between breaths; the baseline now sits at 8 mmHg. What does this indicate?
qs.a: Rebreathing of exhaled CO2
qs.x: An elevated baseline means the inhaled gas contains CO2, as with a faulty exhalation valve, inadequate fresh gas flow or a contaminated sensor, so the equipment should be checked.
w: Esophageal intubation
Bronchospasm
Cardiac arrest

qs.q: You intubate a 40-year-old with a pulse who had been drinking soda shortly before he became unresponsive. Capnography shows small waveforms for 4 breaths that steadily fade to zero. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: The tube is in the esophagus
qs.x: CO2 from stomach contents can produce a few waveforms after an esophageal intubation, but they fade within several breaths; a sustained waveform is required to confirm tracheal placement.
w: The tube is in the right mainstem bronchus
He has severe bronchospasm
His cardiac output has suddenly improved

qs.q: An intubated patient's capnogram shows a regular plateau with a small notch dipping into it on each breath. What does this notch most likely mean?
qs.a: The patient is starting to breathe on his own
qs.x: A cleft in the plateau appears when the patient makes spontaneous respiratory efforts, often as paralysis or sedation wears off, and may signal the need for more sedation.
w: The tube has migrated into the esophagus
CO2 is being rebreathed from the circuit
The patient has gone into cardiac arrest

qs.q: A ventilated 58-year-old who had hip surgery 3 days ago suddenly has his ETCO2 drop from 36 to 18 mmHg with an unchanged waveform shape. SpO2 falls to 85 percent and BP to 78/50. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: A large pulmonary embolism
qs.x: An abrupt ETCO2 drop with a preserved waveform plus hypotension and hypoxia suggests a sudden loss of pulmonary blood flow, such as a massive PE; extubation gives a flat line and a kink raises pressures.
w: Accidental extubation
Hyperventilation by the ventilator
A kinked endotracheal tube

qs.q: During CPR on an intubated 63-year-old, ETCO2 has been 14 mmHg. It suddenly jumps to 42 mmHg with no change in ventilation. What does this most likely indicate?
qs.a: Return of spontaneous circulation
qs.x: An abrupt, sustained rise in ETCO2 during CPR is an early sign of ROSC because restored blood flow delivers more CO2 to the lungs; confirm with a pulse check.
w: Displacement of the tube into the esophagus
Fatigue of the person doing compressions
Hypoventilation by the person bagging

qs.q: During CPR you intubate an adult. Capnography shows a consistent waveform with every breath and a value of 12 mmHg. How should you interpret this?
qs.a: Tracheal placement with low blood flow
qs.x: A persistent waveform confirms the tube is in the trachea even during arrest; the low number reflects limited pulmonary blood flow, not misplacement.
w: The tube is in the esophagus and must be removed now
The tube has entered the right mainstem bronchus
The capnography sensor is faulty and should be replaced

qs.q: A 66-year-old on a transport ventilator for acute pulmonary edema has an SpO2 of 86 percent on 100 percent oxygen with PEEP of 5 cm H2O. BP is 148/90 and tube position is confirmed. Which change is most likely to improve oxygenation?
qs.a: Increase the PEEP
qs.x: PEEP holds fluid-filled alveoli open and improves oxygenation; with an adequate blood pressure, raising PEEP is the usual next step when oxygen is already at 100 percent.
w: Reduce the PEEP to zero
Increase the respiratory rate
Lower the tidal volume to 4 mL/kg

qs.q: An intubated 26-year-old asthmatic on a ventilator has high peak pressures, and the expiratory flow does not return to zero before the next breath starts. Which change best reduces air trapping?
qs.a: Slow the rate to allow longer exhalation
qs.x: In severe asthma the lungs need a long time to empty; a slower rate lengthens exhalation, reducing trapped air (auto-PEEP), even if CO2 rises somewhat.
w: Raise the respiratory rate to clear CO2 faster
Increase the PEEP to 15 cm H2O
Increase the tidal volume

qs.q: During a critical care transfer of a patient with ARDS, which ventilator goal reflects a lung-protective strategy?
qs.a: Plateau pressure at or below 30 cm H2O
qs.x: Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS uses small tidal volumes and limits plateau pressure to about 30 cm H2O or less to reduce further lung injury.
w: Tidal volumes of 12 mL/kg to recruit alveoli
PEEP of zero to avoid barotrauma
A PaO2 above 300 mmHg

qs.q: A 45-year-old admitted 2 days ago with severe pancreatitis is being transferred. He has worsening hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen, bilateral infiltrates on chest x-ray, flat neck veins and no cardiac history. What condition is most likely?
qs.a: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
qs.x: ARDS is an inflammatory, noncardiogenic lung injury triggered by conditions such as sepsis, pancreatitis or major trauma, causing refractory hypoxia with bilateral infiltrates.
w: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Acute asthma exacerbation
Spontaneous pneumothorax

qs.q: How does CPAP improve oxygenation in a patient with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
qs.a: It keeps alveoli open and reduces preload
qs.x: CPAP splints alveoli open to improve gas exchange and raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return (preload) to the failing heart.
w: It increases heart rate and contractility
It removes fluid from the alveoli by suction
It raises systemic vascular resistance

qs.q: Compared with CPAP, what does BiPAP add for a patient with a COPD exacerbation and CO2 retention?
qs.a: Higher pressure during inspiration
qs.x: BiPAP delivers a higher inspiratory pressure above the expiratory pressure, increasing tidal volume and helping clear CO2, whereas CPAP holds one constant pressure.
w: A guaranteed higher delivered oxygen concentration
Built-in protection of the airway from aspiration
A lower risk of hypotension because chest pressure is lower

qs.q: A 71-year-old with COPD has been on CPAP for 15 minutes. He is now hard to arouse, respirations are shallow at 8/min and ETCO2 has climbed to 74 mmHg. What should you do?
qs.a: Remove CPAP and ventilate with a bag-valve mask
qs.x: A falling mental status with rising CO2 means noninvasive ventilation is failing; he needs assisted ventilation and likely an advanced airway.
w: Increase the CPAP pressure
Change to a nonrebreather mask
Continue CPAP and recheck in 10 minutes

qs.q: You must perform a surgical cricothyrotomy on a 40-year-old. Where is the incision through the membrane made?
qs.a: Between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages
qs.x: The cricothyroid membrane lies between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid ring below; it is superficial and relatively avascular.
w: Between the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage
Just above the suprasternal notch
Between the first and second tracheal rings

qs.q: A 6-year-old with an obstructed upper airway is being oxygenated through a needle cricothyrotomy. Which problem limits how long this technique can be relied on?
qs.a: Carbon dioxide builds up
qs.x: A needle cricothyrotomy can oxygenate but allows poor exhalation, so CO2 accumulates; it is only a temporary bridge to a definitive airway.
w: Oxygen cannot reach the alveoli
The catheter needs constant suctioning
It cannot deliver high-concentration oxygen

qs.q: A 68-year-old who had a total laryngectomy is apneic. A stoma is visible at the base of his neck. How should you ventilate him?
qs.a: Through the stoma with a small mask
qs.x: After a total laryngectomy the trachea no longer connects to the mouth or nose, so ventilation must be delivered through the stoma, often with an infant or pediatric mask.
w: With a standard adult mask sealed over the mouth and nose
Through the mouth after placing an oropharyngeal airway
With a nasal cannula running at 15 L/min

qs.q: A 3-year-old's tracheostomy tube came out at home and the parents could not replace it. The child is cyanotic. You have a same-size tube and one a half size smaller. What should you do first?
qs.a: Insert a replacement tube into the stoma
qs.x: Reinserting a tube into the existing stoma, trying the smaller size if needed, is the fastest way to restore the airway; if that fails, ventilate through the stoma or by mouth with the stoma covered.
w: Ventilate with a mask over the mouth and nose only
Perform a needle cricothyrotomy
Intubate orally with a tube two sizes larger

qs.q: A 50-year-old choked on steak and became unresponsive. You cannot ventilate him despite several cycles of CPR. Which advanced technique should you use?
qs.a: Laryngoscopy and Magill forceps
qs.x: Paramedics can look directly into the upper airway with a laryngoscope and remove a visible obstruction with Magill forceps; blind sweeps can push the object deeper.
w: Repeated blind finger sweeps of the posterior pharynx
Abdominal thrusts with the patient supine
Insert a supraglottic airway and ventilate through it

qs.q: You are opening the airway of an unresponsive 4-month-old lying supine on the stretcher. His head flexes forward. What should you do?
qs.a: Place a folded towel under the shoulders
qs.x: An infant's large occiput flexes the neck when supine; padding under the shoulders brings the airway into a neutral position.
w: Hyperextend the neck as for an adult
Place a pillow under the head
Turn the head to one side

qs.q: Using the age-based formula for cuffed tubes, which endotracheal tube size is appropriate for a 6-year-old?
qs.a: 5.0 mm cuffed
qs.x: For cuffed tubes the size is about age divided by 4 plus 3.5, so a 6-year-old needs roughly 5.0 mm; a half size larger and smaller should be ready.
w: 6.5 mm cuffed
4.0 mm cuffed
7.0 mm cuffed

qs.q: During intubation of a 2-year-old, the heart rate falls from 140 to 70/min and the SpO2 to 80 percent. What should you do?
qs.a: Stop and ventilate with oxygen by bag-valve mask
qs.x: Bradycardia during pediatric intubation is usually caused by hypoxia; stopping to oxygenate usually reverses it.
w: Give atropine and continue the attempt
Begin chest compressions immediately
Pass the tube as quickly as possible

qs.q: An unvaccinated 5-year-old is sitting upright and drooling, with a muffled voice, a temperature of 39.8 C (103.6 F) and soft inspiratory stridor. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Keep him calm in a position of comfort
qs.x: These signs suggest epiglottitis; agitating the child or instrumenting the throat can cause complete obstruction, so keep him calm, give oxygen as tolerated and transport with airway equipment ready.
w: Examine the throat with a tongue blade to confirm the cause
Place him supine and insert an oropharyngeal airway
Attempt intubation now before he gets worse

qs.q: A 15-year-old with asthma has been wheezing for hours. Now he is drowsy, his chest is nearly silent and SpO2 is 86 percent. What does the silent chest indicate?
qs.a: Minimal air movement and impending arrest
qs.x: A silent chest in a tiring asthmatic means too little air is moving to produce a wheeze; with drowsiness it signals impending respiratory arrest and the need for assisted ventilation.
w: The bronchospasm is resolving and airflow is improving
Pneumonia has developed and replaced the wheezing
Hyperventilation from anxiety that will settle with coaching

qs.q: A 34-year-old rescued from a house fire has singed nasal hair, soot in his sputum and a hoarse voice that is getting worse. SpO2 is 96 percent. What is the key airway concern?
qs.a: Swelling that may close the airway
qs.x: Progressive hoarseness after inhalation injury signals upper airway edema; early definitive airway management may be needed before swelling makes intubation impossible.
w: Carbon monoxide causing a falsely low SpO2 reading
Bronchospasm that should be managed with CPAP
Aspiration of gastric contents during transport

qs.q: What is an advantage of a second-generation supraglottic airway with a gastric channel?
qs.a: It allows the stomach to be decompressed
qs.x: The gastric channel lets air and fluid vent from the stomach or a gastric tube be passed, reducing the risk of regurgitation, although it does not fully protect against aspiration.
w: It completely protects the lungs from aspiration
It can be inserted in patients with an intact gag reflex
It provides confirmation that the tube is in the trachea

qs.q: A 58-year-old has rapidly progressing tongue and lip swelling with a muffled voice, and you decide he needs an advanced airway. How should you prepare?
qs.a: Be ready for a surgical airway if intubation fails
qs.x: With upper airway swelling, intubation can fail and supraglottic devices may not seal, so a double setup with the neck prepared for cricothyrotomy is essential.
w: Plan blind nasal intubation as the only option
Use a supraglottic airway as the primary device
Wait until he becomes apneic before intervening

qs.q: A septic 70-year-old has an ABG of pH 7.24, PaCO2 26 mmHg and HCO3 11 mEq/L. How should it be interpreted?
qs.a: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
qs.x: A low pH with a low bicarbonate is a metabolic acidosis; the low PaCO2 reflects the lungs blowing off CO2 to compensate.
w: Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic alkalosis together

qs.q: A 22-year-old with severe anxiety, tingling fingers and carpopedal spasm has an ABG of pH 7.53, PaCO2 27 mmHg and HCO3 24 mEq/L. What is the acid-base disorder?
qs.a: Acute respiratory alkalosis
qs.x: A high pH with a low PaCO2 and a normal bicarbonate is an acute respiratory alkalosis; serious causes such as pulmonary embolism should still be considered before blaming anxiety.
w: Metabolic acidosis
Compensated metabolic alkalosis
Acute respiratory acidosis

qs.q: A 40-year-old has vomited repeatedly for 4 days. His ABG shows pH 7.51, PaCO2 47 mmHg and HCO3 35 mEq/L. Which disorder is present?
qs.a: Metabolic alkalosis
qs.x: Losing stomach acid raises bicarbonate; a high pH and high HCO3 identify metabolic alkalosis, and the slightly raised PaCO2 is compensatory hypoventilation.
w: Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis

qs.q: A 74-year-old with long-standing COPD who is at his baseline has an ABG of pH 7.36, PaCO2 62 mmHg and HCO3 34 mEq/L. How should it be interpreted?
qs.a: Compensated chronic respiratory acidosis
qs.x: A near-normal pH with high PaCO2 and high bicarbonate shows the kidneys have retained bicarbonate over time to offset chronic CO2 retention.
w: Acute respiratory acidosis requiring immediate intubation
Primary metabolic alkalosis
A completely normal blood gas

qs.q: You are assessing a 52-year-old for intubation. Which findings predict a difficult laryngoscopy? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Mouth opening of less than two fingerbreadths; A rigid cervical collar limiting neck extension; An expanding hematoma in the neck
qs.x: Limited mouth opening, restricted neck movement and obstruction such as a hematoma all make laryngoscopy harder; missing teeth make bag-mask sealing harder but usually make laryngoscopy easier.
opts: Mouth opening of less than two fingerbreadths
A rigid cervical collar limiting neck extension
An expanding hematoma in the neck
Missing upper front teeth
A thin patient with a long neck
ok: Mouth opening of less than two fingerbreadths
A rigid cervical collar limiting neck extension
An expanding hematoma in the neck

qs.q: Which measures lengthen the safe apnea time before rapid sequence intubation? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Head-up or ramped positioning; Nasal cannula oxygen at high flow left on during laryngoscopy; A PEEP valve on the bag-valve mask for a patient who stays hypoxic
qs.x: Upright positioning, apneic oxygenation and PEEP all improve the oxygen reserve; aggressive bagging inflates the stomach and lying flat or removing oxygen speeds desaturation.
opts: Head-up or ramped positioning
Nasal cannula oxygen at high flow left on during laryngoscopy
A PEEP valve on the bag-valve mask for a patient who stays hypoxic
Bagging at 30 breaths/min before induction
Removing oxygen briefly to check the room air saturation
Laying an obese patient completely flat
ok: Head-up or ramped positioning
Nasal cannula oxygen at high flow left on during laryngoscopy
A PEEP valve on the bag-valve mask for a patient who stays hypoxic

qs.q: You have just intubated an adult with a pulse. Which findings support tracheal placement? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A sustained ETCO2 waveform over several breaths; Seeing the tube pass between the vocal cords; Equal breath sounds with no sounds over the epigastrium
qs.x: Continuous waveform capnography, direct visualization and auscultation support placement; fogging can occur with an esophageal tube, and SpO2 can stay normal for minutes after misplacement.
opts: A sustained ETCO2 waveform over several breaths
Seeing the tube pass between the vocal cords
Equal breath sounds with no sounds over the epigastrium
Fogging inside the tube
A normal SpO2 immediately after the tube is placed
ok: A sustained ETCO2 waveform over several breaths
Seeing the tube pass between the vocal cords
Equal breath sounds with no sounds over the epigastrium

qs.q: An intubated patient's peak airway pressure suddenly rises on the ventilator. Which problems could explain this? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A mucus plug in the tube; Bronchospasm; The patient biting down on the tube
qs.x: Obstruction, bronchospasm and biting all raise resistance to airflow; leaks and disconnections cause low pressure alarms.
opts: A mucus plug in the tube
Bronchospasm
The patient biting down on the tube
A leak in the cuff
Disconnection of the circuit
ok: A mucus plug in the tube
Bronchospasm
The patient biting down on the tube

qs.q: Which situations can produce an elevated ETCO2 with a normal waveform shape? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hypoventilation from an opioid; Return of spontaneous circulation during CPR; Fever with increased metabolism
qs.x: ETCO2 rises when CO2 production or delivery to the lungs increases, or when ventilation falls; hyperventilation, PE and hypothermia lower it.
opts: Hypoventilation from an opioid
Return of spontaneous circulation during CPR
Fever with increased metabolism
Hyperventilation
A massive pulmonary embolism
Hypothermia
ok: Hypoventilation from an opioid
Return of spontaneous circulation during CPR
Fever with increased metabolism

qs.q: Which patients are good candidates for CPAP? Select all that apply.
qs.a: An alert 70-year-old with acute pulmonary edema and BP 170/100; An alert 66-year-old with a COPD exacerbation and accessory muscle use; An alert near-drowning victim with crackles and SpO2 88 percent
qs.x: CPAP needs an alert patient who can protect the airway and is breathing spontaneously; unresponsiveness, vomiting and pneumothorax are contraindications.
opts: An alert 70-year-old with acute pulmonary edema and BP 170/100
An alert 66-year-old with a COPD exacerbation and accessory muscle use
An alert near-drowning victim with crackles and SpO2 88 percent
An unresponsive patient with agonal respirations
A patient who is actively vomiting
A patient with a suspected pneumothorax
ok: An alert 70-year-old with acute pulmonary edema and BP 170/100
An alert 66-year-old with a COPD exacerbation and accessory muscle use
An alert near-drowning victim with crackles and SpO2 88 percent

qs.q: You cannot intubate or oxygenate a patient and need an emergency front-of-neck airway. In which patients is needle cricothyrotomy preferred over a surgical cricothyrotomy? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A 4-year-old with severe facial burns; An 18-month-old with an obstructing foreign body that cannot be removed
qs.x: Young children have a small, pliable cricothyroid membrane, so needle cricothyrotomy is preferred; adults generally receive a surgical cricothyrotomy.
opts: A 4-year-old with severe facial burns
An 18-month-old with an obstructing foreign body that cannot be removed
A 35-year-old with massive facial trauma
A 60-year-old with severe angioedema
A 28-year-old with an expanding neck hematoma
ok: A 4-year-old with severe facial burns
An 18-month-old with an obstructing foreign body that cannot be removed

qs.q: Which anatomic features of a young child's airway differ from an adult's? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A tongue that is large relative to the mouth; A large occiput; A larynx positioned higher and more anterior
qs.x: Children have a large tongue and occiput and a higher larynx; their trachea is short and soft, and their oxygen consumption per kilogram is higher, so they desaturate quickly.
opts: A tongue that is large relative to the mouth
A large occiput
A larynx positioned higher and more anterior
A longer, more rigid trachea
Lower oxygen use per kilogram
ok: A tongue that is large relative to the mouth
A large occiput
A larynx positioned higher and more anterior

qs.q: You are ventilating an intubated patient during a severe asthma attack. Which findings suggest dangerous air trapping? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Blood pressure falling with each breath series; Steadily rising peak airway pressures; Exhalation still occurring when the next breath begins
qs.x: Incomplete exhalation causes stacked breaths, rising pressures and reduced venous return; complete exhalation with matching volumes indicates the lungs are emptying.
opts: Blood pressure falling with each breath series
Steadily rising peak airway pressures
Exhalation still occurring when the next breath begins
Exhaled volumes matching delivered volumes
A long pause after exhalation before the next breath
ok: Blood pressure falling with each breath series
Steadily rising peak airway pressures
Exhalation still occurring when the next breath begins

qs.q: Which arterial blood gas values fall within normal adult ranges? Select all that apply.
qs.a: pH 7.40; PaCO2 40 mmHg; HCO3 24 mEq/L
qs.x: Normal values are about pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45 mmHg and HCO3 22 to 26 mEq/L; a PaO2 of 55 mmHg is hypoxemia and pH 7.30 is acidemia.
opts: PaCO2 40 mmHg
HCO3 24 mEq/L
PaO2 55 mmHg on room air
ok: PaCO2 40 mmHg
HCO3 24 mEq/L

qs.q: A 69-year-old is dizzy. The rhythm strip shows regular P waves at 84/min, with every other P wave followed by a narrow QRS. The PR interval of the conducted beats is constant. What is the rhythm?
qs.a: Second-degree AV block with 2 to 1 conduction
qs.x: When every second P wave is blocked, the block cannot be firmly classified as type I or type II; it is described as 2 to 1 second-degree AV block, and a wide QRS makes an infranodal (more dangerous) block more likely.
w: First-degree AV block
Third-degree AV block
Atrial flutter with 2 to 1 conduction

qs.q: A rhythm strip shows regular P waves at 80/min and regular narrow QRS complexes at 44/min, with no consistent relationship between them; the P waves march through the QRS complexes. What is the rhythm?
qs.a: Third-degree AV block with a junctional escape
qs.x: Atria and ventricles beating independently is complete heart block; a narrow escape rhythm in the 40s to 50s arises from the AV junction and is usually more stable than a wide ventricular escape.
w: Second-degree AV block type I
Sinus bradycardia
Atrial fibrillation with slow response

qs.q: A 54-year-old on methadone collapses. The monitor shows a wide-complex tachycardia whose QRS amplitude repeatedly grows and shrinks, appearing to twist around the baseline. What is this rhythm?
qs.a: Torsades de pointes
qs.x: Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic VT with twisting amplitude linked to a prolonged QT interval, which methadone and many other drugs can cause.
w: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation with aberrancy
Coarse ventricular fibrillation

qs.q: A 73-year-old has had palpitations for an unknown number of days. The monitor shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 128/min. He is alert with BP 132/80. Why is elective cardioversion avoided in the field?
qs.a: It may dislodge a clot from the atria
qs.x: Atrial fibrillation lasting more than about 48 hours, or of unknown duration, may have formed atrial clots that can embolize when sinus rhythm returns, causing a stroke.
w: It will convert the rhythm into asystole
It is ineffective for atrial rhythms
It requires general anesthesia in all patients

qs.q: A 22-year-old with palpitations has an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 240/min with QRS complexes that vary in width. He has a history of an accessory pathway. BP is 118/72. Which treatment approach must be avoided?
qs.a: AV nodal blocking medications
qs.x: In atrial fibrillation with an accessory pathway (pre-excitation), blocking the AV node can push more impulses down the accessory pathway and trigger ventricular fibrillation.
w: Obtaining a 12-lead ECG
Preparing for synchronized cardioversion
Consulting medical direction

qs.q: During CPR on a 66-year-old, the rhythm check shows a flat line in lead II. What should you do?
qs.a: Confirm in another lead and check the gain
qs.x: Before treating as asystole, confirm the leads are connected, the gain is adequate and the flat line persists in another lead, so fine VF is not missed; CPR continues meanwhile.
w: Defibrillate in case it is fine VF
Stop CPR, since asystole is not survivable
Synchronize and cardiovert

qs.q: A 67-year-old on a ventilator for COPD loses his pulse. The monitor shows a narrow-complex rhythm at 130/min. Breath sounds are absent on the right and his neck veins are distended. Which cause of PEA is most likely?
qs.a: Tension pneumothorax
qs.x: A fast, narrow PEA suggests a mechanical problem; absent breath sounds and distended neck veins in a ventilated COPD patient point to tension pneumothorax, which needs decompression.
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypothermia
Acidosis

qs.q: A 58-year-old dialysis patient who has missed two treatments is pulseless. The monitor shows slow, very wide, bizarre complexes at 30/min. Which reversible cause is most likely?
qs.a: Hyperkalemia
qs.x: Slow, wide PEA in a patient who has missed dialysis strongly suggests hyperkalemia, which needs specific treatment along with high-quality CPR.
w: Tension pneumothorax
Cardiac tamponade
Hypovolemia

qs.q: A 77-year-old with several days of black, tarry stools becomes pulseless. The monitor shows a narrow-complex rhythm at 120/min. Which treatment addresses the most likely cause?
qs.a: Rapid volume replacement
qs.x: A fast, narrow PEA after GI bleeding points to hypovolemia; restoring volume, ideally with blood where available, treats the cause while CPR continues.
w: Needle decompression of the chest
Synchronized cardioversion
Transcutaneous pacing

qs.q: A 61-year-old has chest pain with ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 and ST depression in III. Which coronary artery is most likely involved?
qs.a: Left circumflex artery
qs.x: ST elevation limited to the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) usually reflects occlusion of the circumflex artery or one of its branches.
w: Right coronary artery
Posterior descending artery
Proximal left anterior descending artery

qs.q: A 64-year-old has chest pain. His 12-lead shows ST depression in III and aVF and subtle ST elevation in I and aVL. How should this be interpreted?
qs.a: High lateral STEMI with inferior reciprocal changes
qs.x: ST depression in the inferior leads can be the mirror image of a high lateral infarction; subtle elevation in I and aVL with reciprocal inferior depression should be treated as STEMI.
w: Inferior ischemia only, not a STEMI
Pericarditis affecting the inferior wall
A normal variant in an older adult

qs.q: A 59-year-old with an inferior STEMI has more ST elevation in lead III than in lead II, with ST depression in lead I. Which artery is most likely occluded?
qs.a: Right coronary artery
qs.x: In an inferior STEMI, ST elevation greater in III than II with depression in lead I points to the right coronary artery, which also raises concern for right ventricular involvement.
w: Left circumflex artery
Left anterior descending artery
Left main coronary artery

qs.q: A 70-year-old with crushing chest pain and BP 92/60 has ST elevation in aVR and widespread ST depression in most other leads. What does this pattern suggest?
qs.a: Left main or multivessel ischemia
qs.x: ST elevation in aVR with diffuse ST depression suggests severe ischemia from left main or three-vessel disease, a high-risk pattern needing rapid transport to a PCI-capable center.
w: Benign early repolarization
Isolated right ventricular infarction
Acute pericarditis

qs.q: A 51-year-old had chest pain yesterday that has now resolved. His 12-lead shows deep, symmetric T-wave inversions in V2 and V3 with no ST elevation. What is the concern?
qs.a: Critical narrowing of the proximal LAD
qs.x: This Wellens pattern indicates a critical proximal LAD stenosis with a high risk of a large anterior MI in the coming days, so the patient needs cardiology evaluation even though pain-free.
w: A healed old infarction needing no action
Normal T waves for a middle-aged adult
Pericarditis in its late stage

qs.q: A 48-year-old with ongoing chest pain has upsloping ST depression at the J point with tall, symmetric T waves across V1 to V6 and no ST elevation. How should this be handled?
qs.a: As a STEMI equivalent from LAD occlusion
qs.x: This de Winter pattern signals acute proximal LAD occlusion without classic ST elevation and should prompt activation of the STEMI system per protocol.
w: As nonspecific changes needing no special action
As benign early repolarization
As typical findings of hyperventilation

qs.q: A 75-year-old with a known left bundle branch block has chest pain. Which finding on his 12-lead most strongly suggests an acute MI?
qs.a: ST elevation in the same direction as the QRS
qs.x: In LBBB, ST segments normally go opposite the QRS; ST elevation of at least 1 mm in the same direction as the QRS (concordant) is a specific sign of acute infarction.
w: ST elevation opposite to a deep negative QRS in V1
A QRS width of 0.14 seconds
T waves opposite to the main QRS direction

qs.q: A healthy 23-year-old athlete has a 12-lead done after a minor injury. It shows concave ST elevation in V2 to V4 with a notched J point, no reciprocal depression, and no symptoms. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Benign early repolarization
qs.x: Concave ST elevation with J-point notching and no reciprocal changes in a young, asymptomatic person is typical of early repolarization, a common STEMI mimic.
w: Acute anterior STEMI
Brugada pattern
Hyperkalemia

qs.q: A 31-year-old has sharp chest pain and diffuse ST elevation. Which additional ECG finding favors pericarditis over STEMI?
qs.a: PR depression in many leads
qs.x: Pericarditis typically causes widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal ST depression except in aVR; localized elevation with reciprocal depression favors STEMI.
w: ST depression in leads opposite to the elevation
ST elevation confined to II, III and aVF
New Q waves in the anterior leads

qs.q: A 33-year-old fainted at rest. His ECG shows a right bundle branch-like pattern with coved ST elevation in V1 and V2. Why is this important?
qs.a: It indicates a risk of sudden cardiac death
qs.x: Coved ST elevation in V1 and V2 with syncope suggests Brugada syndrome, which predisposes to ventricular fibrillation and requires hospital evaluation.
w: It is a normal finding in young men
It indicates an old septal infarction
It shows that the faint was vasovagal

qs.q: A 25-year-old marathon runner has a heart rate of 42/min in sinus rhythm during a screening exam. He is alert, BP is 118/70 and he has no complaints. What is the appropriate treatment?
qs.a: No treatment for the slow rate
qs.x: Bradycardia is treated only when it causes symptoms or poor perfusion; well-conditioned athletes often have resting rates in the 40s.
w: Atropine to raise the rate
Transcutaneous pacing on standby at 60/min
An immediate fluid bolus

qs.q: You are pacing a 74-year-old with complete heart block. Each pacer spike is followed by a wide QRS on the monitor. How should you confirm mechanical capture?
qs.a: Palpate a femoral pulse that matches the paced rate
qs.x: Electrical capture on the monitor does not prove the heart is pumping; a femoral pulse matching the paced rate confirms mechanical capture, and carotid checks are confused by muscle twitching.
w: Palpate a carotid pulse during pacing
See that the pacer spikes appear on the screen
Watch for chest wall muscle twitching

qs.q: A 72-year-old has second-degree AV block type II with a wide QRS at 54/min. He is alert, BP 118/70, with no chest pain or dizziness. What is the most appropriate action?
qs.a: Apply pacing pads and monitor closely
qs.x: Type II block can suddenly progress to complete heart block, so pads should be on and ready for pacing even in a stable patient.
w: Begin pacing immediately at 80/min
Perform synchronized cardioversion
No monitoring is needed since he is stable

qs.q: A 60-year-old who had a heart transplant 5 years ago has symptomatic bradycardia at 38/min with BP 78/44. Why is atropine unlikely to help?
qs.a: The transplanted heart lacks vagal innervation
qs.x: A transplanted heart is denervated, so blocking vagal tone has little effect; pacing or an adrenergic infusion is usually needed.
w: Transplant patients are allergic to atropine
Atropine only works for wide-complex rhythms
Atropine is used only in children

qs.q: A 34-year-old with 2 days of fever and vomiting has a regular narrow-complex rhythm at 142/min with visible P waves before each QRS. The rate varies slightly with movement. BP is 104/66. What is the best management?
qs.a: Treat the dehydration and fever
qs.x: Sinus tachycardia is a response to an underlying problem, such as fever, pain or hypovolemia; treating the cause is correct, and cardioversion or vagal maneuvers are not.
w: Synchronized cardioversion
Vagal maneuvers to break the rhythm
Transcutaneous pacing

qs.q: You deliver a synchronized shock to a hypotensive 66-year-old in atrial fibrillation with rapid response, but the rhythm does not change. Before delivering the next synchronized shock, what must you check?
qs.a: That the sync mode is still selected
qs.x: Many monitors return to unsynchronized mode after each shock, so sync must be confirmed before every shock to avoid delivering it on the T wave.
w: That the pads have been moved to the back
That the monitor is in pacing mode
That the patient's pulse is absent

qs.q: A 29-year-old with stable SVT at 188/min is alert and normotensive. Which vagal technique is most likely to convert the rhythm?
qs.a: Modified Valsalva with leg raise
qs.x: The modified Valsalva maneuver, a strain against resistance followed immediately by lying flat with legs raised, converts SVT more often than a standard Valsalva; eyeball pressure and bilateral carotid massage are dangerous.
w: Carotid massage on both sides at once
Pressing firmly on both eyeballs
Holding the breath for 5 seconds

qs.q: A 48-year-old had a witnessed collapse with immediate bystander CPR. He remains in VF after three shocks. A mechanical CPR device is in place and your system has an ECPR center 15 minutes away. What is the most appropriate step?
qs.a: Early transport to the ECPR center per protocol
qs.x: Refractory VF in a young patient with a witnessed arrest and good bystander CPR is the classic ECPR candidate; early transport with mechanical CPR is needed because outcomes depend on the time to bypass.
w: Continue on scene for 60 minutes before moving
Stop resuscitation after the third failed shock
Transport to the nearest non-ECPR hospital

qs.q: You are ventilating an intubated 59-year-old after ROSC. Which ETCO2 range is generally targeted?
qs.a: 35 to 45 mmHg
qs.x: Post-arrest ventilation aims for normal CO2 levels; hyperventilation lowers CO2 and reduces cerebral blood flow, while hypoventilation worsens acidosis.
w: 15 to 20 mmHg
20 to 25 mmHg
55 to 65 mmHg

qs.q: A 57-year-old has ROSC after a VF arrest. His post-ROSC 12-lead shows ST elevation in V1 to V4. Where should he be transported?
qs.a: A PCI-capable center
qs.x: Post-arrest patients with STEMI benefit from emergency coronary angiography, so they should go to a PCI-capable center, ideally a designated cardiac arrest center.
w: The closest emergency department regardless of capability
A stroke center
A trauma center

qs.q: A comatose 62-year-old has ROSC after a cardiac arrest. Which temperature-related practice is not recommended in the prehospital setting?
qs.a: Rapid infusion of cold IV fluids
qs.x: Routine prehospital cooling with rapid cold IV fluid infusion has not improved outcomes and has caused pulmonary edema and re-arrest; preventing fever remains part of post-arrest care.
w: Avoiding fever
Monitoring temperature when possible
Preventing hyperthermia from heavy blankets

qs.q: A 3-month-old has a heart rate of 270/min with a narrow QRS, no visible P waves and no beat-to-beat variation. The parents say he was feeding normally an hour ago. What is the most likely rhythm?
qs.a: Supraventricular tachycardia
qs.x: In infants, SVT is usually above 220/min with absent P waves, a fixed rate and abrupt onset; sinus tachycardia is usually lower, varies with activity and follows a cause such as fever or dehydration.
w: Sinus tachycardia from fever
Ventricular tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation

qs.q: A 6-month-old has a narrow-complex tachycardia at 280/min. He is lethargic and mottled with weak pulses. No vascular access has been obtained yet. What is the appropriate treatment?
qs.a: Synchronized cardioversion
qs.x: Unstable SVT with poor perfusion needs immediate synchronized cardioversion when vascular access is not available; delaying for access worsens shock.
w: Unsynchronized defibrillation
Wait for IO access before any treatment
Begin chest compressions

qs.q: A 20-kg child is in ventricular fibrillation. What energy should be used for the first defibrillation?
qs.x: The initial pediatric defibrillation dose is 2 J/kg, so 40 J for a 20-kg child; later shocks are increased to 4 J/kg or more.

qs.q: You are preparing to defibrillate a 5-month-old in VF, but the adult-size pads would touch each other on the front of the chest. What should you do?
qs.a: Place one pad on the front and one on the back
qs.x: Pads must not touch; when the chest is too small, anterior-posterior placement allows the current to pass through the heart without arcing between pads.
w: Overlap the pads slightly on the front of the chest
Cut the pads to a smaller size
Place both pads on the back

qs.q: A 10-month-old with bronchiolitis is limp, with a heart rate of 58/min, SpO2 of 70 percent and poor perfusion. No ventilation has been given yet. What is the first priority?
qs.a: Ventilate with oxygen by bag-valve mask
qs.x: Bradycardia in children is most often caused by hypoxia; oxygenation and ventilation come first, and compressions start if the rate stays below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective ventilation.
w: Begin transcutaneous pacing
Give atropine
Synchronized cardioversion

qs.q: A 66-year-old dialysis patient has weakness. The 12-lead shows tall, narrow, peaked T waves with otherwise normal intervals. What do these findings suggest?
qs.a: Early hyperkalemia
qs.x: Peaked T waves are usually the first ECG sign of rising potassium; with further rises the P wave flattens, the QRS widens and a sine-wave pattern can precede arrest.
w: Hypokalemia
Acute pericarditis
Digoxin effect

qs.q: A 79-year-old found outdoors in winter has a core temperature of 30 C (86 F). The ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a distinct hump at the end of each QRS complex. What is this finding?
qs.a: Osborn (J) waves from hypothermia
qs.x: Osborn waves, an extra deflection at the J point, are characteristic of hypothermia and tend to grow as the temperature falls.
w: Delta waves from pre-excitation
U waves from hypokalemia
Epsilon waves from cardiomyopathy

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman is sitting bolt upright with pink, frothy sputum, crackles throughout, BP 222/124 and SpO2 84 percent. She is alert and follows commands. Which intervention should be started first?
qs.a: CPAP
qs.x: Hypertensive acute pulmonary edema responds rapidly to CPAP, usually combined with nitrates per protocol; fluids and lying flat worsen the congestion.
w: A 1-liter fluid bolus
Supine positioning with legs raised
Nebulized bronchodilator alone

qs.q: A 64-year-old with an anterior STEMI is cool and clammy, with BP 76/48, crackles to the mid-lung fields and SpO2 89 percent. What should be avoided?
qs.a: Nitroglycerin and large fluid boluses
qs.x: This is cardiogenic shock; nitrates worsen hypotension and large fluid volumes worsen pulmonary edema, so management focuses on careful hemodynamic support and rapid reperfusion.
w: Rapid transport to a PCI-capable center
Oxygen to keep SpO2 above 90 percent
A repeat 12-lead ECG during transport

qs.q: A 71-year-old with severe COPD has distended neck veins, swollen ankles and an enlarged, tender liver. His lungs have scattered wheezes but no crackles. Which condition do these findings suggest?
qs.a: Right-sided heart failure
qs.x: Right heart failure, often from chronic lung disease, causes systemic venous congestion such as JVD, edema and liver enlargement, without the pulmonary crackles of left-sided failure.
w: Left-sided heart failure
Hypovolemic shock
Acute pericarditis

qs.q: A 63-year-old has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back, a weak left radial pulse and ST elevation in II, III and aVF. What is the key concern?
qs.a: A dissection extending into the right coronary artery
qs.x: An aortic dissection can involve a coronary artery and cause STEMI; recognizing it matters because antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy can be catastrophic, so the receiving center must be told.
w: A routine inferior STEMI needing standard treatment only
Acute pericarditis from a viral illness
Gastroesophageal reflux with a nonspecific ECG

qs.q: A 72-year-old man suddenly developed severe low back and flank pain, then fainted. He has a pulsatile abdominal mass and BP 84/50. What is the most appropriate approach?
qs.a: Rapid transport to a center with vascular surgery
qs.x: A suspected ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm needs surgery; limit scene time, avoid raising the BP to normal, and transport to a facility that can repair it.
w: Large fluid boluses to bring the systolic BP to 140 mmHg
Prolonged scene stabilization before transport
Transport to the nearest clinic for imaging

qs.q: A 69-year-old has left arm weakness, right gaze deviation and neglect starting 50 minutes ago. Your regional plan allows bypassing a primary stroke center 10 minutes away for a thrombectomy-capable center 25 minutes away when an LVO is suspected. Where should she go?
qs.a: The thrombectomy-capable center
qs.x: With a positive LVO screen and modest added time, direct transport to a thrombectomy-capable center speeds clot retrieval, as regional stroke plans allow.
w: The primary stroke center 10 minutes away
The nearest urgent care clinic
Her primary care physician's office

qs.q: A 58-year-old suddenly develops right-sided weakness. Which feature most suggests a hemorrhagic rather than an ischemic stroke?
qs.a: Severe headache, vomiting and falling LOC
qs.x: Sudden severe headache with vomiting and a declining level of consciousness suggests raised intracranial pressure from bleeding, although only imaging can confirm the stroke type.
w: Slurred speech that began on waking
Facial droop that is resolving
A history of atrial fibrillation

qs.q: A 35-year-old with epilepsy had a witnessed generalized seizure 20 minutes ago and now has right arm weakness. Glucose is 112 mg/dL. Which condition can mimic a stroke in this patient?
qs.a: Postictal (Todd) paralysis
qs.x: Temporary weakness after a seizure (Todd paralysis) is a common stroke mimic, though a stroke cannot be ruled out in the field and the history should be clearly reported.
w: Bell palsy
Hypoglycemia
Transient global amnesia

qs.q: A 74-year-old with an acute ischemic stroke 1 hour ago has BP 196/104. She is alert with stable vital signs otherwise. What is the appropriate field management of her blood pressure?
qs.a: Monitor it without trying to lower it
qs.x: Elevated blood pressure helps perfuse threatened brain tissue, so it is not lowered in the field unless directed by medical control; the hospital manages it according to treatment plans.
w: Lower it to 120/80 within 15 minutes
Give a large fluid bolus to protect the brain
Lay her flat with legs raised

qs.q: A 61-year-old has sudden vertigo, vomiting, double vision and cannot walk without falling. His face, arm drift and speech are normal. What should you suspect?
qs.a: Posterior circulation stroke
qs.x: Posterior circulation strokes often spare the face, arms and speech, so screening tools that include balance and eye findings help detect them.
w: Benign inner ear vertigo
Migraine with aura
Simple dehydration

qs.q: A 57-year-old with lung cancer is short of breath and hypotensive. The 12-lead shows low voltage, and the QRS height alternates from beat to beat. What does this suggest?
qs.a: A large pericardial effusion
qs.x: Low voltage with electrical alternans, the heart swinging within a large fluid-filled pericardium, suggests a large effusion and possible tamponade.
w: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Hyperkalemia
Acute anterior STEMI

qs.q: A 63-year-old with a left ventricular assist device is alert and talking. You cannot palpate a radial pulse and the automatic BP cuff gives no reading. What is the best interpretation?
qs.a: This can be normal with a continuous-flow device
qs.x: Continuous-flow LVADs often produce no palpable pulse or measurable cuff pressure; perfusion is judged by mental status, skin signs and device alarms, and an alert patient is not in arrest.
w: He is in cardiac arrest and needs compressions
The device has failed and must be switched off
He is in hypovolemic shock and needs fluids

qs.q: A rhythm strip shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at 50/min. In lead II the P waves are inverted and appear just before each QRS with a very short PR interval. What is the rhythm?
qs.a: Junctional rhythm
qs.x: Impulses from the AV junction spread backward through the atria, producing inverted P waves just before, during or after the QRS, at a rate of about 40 to 60.
w: Sinus bradycardia
First-degree AV block
Atrial flutter

qs.q: A 76-year-old with a COPD exacerbation and SpO2 of 84 percent has an irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 118/min with at least three different P wave shapes. What is the best approach to this rhythm?
qs.a: Treat the hypoxia and lung disease
qs.x: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is driven by underlying illness, especially lung disease and hypoxia; it does not respond to cardioversion and improves when the cause is treated.
w: Synchronized cardioversion
Transcutaneous pacing
Unsynchronized defibrillation

qs.q: After reperfusion of an inferior STEMI, a 62-year-old's monitor shows a regular wide-complex rhythm at 72/min. He has a strong pulse and BP 124/76. What is this rhythm most likely to be?
qs.a: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
qs.x: A wide ventricular rhythm at 40 to 100 after reperfusion is usually accelerated idioventricular rhythm; it is generally benign and should not be suppressed with antiarrhythmics.
w: Ventricular tachycardia needing cardioversion
Ventricular fibrillation
Third-degree AV block with slow escape

qs.q: A newborn's heart rate remains 50/min after 30 seconds of positive pressure ventilation that moves the chest. What is the next step?
qs.a: Start compressions at a 3 to 1 ratio
qs.x: NRP calls for chest compressions coordinated with ventilations at 3 to 1, with increased oxygen, when the heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation.
w: Continue ventilation alone for 2 more minutes
Start compressions at a 15 to 2 ratio
Stop resuscitation

qs.q: Which conditions can cause ST elevation without an acute coronary occlusion? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Left ventricular hypertrophy; Left bundle branch block; Benign early repolarization
qs.x: LVH, LBBB and early repolarization are common STEMI mimics; reciprocal depression actually makes a true STEMI more likely.
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left bundle branch block
Benign early repolarization
Reciprocal ST depression in the opposite leads
A ventricular rate of 72 in sinus rhythm
ok: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left bundle branch block
Benign early repolarization

qs.q: A 29-year-old had a flu-like illness last week and now has chest pain. Which findings support acute pericarditis? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Pain that is worse lying flat and better leaning forward; A scratchy friction rub heard over the chest; Pain that is sharp and worse with deep breaths
qs.x: Pericarditis causes sharp, pleuritic, positional pain and sometimes a friction rub, often after a viral illness; exertional crushing pain and localized elevation with reciprocal changes suggest ischemia.
opts: Pain that is worse lying flat and better leaning forward
A scratchy friction rub heard over the chest
Pain that is sharp and worse with deep breaths
Crushing pain relieved by rest
ST elevation in V1 to V4 with reciprocal inferior depression
ok: Pain that is worse lying flat and better leaning forward
A scratchy friction rub heard over the chest
Pain that is sharp and worse with deep breaths

qs.q: Which patients are at increased risk of hyperkalemia? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A dialysis patient who missed two treatments; A worker freed after hours trapped under heavy debris; A patient with acute kidney failure
qs.x: Kidney failure and muscle breakdown from crush injury raise serum potassium; vomiting and loop diuretics typically lower it.
opts: A dialysis patient who missed two treatments
A worker freed after hours trapped under heavy debris
A patient with acute kidney failure
A patient with several days of vomiting
A patient taking a high-dose loop diuretic
ok: A dialysis patient who missed two treatments
A worker freed after hours trapped under heavy debris
A patient with acute kidney failure

qs.q: A 58-year-old has a sudden tearing chest pain. Which findings support aortic dissection? Select all that apply.
qs.a: A pulse deficit in one arm; New weakness on one side of the body; A new diastolic heart murmur
qs.x: Dissection can block branch arteries, causing pulse deficits or stroke symptoms, and can disrupt the aortic valve, causing a new diastolic murmur.
opts: A pulse deficit in one arm
New weakness on one side of the body
A new diastolic heart murmur
Pain that built up slowly over several days and eases with rest
Sharp pain that changes with position and improves leaning forward
ok: A pulse deficit in one arm
New weakness on one side of the body
A new diastolic heart murmur
