qs.a: 6 to 8 mL/kg of predicted body weight
qs.x: Lung-protective ventilation sets tidal volume by predicted body weight, from height and sex, at about 6 to 8 mL/kg. Larger volumes based on actual weight raise the risk of lung injury.
w: 10 to 12 mL/kg of actual body weight
15 mL/kg of predicted body weight
Any volume that keeps SpO2 at 100 percent

qs.q: After extubation in prolonged care, a casualty develops inspiratory stridor from airway swelling. Which nebulized drug is most appropriate?
qs.a: Racemic epinephrine
qs.x: Racemic epinephrine causes vasoconstriction of the swollen upper airway mucosa and is used for post-extubation stridor and croup. Albuterol and ipratropium target lower airway bronchospasm.
w: Ipratropium
Albuterol
Hypertonic saline

qs.q: A casualty with severe bronchospasm is not improving after albuterol and ipratropium. Which IV drug is a standard adjunct?
qs.a: Magnesium sulfate
qs.x: IV magnesium relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and is used in severe asthma not responding to inhaled therapy. Beta-blockers such as metoprolol can worsen bronchospasm.
w: Adenosine
Metoprolol
Famotidine

qs.q: A casualty stung by a wasp has wheezing, throat tightness, and hives. What is the first drug?
qs.a: Intramuscular epinephrine into the thigh
qs.x: Epinephrine is the only first-line drug for anaphylaxis; it reverses bronchospasm, airway edema, and vasodilation. IM injection in the anterolateral thigh is preferred.
w: Intravenous diphenhydramine
Oral methylprednisolone
Nebulized ipratropium

qs.q: A stable casualty has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 that did not respond to vagal maneuvers. What is the next drug and technique?
qs.a: Adenosine by rapid push and flush
qs.x: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds, so it is given by rapid IV push into a large proximal vein followed immediately by a flush. A slow push lets it break down before reaching the heart.
w: Adenosine by slow push over minutes
Amiodarone by rapid IV push
Diltiazem by intramuscular route

qs.q: A casualty with known Wolff-Parkinson-White has an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 240, a systolic pressure of 76, and confusion. What is the best treatment?
qs.a: Synchronized cardioversion
qs.x: This is unstable pre-excited atrial fibrillation, which calls for synchronized cardioversion. AV nodal blockers can speed conduction down the accessory pathway and cause ventricular fibrillation.
w: Adenosine by rapid push
Diltiazem by slow IV push
Metoprolol by slow IV push

qs.q: A casualty has symptomatic bradycardia that does not respond to atropine. What are the next options per AHA?
qs.a: Pacing or an epinephrine or dopamine infusion
qs.x: When atropine fails, AHA guidance moves to transcutaneous pacing or a chronotropic infusion of epinephrine or dopamine. Adenosine and diltiazem would slow the heart further.
w: Adenosine by rapid IV push with a flush
Diltiazem infusion to slow conduction further
Repeat vagal maneuvers and then observe

qs.q: A casualty on several QT-prolonging drugs develops polymorphic VT with a twisting pattern and a pulse. Which drug is first-line?
qs.a: Magnesium sulfate
qs.x: Torsades de pointes with a long QT is treated with IV magnesium. Amiodarone further prolongs the QT and can worsen it.
w: Amiodarone
Adenosine
Diltiazem

qs.q: Which vasopressor is first-line for septic shock in a PCC casualty after fluid resuscitation?
qs.a: Norepinephrine
qs.x: Surviving Sepsis guidance lists norepinephrine first, with vasopressin added if needed. Dopamine causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine in shock.
w: Phenylephrine
Dopamine
Vasopressin

qs.q: A casualty in hemorrhagic shock is hypotensive with blood not yet available. What is the role of norepinephrine?
qs.a: It does not replace volume; blood remains the priority
qs.x: Pressors constrict vessels but do not replace lost blood volume or clotting capacity, and they can worsen tissue perfusion in hypovolemia. Hemorrhage control and blood products are the treatment.
w: It is the first-line treatment for hemorrhagic shock in the field
It restores clotting factors lost in bleeding
It is given to reach a systolic pressure of 140

qs.q: A deployed contractor with crushing chest pain and ST elevation has no trauma or bleeding. Which drug is given early?
qs.a: Aspirin, chewed
qs.x: Chewed aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet thromboxane and reduces death in acute MI. It is avoided in bleeding casualties for the same reason.
w: Ketorolac IV
Enoxaparin IM
Meloxicam oral

qs.q: A casualty pulled from a burning enclosed vehicle is confused and hypotensive with a high lactate. Which antidote best fits?
qs.a: Hydroxocobalamin
qs.x: Smoke from burning plastics releases cyanide, which blocks cellular oxygen use and drives lactate up. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted in urine.
w: Flumazenil
Naloxone
Atropine

qs.q: Which effect of hydroxocobalamin is expected and can mislead later care?
qs.a: Red skin and urine that distort color-based labs
qs.x: Hydroxocobalamin turns skin, mucous membranes, and urine red and interferes with colorimetric lab tests and some monitoring. Draw needed labs before giving it when practical.
w: Severe bradycardia and prolonged complete heart block
Rapid hypoglycemia lasting several hours
Blue skin from methemoglobin formation

qs.q: How does amyl nitrite treat cyanide poisoning, and what is the main caution?
qs.a: It forms methemoglobin; caution with carbon monoxide
qs.x: Nitrites oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which binds cyanide. In smoke inhalation with carbon monoxide this further reduces oxygen carrying, so hydroxocobalamin is preferred.
w: It binds cyanide directly; caution with asthma
It speeds cyanide excretion; caution in renal failure
It blocks cyanide uptake; caution in children

qs.q: A casualty exposed to a nerve agent is receiving atropine. Which finding is the main endpoint for titration?
qs.a: Drying of airway secretions with easier breathing
qs.x: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects such as bronchorrhea and bronchospasm, so titration targets dry secretions and easier ventilation. Pupils may stay small and twitching is a nicotinic effect atropine does not treat.
w: Return of pupil size to normal
Heart rate above 140 beats per minute
Complete stop of muscle twitching

qs.q: A casualty with a tricyclic antidepressant overdose has a QRS of 140 ms and hypotension. Which drug is first-line?
qs.a: Sodium bicarbonate
qs.x: Bicarbonate's sodium load and alkalinization overcome the sodium channel blockade that widens the QRS. Flumazenil can trigger seizures in this setting.
w: Amiodarone
Flumazenil
Diltiazem

qs.q: A casualty develops perioral numbness, tinnitus, and then a seizure after a large lidocaine nerve block. What is the specific treatment besides seizure control?
qs.a: Intravenous lipid emulsion
qs.x: These are signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity, which can progress to arrhythmia and arrest. Lipid emulsion is the specific therapy, with benzodiazepines for seizures.
w: Intravenous naloxone
Intravenous flumazenil
Intravenous calcium chloride

qs.q: A casualty with a severe head injury develops a unilateral dilated pupil and posturing. Which TCCC medication is indicated?
qs.a: Hypertonic saline
qs.x: Signs of herniation call for hyperosmolar therapy, and TCCC uses hypertonic saline along with head elevation and brief controlled hyperventilation. Steroids worsen outcomes in TBI.
w: Methylprednisolone
Ketorolac
Dexmedetomidine

qs.q: A hypotensive casualty with TBI shows signs of herniation. Why is hypertonic saline favored over mannitol?
qs.a: Mannitol causes diuresis that worsens hypotension
qs.x: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic, and the fluid loss can drop blood pressure in an already hypovolemic casualty. Hypertonic saline lowers brain pressure while supporting volume.
w: Mannitol cannot be given through an IO line
Mannitol raises intracranial pressure further in shock
Mannitol contains potassium that stops the heart

qs.q: What is the key route consideration for 23.4 percent sodium chloride?
qs.a: It is given through a central line only
qs.x: The very high osmolarity of 23.4 percent saline injures peripheral veins and tissue, so it is given through a central line. Lower concentrations such as 3 percent are used peripherally or by IO.
w: It is given safely by any peripheral IV
It is given by intramuscular injection
It is given orally for brain swelling

qs.q: A casualty with TBI shows signs of herniation and is intubated. During brief controlled hyperventilation, what end-tidal CO2 target does TCCC use?
qs.a: 30 to 35 mmHg
qs.x: Brief hyperventilation to an EtCO2 of 30 to 35 mmHg lowers intracranial pressure through vasoconstriction. Lower values risk brain ischemia, and routine hyperventilation without herniation is avoided.
w: 20 to 25 mmHg
40 to 45 mmHg
Below 15 mmHg

qs.q: A 70 kg casualty has 40 percent TBSA burns. Using the USAISR Rule of Ten, what is the initial fluid rate?
qs.a: 400 mL per hour
qs.x: The Rule of Ten multiplies percent TBSA by 10 to give mL per hour for adults weighing 40 to 80 kg, adding 100 mL per hour for each 10 kg above 80 kg. 40 times 10 is 400.
w: 700 mL per hour
280 mL per hour
1,000 mL per hour

qs.q: A casualty has 30 percent TBSA burns and a penetrating thigh wound with hemorrhagic shock. What takes priority for fluids?
qs.a: Hemorrhagic shock resuscitation with blood
qs.x: TCCC states that resuscitation for hemorrhagic shock takes precedence over burn fluids. Blood products restore volume and clotting, and the burn formula follows once shock is addressed.
w: The burn formula with lactated Ringer's first
Hetastarch for both conditions at once
Delaying fluids until burns are dressed

qs.q: A casualty with a penetrating abdominal wound is in shock and cannot take oral medication. Which antibiotic approach fits TCCC?
qs.a: IV or IM ertapenem
qs.x: Casualties who cannot take oral medication receive a parenteral option such as ertapenem or ceftriaxone. Metronidazole alone misses many aerobic gut and skin organisms.
w: Oral moxifloxacin
Oral cephalexin
IV metronidazole alone

qs.q: Which pairing creates a precipitation risk in the same IV line?
qs.a: Ceftriaxone and calcium solutions
qs.x: Ceftriaxone binds calcium to form a precipitate, which has caused fatal deposits in neonates. In adults the line is flushed between them, and calcium-containing fluids such as LR are not used to dilute it.
w: Ceftriaxone and normal saline
Ertapenem and normal saline
Cefazolin and normal saline

qs.q: A casualty taking oral moxifloxacin also takes an antacid for heartburn at the same time. What is the concern?
qs.a: The antacid reduces moxifloxacin absorption
qs.x: Fluoroquinolones chelate magnesium, aluminum, calcium, iron, and zinc, sharply reducing absorption. Separate the doses by several hours.
w: The antacid raises moxifloxacin to toxic levels
The combination causes severe hyperkalemia
The combination causes immediate hemolysis

qs.q: A PCC casualty on valproic acid for a seizure disorder is started on ertapenem. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Valproate levels drop, raising seizure risk
qs.x: Carbapenems such as ertapenem sharply lower valproic acid levels and can cause breakthrough seizures. The combination is generally avoided.
w: Ertapenem levels rise to toxic levels in the blood
The pair causes severe QT prolongation
Both drugs strongly inhibit platelets

qs.q: Which antibiotic is used in JTS guidance for gram-positive skin flora coverage of open extremity wounds?
qs.a: Cefazolin
qs.x: Cefazolin, a first-generation cephalosporin, covers staphylococci and streptococci that cause extremity wound infections. Metronidazole covers anaerobes and is added for abdominal wounds.
w: Metronidazole
Ondansetron
Famotidine

qs.q: Per TCCC, when are antibiotics given for open combat wounds?
qs.a: As soon as possible after injury
qs.x: Early antibiotics after injury reduce wound infection, so TCCC gives them for all open combat wounds as soon as practical. Waiting for signs of infection loses the benefit.
w: Only once signs of infection appear
Only after the casualty reaches a hospital
Only for wounds larger than 10 cm

qs.q: A PCC casualty is being considered for enoxaparin VTE prophylaxis. Which finding most argues against starting it?
qs.a: Ongoing bleeding or untreated coagulopathy
qs.x: Enoxaparin is an anticoagulant, so active bleeding or uncorrected coagulopathy outweighs its benefit. Immobility and fractures are reasons to consider prophylaxis once bleeding is controlled.
w: Immobility on a litter for more than 24 hours
A femur fracture splinted in traction
Ventilation through an endotracheal tube

qs.q: Which statement about concentrated potassium chloride is correct?
qs.a: It is not given by IV push and is diluted first
qs.x: Undiluted or rapid IV potassium can cause fatal arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. It is diluted and infused slowly with monitoring.
w: It is pushed quickly to correct low potassium levels
It is safe to give by intramuscular injection
It is the first drug for hyperkalemia

qs.q: Succinylcholine is normally refrigerated. Per its label, how long may it be kept at room temperature?
qs.a: Up to 14 days
qs.x: The succinylcholine label allows room-temperature storage for up to 14 days, so out-of-fridge dates are written on the vial in field kits. Rocuronium has a 60-day allowance.
w: Up to 6 months
Up to 1 year
Up to 6 hours

qs.q: Rocuronium is normally refrigerated. Per its label, how long may it be kept at room temperature after removal?
qs.a: Up to 60 days
qs.x: Rocuronium may be stored at room temperature for 60 days after removal from refrigeration. Marking the date keeps a field kit current.
w: Up to 24 hours
Up to 7 days
Up to 2 years

qs.q: A team is still receiving effective enemy fire when a teammate is shot in the thigh with bright red, spurting bleeding. What is the priority in this phase of care?
qs.a: Return fire, then apply a limb tourniquet high and tight
qs.x: In Care Under Fire, fire superiority and a rapidly applied tourniquet for life-threatening extremity bleeding are the only interventions; airway care, packing and full exposure wait for Tactical Field Care.
w: Open the airway with a jaw thrust before addressing the bleeding
Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze and hold pressure for 3 minutes
Expose the wound fully and apply a pressure dressing

qs.q: What does the MARCH sequence stand for in TCCC?
qs.a: Massive hemorrhage, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia and head injury
qs.x: MARCH puts massive hemorrhage first because extremity bleeding is the leading preventable cause of combat death, ahead of airway problems.
w: Mechanism, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hemorrhage
Massive hemorrhage, Analgesia, Resuscitation, Cervical spine, Hypothermia prevention
Mental status, Airway, Respiration, Cardiac, Heat injury

qs.q: After MARCH is complete in Tactical Field Care, what does PAWS cover?
qs.a: Pain, Antibiotics, Wounds, Splinting
qs.x: PAWS is the secondary set of tasks after life threats: pain control, antibiotics for open wounds, wound reassessment and dressing, and splinting of fractures.
w: Pulses, Airway, Warming, Spine
Positioning, Analgesia, Wound packing, Shock
Pressure, Antibiotics, Wound closure, Sedation

qs.q: Which phase of TCCC begins once the casualty and team are no longer under effective hostile fire?
qs.a: Tactical Field Care
qs.x: Tactical Field Care starts when the immediate threat is suppressed, allowing a full MARCH assessment; TACEVAC care begins once the casualty is on an evacuation platform.
w: Care Under Fire
Tactical Evacuation Care
Prolonged Casualty Care

qs.q: In Tactical Field Care, a casualty has a hasty tourniquet high on the thigh over the uniform. The wound is now exposed and is 5 cm above the knee. What is the next best step?
qs.a: Place a deliberate tourniquet on skin 5 to 8 cm above the wound, then loosen the hasty one
qs.x: Hasty tourniquets placed over clothing are replaced by a deliberate one on skin 5 to 8 cm above the wound, minimizing the amount of limb at risk; removing a tourniquet without a replacement risks fatal rebleeding.
w: Leave the hasty tourniquet in place, unchanged, until arrival at a surgical facility
Remove the hasty tourniquet and watch for rebleeding before deciding
Add a pressure dressing over the hasty tourniquet to reinforce it

qs.q: A tourniquet has been tightened on a casualty's leg, but a distal pulse is still present and bleeding continues. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Tighten further or apply a second tourniquet just above the first
qs.x: A tourniquet that leaves a distal pulse is not occluding arterial flow and can increase bleeding by blocking venous return; tighten it or add a second one side by side above it.
w: Loosen it and convert to a pressure dressing
Elevate the leg and wait for clotting to occur
Move the tourniquet below the knee to compress the artery more directly

qs.q: Which situation is a contraindication to tourniquet conversion in the field?
qs.a: The casualty is in hemorrhagic shock
qs.x: Conversion is not attempted when the casualty is in shock, cannot be closely monitored, or has a traumatic amputation; a short tourniquet time is actually a good reason to attempt conversion.
w: The tourniquet has been on for 45 minutes
The wound can be packed with hemostatic gauze
The casualty is awake and reporting pain

qs.q: Within what time frame does TCCC aim to reassess and, when appropriate, convert a tourniquet to reduce ischemic injury?
qs.a: Within 2 hours of application
qs.x: TCCC aims to convert eligible tourniquets within 2 hours, since ischemic nerve and muscle injury rises with time; tourniquets in place longer than about 6 hours are generally left for surgical teams.
w: Within 15 minutes of application
Within 12 hours of application
Only after arrival at a Role 3 facility

qs.q: A casualty has a gunshot wound to the groin with heavy bleeding that a limb tourniquet cannot control. What is the best initial treatment?
qs.a: Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze and hold firm pressure
qs.x: Junctional wounds are controlled with hemostatic gauze packed into the wound and firm pressure for at least 3 minutes, followed by a junctional tourniquet if available; a limb tourniquet cannot reach the bleeding vessel.
w: Apply a limb tourniquet as high as possible on the thigh
Apply a pressure dressing without packing and elevate the leg
Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the iliac crests and elevate the legs

qs.q: What is the purpose of holding firm pressure for at least 3 minutes after packing Combat Gauze into a wound?
qs.a: To let the hemostatic agent and a clot form at the bleeding site
qs.x: Hemostatic dressings work by speeding clot formation where they contact the bleeding vessel, which needs sustained pressure; releasing early dislodges the forming clot.
w: To let the casualty adjust to the pain of packing before evacuation
To check whether a tourniquet is still needed above it
To dry the wound so the dressing adheres to skin

qs.q: A casualty has a deep, narrow fragment wound in the axilla with brisk bleeding. Gauze packing is difficult because of the small entry tract. Which device is designed for this wound?
qs.a: An expanding mini-sponge injector (XStat)
qs.x: XStat injects compressed expanding sponges into deep, narrow junctional wound tracts where gauze packing is hard; a limb tourniquet cannot occlude an axillary vessel.
w: A limb tourniquet applied around the upper arm
A vented chest seal placed over the wound
A cervical collar to stabilize the area

qs.q: A casualty with a suspected unstable pelvic fracture after a blast is hypotensive. Where is a pelvic binder placed?
qs.a: Over the greater trochanters
qs.x: A pelvic binder is centered over the greater trochanters to close the pelvic ring and reduce venous bleeding; placement at the iliac crests is a common error that does not reduce pelvic volume.
w: Over the iliac crests at the waistline
Over the lower abdomen just above the pubis
Around the upper thighs below the groin

qs.q: An unconscious casualty is breathing without airway obstruction after a gunshot wound to the leg. What is the most appropriate airway management in Tactical Field Care?
qs.a: Chin lift or jaw thrust and an NPA, then place in the recovery position
qs.x: An unconscious casualty without obstruction is managed with simple maneuvers, a nasopharyngeal airway and the recovery position; invasive airways are reserved for failure of these measures or obstruction.
w: Immediate surgical cricothyroidotomy before any other airway step
Endotracheal intubation before any other intervention
No airway intervention until evacuation arrives

qs.q: A conscious casualty with severe maxillofacial injuries is bleeding into his mouth and struggling to breathe while lying flat. What is the best first step?
qs.a: Let him sit up and lean forward
qs.x: A conscious casualty with facial trauma often protects his own airway best sitting up and leaning forward so blood drains out; forcing him supine can cause obstruction.
w: Lay him supine and apply a cervical collar to protect the spine
Perform an immediate surgical cricothyroidotomy
Insert an NPA through the injured nose

qs.q: Which landmark identifies the site for a surgical cricothyroidotomy?
qs.a: The membrane between the thyroid cartilage and the cricoid cartilage
qs.x: The cricothyroid membrane lies just below the thyroid cartilage and above the cricoid ring; incision above the thyroid cartilage or below the cricoid risks vessels and the thyroid gland.
w: The space between the cricoid cartilage and the first tracheal ring
The notch at the top of the sternum
The membrane between the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage

qs.q: A casualty with massive facial trauma has an obstructed airway that cannot be cleared, and an NPA and positioning have failed. What is the next step in TCCC?
qs.a: Surgical cricothyroidotomy
qs.x: When the upper airway cannot be opened by simpler means, especially with facial destruction, surgical cricothyroidotomy is the definitive field airway in TCCC.
w: Repeated attempts at nasal intubation
Needle decompression of the chest
High-flow oxygen by face mask

qs.q: After a surgical cricothyroidotomy, which method best confirms the tube is in the trachea?
qs.a: Waveform capnography showing a sustained EtCO2 trace
qs.x: A sustained capnography waveform is the most reliable confirmation of tracheal placement; tube fogging and color change occur with misplaced tubes, and SpO2 lags behind by a minute or more.
w: Fogging inside the tube during each exhalation
Pulse oximetry rising within 10 seconds of the first breath
The casualty's skin color improving over the next minute

qs.q: A casualty with a penetrating chest wound develops progressive respiratory distress, absent breath sounds on the injured side and a weak radial pulse. What is the treatment?
qs.a: Needle decompression on the injured side
qs.x: Progressive distress with unilateral absent breath sounds and shock after torso trauma is presumed tension pneumothorax, treated by decompressing the injured side.
w: A second chest seal over the first
Fluid bolus and reassess in 15 minutes
Needle decompression on the uninjured side

qs.q: Which needle decompression sites does TCCC accept for suspected tension pneumothorax?
qs.a: 5th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line or 2nd intercostal space at the midclavicular line
qs.x: TCCC lists the 5th ICS anterior axillary line and the 2nd ICS midclavicular line; staying lateral to the nipple line in the 2nd space avoids the heart and great vessels.
w: 2nd intercostal space at the anterior axillary line or 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line
4th intercostal space at the sternal border only
7th intercostal space at the posterior axillary line only

qs.q: When performing needle decompression, why is the needle passed over the top of the rib below the chosen space?
qs.a: The nerve, artery and vein run along the lower rib edge
qs.x: The neurovascular bundle runs in the groove under each rib, so entering over the superior margin of the lower rib avoids lacerating the intercostal vessels.
w: The parietal pleura is thinnest along the upper border of each rib
It places the needle tip directly into the lung tissue
It reduces the depth of the needle needed by half

qs.q: What needle and catheter length does TCCC recommend for needle decompression in adults?
qs.a: A 3.25-inch, 10- or 14-gauge needle-catheter
qs.x: Short catheters often fail to reach the pleural space in muscular, armored service members, so TCCC specifies a 3.25-inch, 10- or 14-gauge device.
w: A 2-inch, 22-gauge needle-catheter from a standard IV start kit
A 2-inch, 22-gauge needle-catheter
A 6-inch spinal needle of any gauge

qs.q: A casualty has an open chest wound that is sucking air. What is the initial treatment?
qs.a: Apply a vented or non-vented chest seal and monitor for tension pneumothorax
qs.x: An open pneumothorax is sealed with a vented or non-vented occlusive dressing; the casualty is then watched for tension, which is managed by burping or removing the seal or needle decompression.
w: Pack the wound tightly with hemostatic gauze and cover it with tape
Leave the wound open to allow air to escape
Immediately perform a finger thoracostomy through the wound

qs.q: After a non-vented chest seal is applied, the casualty becomes more short of breath and hypotensive. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Burp or remove the seal, and decompress if signs persist
qs.x: Rising distress and shock after sealing a chest wound suggest tension pneumothorax; releasing the seal lets air escape, and needle decompression follows if that fails.
w: Apply a second non-vented seal over the first
Give a fluid bolus and recheck in 30 minutes
Place the casualty supine with legs elevated

qs.q: During prolonged care, a casualty has had two needle decompressions for a recurring tension pneumothorax. What is the next definitive field procedure for a trained provider?
qs.a: Finger thoracostomy at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior to the midaxillary line
qs.x: When needle decompression fails or tension recurs, an open finger thoracostomy at the 4th to 5th ICS just anterior to the midaxillary line creates a larger opening that does not kink or clot off.
w: A third needle decompression in the same 2nd intercostal space at the midclavicular line
A chest seal over the needle site
Pericardiocentesis below the xiphoid process

qs.q: Which two findings does TCCC use as the primary field signs of hemorrhagic shock?
qs.a: Altered mental status without head injury and a weak or absent radial pulse
qs.x: In the field, decreased mental status not explained by TBI and a weak or absent radial pulse are the practical triggers for resuscitation in TCCC.
w: Bradycardia below 60 with warm, flushed skin over the trunk and limbs
Elevated blood pressure and pinpoint pupils
Fever above 38.5 degrees C and a productive cough

qs.q: A casualty in hemorrhagic shock is ready for resuscitation. What is the preferred fluid in current TCCC guidance?
qs.a: Cold-stored low-titer O whole blood
qs.x: Whole blood replaces volume, oxygen carrying capacity and clotting factors at once; crystalloids and colloids dilute clotting factors and are not used for hemorrhagic shock when blood is available.
w: Lactated Ringer solution warmed to body temperature
Hetastarch
Normal saline

qs.q: If whole blood is unavailable, what does TCCC list next for a casualty in hemorrhagic shock?
qs.a: Plasma, red cells and platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio
qs.x: Component therapy in a balanced 1:1:1 ratio approximates whole blood; plasma or red cells alone come next, and crystalloid is a last resort.
w: Hetastarch followed by red cells
Lactated Ringer's solution until the radial pulse returns
Red cells alone without plasma

qs.q: What is the end point for blood product resuscitation in a casualty with hemorrhagic shock and no head injury?
qs.a: Improved mental status and a palpable radial pulse
qs.x: TCCC uses permissive hypotension until surgical control: restore mentation and a radial pulse without driving pressure high enough to dislodge clots.
w: A systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg
A heart rate below 60 beats per minute
Clear urine output of at least 200 mL per hour

qs.q: Why does TCCC recommend giving calcium with the first blood product in hemorrhagic shock?
qs.a: Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and low calcium impairs clotting and contraction
qs.x: Hypocalcemia is common on arrival in severe trauma and worsens with citrated products; calcium supports clotting and myocardial function.
w: Calcium prevents febrile and allergic transfusion reactions to low-titer O whole blood
Calcium raises the core temperature of a hypothermic casualty
Calcium neutralizes the potassium released from burned tissue

qs.q: Why is permissive hypotension avoided in a casualty who has a traumatic brain injury and hemorrhagic shock?
qs.a: Low blood pressure reduces cerebral perfusion and worsens secondary brain injury
qs.x: A single episode of hypotension is linked to markedly worse outcomes in TBI, so resuscitation targets a normal radial pulse and an adequate systolic pressure instead of permissive hypotension.
w: Low blood pressure raises intracranial pressure directly by compressing the brainstem
Blood products cannot be used in casualties with TBI
Permissive hypotension causes hyperkalemia in brain injury

qs.q: Which factors form the lethal triad of trauma?
qs.a: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy
qs.x: Cold, acid and clotting failure each worsen the others; prevention of heat loss and early blood products interrupt the cycle.
w: Hypoxia, hypertension and bradycardia
Hyperthermia, alkalosis and anemia
Hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia and tachycardia

qs.q: A casualty has a heart rate of 130 and a systolic blood pressure of 100. What is the shock index, and what does it suggest?
qs.a: 1.3, suggesting significant hemorrhage
qs.x: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure; values above about 1.0 suggest substantial blood loss even when the blood pressure still appears acceptable.
w: 0.8, which is within the normal range for a fit adult
2.3, suggesting cardiogenic shock
0.3, suggesting overhydration

qs.q: In which casualty does TCCC recommend tranexamic acid?
qs.a: Hemorrhagic shock or signs of significant TBI, within 3 hours of injury
qs.x: TXA reduces bleeding death when given early; benefit is greatest in the first hour, and use after 3 hours was associated with harm in CRASH-2.
w: Any casualty with a minor laceration to reduce dressing changes
A casualty with significant bleeding more than 6 hours after injury
Only casualties who have already received a massive transfusion of blood products

qs.q: Before transfusing fresh whole blood from a walking blood bank, which donor issue is a key safety concern?
qs.a: ABO compatibility and screening for transfusion-transmitted infection
qs.x: Fresh whole blood is collected under field conditions, so correct ABO matching and prescreened, tested donors are central to avoiding hemolytic reactions and infections.
w: The donor's caffeine and energy drink intake during the past day
The donor's rank and duty position
Whether the donor has eaten in the past 2 hours

qs.q: Why is crystalloid avoided as the primary fluid for hemorrhagic shock?
qs.a: It dilutes clotting factors and worsens acidosis and hypothermia
qs.x: Large crystalloid volumes cause dilutional coagulopathy, edema and acidosis; blood products restore oxygen delivery and clotting.
w: It contains too much potassium for most casualties with kidney injury
It is too viscous to run through an IO needle
It cannot be warmed before infusion

qs.q: During a whole blood transfusion, a casualty develops sudden fever, hypotension and dark urine. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Stop the transfusion and treat a suspected hemolytic reaction
qs.x: Fever, hypotension and hemoglobinuria during transfusion suggest an acute hemolytic reaction; stopping the product and supporting circulation are the first actions.
w: Speed up the transfusion to correct the hypotension and recheck in 15 minutes
Add calcium and continue the same bag of blood
Give antibiotics and continue the transfusion

qs.q: Which device is used to warm blood products in the field to help prevent hypothermia?
qs.a: A portable inline fluid warmer
qs.x: Inline warmers deliver blood at body temperature; cold products are a major source of heat loss in casualties already at risk of the lethal triad.
w: A chemical heat pack placed directly on the IV bag
A heated blanket wrapped around the IO site
A vacuum mattress

qs.q: A casualty with a head injury has a GCS that drops from 13 to 9, a dilated right pupil and left-sided weakness. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Impending transtentorial herniation
qs.x: A falling GCS with a unilateral dilated pupil and opposite-side weakness are signs of brain herniation requiring urgent measures to lower intracranial pressure and rapid evacuation.
w: A simple concussion that will resolve
A spinal cord injury in the neck
Alcohol intoxication

qs.q: A casualty shows signs of herniation after head trauma. Which temporary measures are used in the field?
qs.a: Hypertonic saline, head up 30 degrees, brief hyperventilation to EtCO2 30 to 35 mmHg
qs.x: Hypertonic saline and head elevation lower ICP; mild hyperventilation is used only briefly for herniation because deep hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia.
w: Lay flat, restrict fluids and hold ventilations
Hyperventilate to an EtCO2 below 20 mmHg for the whole evacuation and lay flat
Place in Trendelenburg position and give hypotonic fluids

qs.q: For a casualty with TBI and no signs of herniation, what EtCO2 target is maintained during ventilation?
qs.a: 35 to 40 mmHg
qs.x: Normocapnia preserves cerebral blood flow; hyperventilation is reserved for active herniation, and hypoventilation raises ICP through vasodilation.
w: 20 to 25 mmHg
45 to 55 mmHg
10 to 15 mmHg

qs.q: Which oxygen saturation target is maintained in a casualty with a traumatic brain injury?
qs.a: At least 90 percent
qs.x: Hypoxia below 90 percent is strongly linked to worse outcome after TBI, so oxygen and airway support aim to keep saturation at or above 90 percent.
w: At least 75 percent
Between 80 and 85 percent
Any value as long as he is breathing

qs.q: A casualty with a closed head injury has a blood pressure of 190/100, a heart rate of 48 and irregular respirations. What is this pattern called?
qs.a: Cushing triad
qs.x: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing form the Cushing triad, a late sign of rising intracranial pressure; Beck triad describes cardiac tamponade.
w: Beck triad
Neurogenic shock
Virchow triad

qs.q: A casualty was shot in the neck and is awake, breathing well and moving all limbs. What is the TCCC approach to spinal immobilization?
qs.a: Spinal immobilization is not used for isolated penetrating injury
qs.x: Spinal injury after penetrating trauma is rarely unstable, and immobilization can hide neck wounds and delay airway care; it is reserved for blunt mechanisms with suspected spinal injury.
w: Full spinal immobilization on a long board before moving
A cervical collar and head blocks for all neck wounds
Keep the casualty sitting upright without moving his neck for transport

qs.q: A casualty fell from a vehicle rollover and has neck pain and numbness in his hands. What is the appropriate approach?
qs.a: Spinal motion restriction during movement and evacuation
qs.x: Blunt mechanisms with neck pain or neurologic signs call for spinal motion restriction; penetrating injury alone is where TCCC drops routine immobilization.
w: No spinal precautions because the injury is blunt
Have him walk to the evacuation point to assess function
Apply traction to the neck to relieve pressure

qs.q: A casualty with a suspected cervical spinal cord injury has a blood pressure of 78/40, a heart rate of 54 and warm, dry skin below the injury. What is the likely cause?
qs.a: Neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone
qs.x: High cord injury removes sympathetic outflow, causing hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin; hemorrhage usually causes tachycardia and cool skin, and hemorrhage is excluded before attributing shock to the cord.
w: Hemorrhagic shock from internal bleeding
Septic shock from wound infection
Cardiogenic shock from a cardiac contusion

qs.q: Using the rule of nines, what is the TBSA of partial- and full-thickness burns covering the entire front of the torso and the whole of one arm?
qs.a: 27 percent
qs.x: In the adult rule of nines the anterior trunk is 18 percent and each arm is 9 percent, for a total of 27 percent.
w: 18 percent
36 percent
45 percent

qs.q: When estimating burn size, which burn depth is excluded from the TBSA calculation?
qs.a: Superficial (first-degree) burns
qs.x: Only partial- and full-thickness burns are counted; superficial burns resembling sunburn do not cause the fluid shifts that drive resuscitation.
w: Superficial partial-thickness burns with blisters
Deep partial-thickness burns
Full-thickness burns

qs.q: For small or scattered burns, what is the approximate TBSA of the casualty's own palm including the fingers?
qs.a: 1 percent
qs.x: The palm including the fingers approximates 1 percent of body surface area, which helps estimate irregular burns that do not fit the rule of nines.
w: 5 percent
9 percent
0.1 percent

qs.q: Using the USAISR Rule of Ten, what is the initial fluid rate for a 70 kg casualty with 40 percent TBSA burns?
qs.a: 400 mL per hour
qs.x: The Rule of Ten multiplies TBSA by 10 to give mL per hour for adults 40 to 80 kg: 40 x 10 = 400 mL per hour, adjusted later to urine output.
w: 40 mL per hour
700 mL per hour
2800 mL per hour

qs.q: Using the USAISR Rule of Ten, what is the initial fluid rate for a 100 kg casualty with 30 percent TBSA burns?
qs.a: 500 mL per hour
qs.x: The rate is TBSA x 10 (300 mL per hour) plus 100 mL per hour for every 10 kg above 80 kg (200 mL per hour), giving 500 mL per hour.
w: 300 mL per hour
1000 mL per hour
3000 mL per hour

qs.q: In TCCC, above what burn size is fluid resuscitation started in the field?
qs.a: Greater than 20 percent TBSA
qs.x: TCCC starts burn fluid resuscitation when partial- and full-thickness burns exceed 20 percent TBSA; hemorrhagic shock in a burned casualty is treated with blood first.
w: Greater than 5 percent TBSA
Greater than 50 percent TBSA
Any burn regardless of size

qs.q: Which urine output target is used to adjust fluid resuscitation in an adult burn casualty?
qs.a: 30 to 50 mL per hour
qs.x: Adult burn fluids are titrated to 30 to 50 mL per hour of urine; less suggests under-resuscitation and much more suggests fluid creep, which causes edema and compartment syndromes.
w: 5 to 10 mL per hour
150 to 200 mL per hour
Urine output is not used to guide burn fluids

qs.q: A casualty pulled from a burning vehicle has singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth and a hoarse voice. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Inhalation injury with risk of rapid airway swelling
qs.x: Facial burns with soot, hoarseness or stridor signal inhalation injury; swelling can close the airway over hours, so early definitive airway control is considered before evacuation.
w: A simple superficial facial burn
Anxiety-related hyperventilation
Isolated carbon monoxide exposure with no airway risk

qs.q: A casualty from an enclosed-space fire has a headache and confusion, and the pulse oximeter reads 99 percent. Why is the reading misleading?
qs.a: Standard oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin
qs.x: Carbon monoxide-bound hemoglobin reads as saturated on standard oximeters, so a normal SpO2 does not exclude CO poisoning; high-flow oxygen is given.
w: Pulse oximeters read falsely low in all burn casualties because of skin damage
Fire smoke speeds the pulse oximeter's light signal
Confusion alters the sensor's detection of saturation

qs.q: A casualty has circumferential full-thickness burns of the chest, and ventilation is becoming difficult with rising airway pressures. What procedure addresses this?
qs.a: Escharotomy of the chest wall
qs.x: Rigid circumferential eschar restricts chest expansion; escharotomy through the burned tissue releases it. Extra fluids worsen edema and do not relieve the constriction.
w: Needle decompression on both sides
Tighter chest bandaging
Increase the fluid rate

qs.q: Which finding in a limb with a circumferential full-thickness burn suggests the need for escharotomy?
qs.a: Progressive loss of distal pulses and capillary refill
qs.x: As edema builds under inelastic eschar, distal perfusion fails; loss of pulses or delayed capillary refill indicates escharotomy is needed to restore circulation.
w: Blisters forming on the unburned skin surrounding the circumferential burn
Pain at the edges of the burn
Mild redness above the burn

qs.q: A casualty with 45 percent TBSA burns from 4 days ago needs rapid sequence intubation. Which paralytic is avoided?
qs.a: Succinylcholine
qs.x: Upregulated acetylcholine receptors after burns cause a dangerous potassium surge with succinylcholine beginning roughly 24 to 48 hours after injury; rocuronium is the usual alternative.
w: Rocuronium
Both paralytics are equally safe
Neither paralytic can be used after burns

qs.q: Which other conditions share the same succinylcholine risk as major burns?
qs.a: Crush injury and prolonged immobilization
qs.x: Denervation, massive muscle injury and prolonged immobility upregulate receptors and can cause life-threatening hyperkalemia with succinylcholine.
w: Simple fractures treated within 1 hour
Isolated eye injuries
Mild dehydration

qs.q: What is the correct way to cool a fresh burn in the field?
qs.a: Stop the burning, cover with dry sterile dressings and prevent hypothermia
qs.x: Burned casualties lose heat rapidly through damaged skin; ice, prolonged wet dressings and open exposure drive hypothermia, which worsens coagulopathy and mortality, while ointments and butter trap heat and contaminate the wound.
w: Apply butter or a thick ointment and leave the burn open to the air
Apply butter or ointment and leave open to air
Keep the burn wet with soaked dressings during evacuation

qs.q: A casualty has an open tibia fracture with bone visible. What is part of field management?
qs.a: Cover with a dressing, splint, and give TCCC open-wound antibiotics
qs.x: Open fractures are dressed, splinted in position and treated early with antibiotics; reducing contaminated bone back into the wound and tourniquets for non-severe bleeding add harm.
w: Push the bone back under the skin before splinting
Push the exposed bone back under the skin before applying the splint
Apply a tourniquet routinely for all open fractures

qs.q: What is checked before and after applying a splint to an injured limb?
qs.a: Distal pulse, motor function and sensation
qs.x: Splints can compress vessels and nerves, so distal circulation, movement and sensation are checked before and after, and the splint is loosened if they worsen.
w: Blood pressure on the injured limb
Core temperature
Pupil response

qs.q: Which finding is an early sign of acute compartment syndrome in an injured leg?
qs.a: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain with passive stretch
qs.x: Pain with passive stretch and disproportionate pain occur early; loss of pulses and paralysis are late findings once damage is advanced.
w: Loss of the distal pulse in the foot compared with the uninjured side
Complete paralysis of the foot
Pale, cold toes

qs.q: Which compartment pressure finding supports the diagnosis of acute compartment syndrome?
qs.a: A diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure of less than 30 mmHg
qs.x: A delta pressure (diastolic minus compartment) below 30 mmHg indicates inadequate perfusion and supports fasciotomy; low compartment pressures are normal.
w: A compartment pressure below 10 mmHg
A mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg
A difference of more than 60 mmHg between systolic and compartment pressure

qs.q: During prolonged care, a casualty with a crush injury of the leg is suspected of compartment syndrome. What is avoided while awaiting surgical care?
qs.a: Elevating the limb well above the level of the heart
qs.x: Elevation above the heart lowers arterial inflow and worsens compartment perfusion; the limb is kept at heart level and constricting dressings are loosened.
w: Removing tight dressings, casts or circumferential wraps from the limb
Frequent reassessment of the limb
Documenting the time symptoms started

qs.q: A casualty's legs were trapped under rubble for 6 hours. Just after release, he develops weakness and peaked T waves on the monitor. What is the likely cause?
qs.a: Hyperkalemia from potassium released by damaged muscle
qs.x: Reperfusion of crushed muscle releases potassium, acid and myoglobin; peaked T waves suggest hyperkalemia, which can cause sudden cardiac arrest.
w: Hypoglycemia from prolonged fasting while he was trapped under the rubble
Hypothermia from exposure
A tension pneumothorax

qs.q: Before releasing a casualty from prolonged entrapment of a limb, what is the priority when possible?
qs.a: Start IV fluids and prepare to treat hyperkalemia
qs.x: Fluids before release help dilute the potassium and myoglobin surge; cardiac monitoring and medications for hyperkalemia are ready for release.
w: Give oral water only after release
Withhold fluids to avoid swelling
Apply ice to the limb

qs.q: Which medication class is given first to stabilize the heart during hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
qs.a: IV calcium
qs.x: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes; insulin with dextrose, albuterol and sodium bicarbonate shift potassium into cells afterward.
w: IV potassium chloride
IV succinylcholine
Oral famotidine

qs.q: A crush casualty has dark, tea-colored urine. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis
qs.x: Myoglobin from broken-down muscle colors the urine and can injure the kidneys; aggressive fluids to maintain high urine output are the main field treatment.
w: Normal concentrated urine
Dehydration only
Urinary tract infection

qs.q: A casualty has a penetrating eye injury with a fragment embedded in the globe. What is the best field treatment?
qs.a: A rigid eye shield without pressure, plus oral antibiotics
qs.x: Pressure on an open globe can extrude eye contents, so a rigid shield is used; TCCC lists moxifloxacin for penetrating eye injuries.
w: Remove the fragment carefully and apply a tight gauze pressure patch
Irrigate forcefully to wash the fragment out
Apply a tight gauze pressure dressing

qs.q: A casualty has a chemical splash to the eye. What is the first step?
qs.a: Immediate copious irrigation with clean water
qs.x: Chemical injuries are the exception where immediate, prolonged irrigation is the priority, since damage continues while the chemical remains on the eye.
w: Rigid eye shield and wait for evacuation
Instill a neutralizing acid or base
Pressure patch the eye closed

qs.q: A casualty has an abdominal wound with loops of bowel protruding. What is the best field management?
qs.a: Cover with a moist sterile dressing and do not push the bowel back in
qs.x: Eviscerated bowel is kept moist and covered; reducing it in the field risks contamination and injury, while dry gauze sticks and damages tissue.
w: Gently push the bowel back into the abdomen and close the wound with tape
Leave uncovered to allow inspection
Cover with a dry, adherent gauze dressing

qs.q: Which blast injury mechanism causes most wounds in combat casualties?
qs.a: Secondary blast injury from fragments and debris
qs.x: Fragments propelled by the explosion (secondary blast injury) cause most combat wounds; primary blast injury affects air-filled organs.
w: Primary blast injury from the pressure wave
Quaternary blast injury from burns and toxins
Tertiary blast injury from being thrown

qs.q: Which organs are most vulnerable to primary blast injury from the pressure wave?
qs.a: Air-filled organs such as the lungs, ears and bowel
qs.x: The blast wave damages tissue at air-fluid interfaces, causing blast lung, eardrum rupture and bowel injury.
w: Solid organs such as the liver and spleen
Long bones of the legs
The skin and fat layers only

qs.q: After a close blast, a casualty without visible chest wounds develops shortness of breath, hemoptysis and falling oxygen saturation. What is the likely cause?
qs.a: Blast lung from primary blast injury
qs.x: Blast lung presents with dyspnea, hemoptysis and hypoxia, sometimes hours after exposure; aggressive fluid use is avoided because it worsens pulmonary edema.
w: Heat exhaustion
Anxiety hyperventilation
Isolated eardrum rupture

qs.q: Which item is part of the hypothermia prevention kit used in TCCC?
qs.a: An active heating blanket and heat-reflective shell
qs.x: Hypothermia prevention uses active heating and an insulating, heat-reflective barrier; wet materials and exposure increase heat loss.
w: An ice pack and a fan
A wet blanket to reduce burns
An open-sided litter cover

qs.q: When is hypothermia prevention started for a casualty in TCCC?
qs.a: As early as possible, regardless of the environment or ambient temperature
qs.x: Trauma casualties lose heat even in warm climates; hypothermia worsens clotting, so prevention starts early in all environments.
w: Only after the core temperature has fallen below 32 degrees C
Only after the core temperature falls below 32 degrees C
Only after arrival at surgical care

qs.q: A soldier collapses during a ruck march in the heat. He is confused and combative with a core temperature of 41.2 degrees C. What is the best treatment?
qs.a: Immediate whole-body cold water immersion, cooling before evacuation
qs.x: Exertional heat stroke is treated with rapid cooling on site, since survival depends on time above 40 degrees C; antipyretics do not work on heat stroke.
w: Oral fluids and shade, then reassess core temperature in 30 minutes
Transport first, then cool at the hospital
Give acetaminophen to lower the temperature

qs.q: What distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
qs.a: Altered mental status with a core temperature above 40 degrees C
qs.x: Heat stroke involves altered mental status with high core temperature, while heat exhaustion has normal mental status; sweating may persist in exertional heat stroke.
w: Heavy sweating with pale, moist skin and a rapid, weak pulse
Painful muscle cramps in the legs and abdomen after exertion
Feeling tired and thirsty

qs.q: A soldier who drank large volumes of water during a long training event is confused and vomiting with a normal core temperature. What is the likely cause?
qs.a: Exertional hyponatremia
qs.x: Excess water intake with salt loss dilutes serum sodium, causing confusion and seizures; giving more water worsens it, and hypertonic saline treats severe cases.
w: Heat stroke
Hypoglycemia
Dehydration

qs.q: A soldier has a frostbitten foot during a mountain operation, and evacuation will require walking through snow. What is the best approach?
qs.a: Avoid rewarming until there is no risk of refreezing
qs.x: Thaw-refreeze cycles cause far more tissue damage than delayed thawing; rubbing and high heat also injure tissue.
w: Rewarm by rubbing the foot vigorously
Rewarm in hot water above 45 degrees C
Rewarm with a fire and then walk

qs.q: Which water temperature is used for rapid rewarming of frostbite?
qs.a: 37 to 39 degrees C
qs.x: Warm water at about 37 to 39 degrees C rewarms frozen tissue quickly without burning it; hotter water causes injury in numb tissue.
w: 20 to 25 degrees C
45 to 50 degrees C
Ice water

qs.q: A soldier has cold, swollen, numb feet after days in wet, non-freezing conditions. What is the diagnosis?
qs.a: Non-freezing cold injury (trench foot)
qs.x: Prolonged cold, wet exposure above freezing causes nerve and vessel injury known as trench foot; it is prevented by dry socks and foot care.
w: Frostbite
Cellulitis
Compartment syndrome

qs.q: A severely hypothermic casualty with a core temperature of 27 degrees C is being moved. Why is gentle handling important?
qs.a: Rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation
qs.x: The cold heart is irritable, and rough movement can precipitate ventricular fibrillation; casualties are kept horizontal and handled gently.
w: Rough handling causes frostbite
Rough handling increases shivering
Rough handling lowers blood sugar

qs.q: At 4,000 meters, a soldier develops confusion and ataxia after a headache for 2 days. What is the best treatment?
qs.a: Immediate descent
qs.x: Confusion and ataxia indicate high-altitude cerebral edema; descent is the most important treatment, with oxygen and medications as adjuncts.
w: Continue ascent
Rest at the same altitude
Increase exertion to acclimatize

qs.q: At high altitude, a soldier has worsening breathlessness at rest, a cough with frothy sputum and crackles. What is the likely diagnosis?
qs.a: High-altitude pulmonary edema
qs.x: HAPE causes dyspnea at rest, cough and crackles from fluid in the lungs; descent and oxygen are the main treatment.
w: Acute mountain sickness only
Asthma
Pneumothorax

qs.q: A diver surfaces rapidly and within minutes develops one-sided weakness and confusion. What is the likely cause?
qs.a: Arterial gas embolism
qs.x: Neurologic deficits within minutes of surfacing suggest arterial gas embolism from lung overpressure; treatment is oxygen and urgent recompression.
w: Decompression sickness type I
Nitrogen narcosis
Hypothermia

qs.q: A diver has joint pain several hours after a dive. What is the most important treatment?
qs.a: 100 percent oxygen and recompression in a hyperbaric chamber
qs.x: Decompression sickness is treated with high-flow oxygen and recompression; returning to the water without a chamber is dangerous.
w: Return to depth on the remaining air supply to recompress in the water
Hot shower and rest
Analgesics only

qs.q: A casualty with decompression sickness needs air evacuation. What is a key consideration?
qs.a: Fly at the lowest safe altitude or with cabin pressure near sea level
qs.x: Reduced pressure at altitude enlarges nitrogen bubbles and worsens DCS, so evacuation is low altitude or with a pressurized cabin.
w: Fly as high as possible to shorten the trip and the time to the chamber
Delay evacuation for 24 hours
Altitude does not matter

qs.q: A soldier exposed to a vapor develops pinpoint pupils, runny nose, drooling, wheezing and muscle twitching. What is the likely agent class?
qs.a: Nerve agent (organophosphate)
qs.x: Pinpoint pupils, secretions, bronchospasm and fasciculations are cholinergic signs of nerve agent exposure.
w: Cyanide
Lung agent
Blister agent

qs.q: In nerve agent poisoning, what is the main end point for atropine treatment?
qs.a: Drying of bronchial secretions and easier breathing
qs.x: Atropine is titrated to drying of airway secretions and improved ventilation; pupils and heart rate are unreliable end points.
w: Return of normal pupil size in both eyes after each dose
A heart rate above 140
Complete absence of muscle twitching

qs.q: A casualty exposed to a nerve agent begins seizing. Which medication class is used to treat the seizures?
qs.a: Benzodiazepines
qs.x: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam or midazolam treat nerve agent seizures; atropine does not control them.
w: Opioids
Beta blockers
Antibiotics

qs.q: A soldier in an enclosed space collapses suddenly with seizures, hypotension and bright red skin. What is the likely toxin?
qs.a: Cyanide
qs.x: Cyanide blocks cellular use of oxygen, producing sudden collapse, seizures and cherry-red skin without cyanosis; nerve agents cause miosis and secretions, and phosgene injury is delayed for hours.
w: Nerve agent
Phosgene
Chlorine

qs.q: Which antidote is used for cyanide poisoning in a casualty from a smoke-filled enclosed space?
qs.a: Hydroxocobalamin
qs.x: Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted; it causes red discoloration of skin and urine.
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Atropine

qs.q: Several hours after exposure to a gas that smelled like fresh-mown hay, a soldier develops severe shortness of breath and frothy sputum. What is the likely agent?
qs.a: Phosgene
qs.x: Phosgene smells like fresh-mown hay and causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema hours after a quiet exposure; exertion accelerates it, so exposed soldiers rest and are observed, unlike chlorine, which irritates immediately.
w: Nerve agent
Cyanide
Tear gas

qs.q: What is the first step in decontaminating a casualty exposed to a chemical agent?
qs.a: Remove clothing
qs.x: Removing clothing removes most of the contaminating agent and is the single most effective early decontamination step; washing the skin follows, and covering a contaminated casualty traps vapor against the skin.
w: Apply ointment
Give antibiotics
Cover with a blanket

qs.q: In military mass casualty triage, which category is used for a casualty with injuries so severe that survival is unlikely given available resources?
qs.a: Expectant
qs.x: Expectant casualties have wounds unlikely to be survivable with current resources; they receive comfort care and are reassessed, since the category can change as resources arrive.
w: Immediate
Delayed
Minimal

qs.q: In military triage, which category is used for a casualty who needs life-saving intervention immediately?
qs.a: Immediate
qs.x: Immediate casualties need life-saving intervention now and are likely to survive with it; Delayed casualties need care but can wait, and Minimal casualties have minor wounds.
w: Delayed
Minimal
Expectant

qs.q: Which information is on line 3 of the 9-line MEDEVAC request?
qs.a: Number of patients by precedence
qs.x: Line 3 gives the number of patients by precedence (urgent, urgent-surgical, priority, routine, convenience); location is line 1, special equipment line 4 and marking method line 7.
w: Location of the pickup site
Special equipment required
Method of marking the pickup site

qs.q: What does a MIST report contain?
qs.a: Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment
qs.x: MIST (Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment) is a short structured handoff that gives the receiving team the key facts in a predictable order during evacuation.
w: Medication, Injury, Status, Time
Mental status, Injuries, Signs, Triage
Mechanism, Intervention, Status, Transport

qs.q: Which form is used to document casualty care in TCCC?
qs.a: DD Form 1380 (TCCC Card)
qs.x: The DD Form 1380 TCCC Card travels with the casualty and records injuries, vital signs, tourniquet times and medications so the next level of care can act on them.
w: DD Form 214
SF 600
DA Form 31

qs.q: A male casualty who is 71 inches (180 cm) tall is intubated for prolonged care. Using lung-protective ventilation, what is the target tidal volume range?
qs.a: About 450 to 600 mL
qs.x: Predicted body weight for a male is 50 + 2.3 x (height in inches - 60), about 75 kg here, and 6-8 mL/kg PBW gives roughly 450-600 mL; dosing tidal volume by actual weight or a fixed large volume over-distends the lungs.
w: About 750 to 900 mL
About 300 to 350 mL
About 900 to 1,050 mL

qs.q: On volume assist-control, a ventilated casualty has a plateau pressure of 34 cmH2O. What is the best adjustment?
qs.a: Lower the tidal volume toward 6 mL/kg PBW
qs.x: Plateau pressure reflects alveolar distending pressure and is kept under 30 cmH2O, so tidal volume is reduced (raising the rate to protect minute ventilation); faster flow changes peak, not plateau, and removing PEEP causes derecruitment.
w: Raise the tidal volume to improve CO2 clearance
Increase the inspiratory flow rate only
Remove PEEP entirely to drop the pressure

qs.q: On a volume-control mode, what happens to airway pressures if the casualty's lung compliance falls?
qs.a: Peak and plateau pressures rise at the same set volume
qs.x: Volume control guarantees the set volume, so stiffer lungs show up as higher pressures; a falling tidal volume at fixed pressure describes pressure control instead.
w: Delivered tidal volume falls while pressures stay fixed
The rate automatically drops to compensate
Pressures fall because less air enters the lungs

qs.q: On pressure control ventilation, a casualty develops worsening abdominal distension and stiffer lungs. What change is expected?
qs.a: Delivered tidal volume decreases
qs.x: In pressure control the inspiratory pressure is fixed, so lower compliance means less volume per breath and possible hypoventilation; monitoring exhaled tidal volume and EtCO2 catches it.
w: Peak pressure climbs well above the set level
Delivered tidal volume increases
The respiratory rate doubles on its own

qs.q: Which ventilator mode delivers a set number of mandatory breaths and lets the casualty take additional spontaneous breaths that are not full machine breaths?
qs.a: SIMV
qs.x: SIMV synchronizes mandatory breaths with effort and allows unassisted or pressure-supported spontaneous breaths between them; in assist-control every triggered breath is a full set breath.
w: Assist-control volume
CPAP alone
Pressure control assist-control

qs.q: A casualty on assist-control volume is agitated and triggering at 34 breaths per minute, with rising measured PEEP. What is the main hazard of this mode here?
qs.a: Breath stacking and auto-PEEP from full breaths each trigger
qs.x: Every triggered breath in AC receives the full set volume, so rapid triggering shortens exhalation and traps air; the fix is treating pain, agitation and the cause of tachypnea.
w: Apnea because the mode has no backup rate
Hypercapnia because spontaneous breaths are unsupported
Barotrauma only from the PEEP valve itself

qs.q: Pressure support ventilation is best suited for which casualty?
qs.a: One with an intact respiratory drive being weaned
qs.x: PSV augments only patient-triggered breaths and has no guaranteed rate, so it depends on a reliable drive; paralyzed, deeply sedated or apneic casualties need a mandatory mode.
w: One paralyzed for transport with no drive
One in deep sedation with frequent apnea
One with fresh herniation signs after a TBI

qs.q: On a ventilator, which two settings mainly determine oxygenation?
qs.a: FiO2 and PEEP
qs.x: Oxygenation depends on FiO2 and mean airway pressure, which PEEP drives; rate and tidal volume set minute ventilation and so control CO2.
w: Respiratory rate and tidal volume
Inspiratory flow and trigger sensitivity
Rate and inspiratory time

qs.q: A ventilated casualty's EtCO2 has risen from 38 to 52 mmHg with stable vital signs and a good waveform. Which change most directly lowers CO2?
qs.a: Increase the respiratory rate
qs.x: CO2 removal follows minute ventilation (rate x tidal volume), and raising rate keeps tidal volume lung-protective; FiO2 and PEEP improve oxygenation, not ventilation.
w: Increase the FiO2
Increase the PEEP
Decrease the inspiratory flow

qs.q: A conscious casualty with pulmonary edema after a blast has SpO2 87% on a mask, protects his airway and follows commands. Which noninvasive support adds both inspiratory and expiratory pressure?
qs.a: BiPAP
qs.x: BiPAP gives a higher inspiratory pressure (IPAP) and a lower expiratory pressure (EPAP), assisting ventilation as well as oxygenation; CPAP holds one continuous pressure throughout the cycle.
w: CPAP
High-flow nasal cannula
Simple face mask

qs.q: Which finding makes CPAP or BiPAP unsuitable for a casualty in respiratory distress?
qs.a: Vomiting with a falling level of consciousness
qs.x: Noninvasive ventilation needs a casualty who can protect the airway and cooperate, so vomiting and decreasing mental status point to intubation; hypoxia and tachypnea are the reasons to try it.
w: SpO2 of 89% on supplemental oxygen
Respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute
Bilateral crackles after smoke exposure

qs.q: In the Berlin definition, what PaO2/FiO2 ratio defines severe ARDS?
qs.a: 100 or less
qs.x: Berlin grades ARDS on PEEP of at least 5 as mild (P/F 201-300), moderate (101-200) and severe (100 or less); 400 is near normal lung function.
w: 200 or less
300 or less
400 or less

qs.q: A casualty on 50% FiO2 has a PaO2 of 75 mmHg on an i-STAT blood gas. What is the P/F ratio?
qs.x: P/F = PaO2 divided by FiO2 as a decimal, so 75 / 0.5 = 150, which is moderate ARDS range if the other criteria are met; dividing by the percent or multiplying gives meaningless numbers.

qs.q: In a casualty with ARDS on lung-protective settings, which oxygen saturation target is standard in ARDSNet practice?
qs.x: ARDSNet targets SpO2 88-95% (PaO2 55-80 mmHg) to limit oxygen toxicity and the high FiO2 and PEEP needed to chase 100%; persistent saturations in the low 80s risk hypoxic injury.
w: Any level above 75%

qs.q: A casualty with severe ARDS remains hypoxic with a P/F under 150 despite optimized PEEP and FiO2. Which intervention has shown a mortality benefit?
qs.a: Prone positioning for prolonged sessions
qs.x: The PROSEVA trial showed lower mortality with prolonged prone sessions in severe ARDS; large tidal volumes raise mortality and removing PEEP worsens derecruitment.
w: Increasing tidal volume to 12 mL/kg PBW
Routine high-dose steroids on day one
Removing PEEP to lower intrathoracic pressure

qs.q: When lung-protective ventilation causes the PaCO2 to rise to 55 mmHg with a pH of 7.28 in a casualty without head injury, what is the usual approach?
qs.a: Accept it as permissive hypercapnia
qs.x: Modest respiratory acidosis is tolerated to keep volumes and pressures protective; it is avoided in TBI, where CO2 raises intracranial pressure.
w: Raise tidal volume to 10 mL/kg PBW
Give bicarbonate to normalize the pH
Stop PEEP to improve CO2 clearance

qs.q: How is plateau pressure measured on a ventilated casualty?
qs.a: An inspiratory hold at end inspiration
qs.x: An inspiratory pause removes flow so the reading reflects alveolar pressure; the peak includes airway resistance, and an expiratory hold measures auto-PEEP instead.
w: An expiratory hold at end exhalation
Reading the highest pressure during each breath
Subtracting PEEP from the peak pressure

qs.q: A ventilated casualty suddenly desaturates and the EtCO2 waveform drops to a flat line. What is the first step?
qs.a: Disconnect from the vent and hand-bag with oxygen
qs.x: Sudden deterioration is approached with DOPE (Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment); bagging off the vent separates the casualty from the equipment while tube position and breath sounds are checked.
w: Increase PEEP and FiO2 on the ventilator
Push additional sedation and reassess
Order a chest X-ray before acting

qs.q: A ventilated casualty has a high peak pressure alarm. Peak is 45 cmH2O and plateau is 22 cmH2O. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: Mucus plug or kinked tube
qs.x: A wide gap between peak and plateau means high airway resistance, such as secretions, kinking, biting or bronchospasm; pneumothorax, mainstem intubation and ARDS lower compliance and raise both pressures.
w: Tension pneumothorax
Right mainstem intubation
Worsening ARDS

qs.q: A ventilated blast casualty becomes hypotensive with both peak and plateau pressures rising sharply and absent breath sounds on the left. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Needle decompression of the left chest
qs.x: Rising peak and plateau with unilateral absent breath sounds and shock indicate tension pneumothorax, which positive pressure worsens quickly; suctioning treats resistance problems, not this.
w: Suction the tube and give a bronchodilator
Deflate and reinflate the tube cuff
Lower the alarm limits and observe

qs.q: A ventilated casualty has a low-pressure alarm and the exhaled tidal volume is far below the set volume. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a: A circuit disconnection or cuff leak
qs.x: Low pressure with lost exhaled volume means gas is escaping, so check connections, the cuff and the tube depth; obstruction and pneumothorax set off high-pressure alarms.
w: Bronchospasm with air trapping
Mucus plug in the tube
A tension pneumothorax

qs.q: During transport, an intubated casualty's EtCO2 waveform shows a shark-fin shape with an upsloping plateau. What does this suggest?
qs.a: Bronchospasm or expiratory obstruction
qs.x: The shark-fin shape reflects slow, uneven emptying of narrowed airways, as in asthma or COPD; esophageal placement gives no sustained waveform.
w: Esophageal intubation
Return of spontaneous circulation
Malignant hyperthermia

qs.q: What is the usual target endotracheal tube cuff pressure measured with a manometer?
qs.a: 20 to 30 cmH2O
qs.x: A cuff pressure of 20-30 cmH2O seals the airway while staying below tracheal mucosal perfusion pressure; low pressure allows leaks and aspiration, high pressure causes ischemic injury.
w: 5 to 10 cmH2O
40 to 50 cmH2O
60 to 80 cmH2O

qs.q: When setting the ventilator for an intubated casualty with severe asthma, which strategy is preferred?
qs.a: Low rate with long expiratory time
qs.x: Air trapping is the danger in asthma, so a low rate, short inspiratory time and prolonged exhalation reduce auto-PEEP, with permissive hypercapnia accepted; high rates worsen trapping.
w: High rate to wash out CO2 quickly
Large tidal volumes to open airways
High PEEP to splint the bronchi

qs.q: Minutes after intubation, a casualty with status asthmaticus becomes hypotensive and pressures climb. Breath sounds are equal and quiet. What is the best immediate action?
qs.a: Disconnect the vent to let trapped air escape
qs.x: Dynamic hyperinflation compresses venous return; disconnecting and gently pressing the chest lets trapped air out, then lower rate and longer exhalation prevent recurrence. Higher rate or PEEP worsens it.
w: Increase the rate to improve ventilation
Raise PEEP to recruit collapsed alveoli
Give a fluid bolus and leave settings unchanged

qs.q: How is intrinsic PEEP (auto-PEEP) measured on a ventilated casualty?
qs.a: An end-expiratory hold maneuver
qs.x: An expiratory hold lets alveolar and circuit pressure equilibrate, and the total minus set PEEP is auto-PEEP; an inspiratory hold measures plateau pressure.
w: An end-inspiratory hold maneuver
The peak inspiratory pressure reading
The set PEEP shown on the display

qs.q: An intubated casualty with a moderate TBI and no signs of herniation is being ventilated. What EtCO2 range is the target?
qs.a: 35 to 40 mmHg
qs.x: TCCC and JTS guidance targets normocapnia at 35-40 mmHg; hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia, and hypercapnia raises intracranial pressure.
w: 25 to 30 mmHg
45 to 50 mmHg
50 to 55 mmHg

qs.q: A ventilated TBI casualty develops a unilateral dilated pupil and extensor posturing. Along with hyperosmolar therapy, which ventilation change is a reasonable brief temporizing step?
qs.a: Mild hyperventilation keeping EtCO2 near 30-35
qs.x: Brief, monitored hyperventilation lowers intracranial pressure as a bridge for impending herniation; prolonged or deep hypocapnia under 30 risks cerebral ischemia, and hypercapnia raises ICP.
w: Lower the rate to raise EtCO2 above 45
Remove PEEP and cut FiO2 to room air
Aggressive hyperventilation to EtCO2 of 20

qs.q: Which positioning measure helps lower intracranial pressure in an intubated TBI casualty without spinal concerns?
qs.a: Head of the litter raised about 30 degrees
qs.x: Elevating the head about 30 degrees with the neck midline improves venous drainage; head-down positions and neck flexion or tight collars raise ICP.
w: Flat supine with legs elevated
Trendelenburg to support blood pressure
Lateral position with the neck flexed

qs.q: In a TBI casualty, which pair of secondary insults most worsens outcome and is the focus of prolonged care?
qs.a: Hypotension and hypoxia
qs.x: Even single episodes of hypotension or hypoxia markedly raise TBI mortality, so oxygenation and perfusion are the priorities; an EtCO2 of 38 is within target.
w: Mild fever and anemia
Tachycardia and hypocapnia of 38
Hyperglycemia and bradycardia

qs.q: On the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS), what score describes a casualty who is alert and calm?
qs.x: RASS runs from +4 (combative) to -5 (unarousable), with 0 meaning alert and calm; -3 is moderate sedation with movement to voice but no eye contact.

qs.q: A ventilated casualty opens his eyes and makes eye contact for more than 10 seconds to voice, then drifts off. What is his RASS score?
qs.x: Sustained awakening to voice with eye contact over 10 seconds is -1 (drowsy); -2 is under 10 seconds, -3 is movement without eye contact, and -4 needs physical stimulation.

qs.q: For most ventilated casualties without severe ARDS or paralysis, what sedation target is preferred?
qs.a: Light sedation around RASS 0 to -2
qs.x: Light sedation reduces ventilator days, delirium and hypotension; deep sedation is reserved for specific needs such as neuromuscular blockade or severe dyssynchrony.
w: Deep sedation around RASS -4 to -5
Agitation around RASS +2 to +3
No sedation goal, titrated to vital signs

qs.q: What is the analgesia-first approach to sedation in ventilated casualties?
qs.a: Treat pain first, then add sedatives only as needed
qs.x: Pain drives much of the agitation and ventilator dyssynchrony in trauma, so analgesia comes first and lowers sedative needs; paralysis without sedation risks awareness.
w: Give sedatives first and pain medication later
Avoid analgesics to allow neurologic exams
Use a paralytic in place of sedation

qs.q: A ventilated casualty receives rocuronium for transport. What is the key safety requirement?
qs.a: Adequate sedation and analgesia before and during paralysis
qs.x: Neuromuscular blockers provide no sedation or pain relief, so a paralyzed casualty without them is awake and in pain; paralysis also hides seizures and agitation, making monitoring more important.
w: Stopping all sedation so the exam is reliable
Turning off the high-pressure alarm
Removing the EtCO2 monitor to save battery

qs.q: A hypotensive, intubated casualty in hemorrhagic shock needs ongoing sedation. Which agent best preserves blood pressure?
qs.a: Ketamine
qs.x: Ketamine supports sympathetic tone and is favored for sedation and analgesia in shock; propofol and dexmedetomidine commonly cause hypotension and benzodiazepines add hypotension in shock states.
w: Propofol
Dexmedetomidine
Midazolam infusion

qs.q: Which feature makes dexmedetomidine useful in a ventilated casualty being prepared for extubation?
qs.a: Arousable sedation with little respiratory depression
qs.x: Dexmedetomidine, an alpha-2 agonist, gives cooperative sedation without much respiratory depression; its common effects are bradycardia and hypotension, and it is not suited to deep sedation.
w: Strong analgesia that replaces all opioids
Rapid blood pressure support in shock
Deep sedation for neuromuscular blockade

qs.q: A ventilated casualty has received prolonged high-rate propofol and develops unexplained metabolic acidosis, rising potassium and dark urine. What is suspected?
qs.a: Propofol infusion syndrome
qs.x: Propofol infusion syndrome brings metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, arrhythmias and cardiac failure with prolonged or high-rate use; stopping the infusion is the key step.
w: Serotonin syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Hypoglycemic reaction

qs.q: A casualty on a fentanyl infusion has worsening sedation, pinpoint pupils and a falling respiratory rate after extubation. Which medication reverses this effect?
qs.a: Naloxone
qs.x: Naloxone reverses opioid effects, titrated to breathing rather than full wakefulness; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures.
w: Flumazenil
Glycopyrrolate
Ondansetron

qs.q: A casualty on day 3 of prolonged care has a temperature of 39.2 C (102.6 F), heart rate 124, respiratory rate 26, confusion and SBP 92. Which qSOFA criteria are met?
qs.a: All three: RR 22 or higher, altered mentation, SBP 100 or lower
qs.x: qSOFA uses respiratory rate of 22 or more, altered mentation and SBP of 100 or less; temperature and heart rate are not part of it, and two or more criteria flag high risk.
w: Only the fever and the heart rate
Only the respiratory rate
None, because the SBP is above 90

qs.q: In suspected septic shock, when are antibiotics given relative to recognition?
qs.a: As soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour
qs.x: Each hour of delay in septic shock is linked to higher mortality, so broad-spectrum antibiotics are given within 1 hour; cultures are drawn first only if that causes no delay.
w: After culture results return in 48 hours
Only after fluids fail to correct the BP
Once the fever has lasted 24 hours

qs.q: A wounded casualty becomes septic on day 2 with a contaminated open fracture. Which TCCC/JTS-supported IV option covers broad gram-negative and anaerobic organisms?
qs.a: Ertapenem
qs.x: Ertapenem covers gram-negative, gram-positive and anaerobic organisms and is a TCCC wound antibiotic; oral first-generation cephalosporins and metronidazole alone are too narrow for this.
w: Cephalexin
Cefadroxil
Metronidazole alone

qs.q: A septic casualty remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation. Which vasopressor is first-line?
qs.a: Norepinephrine
qs.x: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock; dopamine causes more arrhythmias, and vasopressin is usually added rather than used alone.
w: Phenylephrine
Dopamine
Vasopressin alone

qs.q: A casualty in prolonged care has a red, warm, tender wound with purulent drainage and fever on day 3. What is the most important step besides antibiotics?
qs.a: Source control by opening and draining the wound
qs.x: Antibiotics penetrate pus poorly, so drainage, debridement and irrigation are the definitive source control; closing an infected wound traps the infection.
w: Closing the wound tightly to keep bacteria out
Applying a tourniquet above the wound
Covering it with an occlusive dressing for a week

qs.q: A casualty with spreading skin discoloration, crepitus and pain out of proportion around a wound on day 2 is suspected of having which condition?
qs.a: Necrotizing soft tissue infection
qs.x: Crepitus, rapid spread and pain out of proportion suggest necrotizing infection, a surgical emergency needing early teleconsult, broad antibiotics and urgent evacuation.
w: Simple cellulitis
Contact dermatitis
Superficial abrasion

qs.q: For a casualty in hemorrhagic shock, which resuscitation fluid does TCCC prefer?
qs.a: Low-titer O whole blood
qs.x: TCCC prefers whole blood, then blood components; crystalloids and colloids dilute clotting factors and worsen coagulopathy, so they are not the fluids for bleeding.
w: Lactated Ringer's
Hetastarch
Normal saline

qs.q: Using the USAISR Rule of Ten, what initial fluid rate is calculated for a 70 kg casualty with a 40% TBSA burn?
qs.a: 400 mL/hr
qs.x: The Rule of Ten multiplies %TBSA by 10 for casualties 40-80 kg, so 40 x 10 = 400 mL/hr; 100 mL/hr is added for every 10 kg above 80 kg.
w: 280 mL/hr
700 mL/hr
1,000 mL/hr

qs.q: Using the Rule of Ten, what initial burn fluid rate is calculated for a 100 kg casualty with a 30% TBSA burn?
qs.a: 500 mL/hr
qs.x: 30 x 10 = 300 mL/hr, plus 100 mL/hr for each 10 kg above 80 kg (2 x 100), totaling 500 mL/hr.
w: 300 mL/hr
1,000 mL/hr
400 mL/hr

qs.q: Using the rule of nines, what TBSA percentage is burned in an adult with full-thickness burns of the entire front of the torso and the entire left arm?
qs.x: The anterior trunk is 18% and one entire arm is 9%, totaling 27%; superficial (first-degree) burns are not counted in TBSA.

qs.q: In an adult burn casualty, what urine output target guides adjustment of burn resuscitation fluids?
qs.a: 30 to 50 mL/hr
qs.x: JTS burn guidance titrates fluids to 30-50 mL/hr of urine in adults; low output signals under-resuscitation, and far higher output signals over-resuscitation and edema.
w: 5 to 10 mL/hr
