qs.q: A casualty with a pelvic injury still has a weak radial pulse after the first unit of whole blood. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.24, PCO2 31 mmHg, HCO3 13 mmol/L, Base excess -15 mmol/L, Lactate 6.8 mmol/L, PO2 94 mmHg. What is the main problem these results point to?
qs.a: Ongoing hemorrhagic shock with lactic acidosis and breathing compensation
qs.x: Low pH, low bicarbonate, a deep base deficit and high lactate together show tissue hypoperfusion from continued bleeding. Low pH, low bicarbonate, a negative base excess and high lactate form the signature of hemorrhagic shock. Hemorrhage control and blood are the core of care, and lactate and base deficit are trended to judge whether resuscitation is catching up.
w: Primary respiratory alkalosis from pain
Respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation
Low blood oxygen from a chest injury

qs.q: Fifteen minutes after a thigh gunshot wound, a tourniquet is in place. Heart rate is 128 and the casualty is pale. A sample is run before any fluid or blood. i-STAT (CG8+): Hematocrit 42%, Hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, pH 7.31, PCO2 34 mmHg, HCO3 16.5 mmol/L, Base excess -10 mmol/L, Potassium 4.0 mmol/L, Glucose 142 mg/dL. How is the normal hemoglobin best interpreted here?
qs.a: It reflects the lag of hemoglobin after acute bleeding; the base deficit is the earlier warning
qs.x: Hemoglobin falls only after dilution. Base deficit and lactate rise sooner and track hemorrhage severity better. In the first hour after injury, hemoglobin and hematocrit can look normal even after large blood loss. Base deficit, lactate and the clinical exam are the earlier markers. Hematocrit is trended, and a falling value later can reflect both ongoing bleeding and dilution.
w: It shows the blood loss was minor
It suggests the acidosis is a lab error
It means the tourniquet has fully stopped the shock process

qs.q: A casualty with an abdominal wound had a lactate of 6.1 mmol/L and base excess of -12 an hour ago. After two units of whole blood and calcium, a repeat arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.36, PCO2 37 mmHg, HCO3 20 mmol/L, Base excess -5 mmol/L, Lactate 2.8 mmol/L, PO2 98 mmHg, sO2 97%. What does the trend suggest?
qs.a: Resuscitation is restoring perfusion and acid is clearing
qs.x: Lactate fell by more than half and the base deficit narrowed from -12 to -5, a strong sign that shock is reversing. Lactate clearance (the percent fall over time) and an improving base deficit are among the best signs that resuscitation is working. A single high lactate means less than the trend. Ongoing values guide whether more blood or surgical control is needed.
w: The casualty is getting worse because lactate is still high
A new respiratory problem has appeared
The results are normal, so no more trending is needed

qs.q: A casualty has a fragment wound to the forearm with minimal bleeding, now dressed. Heart rate is 96 and the casualty is anxious. An arterial sample is run as part of a routine work-up. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.41, PCO2 39 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, Lactate 1.3 mmol/L, PO2 96 mmHg, sO2 98%. What do these results show?
qs.a: No lab evidence of shock at this time
qs.x: Every value is within range. The mild tachycardia fits anxiety and pain, and the exam and vital signs remain the main tools going forward. Most results in a minor injury are normal, and reading them as normal is a skill. A normal lactate and base excess make significant hidden hemorrhage unlikely at the time of the sample. A change in vital signs or exam is a reason to repeat the panel.
w: Compensated shock hidden by a normal pH
Respiratory alkalosis from anxiety
Early metabolic acidosis

qs.q: A casualty has received four units of cold-stored whole blood and tranexamic acid (TXA) during a long hold. Calcium has not yet been given. i-STAT (CG8+): pH 7.29, Ionized calcium 0.91 mmol/L, Potassium 5.6 mmol/L, Sodium 141 mmol/L, Glucose 128 mg/dL, Hematocrit 33%, Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL. Which finding is most directly caused by the transfusion and most urgent?
qs.a: Low ionized calcium from citrate in the stored blood
qs.x: Citrate binds calcium. Low ionized calcium weakens clotting and heart contraction, which is why TCCC pairs calcium with the first unit of blood. Low ionized calcium is one of the most common and most treatable findings after transfusion. Citrate in each unit binds calcium, and hypocalcemia worsens bleeding and blood pressure. Ionized calcium is trended with each few units, alongside potassium.
w: The glucose of 128 mg/dL
Low calcium caused by the TXA
The hematocrit, which proves the transfusion failed

qs.q: During a massive transfusion of stored red cells and plasma, the cardiac monitor shows taller, peaked T waves. A sample is run. i-STAT (EG7+): Potassium 6.6 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 0.88 mmol/L, pH 7.22, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Hematocrit 30%. Which combination raises the most concern for a dangerous heart rhythm?
qs.a: High potassium together with low ionized calcium and acidosis
qs.x: Each one adds to cardiac risk, and calcium stabilizes the heart muscle against potassium. The peaked T waves fit this combination. Massive transfusion can raise potassium (from stored red cells and acidosis) while lowering calcium (from citrate). The pair is especially dangerous for the heart. Calcium, correction of acidosis and fresher products are part of the response, and potassium and calcium are trended together.
w: Normal sodium with normal PCO2
Low hematocrit alone
Low bicarbonate alone

qs.q: Blood is being given rapidly through a fluid warmer. The casualty reports tingling around the mouth and fingers, and blood pressure has dropped despite the blood. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Ionized calcium 0.78 mmol/L, Potassium 4.6 mmol/L, Sodium 142 mmol/L, Chloride 104 mmol/L, Glucose 140 mg/dL, Hematocrit 35%, Hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL. What best explains the tingling and low blood pressure?
qs.a: Citrate toxicity causing very low ionized calcium
qs.x: Perioral and finger tingling with low blood pressure during rapid transfusion fits a very low ionized calcium. Calcium supports blood vessel tone and heart contraction. Rapid transfusion, liver injury and hypothermia slow citrate clearance, so ionized calcium can fall quickly. Numbness, tingling, muscle cramps, low blood pressure and a long QT interval are clues. Calcium replacement and ionized calcium trends are standard parts of transfusion care.
w: High potassium from stored blood
Low blood sugar
Anemia alone

qs.q: A casualty received two units of fresh whole blood collected from screened unit members. A blood gas and a clotting test are run together. i-STAT (CG8+ and PT/INR): Potassium 4.1 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 1.08 mmol/L, Hematocrit 37%, Hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, pH 7.34, INR 1.2, PT 13.0 sec. Which statement fits these results?
qs.a: Fresh whole blood supplies working clotting factors with little potassium load, but calcium can still fall
qs.x: Normal potassium and a near-normal INR fit fresh product; the mildly low ionized calcium reflects citrate. Fresh whole blood replaces red cells, plasma and platelets in one product with little stored-cell potassium. It is still anticoagulated with citrate, so ionized calcium is still trended. A stable INR and potassium after transfusion are reassuring signs.
w: Fresh whole blood has no effect on calcium
The INR shows a worsening coagulopathy
The potassium shows a transfusion reaction

qs.q: Midway through a unit of blood, a casualty develops fever, chills, low back pain and dark red urine. Hematocrit was 35% before this unit. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 5.9 mmol/L, Hematocrit 29%, Hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, BUN 24 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.15 mmol/L, Sodium 139 mmol/L, Glucose 118 mg/dL. What is the most likely explanation?
qs.a: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
qs.x: Fever, back pain and dark urine during a unit, with rising potassium, falling hematocrit and rising creatinine, point to destruction of incompatible red cells. An acute hemolytic reaction is usually from blood group incompatibility. Stopping the transfusion and supporting blood pressure and kidney function are the core of care. Potassium, hematocrit and creatinine are trended, and the unit and labels are kept for review.
w: Citrate toxicity
Ongoing hemorrhage only
Stored-blood potassium load

qs.q: Three hours after a blast, a casualty has a GCS of 14, headache and repeated vomiting. The TBI cartridge and a chemistry panel are run. i-STAT (TBI and CHEM8+): GFAP Elevated, UCH-L1 Elevated, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Glucose 98 mg/dL, Hematocrit 43%, Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL. What does an elevated TBI result mean here?
qs.a: It indicates a higher chance of a CT-visible brain injury, supporting the need for CT imaging
qs.x: The i-STAT TBI test is cleared to help decide on CT in mild head injury (GCS 13 to 15) within 24 hours of injury. The TBI cartridge reports GFAP and UCH-L1 against set cutoffs. An elevated result means CT imaging is more likely to show an injury, which affects evacuation priority. It does not replace the neurologic exam, which is trended for any decline.
w: It confirms a severe brain injury requiring surgery
It is explained by the vomiting and dehydration
It rules out concussion

qs.q: Six hours after a nearby blast, a casualty has a GCS of 15, a mild headache and a normal neurologic exam. The TBI cartridge and a chemistry panel are run. i-STAT (TBI and CHEM8+): GFAP Not elevated, UCH-L1 Not elevated, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Potassium 4.1 mmol/L, Glucose 94 mg/dL, Hematocrit 44%. How is this result best interpreted?
qs.a: A CT-visible brain injury is unlikely, but concussion is still possible and symptoms are followed
qs.x: A negative TBI test has a high negative predictive value for CT findings. Concussion is a clinical diagnosis that the test does not exclude. A not-elevated TBI result can help show that a CT scan, and the evacuation needed to get one, may not be needed. It does not rule out concussion, so symptom tracking, rest and repeat neurologic checks continue. A worsening exam overrides a reassuring test.
w: Concussion is ruled out and the casualty is cleared
The test is invalid because the chemistry is normal
A CT scan is urgent because of the headache

qs.q: A head-injured casualty has received hypertonic saline twice for signs of rising brain pressure. Sodium was 141 mmol/L before the first dose. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 156 mmol/L, Chloride 121 mmol/L, TCO2 20 mmol/L, Anion gap 19 mmol/L, Potassium 3.9 mmol/L, Glucose 182 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. How is the sodium of 156 mmol/L best read?
qs.a: It reflects the intended effect of hypertonic saline, with limited room left before about 160 mmol/L
qs.x: Head injury protocols accept a raised sodium to pull fluid out of the brain, and many treat values above about 160 mmol/L as a ceiling. Hypertonic saline raises sodium and chloride by design. Each dose is guided by the sodium trend, with many protocols treating about 160 mmol/L as an upper limit. High chloride can add a mild normal-gap acidosis, and glucose is kept out of the high range.
w: It shows dehydration and the need for more free water
It is a lab error because sodium cannot rise this fast
It explains the brain swelling

qs.q: An intubated head-injured casualty is being bagged quickly during a bumpy ground transport. End-tidal CO2 reads low. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.53, PCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3 21 mmol/L, Base excess -2 mmol/L, PO2 112 mmHg, Lactate 1.4 mmol/L. What is the main problem?
qs.a: Over-ventilation causing respiratory alkalosis, which can reduce blood flow to the injured brain
qs.x: Fast bagging drives PCO2 down. In TBI, a PCO2 well below about 35 mmHg can worsen brain ischemia. In traumatic brain injury, ventilation is usually targeted to a PCO2 of about 35 to 40 mmHg. Over-ventilation is common during hand bagging and transport, and it narrows brain blood vessels. End-tidal CO2 is trended and matched against blood gas PCO2.
w: Metabolic alkalosis from vomiting
Low oxygen in the blood
Hemorrhagic shock

qs.q: A casualty was pinned under a collapsed wall for several hours before extrication. The legs are swollen and tense. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 6.4 mmol/L, Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, BUN 31 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.02 mmol/L, TCO2 18 mmol/L, Anion gap 24 mmol/L, Sodium 139 mmol/L, Glucose 112 mg/dL. What is the greatest immediate threat?
qs.a: High potassium and its effect on heart rhythm
qs.x: A potassium of 6.4 mmol/L, made worse by low calcium and acidosis, can cause sudden cardiac arrest. Crush syndrome releases potassium, acid, myoglobin and phosphate from damaged muscle. Potassium is the most immediate danger, followed by kidney injury. Large-volume fluid resuscitation, cardiac monitoring and repeat potassium values are core features of care.
w: The creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL
The sodium
The mild glucose rise

qs.q: A casualty has been pinned at the thigh for about one hour and is still trapped. IV access is in place and a sample is run before release. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 4.6 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, BUN 18 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.16 mmol/L, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Glucose 132 mg/dL. What do these pre-release results tell you?
qs.a: Values are normal now, but potassium and acid can surge after release, so repeat values matter
qs.x: Reperfusion washes potassium and acid from the crushed muscle into circulation, so the post-release sample matters most. Before release, a crushed limb can hold its potassium and acid. Release restores flow and can cause a sudden potassium spike and cardiac arrest. A baseline panel helps, but post-release values and cardiac monitoring show the real risk.
w: Crush syndrome will not develop
The casualty has hidden hyperkalemia
The glucose shows diabetic ketoacidosis

qs.q: After a long ruck march and heavy exercise in the heat, a soldier has severe thigh pain and cola-colored urine. Core temperature is 37.8 C (100 F) and mental status is normal. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, BUN 28 mg/dL, Potassium 5.3 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 1.08 mmol/L, Sodium 141 mmol/L, Hematocrit 50%, Glucose 96 mg/dL. Which pattern fits best?
qs.a: Exertional rhabdomyolysis with early kidney injury
qs.x: Muscle pain, dark urine, rising creatinine and potassium, and low calcium after heavy exertion fit muscle breakdown. Exertional rhabdomyolysis is common in training. The i-STAT does not measure CK (creatine kinase), so the diagnosis rests on the story, dark urine and lab clues such as rising potassium and creatinine. Fluid resuscitation and trends in potassium and kidney function guide care.
w: Simple dehydration only
Heat stroke
Exercise-associated hyponatremia

qs.q: Twenty minutes after a crushed leg was freed, the casualty's monitor shows widening QRS complexes. A sample is run. i-STAT (CG8+): Potassium 7.1 mmol/L, pH 7.24, HCO3 15 mmol/L, Base excess -12 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 0.98 mmol/L, Sodium 138 mmol/L, Hematocrit 47%. What best explains the sudden potassium rise?
qs.a: Reperfusion of the crushed limb releasing potassium and acid
qs.x: Restored blood flow washes potassium and acid out of dead and injured muscle, and the ECG change matches. The minutes after release are the highest-risk period in crush injury. Potassium above about 6.5 mmol/L with ECG changes is an emergency, and calcium, measures that shift potassium into cells and fluid are part of hospital protocols. A hemolyzed sample can mislead, so the ECG and clinical picture are read alongside the number.
w: Sample hemolysis, which fully explains the result
Kidney failure developing in twenty minutes
Stored blood transfusion

qs.q: Six hours after a 45% body surface area burn, urine output has been low. Lactate was 2.4 mmol/L at the first draw. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.29, PCO2 34 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, Base excess -11 mmol/L, Lactate 4.6 mmol/L, PO2 88 mmHg. What does the rising lactate most likely reflect?
qs.a: Burn shock from under-resuscitation
qs.x: Large burns leak plasma into tissue. Rising lactate, a deepening base deficit and low urine output point to too little circulating volume. Burn shock develops over hours as plasma leaks into burned and unburned tissue. Urine output is the main guide to burn fluids, and rising lactate or base deficit add warning that resuscitation is falling behind. In an enclosed-space burn, carbon monoxide or cyanide are also considered when lactate is high.
w: Normal healing response
Respiratory failure from smoke
Fluid overload

qs.q: Four hours after a large flame burn, the casualty has had limited fluid during a delayed evacuation. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Hematocrit 56%, Hemoglobin 19.0 g/dL, Sodium 147 mmol/L, BUN 30 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, Potassium 4.8 mmol/L, Glucose 168 mg/dL. What does the high hematocrit mean here?
qs.a: Loss of plasma volume with hemoconcentration, a marker of a fluid deficit
qs.x: Burns leak plasma, concentrating red cells. Rising BUN, creatinine and sodium add to the picture of low volume. A rising hematocrit early after a large burn reflects plasma loss, not more red cells. It falls as resuscitation restores volume. Kidney values and urine output show whether perfusion is improving.
w: The casualty has too many red cells and needs no fluid
It is a lab error
It rules out internal bleeding

qs.q: A casualty was pulled from a burning vehicle after several minutes inside. There is a headache, confusion and soot around the nose. Pulse oximetry reads 99% on room air. i-STAT (CG4+): PO2 96 mmHg, sO2 98%, pH 7.30, PCO2 35 mmHg, HCO3 17 mmol/L, Base excess -9 mmol/L, Lactate 5.2 mmol/L. Why is the sO2 of 98% misleading here?
qs.a: It is calculated from PO2 and cannot detect carboxyhemoglobin; co-oximetry is needed
qs.x: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin tightly, but PO2 stays normal. Only co-oximetry measures the true fraction of hemoglobin carrying oxygen. In carbon monoxide poisoning, PO2, calculated sO2 and standard pulse oximetry can all look normal. Headache, confusion, enclosed-space exposure and a high lactate are the clues, and high-concentration oxygen is the core treatment. Cyanide often coexists in smoke, especially when lactate is very high.
w: It is not misleading; oxygen delivery is normal
Smoke raises the PO2 falsely
Pulse oximetry and the i-STAT both measure carbon monoxide directly

qs.q: A casualty touched a high-voltage line. There are small entry and exit burns on the hand and foot, and the forearm is swollen and firm. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 5.8 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.7 mg/dL, BUN 22 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.05 mmol/L, Glucose 120 mg/dL, Hematocrit 45%. What do these results suggest?
qs.a: Deep muscle injury with rhabdomyolysis, similar to crush injury
qs.x: High potassium, rising creatinine and low calcium after high-voltage injury point to deep muscle breakdown. High-voltage electrical injury damages muscle along the current path, often with little skin injury. Labs often look like crush syndrome: high potassium, falling calcium and kidney injury. Burn formulas based on skin area underestimate the fluid needs, and urine output and potassium trends guide care.
w: The injury is minor because the skin burns are small
Simple dehydration
Hemorrhagic shock

qs.q: After several doses of an opioid for a leg fracture, a casualty is difficult to wake, breathing 6 times a minute with pinpoint pupils. An arterial sample is drawn on room air. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.24, PCO2 64 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, PO2 62 mmHg, sO2 88%, Lactate 1.2 mmol/L. What is the primary disturbance?
qs.a: Acute respiratory acidosis from opioid-related hypoventilation
qs.x: A high PCO2 with low pH and near-normal bicarbonate is acute respiratory acidosis, matching the slow breathing and pinpoint pupils. Opioid oversedation suppresses breathing, raising PCO2 and lowering PO2. A normal bicarbonate shows the change is acute. Airway support, ventilation and opioid reversal are the core of care, and capnography (end-tidal CO2) is the field trend to follow.
w: Metabolic acidosis from shock
Mixed metabolic and respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis from pain

qs.q: An intubated casualty on a transport ventilator has a set rate of 8 with a small tidal volume. End-tidal CO2 has been climbing. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.27, PCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, PO2 145 mmHg, Lactate 1.1 mmol/L. What does this pattern point to?
qs.a: Ventilator minute ventilation is too low to clear CO2
qs.x: High PCO2 with normal bicarbonate on a low set rate and small volume points to under-ventilation. Oxygenation and ventilation are separate problems. PO2 mainly reflects oxygen settings and lung function, while PCO2 reflects minute ventilation. A high PCO2 on a ventilator usually means rate or tidal volume is set too low for the casualty. End-tidal CO2 is trended after each change and compared with blood gas PCO2.
w: The ventilator is delivering too little oxygen
Shock is causing metabolic acidosis
The casualty is over-ventilated

qs.q: A casualty with a painful ankle fracture is breathing fast, reports tingling hands and is very anxious. There is no fever, and the chest exam is normal. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.51, PCO2 29 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, PO2 104 mmHg, sO2 98%, Lactate 1.2 mmol/L. What is the most likely disturbance?
qs.a: Acute respiratory alkalosis from pain and anxiety
qs.x: High pH, low PCO2 and normal bicarbonate is acute respiratory alkalosis. Normal PO2 and lactate make low oxygen or sepsis less likely. Pain and anxiety commonly cause respiratory alkalosis, and the low CO2 can cause tingling and cramps. Before settling on that explanation, low oxygen, early sepsis, pulmonary embolism and chest injury are considered. A normal PO2 and lactate help narrow the cause.
w: Metabolic alkalosis
Compensated metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis

qs.q: A team has been operating at about 10,000 feet for two days. One member reports mild headache and breathlessness on exertion. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.47, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 21 mmol/L, Base excess -3 mmol/L, PO2 60 mmHg, sO2 91%, Lactate 1.4 mmol/L. What best describes these results?
qs.a: An expected altitude pattern: hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis and early kidney compensation
qs.x: Low PO2 drives hyperventilation, and the mildly low bicarbonate shows the kidneys adjusting over days. At altitude, low PO2 and respiratory alkalosis are expected, and the kidneys lower bicarbonate over days. Values that move outside this pattern, such as worsening PO2 or rising lactate, can signal altitude illness such as high-altitude pulmonary edema. Symptoms and trends matter more than one sample.
w: Severe lactic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis from altitude
Carbon monoxide poisoning

qs.q: The casualty from an earlier under-ventilation case had the ventilator rate increased. A repeat arterial sample is run twenty minutes later. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.39, PCO2 41 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, PO2 118 mmHg, Lactate 1.0 mmol/L. What do the repeat results show?
qs.a: The ventilator change corrected the CO2, and oxygenation is more than adequate
qs.x: pH and PCO2 are normal. The only value out of range is a high PO2 from supplemental oxygen. After a ventilator change, a repeat gas confirms the effect. Normal pH and PCO2 show ventilation now matches the casualty's needs. A PO2 well above range on oxygen is not harmful in the short term but often allows oxygen to be reduced, which conserves supply in the field.
w: A new metabolic acidosis
Ongoing hypoventilation
Dangerous hypoxemia

qs.q: During a long training day in the heat, a trainee drank large amounts of water. The trainee is now confused and vomiting, with swollen hands. Core temperature is 38.0 C (100.4 F). i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 124 mmol/L, Chloride 91 mmol/L, Potassium 3.7 mmol/L, BUN 7 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, Glucose 92 mg/dL, Anion gap 14 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause of the confusion?
qs.a: Exercise-associated hyponatremia from excess water intake
qs.x: A sodium of 124 mmol/L with low BUN after heavy drinking fits dilution. Low sodium causes brain swelling and confusion. Exercise-associated hyponatremia and heat stroke can look alike in the field, with confusion after exertion in the heat. Sodium separates them: low in overhydration, normal or high in heat stroke. Giving more plain water worsens hyponatremia, and treatment centers on restricting water and, for severe symptoms, hypertonic saline.
w: Heat stroke with dehydration
Hypoglycemia
Diabetic ketoacidosis

qs.q: A soldier collapsed near the end of a timed run. Core temperature is 41.5 C (106.7 F) and the soldier is combative and confused. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 148 mmol/L, BUN 32 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, Potassium 5.2 mmol/L, Glucose 64 mg/dL, Hematocrit 52%, Hemoglobin 17.7 g/dL, TCO2 19 mmol/L. Which pattern fits best?
qs.a: Heat stroke with dehydration, early kidney injury and low glucose
qs.x: Very high core temperature with altered mental status is heat stroke. High sodium, BUN and hematocrit show dehydration, and creatinine shows organ injury. Heat stroke is defined by high core temperature with central nervous system dysfunction. Rapid cooling, such as cold-water immersion, is the most important treatment and comes first. Labs show the organ damage: kidney injury, muscle breakdown, low glucose and, later, clotting problems.
w: Exercise-associated hyponatremia
Simple heat exhaustion
Diabetic ketoacidosis

qs.q: A casualty with a leg wound was pulled from a cold river after 40 minutes. Core temperature is 31 C (87.8 F). The analyzer and cartridges were kept warm in a chest pocket. Results are reported at 37 C (98.6 F). i-STAT (CG8+): pH 7.28, PCO2 47 mmHg, HCO3 21 mmol/L, Base excess -5 mmol/L, Potassium 3.2 mmol/L, Glucose 185 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.10 mmol/L, Hematocrit 49%. Which statement best fits these results?
qs.a: Cold is contributing to the acidosis, glucose rise and potassium shift, and these change during rewarming
qs.x: Hypothermia slows breathing, impairs perfusion, suppresses insulin and moves potassium into cells. Rewarming changes all of these, so values are trended. Hypothermia, acidosis and bleeding form the trauma lethal triad. Blood gases are analyzed at 37 C (98.6 F), and many clinicians read them uncorrected. The i-STAT has an ambient operating range, so cartridges and the device are kept within it in cold environments.
w: The low potassium means potassium is low in the whole body
The high glucose means diabetes
The results are invalid because the patient is cold

qs.q: After a long patrol in the heat, a soldier is tired, nauseated and dizzy on standing. Core temperature is 38.4 C (101.1 F) and mental status is normal. The soldier has been drinking a mix of water and electrolyte drinks. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 141 mmol/L, Potassium 4.0 mmol/L, BUN 20 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, Glucose 98 mg/dL, Hematocrit 47%. What do these results suggest?
qs.a: Heat exhaustion without electrolyte or kidney problems
qs.x: Symptoms with normal mental status and normal labs fit heat exhaustion. Cooling, rest and oral fluids are typical care, with reassessment for any change. Heat exhaustion causes fatigue, dizziness and nausea without central nervous system dysfunction or organ injury. Normal sodium, potassium, BUN and creatinine help rule out the dangerous look-alikes. Any confusion or a rising core temperature changes the picture to possible heat stroke.
w: Heat stroke
Exercise-associated hyponatremia
Exertional rhabdomyolysis

qs.q: A casualty was rescued from a burning building filled with smoke from burning plastics. Breathing is labored, blood pressure is low, and the casualty is on high-flow oxygen. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.12, PCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 9 mmol/L, Base excess -21 mmol/L, Lactate 11.8 mmol/L, PO2 210 mmHg. Which cause best explains a very high lactate with a high PO2?
qs.a: Cyanide poisoning from burning plastics
qs.x: Cyanide stops cells from using oxygen. A lactate above about 8 to 10 mmol/L after smoke exposure strongly suggests cyanide, even with good PO2. Burning plastics, foam and wool release hydrogen cyanide. A very high lactate with good oxygenation, low blood pressure and altered mental status after smoke exposure is the classic clue. Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) is the antidote used in this setting, and carbon monoxide often coexists.
w: Respiratory acidosis from smoke in the airway
Low oxygen in the blood
Mild heat exhaustion

qs.q: After a suspected nerve agent exposure, a casualty has heavy secretions, wheezing, pinpoint pupils and muscle twitching. An arterial sample is drawn on room air. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.22, PCO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 24.5 mmol/L, Base excess -3 mmol/L, PO2 58 mmHg, sO2 86%, Lactate 3.4 mmol/L. What is the dominant problem?
qs.a: Respiratory failure: high PCO2 and low PO2 from secretions and weak breathing
qs.x: The high PCO2 with normal bicarbonate and low PO2 show the lungs and breathing muscles are failing, the main cause of death in nerve agent poisoning. Nerve agents cause excess secretions, bronchospasm and breathing muscle weakness, leading to combined respiratory failure. Lab values show severity but do not make the diagnosis, which is clinical. Drying secretions and supporting ventilation are central to care.
w: Pure metabolic acidosis from shock
Respiratory alkalosis
Carbon monoxide poisoning

qs.q: A service member found confused in the motor pool admits drinking from an unmarked bottle several hours ago. There is no injury, no history of diabetes, and blood pressure is normal. i-STAT (CHEM8+): TCO2 10 mmol/L, Anion gap 32 mmol/L, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Chloride 102 mmol/L, Potassium 4.5 mmol/L, Glucose 101 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, BUN 15 mg/dL. What best explains this high anion gap acidosis?
qs.a: Toxic alcohol poisoning such as ethylene glycol (antifreeze)
qs.x: A large gap with normal glucose, normal blood pressure and a history of drinking an unknown liquid fits a toxic alcohol. A high anion gap acidosis has a short list of causes: lactate, ketones, kidney failure and toxins such as toxic alcohols and salicylates. Lactate measurement helps rule out shock, and some lab methods can read glycolate from ethylene glycol as lactate. Antifreeze and windshield fluid are found in motor pools, and specific antidotes and dialysis are used in hospital care.
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Uremia from kidney failure
Hyperchloremic acidosis from saline

qs.q: A service member took most of a bottle of aspirin after a personal crisis. There is ringing in the ears, vomiting and fast, deep breathing. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.44, PCO2 24 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, Base excess -8 mmol/L, Lactate 2.6 mmol/L, PO2 104 mmHg. What does the normal pH hide?
qs.a: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, typical of salicylate poisoning
qs.x: Salicylate stimulates breathing and also creates metabolic acid. The two offset each other, leaving a deceptively normal pH. When pH is normal but PCO2 and bicarbonate are both abnormal, two disorders are present. Salicylate poisoning classically causes this mix. Losing the breathing compensation, for example from sedation or a ventilator set too low, lets the pH drop sharply, which is why ventilation is managed carefully in these patients. Behavioral health care is part of the full response.
w: Nothing; the acid-base status is normal
Simple respiratory alkalosis from anxiety
Compensated respiratory acidosis

qs.q: Three days after a fragment wound to the calf during a prolonged hold, a casualty has fever, a heart rate of 112 and a breathing rate of 26. The wound is red and draining. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.48, PCO2 31 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, Lactate 2.6 mmol/L, PO2 88 mmHg, sO2 97%. What do these results most likely represent?
qs.a: Early sepsis with respiratory alkalosis and a rising lactate
qs.x: Fast breathing with a low PCO2 is often one of the earliest sepsis signs, and a lactate above 2 mmol/L adds concern. Respiratory alkalosis is a common early sign of sepsis, before acidosis develops. A lactate above 2 mmol/L in suspected infection marks higher risk. Source control of the wound, antibiotics and fluids are core sepsis care, and a repeat lactate shows the direction.
w: Anxiety only
Hemorrhagic shock
Acute respiratory acidosis

qs.q: A casualty with a known abdominal wound infection now has low blood pressure despite fluids, cool mottled skin and confusion. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.27, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 13 mmol/L, Base excess -14 mmol/L, Lactate 5.4 mmol/L, PO2 76 mmHg. What is the main problem?
qs.a: Septic shock with lactic acidosis
qs.x: Low blood pressure despite fluids, with a lactate over 4 mmol/L and a deep base deficit, fits septic shock. Septic shock combines infection, low blood pressure needing support and a raised lactate. Fluids, antibiotics, source control and blood pressure support are central, and the lactate trend over hours shows whether perfusion is improving. In prolonged casualty care, early evacuation or telemedicine consultation is part of planning.
w: Primary respiratory failure
Metabolic alkalosis
Mild infection without organ dysfunction

qs.q: Five days into a prolonged hold, a casualty with an infected burn has had little urine output over the last 12 hours. The casualty has no history of diabetes. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, BUN 48 mg/dL, Potassium 5.4 mmol/L, Sodium 135 mmol/L, Glucose 182 mg/dL, TCO2 17 mmol/L, Chloride 99 mmol/L, Anion gap 24 mmol/L. What best fits these results?
qs.a: Sepsis with acute kidney injury and rising potassium
qs.x: Low urine output with rising creatinine, BUN and potassium in an infected casualty points to sepsis-related kidney injury. Acute kidney injury is a common organ failure in sepsis. Rising creatinine and BUN with falling urine output are the markers, and potassium becomes a growing danger. Kidney injury also changes how fluids and many medications are handled, which is part of prolonged care planning.
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Simple dehydration
Hyperchloremic acidosis

qs.q: A casualty has a mildly red, warm wound edge and a temperature of 38.2 C (100.8 F). Heart rate is 92 and blood pressure is normal. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.40, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, Lactate 1.1 mmol/L, PO2 95 mmHg. How are these results best interpreted?
qs.a: No lab sign of sepsis-related hypoperfusion now; the wound and vital signs are trended
qs.x: Normal lactate and acid-base values are reassuring, but a local infection can still progress. A normal lactate and blood gas in a local infection is a good sign but not a final answer. Infections can progress over hours, especially in prolonged care. Vital signs, wound appearance and a repeat lactate if things change are the key trends.
w: They rule out infection
They show early septic shock
They show hidden respiratory alkalosis

qs.q: A service member with type 1 diabetes ran out of insulin during a long mission. There is vomiting, abdominal pain, deep fast breathing and a fruity breath odor. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Glucose 486 mg/dL, TCO2 8 mmol/L, Anion gap 32 mmol/L, Potassium 4.8 mmol/L, Sodium 131 mmol/L, Chloride 96 mmol/L, BUN 30 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL. How is the potassium of 4.8 mmol/L best interpreted?
qs.a: The blood value looks normal, but the body is depleted, and potassium will fall when insulin is started
qs.x: Insulin drives potassium back into cells. In DKA, a normal starting value often drops into a dangerous low range during treatment. DKA shows high glucose, low bicarbonate and a high anion gap. Potassium may look normal or even high at first, yet total body potassium is low. DKA protocols track potassium closely, often every one to two hours, because insulin moves it into cells.
w: Potassium is normal and needs no attention
Potassium is high and dangerous
Potassium does not change in DKA

qs.q: The DKA casualty from the earlier case has had four hours of IV fluids and an insulin infusion. The casualty now reports muscle weakness and the monitor shows flattened T waves. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 3.1 mmol/L, Glucose 238 mg/dL, TCO2 15 mmol/L, Anion gap 21 mmol/L, Sodium 137 mmol/L, Chloride 104 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Why has the potassium fallen?
qs.a: Insulin is driving potassium into cells, exposing the total-body deficit
qs.x: Insulin moves potassium into cells. DKA protocols typically pause insulin when potassium falls below about 3.3 mmol/L until it is replaced. Low potassium is a major cause of preventable harm during DKA treatment. As insulin works, potassium drops, often fast. Weakness and ECG changes such as flattened T waves or U waves are warning signs, and potassium replacement is part of every DKA protocol.
w: The lab has made an error
Potassium is being lost in vomit only
The kidneys have failed

qs.q: After a long patrol with little food, a soldier who uses insulin is sweating, shaky and confused. There is no head injury and core temperature is normal. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Glucose 38 mg/dL, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Potassium 3.9 mmol/L, BUN 14 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, Hematocrit 45%. What explains the confusion?
qs.a: Hypoglycemia from insulin use with little food intake
qs.x: A glucose of 38 mg/dL explains sweating, shaking and confusion. All other values are normal. Hypoglycemia is quick to identify and correct, and it can mimic head injury, intoxication or heat illness. A glucose check belongs early in any altered mental status work-up. The other normal values here help rule out the look-alikes.
w: Exercise-associated hyponatremia
Heat stroke
Kidney failure

qs.q: A service member has had several days of vomiting from a stomach illness with little intake. A blood gas and chemistry panel are run together. i-STAT (CG4+ and CHEM8+): pH 7.52, HCO3 37 mmol/L, PCO2 47 mmHg, Potassium 3.0 mmol/L, Chloride 88 mmol/L, TCO2 38 mmol/L, BUN 30 mg/dL. What is the primary disturbance?
qs.a: Metabolic alkalosis from vomiting with low chloride and potassium
qs.x: High pH and bicarbonate after vomiting, with low chloride and potassium, is a classic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation. Vomiting removes acid and chloride, raising bicarbonate. The kidneys then hold sodium and lose potassium, which worsens the alkalosis. Fluid and electrolyte replacement, especially chloride and potassium, corrects this pattern.
w: Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis

qs.q: A casualty received large volumes of normal saline during a long delay before blood was available. Bleeding is controlled and blood pressure is now normal. i-STAT (CG4+ and CHEM8+): Chloride 116 mmol/L, TCO2 18 mmol/L, Sodium 144 mmol/L, Anion gap 14 mmol/L, pH 7.31, Lactate 1.3 mmol/L, Potassium 4.2 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. What is the cause of the acidosis?
qs.a: Hyperchloremic (normal anion gap) acidosis from large-volume saline
qs.x: High chloride, low bicarbonate and a normal gap with normal lactate point to the saline itself. Large volumes of normal saline cause a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap acidosis. It can be mistaken for ongoing shock, but a normal lactate and gap tell them apart. TCCC favors blood products for hemorrhagic shock, and balanced crystalloids such as lactated Ringer's carry less chloride than saline.
w: Lactic acidosis from ongoing shock
Ketoacidosis
Kidney failure

qs.q: A casualty had hours of low blood pressure before reaching a surgical team. Two days later in a prolonged care setting, urine output has fallen. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, BUN 54 mg/dL, Potassium 5.8 mmol/L, TCO2 17 mmol/L, Anion gap 24 mmol/L, Sodium 137 mmol/L, Hematocrit 32%, Hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL. What best explains these results?
qs.a: Acute kidney injury from prolonged shock
qs.x: Rising creatinine, BUN and potassium with low urine output after hours of low blood pressure fit kidney injury from poor perfusion. Shock-related kidney injury shows rising creatinine and BUN, falling urine output, high potassium and high anion gap acidosis. Fluid balance becomes delicate because the kidneys cannot clear excess. Potassium, creatinine and urine output are the key trends, and severe cases need dialysis.
w: Normal recovery after surgery
Simple dehydration
Hyperchloremic acidosis

qs.q: A soldier has had diarrhea for two days during a field exercise and has been drinking little. The soldier is dizzy on standing but alert. i-STAT (CHEM8+): BUN 38 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, Sodium 147 mmol/L, Hematocrit 50%, Potassium 4.4 mmol/L, Glucose 102 mg/dL. What does the BUN to creatinine ratio suggest?
qs.a: Prerenal kidney stress from dehydration
qs.x: A ratio above 20 with high sodium after fluid loss points to low volume. This often reverses with fluids. A high BUN to creatinine ratio with signs of dehydration suggests a prerenal problem that usually reverses with fluid. Creatinine returning toward normal after fluids confirms it. A rising creatinine despite fluids suggests the kidney itself is injured.
w: Intrinsic kidney damage
Rhabdomyolysis
Exercise-associated hyponatremia

qs.q: A casualty had a sodium of 118 mmol/L that had fallen slowly over several days. Twelve hours after treatment began, a repeat sample is run. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 130 mmol/L, Chloride 96 mmol/L, Potassium 3.8 mmol/L, Glucose 96 mg/dL, BUN 9 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. What is the main concern?
qs.a: Sodium has risen too fast, raising the risk of osmotic demyelination
qs.x: With slowly developing hyponatremia, the brain adapts. A rise faster than about 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours can damage brain cells. In hyponatremia that developed over more than about 48 hours, rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination, a severe and sometimes permanent brain injury. Many guidelines limit the rise to about 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours. Frequent sodium checks are how the rate is tracked.
w: Sodium is still low, so correction is too slow
No concern because the casualty is improving
Potassium is the problem

qs.q: Before blood was available, a casualty received large volumes of crystalloid and then red cells only, with no plasma or whole blood. The casualty is now oozing from IV sites. i-STAT (PT/INR and CHEM8+): INR 1.9, PT 21.5 sec, Hematocrit 28%, Hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, Ionized calcium 0.95 mmol/L, Sodium 141 mmol/L. What explains the rising INR?
qs.a: Dilution of clotting factors by crystalloid and plasma-free red cells
qs.x: Fluids and red cells without plasma replace volume but not clotting factors, so the INR rises. Dilutional coagulopathy develops when volume is replaced without clotting factors. Whole blood or balanced plasma, platelets and red cells limit it, which is why TCCC prefers whole blood. INR and calcium trends help track it.
w: Warfarin use
Lab error from the low hematocrit
Normal response to injury that needs no attention

qs.q: A hypothermic trauma casualty (core temperature 33 C (91.4 F)) is oozing from every wound. A clotting test and a blood gas are run. i-STAT (PT/INR and CG8+): INR 1.1, PT 12.0 sec, pH 7.25, Ionized calcium 1.05 mmol/L, Potassium 4.0 mmol/L, Hematocrit 36%. Why is the casualty bleeding despite a normal INR?
qs.a: The INR is measured at 37 C (98.6 F), so it misses cold-related clotting failure; acidosis and low calcium add to it
qs.x: Clotting enzymes slow down in the cold. The INR test warms the blood, hiding this, and it does not assess platelets. Hypothermia, acidosis and low calcium all impair clotting, and none of them show up fully in a standard INR run at 37 C (98.6 F). Warming, correcting calcium and acidosis and using whole blood address this. A normal INR in a cold, bleeding casualty is not reassuring.
w: The INR proves clotting is normal
The oozing is from high potassium
The low hematocrit alone explains the bleeding

qs.q: Within an hour of a severe blast injury, before any fluid or blood has been given, a clotting test and blood gas are run. The casualty is in shock. i-STAT (PT/INR and CG4+): INR 1.5, PT 17.4 sec, pH 7.26, PCO2 33 mmHg, HCO3 14 mmol/L, Base excess -13 mmol/L, Lactate 5.9 mmol/L. What best explains the INR rise?
qs.a: Acute traumatic coagulopathy from shock and tissue injury
qs.x: Severe injury and shock trigger clotting failure within minutes, before any dilution. It is linked to higher mortality. Acute traumatic coagulopathy appears early in severe injury with shock. It is a reason that TCCC emphasizes early whole blood, TXA and calcium. Shock severity markers such as base deficit and lactate often move with it.
w: Dilution from fluids
Warfarin use
Lab error from acidosis

qs.q: An older civilian casualty fell and struck the head. Family members report the casualty takes warfarin. The neurologic exam is normal so far. i-STAT (PT/INR and CHEM8+): INR 3.4, PT 36 sec, Hematocrit 40%, Hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Why does this INR matter for a head injury?
qs.a: Anticoagulation raises the risk of delayed brain bleeding, which raises evacuation and imaging priority
qs.x: An INR of 3.4 means slower clotting, and head injury in anticoagulated patients carries a high risk of delayed intracranial bleeding. The i-STAT PT/INR test is designed for monitoring warfarin. It is not reliable for heparin or the newer direct oral anticoagulants. In head injury, a raised INR from warfarin raises the priority for CT and reversal at a higher level of care.
w: It does not matter if the exam is normal
It shows dilutional coagulopathy
It shows acute traumatic coagulopathy from shock

w: In the Notes box only
On the casualty's forehead only
They are not recorded on the card

qs.q: At 2210 local, a 19-year-old private is shot through the left arm and right thigh. Buddy aid places a tourniquet on the right thigh at 2212; the medic, call sign Granite 8, adds a left arm tourniquet at 2215 and packs the thigh wound with hemostatic gauze. At 2225 vitals are heart rate 120, blood pressure 100/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 percent, alert, pain 8 of 10. Ketamine is given at 2228 and tranexamic acid at 2230. The private reports an allergy to penicillin. How are the medications recorded?
qs.a: Analgesic row: ketamine, route, time 2228; Other row: tranexamic acid, route, time 2230
qs.x: Each medication goes in its category row with name, dose, route and time.
w: A note saying meds given
Only the time of the last medication
In the mechanism of injury section

qs.q: At 2210 local, a 19-year-old private is shot through the left arm and right thigh. Buddy aid places a tourniquet on the right thigh at 2212; the medic, call sign Granite 8, adds a left arm tourniquet at 2215 and packs the thigh wound with hemostatic gauze. At 2225 vitals are heart rate 120, blood pressure 100/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 percent, alert, pain 8 of 10. Ketamine is given at 2228 and tranexamic acid at 2230. The private reports an allergy to penicillin. Where is the penicillin allergy recorded?
qs.a: In the Allergies field on the front of the card
qs.x: The allergy field sits in the identity block on the front.
w: Under Notes only
It is left off because no antibiotic was given yet
In the medication rows

qs.q: At 2210 local, a 19-year-old private is shot through the left arm and right thigh. Buddy aid places a tourniquet on the right thigh at 2212; the medic, call sign Granite 8, adds a left arm tourniquet at 2215 and packs the thigh wound with hemostatic gauze. At 2225 vitals are heart rate 120, blood pressure 100/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 percent, alert, pain 8 of 10. Ketamine is given at 2228 and tranexamic acid at 2230. The private reports an allergy to penicillin. Which EVAC box on the card fits this casualty?
qs.a: Urgent
qs.x: Two extremity wounds needing tourniquets with tachycardia and borderline pressure fit Urgent; the card offers only Urgent, Priority and Routine.
w: Routine
Convenience
Urgent-Surgical

qs.q: At 1730 local, after a blast, a 29-year-old specialist with bilateral leg wounds is in shock with a heart rate of 140 and absent radial pulses. The medic, call sign Sabre 3, starts cold-stored low-titer O whole blood at 1740 through a humeral IO, followed at 1825 by fresh whole blood from a pre-screened walking blood bank donor. Calcium is given at 1742 and tranexamic acid at 1745. At 1830 the heart rate is 112, radial pulses are back, and the casualty is responding to voice. Which entries best document the transfusion on the DD 1380?
qs.a: Blood products row: product name (LTOWB, then fresh whole blood), volume, route (IO), and time of each
qs.x: The card's blood product row asks for name, volume, route and time for each product.
w: Fluids row only
A note saying blood given
Nothing; blood is tracked by the lab

qs.q: At 1730 local, after a blast, a 29-year-old specialist with bilateral leg wounds is in shock with a heart rate of 140 and absent radial pulses. The medic, call sign Sabre 3, starts cold-stored low-titer O whole blood at 1740 through a humeral IO, followed at 1825 by fresh whole blood from a pre-screened walking blood bank donor. Calcium is given at 1742 and tranexamic acid at 1745. At 1830 the heart rate is 112, radial pulses are back, and the casualty is responding to voice. Which additional detail is most important to capture for a walking blood bank unit?
qs.a: The donor's identity and unit number, blood type and screening result
qs.x: Traceability links the unit to the donor if a reaction or infection question arises later; JTS whole blood guidance includes donor and unit tracking.
w: The donor's favorite food
The color of the blood bag
Only the time the donor arrived

qs.q: At 1730 local, after a blast, a 29-year-old specialist with bilateral leg wounds is in shock with a heart rate of 140 and absent radial pulses. The medic, call sign Sabre 3, starts cold-stored low-titer O whole blood at 1740 through a humeral IO, followed at 1825 by fresh whole blood from a pre-screened walking blood bank donor. Calcium is given at 1742 and tranexamic acid at 1745. At 1830 the heart rate is 112, radial pulses are back, and the casualty is responding to voice. Which observation pairs best with a transfusion entry on a flowsheet?
qs.a: Vitals before, during and after the transfusion, plus any reaction signs such as fever, hives or hypotension
qs.x: Response and reaction monitoring around each unit is documented alongside the product.
w: The time the radio was checked
The weather
The battle roster numbers of the rest of the squad

qs.q: At 1730 local, after a blast, a 29-year-old specialist with bilateral leg wounds is in shock with a heart rate of 140 and absent radial pulses. The medic, call sign Sabre 3, starts cold-stored low-titer O whole blood at 1740 through a humeral IO, followed at 1825 by fresh whole blood from a pre-screened walking blood bank donor. Calcium is given at 1742 and tranexamic acid at 1745. At 1830 the heart rate is 112, radial pulses are back, and the casualty is responding to voice. How would the vitals trend be presented in MIST Signs?
qs.a: Heart rate 140 with absent radials at 1730, improving to 112 with radials present after whole blood at 1830; responds to voice
qs.x: The trend tied to the intervention shows the transfusion response.
w: Heart rate 112
Responding to voice
Bilateral leg wounds

qs.q: A 30-year-old sergeant with a severe head injury from a rollover at 0600 local has been held for 30 hours by the team's 18D, call sign Ember 4. He is intubated on a portable ventilator, sedated with ketamine and midazolam infusions, has a Foley catheter and an orogastric tube, and has received levetiracetam, ceftriaxone and hypertonic saline, all with recorded times. A Critical Care Air Transport team arrives to take the patient. The flowsheet shows hourly vitals, EtCO2, urine output and pupil checks. Which item is most important to hand over for the ventilator?
qs.a: Current settings (mode, tidal volume, rate, FiO2, PEEP), pressures, EtCO2 trend and tube position at the teeth
qs.x: The receiving team needs settings, pressures, the EtCO2 target being held and the tube depth to continue care safely.
w: Brand of the batteries
The time the ventilator was unpacked
Only the SpO2

qs.q: A 30-year-old sergeant with a severe head injury from a rollover at 0600 local has been held for 30 hours by the team's 18D, call sign Ember 4. He is intubated on a portable ventilator, sedated with ketamine and midazolam infusions, has a Foley catheter and an orogastric tube, and has received levetiracetam, ceftriaxone and hypertonic saline, all with recorded times. A Critical Care Air Transport team arrives to take the patient. The flowsheet shows hourly vitals, EtCO2, urine output and pupil checks. Which neuro data are most relevant to a head-injured handoff?
qs.a: Pupil size and reactivity trend, GCS before sedation, RASS, and any seizure activity or hypertonic saline response
qs.x: These tell the receiving team whether intracranial pressure is changing and how the patient has responded to treatment.
w: Pain score only
Hair color
Time of the last meal

qs.q: A 30-year-old sergeant with a severe head injury from a rollover at 0600 local has been held for 30 hours by the team's 18D, call sign Ember 4. He is intubated on a portable ventilator, sedated with ketamine and midazolam infusions, has a Foley catheter and an orogastric tube, and has received levetiracetam, ceftriaxone and hypertonic saline, all with recorded times. A Critical Care Air Transport team arrives to take the patient. The flowsheet shows hourly vitals, EtCO2, urine output and pupil checks. How are infusions and medications handed over?
qs.a: By drug name, current rate or last time given, and response
qs.x: Each infusion and scheduled drug is passed with its current status and timing so nothing is duplicated or missed.
w: By the color of the syringe
As 'the usual meds'
Only the most recent drug

qs.q: A 30-year-old sergeant with a severe head injury from a rollover at 0600 local has been held for 30 hours by the team's 18D, call sign Ember 4. He is intubated on a portable ventilator, sedated with ketamine and midazolam infusions, has a Foley catheter and an orogastric tube, and has received levetiracetam, ceftriaxone and hypertonic saline, all with recorded times. A Critical Care Air Transport team arrives to take the patient. The flowsheet shows hourly vitals, EtCO2, urine output and pupil checks. Which document best supports this handoff?
qs.a: The prolonged care flowsheet together with the DD 1380 and a verbal handoff with readback
qs.x: The flowsheet carries the hours of trends, the DD 1380 the point-of-injury care, and the verbal handoff with readback closes the loop.
w: Only the original DD 1380
The 9-line request
A verbal report alone

qs.q: A 30-year-old sergeant with a severe head injury from a rollover at 0600 local has been held for 30 hours by the team's 18D, call sign Ember 4. He is intubated on a portable ventilator, sedated with ketamine and midazolam infusions, has a Foley catheter and an orogastric tube, and has received levetiracetam, ceftriaxone and hypertonic saline, all with recorded times. A Critical Care Air Transport team arrives to take the patient. The flowsheet shows hourly vitals, EtCO2, urine output and pupil checks. Which lines and drains are handed off?
qs.a: Airway tube, IV or IO sites with placement times, Foley with hourly output, and orogastric tube with output
qs.x: Each device with its placement time and output is part of a complete handoff.
w: Only the IV
None; the receiving team will check
Only the Foley

qs.q: At 1100 local, a 37-year-old partner-force officer arrives at a Role 2 after a 6-hour ground evacuation. The flight medic, call sign Hawk 9, reports that he was shot in the right flank at 0500, was given whole blood and tranexamic acid early, and that his heart rate has climbed from 100 to 130 over the last hour, with a firm, distended abdomen. Ketamine and ertapenem were also given with recorded times. The medic calls the on-call surgeon by phone. Which line is the best Situation statement?
qs.a: This is Hawk 9; I have a 37-year-old with a right flank gunshot wound from 0500 who is getting worse with a rising heart rate and distending abdomen
qs.x: Situation is a short statement of who is calling, who the patient is and the immediate concern.
w: He was given whole blood and tranexamic acid
I think he is bleeding inside
I would like you to come now

qs.q: At 1100 local, a 37-year-old partner-force officer arrives at a Role 2 after a 6-hour ground evacuation. The flight medic, call sign Hawk 9, reports that he was shot in the right flank at 0500, was given whole blood and tranexamic acid early, and that his heart rate has climbed from 100 to 130 over the last hour, with a firm, distended abdomen. Ketamine and ertapenem were also given with recorded times. The medic calls the on-call surgeon by phone. Which line fits Recommendation?
qs.a: I am requesting surgical evaluation now and asking whether to continue whole blood while waiting
qs.x: The R in SBAR is the specific request.
w: The patient is 37
Heart rate 130
The flank wound was at 0500

qs.q: At 1100 local, a 37-year-old partner-force officer arrives at a Role 2 after a 6-hour ground evacuation. The flight medic, call sign Hawk 9, reports that he was shot in the right flank at 0500, was given whole blood and tranexamic acid early, and that his heart rate has climbed from 100 to 130 over the last hour, with a firm, distended abdomen. Ketamine and ertapenem were also given with recorded times. The medic calls the on-call surgeon by phone. What closes the SBAR loop?
qs.a: A readback of the surgeon's instructions
qs.x: Readback confirms the plan and catches errors.
w: Hanging up after the request
Sending the 9-line
Repeating the mechanism

qs.q: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+0:02 (Point of injury): Both stumps are pumping bright red blood. He is awake, screaming and trying to sit up. The area is now secure. What comes first?
qs.a: Limb tourniquets placed high and tight on both legs
qs.x: Life-threatening extremity bleeding is controlled first, and a traumatic amputation is a clear tourniquet indication. MARCH starts with massive hemorrhage. Tourniquets go on high and tight for amputations, and a second tourniquet above the first is used when one does not stop the bleeding. The time is written on the tourniquet and on the DD1380.
w: IV access before anything else so fluids can start
Airway assessment with a jaw thrust
Pressure dressings wrapped over both stumps

qs.q: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+0:15 (Casualty collection point): Bleeding has stopped. His radial pulse is weak and thready, he is pale and slow to answer questions. IO access is in the sternum. Which resuscitation plan fits best?
qs.a: Low titer O whole blood transfused, with TXA started as soon as possible within 3 hours of injury
qs.x: Whole blood is the preferred TCCC resuscitation fluid, and TXA in the first 3 hours reduces death from bleeding. TCCC lists cold-stored low titer O whole blood as the preferred fluid, then plasma with red cells, plasma alone, or red cells alone. The end point is a palpable radial pulse, improved mentation, or a systolic pressure near 100, not a normal blood pressure.
w: Lactated Ringer's boluses until blood pressure is normal
Hetastarch to expand volume and save the blood for later
No fluid until the radial pulse is lost completely

qs.q: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): Two units of whole blood are in. He reports tingling around his mouth. An i-STAT CG8+ is run. How is the low ionized calcium handled?
qs.a: Calcium replacement alongside ongoing blood products, with a repeat i-STAT
qs.x: Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and hypocalcemia is part of the lethal diamond with acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy. The lethal diamond is hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy and hypocalcemia. TCCC calls for calcium with or right after the first unit of blood product, and i-STAT ionized calcium guides further replacement.
w: Sodium bicarbonate to fix the pH first, then a calcium recheck
Calcium deferred until four units are in
No treatment because he has no arrhythmia

qs.q: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+1:30 (Patrol base): He is moved into an abandoned stone building. His uniform is soaked and he is shivering on the concrete floor. What is the best way to address his temperature?
qs.a: Wet clothing removed, insulation under him, a hypothermia prevention kit with an active heater, and warmed blood products
qs.x: Insulation from the ground, dry layers, active heat and warmed fluids together limit heat loss from every route. Even mild hypothermia worsens clotting. In TCCC, hypothermia prevention starts at the point of injury and continues through every move: off the ground, out of the wind, dry, covered and actively warmed.
w: Warm Lactated Ringer's boluses to heat him from the inside
A blanket over the torso, leaving the stumps exposed for monitoring
Shivering allowed to continue since it is the body's own warming

qs.q: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+2:30 (Patrol base): The tourniquets have been on for about 2.5 hours. A teammate asks whether it is time to convert them to pressure dressings. Blood pressure is rising, and there is new oozing past the left tourniquet. What fits best for the tourniquets?
qs.a: Tourniquets left in place, the left one tightened or a second added above it, and times recorded on the DD1380
qs.x: Amputation tourniquets stay on. As resuscitation raises blood pressure, a tourniquet that was effective can start to leak and needs reassessment. TCCC: tourniquet conversion is not attempted on an amputation, on a casualty in shock, or when the casualty cannot be watched closely. Every tourniquet is reassessed after each move and as blood pressure recovers.
w: Both tourniquets converted to pressure dressings now that the 2-hour mark has passed
Tourniquets loosened every 30 minutes to let the limbs perfuse
A pressure dressing added over the left stump while the tourniquet stays loose

qs.q: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+3 (Patrol base): He is nauseated and has vomited once. Both stumps are open, contaminated wounds packed with dirt and fabric. No antibiotic has been given yet. Which antibiotic plan fits best?
qs.a: IV ertapenem or ceftriaxone now, with the time recorded
qs.x: TCCC calls for antibiotics as soon as possible for open combat wounds, by IV, IO or IM route when oral intake is not possible. TCCC antibiotics: moxifloxacin by mouth when the casualty can swallow; ertapenem or ceftriaxone IV, IO or IM when the casualty cannot. The time each dose is given goes on the DD1380 so redosing stays on schedule during the hold.
w: Oral moxifloxacin from the combat wound medication pack
Antibiotics held until signs of infection appear
Topical antiseptic poured into the wounds instead of systemic antibiotics

qs.q: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+6 (Patrol base): He rates his pain 8 out of 10 and is grimacing. His blood pressure is better but he is still tachycardic. Which analgesic approach fits best?
qs.a: Ketamine titrated to effect, with pain and sedation scores recorded and an antiemetic as needed
qs.x: Ketamine provides strong analgesia while preserving blood pressure and breathing, which makes it the TCCC choice for a casualty in or at risk of shock. TCCC analgesia: the combat wound medication pack for mild pain, fentanyl or ketamine for moderate to severe pain, and ketamine preferred when shock or respiratory distress is present. Pain scores are recorded with each dose on the PCC flowsheet.
w: Repeated IV morphine until he is comfortable
Meloxicam, since it does not depress breathing
Analgesia withheld until his blood pressure is completely normal

qs.q: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+12 (Patrol base): A Foley catheter has been placed. All four stored units are used. Urine output over the last two hours is low and dark. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Fresh whole blood from prescreened walking blood bank donors, calcium as needed, and a teleconsult
qs.x: Low urine output, falling hemoglobin and persistent lactate point to ongoing under-resuscitation that blood corrects. In prolonged care, urine output via a Foley, lactate and hemoglobin trends guide resuscitation better than one blood pressure. Teleconsultation through the ADVISOR line helps plan ongoing blood needs and donor use.
w: Norepinephrine to raise blood pressure
Large crystalloid boluses to bring up urine output
Current status accepted because his systolic pressure is above 90

qs.q: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+40 (Long hold, day 2): He has a new fever and a foul smell from the right stump dressing. The skin above the wound is red and warm. What is the best response?
qs.a: Wound exposed, irrigated and debris removed, clean dressing applied, antibiotic redosing verified, sepsis screen and teleconsult
qs.x: Source control in the field means cleaning and opening the wound, confirming antibiotics are on time, and getting expert input. JTS Prolonged Casualty Care guidance includes daily wound checks, irrigation and dressing changes. New fever with a rising heart rate prompts a sepsis screen, lactate check, antibiotic review and a teleconsult, and the casualty's evacuation priority may change.
w: More dressing layers added on top to contain the smell
Acetaminophen for the fever and observation
Antibiotics stopped because they appear to have failed

qs.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+0:10 (Point of injury): His abdomen is firm and slowly distending. He is pale and anxious with a weak radial pulse. No external bleeding is visible. Which plan fits best?
qs.a: Whole blood resuscitation to a radial pulse and clear mentation, TXA early, and an urgent surgical evacuation request
qs.x: Non-compressible bleeding needs blood, TXA and a surgeon. Hypotensive resuscitation limits clot disruption until surgery. Non-compressible torso hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable combat death. TCCC: resuscitate to a palpable radial pulse, normal mentation or a systolic pressure near 100, with whole blood and TXA, while pushing for surgical care.
w: Hemostatic gauze packed deep into the abdominal wound
An abdominal aortic junctional tourniquet applied over the abdomen
Crystalloid to bring blood pressure back to normal

qs.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+0:30 (Casualty collection point): He is thirsty and asks for water. A teammate offers the combat wound medication pack. Which antibiotic plan fits best?
qs.a: IV or IO ertapenem now, nothing by mouth, mouth moistened with a damp gauze
qs.x: Ertapenem covers bowel flora including anaerobes and suits a casualty who cannot take oral medication. Penetrating abdominal wounds are presumed to involve bowel. Ertapenem is the TCCC parenteral choice. Keeping the casualty without food or drink protects the airway and a later surgery, and a damp gauze eases thirst.
w: Oral moxifloxacin with a sip of water
Oral cephalexin to cover the skin bacteria
Antibiotics deferred until the surgeon sees him

qs.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+1 (Casualty collection point): Both stored units are in. His pressure has dipped again. i-STAT results are back. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Walking blood bank activated with ABO confirmation on donors and recipient, and calcium replacement
qs.x: Fresh whole blood supplies red cells, plasma and working platelets. Calcium corrects the citrate effect seen on the i-STAT. The walking blood bank uses prescreened donors whose type is confirmed in the field with a rapid typing card. Ionized calcium falls with every citrated unit, and repeat i-STAT checks guide replacement.
w: Hetastarch to stretch the remaining resources
Vasopressin to support blood pressure until surgery
No more blood because systolic pressure is above 80

qs.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+3 (Patrol base): After a unit of fresh whole blood, his radial pulse is stronger and he answers questions clearly. The team plans the night. Which monitoring plan fits best?
qs.a: A Foley with hourly urine output, vitals every 15 to 30 minutes, serial abdominal exams and a PCC flowsheet
qs.x: Frequent, structured reassessment catches re-bleeding early and creates the trend record for teleconsult and handoff. The PCC flowsheet records vitals, intake, urine output, medications and products over time. Trends drive decisions during a long hold and give the receiving surgeon the story.
w: Vital signs every 4 hours to let him sleep
Blood pressure alone as the trigger for action
A nasogastric tube passed blind to check for blood in the stomach

qs.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+6 (Patrol base): His pain is 9 out of 10 and he is guarding his abdomen. A teammate worries that pain medication will hide a worsening exam. Which analgesic approach fits best?
qs.a: Titrated IV fentanyl or ketamine, with pain and sedation scores recorded
qs.x: Both work quickly with IV or IO access and are TCCC options for severe pain. Ketamine is favored if pressure drops again. Pain control is part of care, not a threat to diagnosis. TCCC and the JTS Analgesia and Sedation CPG favor titrated fentanyl or ketamine for severe pain and avoid NSAIDs other than meloxicam in casualties who may bleed.
w: Ketorolac, since it avoids opioid side effects
Analgesia withheld to keep the abdominal exam reliable
IM morphine for its longer effect

qs.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+12 (Patrol base): He is stable through the night. Hemoglobin is holding. A teammate suggests raising his pressure further with fluid and starting clot prevention. What fits best now?
qs.a: Measured maintenance fluid with ongoing reassessment, nothing by mouth, and a teleconsult update
qs.x: With bleeding controlled for now, the goal is steady perfusion without over-resuscitation while surgery is awaited. After the shock phase, prolonged care shifts to careful maintenance and watching for re-bleeding. DVT prophylaxis waits until bleeding is surgically controlled, a decision made with a teleconsult.
w: Enoxaparin started to prevent DVT during the long hold
Large crystalloid boluses to push systolic pressure higher
A regular meal to support healing

qs.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): He is confused and breathing fast. His abdomen is rigid and tender everywhere. His skin is warm and flushed. What is happening, and what fits best?
qs.a: Septic shock from peritonitis; fluid bolus with reassessment, antibiotic coverage reviewed by teleconsult, lactate repeated, evacuation priority raised
qs.x: Fever, confusion, fast breathing, low pressure and high lactate after bowel injury add up to septic shock that needs source control. The JTS Sepsis in PFC CPG uses early recognition, fluid boluses with reassessment, broad antibiotics and vasopressors when needed. Source control means surgery here, so the casualty's evacuation priority rises.
w: Re-bleeding; more whole blood
Fever only; acetaminophen and recheck in 4 hours
Fluids withheld to avoid abdominal swelling

qs.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+32 (Long hold, day 2): After two fluid boluses his lungs are still clear, but his mean arterial pressure stays low and his urine output is falling. What is the best next step?
qs.a: Norepinephrine titrated to a MAP of at least 65 through secure access
qs.x: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor for septic shock once initial fluid has been given. Septic shock: MAP target of 65 or more, norepinephrine first, vasopressin as a second agent. Infusions in the field need a secure line, a pump or careful drip counting, and close blood pressure checks.
w: Dopamine as the first vasopressor
Repeated boluses until crackles appear
A MAP of 58 accepted since he is still mentating

qs.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+48 (Long hold, day 2): A helicopter is inbound. He is on norepinephrine with improving lactate. The team prepares for handoff. Which handoff fits best?
qs.a: DD1380 and PCC flowsheet with trends, all products and donor IDs, antibiotic and infusion times, plus a MIST verbal report
qs.x: Complete documentation lets the surgical team act right away and avoid repeating or missing treatments. The DD1380 and PCC flowsheet travel with the casualty. They include tourniquet and product times, walking blood bank donor information, medications with times, and trends in vitals, urine output and labs.
w: A quick verbal summary to the flight medic
A blank DD1380 sent with a promise to email details later
Only the most recent set of vital signs

qs.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+0:10 (Point of injury): He has snoring respirations and does not open his eyes to pain. External bleeding is controlled. What fits best for his airway?
qs.a: Rapid sequence intubation with a hemodynamically stable induction agent and a paralytic, with preoxygenation and waveform capnography
qs.x: With a GCS of 7 and hypoxia, he needs a definitive airway. Ketamine or etomidate with rocuronium keeps blood pressure stable. In TBI, a single episode of hypoxia or hypotension raises mortality. TCCC and the JTS TBI in PFC CPG aim for SpO2 above 90% and avoid hypotension during airway management. Ketamine is acceptable in TBI.
w: A nasopharyngeal airway and observation
Hyperventilation by bag right away to reduce brain swelling
Midazolam alone to facilitate intubation

qs.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): He is intubated and on the ventilator. A teammate set a high rate to protect his brain. How is ventilation best adjusted?
qs.a: Rate reduced to bring EtCO2 to 35 to 40 mmHg
qs.x: Normal CO2 keeps cerebral blood flow steady. Hyperventilation is a short bridge only for active herniation. JTS TBI in PFC targets: SpO2 above 90%, normal EtCO2 near 35 to 40 mmHg, systolic pressure above 110 mmHg, head of bed raised about 30 degrees, and normal temperature and glucose.
w: EtCO2 kept at 28 to protect the brain
EtCO2 allowed to rise to 50 for lung protection
Only FiO2 adjusted, since EtCO2 is not relevant in TBI

qs.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+1:30 (Casualty collection point): His right pupil is now 6 mm and sluggish, the left is 3 mm. His blood pressure is rising and his heart rate is falling. What fits best now?
qs.a: Hypertonic saline bolus, head of bed at 30 degrees with the neck straight, brief hyperventilation to EtCO2 near 30 to 35 as a bridge, and an urgent teleconsult
qs.x: A blown pupil with the Cushing triad signals herniation. Hypertonic saline draws water from the brain and supports pressure. Herniation signs: a dilated or sluggish pupil, posturing, falling GCS, or the Cushing triad of high blood pressure, slow heart rate and irregular breathing. JTS favors hypertonic saline. Mannitol is an alternative but can lower blood pressure through diuresis.
w: Metoprolol to bring blood pressure down
Atropine for the bradycardia
Observation until both pupils are fixed

qs.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+2 (Casualty collection point): He has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting more than 2 minutes. The ventilator alarms. What fits best?
qs.a: A benzodiazepine to stop the seizure, then levetiracetam for ongoing prophylaxis
qs.x: Midazolam or lorazepam stops the seizure quickly, and levetiracetam covers the early post-injury period. The JTS TBI in PFC CPG recommends seizure prophylaxis with levetiracetam for severe TBI for about 7 days. Active seizures are stopped first with a benzodiazepine while watching blood pressure.
w: A paralytic to stop the movement
Levetiracetam alone, then waiting for it to work
Observation, since seizures stop on their own

qs.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+4 (Patrol base): He is settled after the seizure. Labs come back. A teammate wants to start a dextrose-containing maintenance fluid. Which fluid plan fits best?
qs.a: Isotonic fluid such as Plasma-Lyte or normal saline, with sodium and glucose rechecked every 4 to 6 hours
qs.x: Isotonic fluid avoids pulling water into the brain, and repeat checks catch dangerous sodium or glucose shifts. In TBI, sodium is kept normal to mildly high with a target set by teleconsult, and swings are avoided. Glucose is kept roughly in the 80 to 180 mg/dL range because both low and high glucose harm the injured brain.
w: Dextrose-containing maintenance fluid
Large volumes of Lactated Ringer's to keep the kidneys perfused
Fluids stopped to keep the brain dry

qs.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+8 (Patrol base): He coughs and bucks against the ventilator during suctioning. His heart rate and blood pressure spike. What fits best?
qs.a: Analgesia and sedation deepened with ketamine and fentanyl, propofol only if blood pressure allows
qs.x: Coughing and agitation raise intracranial pressure. Analgesia first, then sedation, protects the brain while keeping pressure up. Analgesia-first sedation reduces intracranial pressure spikes. Ketamine does not raise intracranial pressure in ventilated patients when CO2 is controlled. Propofol lowers intracranial pressure but often drops blood pressure.
w: Rocuronium alone to stop the bucking
Restraints only, since medications cloud the neuro exam
Suctioning stopped completely

qs.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+14 (Patrol base): After propofol was increased, his blood pressure dropped. A teammate says a systolic of 92 is fine under TCCC. What fits best?
qs.a: Propofol reduced, volume status checked, and a vasopressor such as norepinephrine or phenylephrine to keep systolic above 110
