qs.x: Removing the cause and supporting pressure maintains brain perfusion. TBI blood pressure target: systolic above 110 mmHg in the JTS TBI in PFC CPG. When sedation lowers pressure, the sedative is adjusted first and a vasopressor is added as needed.
w: A systolic of 92 accepted as within TCCC targets
Head of bed lowered flat to raise blood pressure
More hypertonic saline only

qs.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): Urine output has jumped to about 300 mL per hour of pale, watery urine. No hypertonic saline has been given in 10 hours. What is most likely, and what fits best?
qs.a: Diabetes insipidus from pituitary injury; teleconsult, hypertonic saline held, and water replacement guided by frequent sodium checks
qs.x: Large volumes of dilute urine with rising sodium after severe TBI point to diabetes insipidus. Central diabetes insipidus can follow severe TBI. Clues are high urine output, dilute urine and rising sodium. Treatment needs teleconsult guidance, and sodium is lowered slowly.
w: Response to earlier hypertonic saline; more hypertonic saline
Normal diuresis; no change
Fluid restriction to slow urine output

qs.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): His temperature is climbing. His eyes are not fully closed, and his skin over the sacrum is pink. Which care fits best?
qs.a: Cooling and acetaminophen, a search for infection, eye lubrication and taping, and repositioning every 2 hours
qs.x: Fever control, eye protection and pressure injury prevention are core nursing tasks in prolonged TBI care. Prolonged TBI nursing includes normal temperature, eye care, oral care, head of bed at 30 degrees, repositioning every 2 hours, and recording GCS and pupil checks on the flowsheet.
w: Fever left alone as a normal response
Ice packs to the head only
Turning stopped to avoid raising intracranial pressure

qs.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+0:10 (Point of injury): His nasal hair is singed, his voice is hoarse and he is coughing up black sputum. Mild stridor has started. What fits best for his airway?
qs.a: Early rapid sequence intubation by the most experienced provider, with a cricothyroidotomy kit ready
qs.x: Hoarseness, stridor and carbonaceous sputum predict airway swelling. Intubating early is easier and safer. Signs of inhalation injury: facial burns, singed hair, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness and stridor. The JTS Burn CPG supports early intubation when these are present and transport will be prolonged.
w: Observation until stridor worsens
Nebulized racemic epinephrine as the main airway treatment
A nasopharyngeal airway

qs.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+0:30 (Casualty collection point): He is intubated. He was confused before intubation and the fire was in an enclosed space. The pulse oximeter reads high, but the i-STAT lactate is very high. What fits best?
qs.a: 100% oxygen and hydroxocobalamin for suspected cyanide poisoning
qs.x: An enclosed-space fire, altered mental status, hypotension and very high lactate suggest cyanide, and hydroxocobalamin is the preferred antidote. Smoke from burning plastics and furnishings contains carbon monoxide and cyanide. High-flow oxygen treats CO, and hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide. Hydroxocobalamin turns skin and urine red and can interfere with some lab tests.
w: SpO2 of 99% taken as proof of good oxygenation
Sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis
Amyl nitrite for cyanide

qs.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+1 (Casualty collection point): His burns are mapped and estimated at 40% TBSA, not counting superficial redness. A teammate wants a large fluid bolus based on the Parkland formula. Which fluid approach fits best?
qs.a: Lactated Ringer's started at the Rule of Ten rate, then titrated hourly to urine output
qs.x: The Rule of Ten gives a quick starting rate from TBSA and weight, and urine output guides changes from there. TCCC and the JTS Burn CPG use the Rule of Ten for adults 40 to 80 kg: TBSA rounded to the nearest 10, times 10, gives the starting hourly rate. Superficial (first-degree) burns are not counted in TBSA.
w: The full first 8-hour Parkland volume given as a bolus
Hetastarch to reduce the total volume
Fluids withheld until 2 hours after the burn

qs.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+3 (Patrol base): A Foley catheter is in. Urine output over the last hour is low and dark. Heart rate is climbing. What is the best adjustment?
qs.a: Lactated Ringer's rate increased stepwise, with urine output rechecked each hour toward a target of about 30 to 50 mL per hour
qs.x: Hourly titration to urine output is the standard way to adjust burn fluid. In burns, urine output is the main resuscitation gauge: about 30 to 50 mL per hour for adults. The fluid rate is raised or lowered in steps, and every hour is recorded on the burn flowsheet.
w: A large bolus to catch up
Mannitol to increase urine output
Low urine output accepted as expected in burns

qs.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+6 (Patrol base): Ventilator peak pressures have risen and his chest barely moves. The circumferential chest burn is leathery and tight. After a quick DOPE check is normal, what fits best?
qs.a: Chest escharotomy with teleconsult guidance
qs.x: A tight chest eschar can restrict ventilation, and releasing it restores chest wall movement. Circumferential burns of the chest or limbs can restrict breathing or circulation. Escharotomy is a high-risk procedure in the field, usually done with teleconsult guidance when ventilation or limb perfusion is failing.
w: Sedation increased
A paralytic to improve compliance
PEEP increased alone

qs.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+10 (Patrol base): The burns are exposed while being checked. The room is cool and his temperature is dropping. Which wound and temperature plan fits best?
qs.a: Clean, dry burn dressings, an active warming blanket, a warm room, and warmed fluids
qs.x: Burned skin cannot hold heat, so covering, warming the room and warming fluids prevent hypothermia. Burn casualties lose heat quickly through damaged skin. The JTS Burn CPG emphasizes dry dressings, active warming and a warm environment. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for burns alone.
w: Cool, wet dressings over all the burns for comfort
Burns left open to air to let them dry
Prophylactic systemic antibiotics for the burns

qs.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+16 (Patrol base): He grimaces during dressing changes and his heart rate jumps. He is ventilated. Which analgesia and sedation approach fits best?
qs.a: Ketamine and fentanyl titrated to pain and sedation scores, with extra analgesia before dressing changes
qs.x: Burn pain is severe and spikes with dressing changes, so analgesia-first sedation with ketamine and fentanyl fits. Burns are among the most painful injuries. Analgesia-first sedation with ketamine and opioids is common. Burn patients often need more than expected, and pain and sedation scores are recorded on the flowsheet.
w: Ketorolac for analgesia
Midazolam alone for sedation
Dressing changes stopped to avoid pain

qs.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): His endotracheal tube cuff fails and he needs re-intubation. A teammate grabs succinylcholine. Which paralytic fits best?
qs.a: Rocuronium
qs.x: Rocuronium avoids the burn-related hyperkalemia risk and still allows rapid sequence intubation. After about 24 hours, burns increase muscle acetylcholine receptors, and succinylcholine can cause a life-threatening rise in potassium. The same risk applies to crush injury, prolonged immobility and denervation injuries.
w: Succinylcholine for its fast onset and short duration
No paralytic, sedation only
Succinylcholine with calcium given ahead of time

qs.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+48 (Long hold, day 2): Urine output has been 80 to 100 mL per hour for several hours. His face, arms and abdomen are very swollen. What fits best?
qs.a: Lactated Ringer's rate reduced stepwise, with abdominal pressure and airway pressures checked
qs.x: Over-resuscitation causes abdominal compartment syndrome, worsening lung function and limb compartment problems. Fluid creep is a major cause of burn complications. When urine output exceeds the target, the rate is lowered stepwise. A tense abdomen with rising airway pressures can signal abdominal compartment syndrome.
w: The fluid rate kept the same
An extra bolus to protect the kidneys
Hetastarch to pull fluid back into the vessels

qs.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+0 (Point of injury): He is awake and talking. Engineers are ready to lift the slab in about 10 minutes. What fits best before release?
qs.a: IV or IO access with isotonic fluid running before the slab is lifted, and the cardiac monitor attached
qs.x: Fluid before release dilutes the potassium, acid and myoglobin that flood in when blood returns to the crushed muscle. Crush syndrome develops after compression of large muscle groups, often more than an hour. Preparation before release includes access, fluid, a cardiac monitor and medications for hyperkalemia ready to give.
w: Immediate lift, with fluids started once he is out
Oral water only
Lift delayed several hours to plan the evacuation

qs.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): Minutes after release, the monitor shows peaked T waves and a widening QRS. His heart rate is slowing. What comes first?
qs.a: Calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane
qs.x: Calcium protects the heart within minutes and buys time for the potassium-lowering treatments. Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: calcium first to stabilize the heart, then shift potassium into cells with insulin and dextrose, albuterol, and bicarbonate if acidotic. Only dialysis or the kidneys remove potassium from the body.
w: Insulin with dextrose to lower potassium
Sodium bicarbonate alone
Potassium recheck in 2 hours

qs.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+0:50 (Casualty collection point): After calcium, the QRS narrows. A teammate says the problem is fixed. What fits best next?
qs.a: Regular insulin with dextrose, nebulized albuterol, and sodium bicarbonate for the acidosis
qs.x: These shift potassium into cells and lower the serum level while the kidneys recover. Calcium stabilizes but does not lower potassium. The JTS Hyperkalemia CPG lists insulin and dextrose, albuterol and bicarbonate as shift therapies, with potassium and glucose rechecked often.
w: No further treatment since the ECG improved
Potassium-containing maintenance fluid
Repeated calcium alone every 30 minutes

qs.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+2 (Patrol base): He is sweaty and confused. The i-STAT is rechecked. What fits best?
qs.a: Dextrose, with glucose checked every hour while insulin effects last
qs.x: Hypoglycemia is a common complication of insulin for hyperkalemia and is quickly reversed with dextrose. Insulin for hyperkalemia commonly causes hypoglycemia 1 to 3 hours later. Hourly glucose checks for several hours are part of the treatment.
w: More insulin to keep potassium falling
Observation since potassium is improving
Albuterol for the confusion

qs.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+4 (Patrol base): His urine is dark brown like tea. A Foley is in, and output is low. Which plan fits best?
qs.a: Isotonic fluid titrated to a high urine output target of about 200 to 300 mL per hour, with lung and edema checks
qs.x: High urine flow flushes myoglobin through the kidneys and lowers the risk of kidney failure. Rhabdomyolysis from crush injury releases myoglobin that damages the kidneys. The goal is high urine output with isotonic fluid, while watching for lung crackles and edema.
w: Fluids restricted to protect the lungs
Mannitol as first-line treatment
Dark urine accepted as expected

qs.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+8 (Patrol base): His left calf is tense and shiny. He has severe pain when his toes are moved and numbness on top of his foot. Pulses are present. What fits best?
qs.a: Leg kept at heart level, tight dressings loosened, hourly compartment checks, and a teleconsult about fasciotomy
qs.x: Pain with passive stretch and numbness suggest compartment syndrome. Present pulses do not rule it out. Compartment syndrome signs: severe pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling and numbness. In crush injury, the fasciotomy decision is complex and is made with expert teleconsult input.
w: Leg elevated high to reduce swelling
Ice packs and more opioid
Waiting until pulses are lost

qs.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+14 (Patrol base): Potassium is rising again. Urine output has dropped despite fluids, and there are new crackles in both lungs. What fits best?
qs.a: Repeat shift therapy, fluids reduced, oxygen, and an urgent teleconsult to raise evacuation priority for dialysis
qs.x: Kidney failure with rising potassium needs dialysis, which only a hospital can provide. Oliguric kidney failure after crush injury needs dialysis. In the field, potassium is managed with repeated shift therapy and the evacuation priority rises.
w: More fluid boluses to restart urine flow
Potassium chloride in the IV fluid
Atropine for prevention

qs.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): He is awake and in severe pain from his legs. Kidney function is poor. Which analgesic approach fits best?
qs.a: Fentanyl or ketamine titrated to pain, with sedation and breathing watched
qs.x: Neither relies on the kidneys for clearance as much as morphine, so they are better choices in kidney failure. In kidney failure, NSAIDs are avoided and morphine is used with caution. Fentanyl and ketamine are preferred. Pain and sedation scores are recorded with each dose.
w: Ketorolac or meloxicam for non-opioid pain control
Morphine repeated as needed
Pain medication withheld because of kidney failure

qs.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+0:05 (Point of injury): The wound bubbles with each breath. He is short of breath but talking in full sentences. Breath sounds are present on both sides. What fits best for the wound?
qs.a: A vented chest seal applied, then close watch for progressive respiratory distress
qs.x: A vented seal stops air entry through the wound while letting pleural air escape, and tension can still develop later. TCCC: open or sucking chest wounds receive a vented or non-vented chest seal, then the casualty is monitored for tension pneumothorax. Placing the casualty in the sitting or recovery position, injured side down, can ease breathing when the casualty is conscious.
w: Wound left open to air so tension cannot build
Needle decompression before the seal goes on
Hemostatic gauze packed into the chest wound

qs.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+0:30 (Casualty collection point): He is gasping and anxious. Breath sounds are absent on the right. The chest seal was burped and briefly removed without improvement. What fits best?
qs.a: Needle decompression at the 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line or the 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line
qs.x: Suspected tension pneumothorax with shock and hypoxia is decompressed right away, and TCCC lists both sites. TCCC: suspected tension pneumothorax with progressive respiratory distress on the injured side is decompressed with a needle, and repeated if signs return. Simple thoracostomy is an option for providers trained in it.
w: Observation until tracheal deviation confirms tension
A fluid bolus to treat the falling blood pressure
Intubation and positive pressure ventilation first

qs.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+1:30 (Casualty collection point): He improved, then tired and was intubated with ketamine and rocuronium. On the ventilator, his oxygen and pressure fall again and peak pressure climbs. What fits best?
qs.a: Finger (simple) thoracostomy at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line
qs.x: Positive pressure keeps refilling the pleural space, and an open finger thoracostomy decompresses it reliably in a ventilated casualty. In a ventilated casualty, recurrent tension after needle decompression is an indication for simple thoracostomy by a trained provider. A chest tube follows when the hold is long and a kit and teleconsult are available.
w: More needle decompressions, one every few minutes
Tidal volume increased to improve oxygen
Sedation deepened for ventilator dyssynchrony

qs.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+3 (Patrol base): A chest tube placed with teleconsult guidance drains about 900 mL of blood at once and then keeps dripping. His pressure is still low. What fits best?
qs.a: Whole blood, TXA because he is within 3 hours of injury, calcium, warming, and hourly chest tube output tracking
qs.x: Hemorrhagic shock from a hemothorax needs blood, and hourly output tells whether surgery is urgent. Surgical bleeding is suggested by about 1,500 mL drained at once, or about 200 mL per hour for 2 to 4 hours. Chest tube output is recorded hourly on the PCC flowsheet alongside vitals and products.
w: Chest tube clamped to tamponade the bleeding
Crystalloid bolus to bring pressure up
Output ignored now that the lung has re-expanded

qs.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+6 (Patrol base): His SpO2 drops suddenly and the ventilator alarms high pressure. The EtCO2 waveform is still present but smaller. The chest tube has stopped draining. What fits best?
qs.a: Disconnection from the ventilator, bag ventilation, and a DOPE check that includes chest tube patency
qs.x: DOPE finds the cause in a structured way; a kinked or clotted tube with a new pneumothorax fits these findings. DOPE: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment. Bagging off the ventilator separates a patient problem from a machine problem, and a chest tube that suddenly stops draining is checked for kinks, clots and position.
w: FiO2 and PEEP raised and the alarm silenced
More sedation for coughing
Paralysis to lower airway pressure

qs.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+10 (Patrol base): Chest tube output has been about 150 to 200 mL per hour for 3 hours. All stored units are used. What fits best?
qs.a: Teleconsult reporting the trend, evacuation priority raised to urgent surgical, and fresh whole blood from the walking blood bank
qs.x: This bleeding likely needs a thoracotomy, so the team raises priority and replaces blood until then. Ongoing hemothorax output is one of the clearest field signals that surgery is needed. The teleconsult report includes hourly output, products given, and vital sign and lab trends.
w: A second chest tube to drain faster
Output accepted as normal after a chest wound
Chest tube clamped to slow the loss

qs.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+18 (Patrol base): Bleeding has slowed. An arterial i-STAT is run on FiO2 0.6. He has a large pulmonary contusion. Which ventilator adjustment fits best?
qs.a: Lung-protective tidal volume kept, PEEP titrated for oxygenation, and rate increased for CO2
qs.x: Rate clears CO2 and PEEP recruits lung without the overstretch of larger breaths. Lung-protective ventilation uses tidal volume based on ideal body weight, a plateau pressure under 30, and PEEP and FiO2 adjusted together. Mild permissive hypercapnia is acceptable when there is no brain injury.
w: Sodium bicarbonate for the low pH
Tidal volume increased well above the lung-protective range to clear CO2
FiO2 at 1.0 for the rest of the hold

qs.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): He has a new fever and thick yellow secretions on suctioning. The head of the litter has been flat most of the night. What fits best?
qs.a: Pneumonia bundle with head of bed at 30 degrees, oral care, suctioning, and an antibiotic chosen with teleconsult
qs.x: Fever with purulent secretions in a ventilated casualty suggests pneumonia, and the bundle limits further aspiration. Ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention includes head of bed at 30 degrees, oral care, suctioning and daily sedation checks. New fever in prolonged care prompts a source search and antibiotic choice guided by teleconsult.
w: Chest tube removed as the likely source
Acetaminophen and recheck later
Suctioning reduced to rest the airway

qs.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0 (Point of injury): He is confused and combative. His skin is hot and still sweaty. A rectal thermometer is in the aid bag. What fits best?
qs.a: Immediate whole-body cooling with cold water immersion or tarp-assisted cooling with ice water
qs.x: Time above about 40 C (104 F) drives organ injury, and rapid cooling within 30 minutes gives the best outcomes. Exertional heat stroke is a high core temperature with central nervous system dysfunction. Sweaty skin does not rule it out. Cold water immersion is the fastest method, with tarp-assisted cooling or ice sheets as field alternatives.
w: Shade, loosened gear and oral water
Evacuation first, with cooling at the aid station
Acetaminophen for the high temperature

qs.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0:20 (Point of injury): His rectal temperature is falling quickly. A teammate wants to keep cooling until it reaches 37 C (98.6 F). When is active cooling stopped?
qs.a: At about 39 C (102.2 F), with continued rectal temperature checks
qs.x: Stopping near 39 C (102.2 F) avoids overshoot, and ongoing checks catch rebound. Active cooling stops near 39 C (about 102 F) measured rectally. Oral, ear and forehead readings are unreliable in heat stroke, and rebound hyperthermia is common in the first hours.
w: When shivering starts
Only once mental status is fully normal

qs.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0:30 (Point of injury): During cooling he has a generalized seizure and fights the tarp. What fits best?
qs.a: A benzodiazepine to stop the seizure, with cooling continued and the airway protected
qs.x: Midazolam or diazepam stops seizures and shivering, both of which generate heat. Benzodiazepines are the agents of choice for seizures, agitation and shivering during heat stroke cooling. Antipsychotics are avoided.
w: Haloperidol for the agitation
Cooling paused until the seizure ends
Restraints to keep him on the tarp

qs.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0:45 (Casualty collection point): Cooling is done but he is still slow to answer. An i-STAT CHEM8+ is run. What fits best?
qs.a: Dextrose, then repeat glucose checks
qs.x: Hypoglycemia after prolonged exertion adds to his confusion and corrects quickly. Glucose is checked in every casualty with altered mental status. Exertional illness can also cause hyponatremia, so sodium guides fluid choice. Both are trended on the PCC flowsheet.
w: Free water by mouth for the low sodium
Insulin with dextrose for the potassium
Observation, since confusion is expected after heat stroke

qs.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+2 (Patrol base): A Foley drains a small amount of cola-colored urine. His legs ache. What fits best?
qs.a: Isotonic fluid titrated to a high urine output target, with lung checks and potassium trends
qs.x: Brisk urine flow protects the kidneys from myoglobin, and potassium is watched as muscle breaks down. Exertional heat stroke often causes rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. Isotonic fluid is titrated to a high urine output, watching for crackles, edema and falling sodium.
w: Fluids restricted to avoid swelling
A diuretic to increase urine flow
Cola-colored urine accepted as dehydration that will clear

qs.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+8 (Patrol base): There is new oozing from IV sites and his gums, and petechiae on his chest. What fits best?
qs.a: Teleconsult, whole blood or plasma if available, and a higher evacuation priority
qs.x: Heat stroke can trigger DIC, which needs factor replacement and hospital care. DIC is a late, ominous complication of heat stroke, often with liver injury. Field care is supportive: blood products when available, avoidance of drugs that worsen bleeding, and urgent evacuation.
w: TXA to stop the oozing
Enoxaparin to treat microclots
Aspirin for the petechiae

qs.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+16 (Patrol base): His temperature rebounds. His right upper abdomen is tender. A teammate reaches for fever medication. What fits best?
qs.a: External cooling restarted with ice water and fanning, with rectal temperature monitored
qs.x: Rebound hyperthermia is treated the same way as the first episode: physical cooling. Rebound hyperthermia is common after heat stroke. External cooling is the treatment, and liver injury from heat stroke is another reason to avoid acetaminophen.
w: Ketorolac to bring the temperature down
Acetaminophen to bring the temperature down
Observation, since the peak has passed

qs.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): He is awake and oriented and says he feels fine. Evacuation is inbound. What fits best?
qs.a: DD1380 and PCC flowsheet with cooling times, temperatures, glucose, labs and urine output, plus a MIST report
qs.x: This record lets the hospital judge kidney, liver and clotting injury and plan follow-up. Feeling well does not mean organ recovery. Kidney, liver and clotting injury evolve over days, and the record of cooling start time, peak temperature and lab trends guides care and return-to-duty decisions.
w: Return to duty since he feels better
A verbal handoff only
The last set of vital signs only

qs.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+2 (Patrol base): He is bucking the ventilator, grimacing and reaching for the tube. What fits best?
qs.a: Analgesia first with ketamine or fentanyl, then sedation titrated to a RASS goal of 0 to -2
qs.x: Pain is the most common driver of agitation in a fresh trauma casualty. The JTS Analgesia and Sedation CPG uses analgesia-first sedation. Pain is scored with a tool such as CPOT or a behavioral scale when the casualty cannot talk, and RASS is recorded with every check.
w: Rocuronium to stop him fighting the ventilator
Midazolam alone to calm him
Soft restraints and observation

qs.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+6 (Patrol base): A teammate added propofol for better sedation, and his pressure dropped. What fits best?
qs.a: Propofol reduced or stopped, with ketamine as the main agent and volume status checked
qs.x: Ketamine supports blood pressure and breathing, which fits a recently bled trauma casualty. Propofol is short acting but causes vasodilation and hypotension. In prolonged casualty care with limited monitoring, ketamine is often the backbone agent, with fentanyl for analgesia.
w: Propofol continued and a vasopressor added to cover it
A switch to dexmedetomidine
Midazolam in place of propofol

qs.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+10 (Patrol base): While turning him, the team hears gurgling at the mouth. The EtCO2 waveform disappears and his SpO2 falls. What fits best?
qs.a: Tube displacement recognized, bag-mask ventilation, and re-intubation confirmed by waveform capnography
qs.x: A lost waveform after moving a casualty is displacement until proven otherwise. Waveform capnography is the fastest monitor for displacement. DOPE starts with D, and tube depth at the teeth is recorded on the flowsheet and checked after every move.
w: FiO2 increased to 100%
Needle decompression on both sides
Suctioning through the tube

qs.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+18 (Patrol base): He does not open his eyes to voice or move to shoulder shaking. His sedation has not been lightened since H+6. What fits best?
qs.a: Sedation lightened toward a RASS of 0 to -2, with pain reassessed as he wakes
qs.x: Light sedation is the goal, and reassessing pain avoids swinging into agitation. Daily sedation lightening and a set RASS target reduce ventilator days and delirium. Reversal agents are for overdose emergencies, not routine sedation adjustment.
w: Deep sedation kept for comfort
Flumazenil to wake him
Naloxone for full opioid reversal

qs.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): Skin checks show a patch of non-blanching redness over the sacrum and red heels. He has been on a litter for a day. What fits best?
qs.a: Repositioning every 2 hours, padding over bony areas, heels floated off the litter, and skin documented
qs.x: Non-blanching redness is a stage 1 pressure injury, and offloading prevents progression. Litters and ventilated immobility cause pressure injuries fast. JTS PCC guidance includes turns every 2 hours, padding, skin checks, and keeping skin dry, all recorded on the PCC flowsheet.
w: Massage of the red area to restore blood flow
Turns every 6 hours to let him rest
A donut-shaped cushion under the sacrum

qs.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): Hemoglobin has been stable on three checks, the leg wound is dry, and he has no brain or spinal cord injury. A teammate asks about clot prevention. What fits best?
qs.a: Enoxaparin started now that bleeding is controlled, after a teleconsult
qs.x: With hemorrhage controlled and no brain injury, the benefit of prophylaxis outweighs the bleeding risk. Trauma casualties are hypercoagulable after the first day. Enoxaparin prophylaxis begins once bleeding is controlled, often around 24 to 36 hours, with teleconsult input. Intermittent compression devices can be used earlier when carried.
w: Aspirin for DVT prevention
No prophylaxis until he reaches a hospital
Enoxaparin given at H+1, right after the wound was packed

qs.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+36 (Long hold, day 2): He has been ventilated with nothing by mouth for 36 hours. There is a small amount of coffee-ground fluid in the mouth during suctioning. What fits best?
qs.a: Stress ulcer prophylaxis, an orogastric tube to decompress the stomach, and a teleconsult about starting enteral feeding
qs.x: Acid suppression protects the stomach, and gastric access allows decompression and early nutrition. Ventilated trauma casualties are at high risk for stress ulcers. Pantoprazole or famotidine and early enteral nutrition through a gastric tube are standard in prolonged care, and nutrition is planned with teleconsult guidance.
w: No action, since the amount is small
An oral diet once he is lighter
IV fluids alone for nutrition

qs.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+48 (Long hold, day 3): Dexmedetomidine was added to ease agitation as sedation was lightened. His heart rate falls and he looks pale. What fits best?
qs.a: Dexmedetomidine reduced or stopped, with atropine or glycopyrrolate ready if he becomes unstable
qs.x: Bradycardia and hypotension are expected effects of dexmedetomidine and usually improve when it is reduced. Dexmedetomidine allows light, rousable sedation but causes bradycardia and hypotension. It is reduced or stopped first. Atropine or glycopyrrolate treats symptomatic bradycardia.
w: Dexmedetomidine increased because he is still restless
Haloperidol added for agitation
Observation only, since heart rate often drops with sedation

qs.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+72 (Long hold, day 3): The evacuation aircraft is inbound. He is on ketamine and fentanyl at a RASS of -1. Which handoff fits best?
qs.a: PCC flowsheet with RASS and pain scores, ventilator settings, tube depth, line and drain times, medications with times, skin checks and intake and output
qs.x: A complete record supports safe continuity of care and avoids missed or repeated treatments. In a 72-hour hold, the PCC flowsheet is the medical record. It includes sedation and pain scores, ventilator settings, devices with placement times, medications with times, skin and wound checks, and intake and output.
w: A verbal report to the flight crew
A blank DD1380 with a note to call later
The last set of vital signs only

qs.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+1 (Casualty collection point): Stored blood is gone and he is still in shock. Several soldiers volunteer to donate. Which donor approach fits best?
qs.a: Prescreened donors from the roster, with ABO confirmed by rapid typing on both donor and recipient and each unit labeled
qs.x: Pre-deployment screening plus field confirmation and labeling lower the risk of mismatch and clerical error. The JTS Whole Blood Transfusion CPG relies on prescreened donors, low titer O when the recipient type is unknown, field ABO confirmation, and careful labeling. Most severe reactions come from identification errors.
w: Any volunteer whose ID tag says type O
The first available volunteer, to save time
No transfusion until evacuation

qs.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+1:40 (Casualty collection point): Fifteen minutes into the first fresh unit he develops a high fever, back and flank pain, oozing around the IV, and dark red urine in the Foley bag. What fits best?
qs.a: Transfusion stopped at once, the line kept open with saline through new tubing, and donor and recipient identity and typing rechecked
qs.x: Fever, flank pain, hypotension, oozing and dark urine early in a unit point to an acute hemolytic reaction. Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: fever, chills, flank or back pain, hypotension, red or dark urine and oozing from DIC, usually early in the unit. The first step for any suspected reaction is stopping the transfusion.
w: Transfusion slowed and the casualty watched closely
Acetaminophen for the fever and the unit continued
Diphenhydramine and the unit continued

qs.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+1:50 (Casualty collection point): The transfusion is stopped. He remains hypotensive and urine output is low and dark. What fits best?
qs.a: Blood pressure supported with fluid and norepinephrine, high urine output maintained, potassium and calcium treated, and a teleconsult
qs.x: Hemolysis causes shock, kidney injury, high potassium and DIC, so support focuses on each. Hemolytic reactions release potassium and free hemoglobin. Support includes blood pressure, urine output to protect the kidneys, treatment of hyperkalemia, and watching for DIC.
w: The same unit restarted once his pressure improves
Sodium bicarbonate as the main treatment
Observation until the fever breaks

qs.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+2:30 (Casualty collection point): Retyping shows the recipient is type A. The donor recorded as O retypes as B. The tube labels were swapped during collection. Which donor fits best for the next unit?
qs.a: Type A or low titer O donor, both confirmed by rapid typing, with one collection labeled at a time
qs.x: These are compatible with a type A recipient, and one-at-a-time labeling prevents another swap. Fresh whole blood is type-specific or low titer O. Collecting and labeling one donor at a time, with two-person checks, prevents most clerical errors.
w: Another type B donor
Any type O donor without a known titer
No more blood after a reaction

qs.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+4 (Casualty collection point): During a type A unit his temperature rises and he shivers. Blood pressure is stable, urine is clear, and there is no pain or rash. What fits best?
qs.a: Transfusion paused, hemolysis and contamination looked for, acetaminophen for fever, and a teleconsult decision on resuming or using a new unit
qs.x: Isolated fever and chills with stable vitals fit a febrile non-hemolytic reaction once worse causes are excluded. Febrile non-hemolytic reactions are common, especially with fresh whole blood. Hemolysis and bacterial contamination are excluded before deciding to resume or use another unit.
w: Transfusion continued without a pause
Epinephrine for the reaction
All transfusion stopped for the rest of the hold

qs.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+5 (Casualty collection point): During the next unit, hives appear on his chest and he itches. Breathing, voice and blood pressure are normal. What fits best?
qs.a: Transfusion paused, diphenhydramine, and the unit resumed if hives resolve and nothing else develops
qs.x: Isolated hives are a mild allergic reaction, which is the one reaction where the same unit is often resumed. Mild allergic reactions cause hives and itching only. Wheezing, throat tightness, swelling or hypotension change the picture to anaphylaxis, which is treated with epinephrine and the transfusion is not resumed.
w: Epinephrine for possible anaphylaxis
All transfusion stopped for the rest of the hold
Methylprednisolone and the unit continued without a pause

qs.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+6:30 (Casualty collection point): About 90 minutes after the last unit he becomes acutely short of breath with frothy secretions and crackles in both lungs. His neck veins are flat. What fits best?
qs.a: Oxygen and ventilatory support with PEEP, any running blood stopped, and a teleconsult, treated as TRALI
qs.x: Hypoxia within 6 hours of transfusion with fever, hypotension and flat neck veins points to TRALI, which is treated with supportive care. TRALI: hypoxia within 6 hours, fever, hypotension and normal or flat neck veins. TACO: hypoxia with high blood pressure, distended neck veins and a positive fluid balance, and it responds to diuresis.
w: A diuretic for fluid overload
Another unit of blood for the low pressure
Observation, since the transfusion is already finished

qs.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+12 (Patrol base): His oxygen requirement is falling and his pressure is stable. The team prepares records for the morning evacuation. Which documentation fits best?
qs.a: Each unit's donor ID, ABO results, start and stop times, reactions with vitals, treatments, and the set-aside unit, recorded on the DD1380 and PCC flowsheet
qs.x: This record supports donor follow-up for infection testing, reaction investigation and safe care at the next level. Walking blood bank records link every unit to a donor for later infection testing and reaction review. The mismatched unit and samples are kept when possible.
w: A verbal handoff only
Records of the mismatched unit discarded to avoid confusion
The last set of vital signs only

qs.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+0:20 (Casualty collection point): The tourniquet has been on for 20 minutes. He is alert with a strong radial pulse. The team can watch him closely. What fits best for the tourniquet?
qs.a: Conversion to a hemostatic or pressure dressing, with the loosened tourniquet left in place and the wound watched
qs.x: He is not in shock, the wound is not an amputation, and he can be monitored, which fits TCCC conversion criteria. TCCC: tourniquets are reassessed and converted when possible within 2 hours if the casualty is not in shock, can be monitored, and does not have an amputation. A loosened tourniquet stays in place for quick re-tightening.
w: Tourniquet left in place until evacuation
Tourniquet loosened every 30 minutes
Tourniquet removed and the leg elevated without a dressing

qs.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): The bleeding is controlled. The thigh is shortened and deformed, and bone is visible. What fits best?
qs.a: Wound dressed, then a traction splint applied, with distal pulses and sensation checked before and after
qs.x: Traction stabilizes the fracture, reduces bleeding and pain, and limits fat embolism risk. Traction splints are used for midshaft femur fractures without contraindications such as pelvic or knee injury. Distal pulse, motor and sensory checks are recorded before and after.
w: No splint, to avoid disturbing the wound
Exposed bone pushed back into the wound before splinting
Tight elastic wrap around the whole thigh

qs.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+1 (Casualty collection point): No antibiotics have been given. He is not vomiting and has IV access. Which antibiotic plan fits best?
qs.a: IV cefazolin, or ertapenem or ceftriaxone if that is what the kit carries, now
qs.x: Early IV antibiotics reduce infection after open fractures, and the JTS favors cefazolin for open extremity fractures. The JTS Prevention of Combat-Related Infections CPG recommends cefazolin for open extremity fractures, ideally within the first hour. TCCC lists moxifloxacin by mouth or ertapenem or ceftriaxone for open combat wounds.
w: Antibiotics deferred until fever appears
Topical antiseptic only
The wound sutured closed to keep bacteria out

qs.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+3 (Patrol base): His pain is 9 out of 10 despite the splint. He is not in shock and is breathing comfortably. Which analgesic approach fits best?
qs.a: Multimodal analgesia: acetaminophen plus titrated ketamine or fentanyl, with pain and sedation scores recorded and an antiemetic as needed
qs.x: Combining agents improves pain control while limiting the side effects of any one drug. Multimodal analgesia is standard in prolonged care. The JTS Analgesia and Sedation CPG includes acetaminophen, ketamine and opioids, and newer non-opioids such as suzetrigine may be used for moderate pain.
w: Midazolam to help him relax
Frequent IM morphine
Analgesia withheld to avoid masking compartment syndrome

qs.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+8 (Patrol base): His lower leg is tense and shiny. Moving his toes causes severe pain, and he reports numbness between the first and second toes. Pedal pulses are present. What fits best?
qs.a: Splint straps and dressings loosened, leg at heart level, hourly checks, and an urgent teleconsult about fasciotomy
qs.x: Pain with passive stretch and numbness suggest compartment syndrome even with pulses present. Compartment syndrome signs: severe pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling and numbness. Fasciotomy in the field is a high-risk procedure usually performed with teleconsult guidance.
w: The leg elevated well above the heart
More opioid until the pain settles
Observation until pulses are lost

qs.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+20 (Patrol base): After a fasciotomy under telementoring, he is alert and asking for food. Urine output has been adequate. What fits best?
qs.a: Oral fluids and calorie-dense rations, with intake and output tracked and fasciotomy wounds checked
qs.x: Early oral nutrition supports healing, and tracking intake and output catches dehydration or kidney injury. Nutrition and hydration are part of prolonged casualty care. Oral intake is preferred when the gut works, and intake and output are recorded on the PCC flowsheet.
w: Nothing by mouth until evacuation
IV crystalloid alone for hydration
Food only after he is evacuated

qs.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+36 (Long hold, day 2): He becomes confused and short of breath. There are pinpoint petechiae on his chest, armpits and inside his eyelids. What fits best?
qs.a: Fat embolism syndrome recognized: oxygen and ventilatory support, the femur kept immobilized, a teleconsult, and a higher evacuation priority
qs.x: Hypoxia, confusion and petechiae 24 to 72 hours after a long bone fracture are classic fat embolism syndrome. Fat embolism syndrome: hypoxia, confusion and petechiae, typically 24 to 72 hours after long bone fracture. Care is supportive with oxygen, ventilation if needed, and fracture stabilization.
w: Sepsis alone assumed, with broader antibiotics
A benzodiazepine for the confusion
Methylprednisolone for the emboli

qs.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+60 (Long hold, day 3): His oxygen has improved, but the thigh wound and fasciotomy sites now have purulent drainage and spreading redness. What fits best?
qs.a: Wounds opened, irrigated and cleaned, antibiotics broadened with teleconsult, fluid bolus with reassessment, lactate repeated, and evacuation priority raised
qs.x: This is sepsis from a wound source, which needs source control and antibiotics. Sepsis from wound infection is common in prolonged care. Field source control means opening, irrigating and cleaning the wound, and the JTS Sepsis in PFC CPG guides fluids, antibiotics and vasopressors.
w: Acetaminophen and observation
More dressing layers to contain the drainage
Antibiotics stopped because they failed

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has crushing chest pain that radiates to his left arm. Protocol allows aspirin. Which findings would lead the EMT to withhold aspirin? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Hives and wheezing the last time he took aspirin; Vomiting dark coffee-ground material today
qs.x: Aspirin allergy (including aspirin-induced asthma) and active GI bleeding are contraindications. Hypertension, diabetes, radiating pain, nausea and sweating are common in ACS and do not prevent aspirin.
opts: History of high blood pressure
Hives and wheezing the last time he took aspirin
Pain radiating to the left arm
Vomiting dark coffee-ground material today
Nausea and sweating
History of type 2 diabetes
ok: Hives and wheezing the last time he took aspirin
Vomiting dark coffee-ground material today

qs.q: An EMT is giving aspirin to an adult with suspected acute coronary syndrome. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Use non-enteric-coated chewable tablets; Instruct the patient to chew the tablets before swallowing; Give a total of 162 to 324 mg (typically four 81 mg tablets)
qs.x: For suspected ACS, 162-324 mg of non-enteric-coated aspirin is chewed so it is absorbed quickly. Swallowing whole, enteric coating or sublingual placement delays or does not fit the intended route.
opts: Use non-enteric-coated chewable tablets
Have the patient swallow the tablets whole with water
Instruct the patient to chew the tablets before swallowing
Choose an enteric-coated tablet to protect the stomach
Give a total of 162 to 324 mg (typically four 81 mg tablets)
Place the tablets under the tongue to dissolve
ok: Use non-enteric-coated chewable tablets
Instruct the patient to chew the tablets before swallowing
Give a total of 162 to 324 mg (typically four 81 mg tablets)

qs.q: A 66-year-old woman with chest pain asks the EMT to help her take her own prescribed nitroglycerin. Which findings would lead the EMT to withhold it? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg; She took sildenafil 6 hours ago; She already took 3 doses in the past 15 minutes
qs.x: Systolic BP under 90, PDE-5 inhibitor use (sildenafil within 24 h) and reaching the maximum of 3 doses in 15 minutes are reasons not to give more. A normal heart rate, ongoing pain and a history of angina do not prevent assisting.
opts: Heart rate of 88/min
Blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg
Chest pain rated 8 out of 10
She took sildenafil 6 hours ago
She already took 3 doses in the past 15 minutes
She has a history of angina
ok: Blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg
She took sildenafil 6 hours ago
She already took 3 doses in the past 15 minutes

qs.q: An EMT has medical direction to assist a patient with chest pain with the patient's own nitroglycerin tablets. Place the steps in order.
qs.a: 1. Confirm the nitroglycerin is the patient's own and unexpired, blood pressure is adequate and no PDE-5 inhibitor was used recently  2. Have the patient lift the tongue and place one tablet underneath  3. Have the patient close the mouth and let the tablet dissolve without swallowing  4. Reassess blood pressure and chest pain within 5 minutes
qs.x: The right patient and drug, an adequate BP and no recent PDE-5 inhibitor are confirmed first because hypotension is the main risk. The tablet is placed and dissolved under the tongue, and BP and pain are rechecked before any repeat dose.
opts: Confirm the nitroglycerin is the patient's own and unexpired, blood pressure is adequate and no PDE-5 inhibitor was used recently
Have the patient lift the tongue and place one tablet underneath
Have the patient close the mouth and let the tablet dissolve without swallowing
Reassess blood pressure and chest pain within 5 minutes
ok: Confirm the nitroglycerin is the patient's own and unexpired, blood pressure is adequate and no PDE-5 inhibitor was used recently
Have the patient lift the tongue and place one tablet underneath
Have the patient close the mouth and let the tablet dissolve without swallowing
Reassess blood pressure and chest pain within 5 minutes

qs.q: A 30-year-old stung by a bee has his own epinephrine auto-injector. Which findings indicate anaphylaxis for which the EMT should assist with the auto-injector? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Wheezing and a feeling of throat tightness; Widespread hives with a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg; Swelling of the tongue and lips
qs.x: Airway swelling, wheezing and hypotension with hives show a systemic reaction that needs epinephrine. Local swelling, local pain, or anxiety with normal vital signs and clear lungs are not anaphylaxis.
opts: Wheezing and a feeling of throat tightness
Redness and swelling only at the sting site
Widespread hives with a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg
Pain at the sting site
Swelling of the tongue and lips
Anxiety with a normal blood pressure and clear lungs
ok: Wheezing and a feeling of throat tightness
Widespread hives with a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg
Swelling of the tongue and lips

qs.q: A 20-kg child in anaphylaxis has been prescribed an epinephrine auto-injector. Which statements about its use are correct? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The 0.15 mg auto-injector matches this child's weight; It is injected into the outer (anterolateral) thigh; Tachycardia, tremor and pallor are expected after the injection
qs.x: The 0.15 mg auto-injector is for 15-30 kg, and the 0.3 mg device is for 30 kg or more. It is given into the lateral thigh without waiting for shock, and its sympathomimetic effects cause tachycardia, tremor and pallor, not drowsiness.
opts: The 0.15 mg auto-injector matches this child's weight
The 0.3 mg auto-injector should be used because anaphylaxis is life-threatening
It is injected into the outer (anterolateral) thigh
It should be held until the child becomes hypotensive
Tachycardia, tremor and pallor are expected after the injection
Drowsiness is the expected effect after the injection
ok: The 0.15 mg auto-injector matches this child's weight
It is injected into the outer (anterolateral) thigh
Tachycardia, tremor and pallor are expected after the injection

qs.q: An EMT finds an adult who is unresponsive in a public restroom with a syringe nearby. Which findings support opioid overdose? Select all that apply.
qs.a: Respiratory rate of 6/min with shallow breaths; Pinpoint pupils; Cyanotic lips with snoring respirations
qs.x: Slow, shallow breathing, pinpoint pupils and signs of hypoxia are the classic opioid toxidrome. Dilated pupils, fast breathing and hot sweaty skin suggest a stimulant or other toxin.
opts: Respiratory rate of 6/min with shallow breaths
Widely dilated pupils
Pinpoint pupils
Respiratory rate of 30/min
Cyanotic lips with snoring respirations
Hot, flushed skin with heavy sweating
ok: Respiratory rate of 6/min with shallow breaths
Pinpoint pupils
Cyanotic lips with snoring respirations

qs.q: An EMT finds an adult with suspected opioid overdose who is breathing 4 times per minute. Place the actions in order.
qs.a: 1. Confirm scene safety and check responsiveness and breathing  2. Open the airway and begin bag-mask ventilation  3. Give intranasal naloxone by inserting the nozzle into a nostril and pressing the plunger  4. Continue ventilating and reassess breathing and responsiveness  5. Prepare a repeat dose if breathing is still inadequate after 2 to 3 minutes
qs.x: Scene safety comes first, then oxygenation and ventilation, because hypoxia is the immediate threat. Naloxone is then given intranasally, the patient is reassessed, and doses may repeat every 2-3 minutes.
opts: Confirm scene safety and check responsiveness and breathing
Open the airway and begin bag-mask ventilation
Give intranasal naloxone by inserting the nozzle into a nostril and pressing the plunger
Continue ventilating and reassess breathing and responsiveness

ok: Confirm scene safety and check responsiveness and breathing
Open the airway and begin bag-mask ventilation
Give intranasal naloxone by inserting the nozzle into a nostril and pressing the plunger
Continue ventilating and reassess breathing and responsiveness
Prepare a repeat dose if breathing is still inadequate after 2 to 3 minutes

qs.q: A 19-year-old with asthma is wheezing and asks the EMT for help with an inhaler. Which conditions must be met before the EMT assists with the metered-dose inhaler? Select all that apply.
qs.a: The inhaler is prescribed to this patient; The patient is alert enough to coordinate a deep breath; Medical direction or protocol authorizes the medication
qs.x: The EMT assists only with the patient's own unexpired inhaler, with authorization, and the patient must be able to inhale on command. An unresponsive patient with agonal breathing needs ventilation, not an MDI.

The inhaler belongs to the patient's roommate, who has the same condition
The patient is alert enough to coordinate a deep breath
The patient is unresponsive with agonal breathing
Medical direction or protocol authorizes the medication

ok: The inhaler is prescribed to this patient
The patient is alert enough to coordinate a deep breath

qs.q: Place the steps for assisting a patient with an albuterol metered-dose inhaler in order.
qs.a: 1. Confirm the right patient, medication and expiration date, then shake the inhaler  2. Have the patient exhale fully  3. Have the patient seal the lips around the mouthpiece or spacer and press the canister while inhaling deeply  4. Have the patient hold the breath as long as comfortable  5. Reassess breath sounds and work of breathing
qs.x: Checks come first, and a full exhalation allows a deep inhalation that carries the medication into the lungs. Holding the breath helps the medication deposit before the EMT reassesses.
opts: Confirm the right patient, medication and expiration date, then shake the inhaler
Have the patient exhale fully
Have the patient seal the lips around the mouthpiece or spacer and press the canister while inhaling deeply
Have the patient hold the breath as long as comfortable
Reassess breath sounds and work of breathing
ok: Confirm the right patient, medication and expiration date, then shake the inhaler
Have the patient exhale fully
Have the patient seal the lips around the mouthpiece or spacer and press the canister while inhaling deeply
Have the patient hold the breath as long as comfortable
Reassess breath sounds and work of breathing

qs.x: Oxygenation, a glucose check and a benzodiazepine (lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg = 2 mg) come first, followed by levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (1,200 mg) over 10-15 minutes if seizures persist. IV midazolam is 0.1 mg/kg (max 5 mg), and 4,500 mg is the levetiracetam maximum, far above 60 mg/kg here.

qs.x: The airway is managed first, and levetiracetam 60 mg/kg is capped at 4,500 mg, infused over 10-15 minutes. Lorazepam is repeated only once, the second-line drug is not delayed for awakening, and glucose is checked in every seizing patient.

qs.q: A 62-year-old in septic shock with lactic acidosis (pH 7.08) is breathing 36/min and tiring, and the sending physician asks about sodium bicarbonate before the flight. Which findings argue against giving it now? Select all that apply.

qs.x: Bicarbonate is contraindicated with inadequate ventilation (the CO2 it generates accumulates, shown by a rising ETCO2), hypocalcemia (it worsens) and hypernatremia. The low pH is the reason it is being considered, and the HR and potassium are not contraindications.

qs.q: A 70-kg patient with 45% TBSA burns from 6 days ago develops respiratory failure in a rural ICU and needs RSI for transfer. The potassium result is pending. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

qs.x: Succinylcholine is contraindicated from about 24 hours after a major burn, by any route, because of the risk of severe hyperkalemia; the risk peaks around 7-10 days, so 6 days is well within the danger window. qs.x: Calcium chloride 1 g (10 mL of 10%) stabilizes the myocardium but does not lower potassium, so shifting therapy such as insulin with dextrose follows. Rapid push can cause bradycardia, extravasation can cause tissue necrosis, and ECG changes such as peaked T waves are an indication.

qs.x: Decontamination protects the crew and aircraft, atropine is doubled every 5 minutes until bronchial secretions dry with no maximum (the 3 mg cap applies to bradycardia), and pralidoxime is added. qs.x: Calcium chloride 1-2 g every 10-20 minutes, high-dose insulin euglycemia therapy and vasopressors support calcium channel blocker poisoning. Diltiazem and nicardipine are calcium channel blockers, and labetalol would worsen bradycardia and hypotension.

qs.x: Ketamine maintains BP and small titrated fentanyl doses limit hypotension. Full-dose propofol, large midazolam boluses and a dexmedetomidine load all commonly cause hypotension, which is dangerous in hemorrhagic shock.

qs.x: Hypotension and hypoxia before RSI raise arrest risk, so resuscitation, a ready push-dose pressor, a reduced induction dose and thorough preoxygenation are used. Propofol in unstable patients is reduced to 0.5-1 mg/kg, and skipping preoxygenation worsens hypoxia.

qs.x: Push-dose epinephrine is 10-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes as a bridge to an infusion. 1 mg is the arrest dose, 0.3 mg IM is the anaphylaxis dose, higher PEEP lowers venous return and BP, and profound post-intubation hypotension should not go untreated.
